docs.title: PINNeAPPle
docs.text:
Physics AI that tells you when to trust it. Solve, simulate, forecast and design with physics-informed AI, and know for every result whether it still holds: checked against references, baselines and physical laws, with its uncertainty and its limits written down.

Get started Experiment catalogue GitHub

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Simulate

    OpenFOAM around any body or through pipes and mixers, CalculiX from Python (pp.fea), lattice Boltzmann, DEM particles, a 3-D finite-element solver, black-hole hydrodynamics. Each one verified on a case with a known answer.

  • Learn

    PINNs, FNO, DeepONet, MeshGraphNet and equivariant GNNs, reduced-order models (POD, DMD, Operator Inference, parametric POD-GPR), forecasters, all trained against their baselines.

  • Trust

    Every result answers six questions: data and geometry, model, physical constraints, benchmark, uncertainty and the engineering decision. The evidence is a passing check, never a claim.

  • Show

    Blender renders, post-processor style FEA figures, process videos with live charts, a browser 3-D viewer and glTF / USD exports, from the same results the checks ran on.

docs.title: Five lines to a validated result
docs.text:
import pinneapple as pp

m = pp.fea.FEModel.from_gmsh(pp.fea.geo_l_bracket(), size=0.0025)     # CAD-like geometry, gmsh C3D10
m.material = pp.fea.Material("steel", E=210e9, nu=0.3)
base, top = m.nodes_where(lambda X: X[:, 2] < 1e-9), m.nodes_where(lambda X: X[:, 2] > 0.08 - 1e-9)
res = pp.fea.solve(m, pp.fea.Static(fix=[(base, (1, 2, 3))], loads=[(top, (2000.0, 0, 0))]), "work/bracket")
print(res.von_mises.max() / 1e6, "MPa")

pip install pinneapple
python -m pinneapple_lab run calculix_case -p case=plate_hole     # run, check, store, and see it in the catalogue

docs.title: Philosophy
docs.text:
PINNeAPPle is built around explicit abstraction layers to keep research workflows clean and extensible:

  • Problem Design
  • Data & Geometry
  • Model
  • Physics / PINN
  • Solver
  • Backend
  • Research / Benchmarking

docs.title: Why PINNeAPPle?
docs.text:
Many PINN codebases couple model, residuals, training loop and runtime.

PINNeAPPle is designed to: - keep physics reusable, - keep solvers interchangeable, - keep execution backends pluggable, - make benchmarking a first-class workflow.

docs.title: Physics Anomaly Detector (day 28)
docs.text:
Which balance broke, by how much, and which sensors are involved. Live at https://anomaly.pinneapple.org. Source: apps/anomaly_detector.

Upload sensor time series and the end of a window you know is normal. Add conservation balances written as formulas over your columns, and optionally a physical reference model. Four detector families run, each calibrated only on the normal window:

Family What it sees Statistical values and rates outside their normal band (robust z-score) AR + CUSUM slow drifts against a signal's own dynamics Conservation balances d(accumulation)/dt = inflow − outflow broken, with the size and direction in the law's units Model residuals a reference model that mispredicts a state from the measured inputs

Flags become events with a severity, the variables involved and explanations. With a label column, the app computes precision, recall, false alarms per hour and detection delays.

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text: The benchmark uses labelled synthetic runs of the heated tank: a leak, a heater loss, a sensor bias, a sensor drift, a stuck meter and a valve fault, on seeds not used during development. The combined detector finds every fault with 80 % point precision and 0.18 false alarms per hour. The balances alone never false-alarm but miss the valve fault, because the outflow is measured and the physics holds. The public BATADAL adapter (PR #731) is not merged yet.

docs.title: Automate it
docs.text: POST /api/analyze with an upload_id, normal_until, balances and constants returns a job. The events and scores are in GET /api/jobs/{id}; the downloads are events.csv and anomaly.study.json. In Python, call pinneapple_systems.operations.anomaly.detect.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• "Normal" is whatever the declared window contains.
  • A broken balance does not say whether the plant or a meter is at fault.
  • The benchmark is synthetic until a public labelled set lands.

Monetization: monitored assets, data volume and analysis frequency.

docs.title: Physics AI Benchmark Arena
docs.text:
arena.pinneapple.org · source apps/benchmark_arena

Which method works best for each physical problem, ranked under one protocol, with only numbers from runs that were actually executed.

Protocol. pinneapple_arena.regimes.run_regime_arena applies the same rules to every method:

  • equal data: one split for every method and seed;
  • equal compute: the same ComputeBudget, enforced by train_within_budget;
  • the same stopping rule;
  • several seeds, with their spread shown;
  • errors measured only on samples that no method trained on or was chosen with.

Regimes. Interpolation, few data, extrapolation, geometry change (held-out groups), and steep fronts (fields only).

Also measured. Training and inference cost, model size, violations of declared constraints, the PDE residual, and numerical-solver baselines. The splits are audited independently by pinneapple_data.audit, which runs the dataset checks of pinneapple check.

Results. Public results are files in apps/benchmark_arena/results/, written by run_public_benchmarks.py with their date, hardware and dataset hash. The published results of pinneapple-benchmark experiment 09 (five problems, pp.benchmark protocol) are shown unchanged with their source commit and hardware. Private benchmarks run the same protocol on an uploaded table as a job.

Library. pinneapple_arena.regimes, pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.methods, pinneapple_analysis.cost.equal_budget, pinneapple_data.audit; guide: Surrogates from simulation results.

Limits.

  • Hyper-parameters are the library defaults; there is no per-method search.
  • Wall-clock budgets depend on the hardware.
  • "Steep fronts" is only a proxy for discontinuities.
  • Graph networks and R-OAMS are not compared; the app states why.

docs.title: Model Calibration Lab (day 18)
docs.text:
Fit model parameters to your measurements, with intervals only where the data determine them, checked on measurements the fit never saw. Live at https://calibration.pinneapple.org. Source: apps/calibration_lab.

Upload measurements: CSV, Excel, Parquet, JSON or a sensor export. Pick a model: built in, your formula, or a table of your solver runs. Set the parameters to adjust and their bounds. The lab returns:

  • calibrated values, with Jacobian and bootstrap 95 % intervals;
  • "not estimable" instead of a number for any parameter the measurements cannot determine, with the combination they do fix (the identifiability core of the Parameter Identifiability Lab, day 25);
  • before / after curves, residuals, and the error on held-out measurements (a separate table, a random fraction, or the last rows as an extrapolation test);
  • the same data solved by other estimators (Bayesian, autodiff, adjoint, a physics-informed network), ranked by held-out error;
  • a StudyResult and a ModelRef of the calibrated model with its held-out metrics, for the other apps.

docs.title: Automate it
docs.text:
curl -X POST https://calibration.pinneapple.org/api/calibrate -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @calibration.json
curl https://calibration.pinneapple.org/api/jobs/<id>

On your own machine, with your own solver: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.calibrate(CallableModel(solver), ...). See the guide Identifiability, calibration and inverse problems.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The intervals assume the model form is right; read the reduced χ² and the held-out error. A table of solver runs adds an interpolation error the intervals do not include. Uploaded code is not run on the server. The app README lists every limit, with the measured results of each example.

docs.title: Physics-Based Control Lab (day 29)
docs.text:
Better control actions from physical models, compared fairly with PID and rules. Live at https://control.pinneapple.org. Source: apps/control_lab.

Simulation and recommendation only. This version has no command path to real equipment: it never writes to a controller, PLC or DCS.

Give the lab a dynamic model, the estimated state, objectives, constraints and actuator limits. The model is the heated tank's balances, or a reduced-order surrogate as a ModelRef. It runs each controller in closed loop on the same simulated plant, with the same noise and disturbances:

  • linear MPC: successive linearisation and a QP;
  • nonlinear MPC: CasADi + IPOPT, with a SciPy fallback;
  • nonlinear MPC with the surrogate as its model;
  • a two-loop PID with anti-windup;
  • hysteresis rules.

It reports tracking error, constraint violations, energy, actuator travel and solve time, plus what the MPC planned at any moment against what then happened.

In the default study, the MPCs reduce the temperature tracking error 4.7x compared with PID, with no constraint violation. They move the heater more, a trade-off set by the move weight. The surrogate MPC tracks the level worse because the ROM cannot see the unmeasured demand change.

docs.title: Automate it
docs.text:
• POST /api/compare with spec, scenario and controllers returns a job. Downloads: control.study.json, trajectories.csv.
  • POST /api/recommend with the Digital Twin Runtime's state and the current readings returns the proposed actions and their predicted effect.
  • In Python, call pinneapple_systems.operations.control.compare_controllers and recommend.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The plant is simulated, so model mismatch is smaller than on a real plant.
  • The baselines are hand-tuned, not optimal.
  • Output constraints are soft; actuator and rate limits are hard.
  • There is no command path to equipment, by design.

Monetization: assets, scenarios and control studies.

docs.title: Engineering Evidence Report (day 30)
docs.text:
Experiments and simulations as reproducible technical evidence. Live at https://evidence.pinneapple.org. Source: apps/evidence_report.

Upload what a study produced, from any app of the series or from your own tools:

  • Validation Lab reports;
  • evidence ledgers;
  • pinneapple check JSON;
  • Simulation Comparator results;
  • StudyResult / ModelRef / DatasetSpec JSON;
  • metrics tables;
  • any other file.

Add the methodology, the conditions and the names of the baseline and candidate runs. The app builds a report (HTML, PDF) with methodology, conditions, baseline comparison, tests, limitations and references, where every original artifact is referenced by SHA-256 and URL. It also builds an evidence package: a zip with the report, the ledger, the figures, the original files and a SHA-256 manifest.

A test is reported as passed only when there is a recorded evidence entry that it ran (inputs SHA-256, outputs, time). Otherwise the report prints "not run", with the source's claim next to it. See the evidence ledger for how records are made and checked.

docs.title: Automate it
docs.text: POST /api/report returns JSON and HTML, /api/report.pdf the PDF and /api/package the zip. Each takes files plus meta (JSON) and urls (JSON: file name → URL). The interactive docs are at /docs. API keys and usage metering (reports and downloads per caller and month) come from the shared app runtime.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The report checks that records exist and are intact; it does not re-run tests.
  • Baseline and candidate are matched by run name, and units are not converted.
  • Contracts are validated against pinneapple_data.contracts; each report is also exported as a StudyResult.
  • Nothing is stored: keep the package.

Monetization: reports, campaigns and private projects.

docs.title: PINNeAPPle Hub
docs.text:
hub.pinneapple.org · source apps/hub · library pinneapple_hub.library

One searchable catalogue of everything ready-made in PINNeAPPle: tools (the public functions of AGENTS.md, Flow Studio nodes, recipes from AGENTS.md and the module reference, the MCP server's tools), trained models (the zoo), geometries (the geometry library), datasets, flows (Flow Studio) and examples (every examples/* manifest and Lab item, with its A–F seal and six-stage trust card). Click an item to see what it is, copy its code in one click, read the output its code printed when it was run, and download its files.

docs.title: An item
docs.text:
• Use it: a minimal snippet (import pinneapple as pp ...) and the recorded run of exactly that code (printed output, seconds, figures). The run is matched to the snippet by its hash, so a snippet that changed shows "not run" until it is run again.
  • Results already run: the measured numbers and figures of the source: a model card's held-out metrics and an example row of the model's own test split (inputs and the stored reference), a Lab run's metrics and figures, the module reference's figures.
  • 3-D preview of a geometry (its committed light glTF, with the three.js copy the library vendors) and downloads: STL / GLB from the repository, fine levels of detail, OBJ, USD and STEP from the Hugging Face Hub; model weights, configuration, card and ONNX graph; dataset files.
  • Try it (models): inputs start at the held-out example row; run the model's ONNX graph and its query checks in the browser (pinneapple_hub/zoo/web/zoo.js, no server) or pp.zoo on the server, with the verdict of the per-query trust checks.
  • Trust card / validation checks: the Lab's six questions for examples, the zoo's validation checks for models.
  • Open in Flow Studio for flows (?example=<name>), Compose for Flow Studio nodes.

docs.title: Tools by task
docs.text:
Every tool (flow nodes, generated library calls, public functions, recipes and the MCP agent tools) is in exactly one of 20 task categories: problem setup, geometry and meshing, equations, classical solvers, PINNs, surrogates, the model zoo, physics checks, verification, benchmarks, uncertainty, inverse problems, design, process and system components, vehicles, electromagnetics, time series and twins, data, visualisation, and automation. The home page lists them with their counts; the Task filter (/?kind=tool&category=uq) and hub.search(index, q, category="uq") select one, and an item page links back to its task.

The assignment is generated, not hand-tagged per item: pinneapple_hub/library/categories.py maps where a tool comes from (node:<flow node type>, lib:<module>:<function>, fn:<dotted name>, mcp:<tool>) to a category by the longest matching prefix, and lists recipes one by one (their ids follow README order). tests/test_hub_library.py fails when a tool matches nothing, a category is empty, a rule places no tool, or a listed recipe is gone, so a new node or module has to be given a task before the index builds clean.

docs.title: Create your own
docs.text: Pick blocks (every curated Flow Studio node type), optionally start from a bundled flow and add a library geometry. Each new block's inputs are wired from the blocks before it by port type (pinneapple_flow.lab_status.insert_nodes) and every parameter is checked against the node's schema. You get the flow JSON and Python that builds, validates and runs it, to copy or download. Validate in a sandbox runs that Python -- regenerated on the server from the blocks, never code a visitor typed -- in a separate interpreter with a time and memory limit, as a job, and shows what it printed. Save to My Hub keeps it (with the validation run when it ran that exact code) in the app's data volume, per login, API key or address. Open in Flow Studio passes the flow in the link (?flow=<base64url JSON>).

docs.title: With Flow Studio
docs.text:
The Hub and Flow Studio read one registry, pinneapple_flow.REGISTRY: every node type of the palette (the curated nodes and the 249 generated library calls of pinneapple_flow/autocalls.json) is a Hub tool with the palette's title, category and parameter schema, and tests/test_hub_flow_link.py fails when the two lists differ.

  • Run it (a node page): a form generated from the node's parameter schema; a node without required inputs runs in the sandbox with those values and shows what it measured. A library call the generator checked ("runs with its defaults") also has a snippet that calls the function with the form's defaults, recorded like every other snippet (those defaults are placeholders, not a physical case).
  • Open in Flow Studio: pinneapple_hub.library.flowlink.flow_for_node builds inputs -> the node with your values -> report: the upstream wiring of a bundled flow that uses the node when there is one, otherwise a producer for each required input, then export.report. Every node type gets a valid flow (tested for all 327).
  • Add to a flow: Flow Studio opens with ?add=<type>&params=<base64url JSON> and asks which flow (an example, a saved flow, the canvas or a new one); the node is wired in by port type (/api/flows/insert-nodes).
  • Publish to Hub (Flow Studio's toolbar): the flow on the canvas opens in "Create your own" (/create?flow=<base64url JSON>); tick the parameters the tool takes and they become variables at the top of the generated Python; validate in the sandbox and save to My Hub.
  • Already run: python -m pinneapple_hub.library flowruns runs each bundled flow headless and records what every node measured (data/web/hub/flow_runs.json, keyed by the flow file's SHA-256); a flow page shows its run, and a node page shows its results in every bundled flow that uses it. A flow that fails is shown as failed, with its error.

  • A public function of the AGENTS.md table links to the node that wraps it.

  • The Flow Studio canvas in "Create your own" (/create?mode=canvas, or the "Flow Studio canvas" tab): the Flow Studio editor itself, embedded. It posts its flow to the Hub on every change and loads the flow the Hub sends (a flow opened with ?flow=); the tick boxes, the generated Python, the sandbox validation and "Save to My Hub" work on that flow. Messages go only between the two configured origins (checked on both sides), and Flow Studio can be embedded only by the origins in FLOW_FRAME_ANCESTORS (its CSP frame-ancestors; unset, nobody may embed it). The Hub frames only HUB_FLOW_STUDIO_URL's origin (frame-src). Serve both on one site (e.g. hub.pinneapple.org and flow.pinneapple.org) so a Flow Studio login also works inside the frame.

Flow Studio's "🍍 Hub" button and links go to FLOW_HUB_URL (default http://127.0.0.1:8116); the Hub's go to HUB_FLOW_STUDIO_URL (default http://127.0.0.1:8765).

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
/ focuses the search, Ctrl+K (⌘K) opens quick search with arrow keys and Enter; filters by type, physical domain (pinneapple_lab.manifest.domain_of) and quality (Lab letter A–F, zoo decision). Light and dark themes follow the system, the moon button switches and remembers. Works from 340 px wide.

Dark Phone

docs.title: The index
docs.text:
data/web/hub/index.json is generated, never written by hand:

python -m pinneapple_hub.library build              # collect every item from the sources
python -m pinneapple_hub.library run --stale        # run new or changed snippets, record output and figures
python -m pinneapple_hub.library check              # current, every run passing, every file and link present
python -m pinneapple_hub.library flowruns           # run the bundled flows headless, record each node's metrics

from pinneapple_hub import library as hub

index = hub.load_index()
item = hub.search(index, "wind turbine", kind="geometry")[0]
print(item["id"], item["run"]["status"], [f["label"] for f in item["files"]][:3])
Kind Source model pinneapple_hub/zoo/manifest.json, the bundled model cards, the first row of each model's held-out split, data/web/zoo dataset the zoo manifest's datasets geometry pinneapple_design.geometry_library.web.index() and its manifest flow pinneapple_flow/flows/*.json, with their recorded headless runs (data/web/hub/flow_runs.json) tool AGENTS.md (its API table and Python blocks), scripts/reference/content.py (recorded by run_examples.py), pinneapple_flow.REGISTRY (every node type: curated nodes and generated library calls), pinneapple_mcp.server example pinneapple_lab.explorer.collect: examples/*/experiment.json and lab/curation.json

Related items link both ways: an example whose scripts name a model, dataset, geometry, flow or node is related to it, and a node to every bundled flow that uses it.

Tests. tests/test_hub_library.py (index current, every recorded run passing for its current code, a sample per kind run again, PINNEAPPLE_HUB_RUN_SNIPPETS=1 runs all of them; quality equal to the Lab's and the zoo's; files and links exist; search, composer, My Hub, sandbox), tests/test_hub_app.py (API, file serving limited to the index's folders, server inference equal to the library's fixed-input answers, validation job, downloads), tests/test_hub_e2e.py (Playwright: search, shortcuts, filters, copy code, 3-D preview, browser vs server inference, composing and validating, My Hub, dark theme, phone layout; HUB_SCREENSHOTS=<dir> saves the pictures above).

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
A service hub in apps/deploy (port 8116, Caddy block {$HUB_DOMAIN}, volume hub_data); see the deploy README.

Limits.

  • The sandbox limits time, memory, CPU and file size, not the network; keep the container without outbound access on a public server if validation runs must be offline.
  • Only the light geometries, small datasets and zoo weights are in the repository; fine levels of detail and large datasets download from the Hugging Face Hub.
  • A recorded run is from the machine that ran python -m pinneapple_hub.library run; timings are that machine's.
  • The interface is in English, like the other apps.

docs.title: Parameter Identifiability Lab (day 25)
docs.text:
Before estimating parameters, check that the measurements can determine them. Live at https://identifiability.pinneapple.org. Source: apps/identifiability_lab.

Describe a model, the unknown parameters with their plausible range, and the measurement plan (where, when, which observable, with what noise). The lab answers four questions on the same problem:

Question Method Can any data of this kind determine each parameter? Rank of the Fisher information; its null directions are the ambiguities, reported with the combination the data do fix (for example h/k) Can these data determine it, and how precisely? Cramér-Rao bounds and the profile likelihood (95 % interval, open or closed) How are the estimates coupled? Expected correlations (Fisher) and posterior correlations (adaptive Metropolis) What should I measure next? Leverage of each measurement, and the greedy D-optimal extra measurements, with the rank and bounds each would give

The result downloads as a report (JSON), as CSV tables, and as a StudyResult contract (study_type="identifiability"). The Model Calibration Lab and the Inverse Model Studio read that contract, and call the same core to decide which parameters get a confidence interval.

docs.title: Automate it
docs.text:
curl -X POST https://identifiability.pinneapple.org/api/analyze -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @problem.json
curl https://identifiability.pinneapple.org/api/jobs/<id>           # status, progress, the report

The same analysis in Python: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.analyze_identifiability. See the guide Identifiability, calibration and inverse problems.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The verdict is local: it holds at the analysis point and within the bounds given. It assumes the model form is right and the noise is independent and Gaussian. The profile and the posterior run only for fast models with at most 6 parameters. The app README lists every limit.

docs.title: Inverse Model Studio (day 21)
docs.text:
From measurements back to the unknown parameters and fields: one problem, five methods, the same data, checked. Live at https://inverse-studio.pinneapple.org. Source: apps/inverse_studio.

Formulate the problem once: measurements, a physical model and its geometry, and the unknowns (parameters, boundary conditions or the zones of a field). The studio solves it with every method that applies, on the same data:

Method Uncertainty Classical least squares (exact sensitivities, autograd or finite differences) Gauss-Newton 95 % Adjoint gradient (one adjoint solve per gradient, whatever the number of unknowns) Gauss-Newton 95 % Automatic differentiation (PyTorch) Gauss-Newton 95 % Bayesian regularisation (Gaussian and smoothness priors, MCMC) posterior 95 % Physics-informed network (the Inverse Heat Lab's fin and plate) none from one run

It then validates the answers:

  • held-out measurements that no method saw, which rank the methods;
  • the identifiability diagnosis (the Parameter Identifiability Lab's core);
  • on the examples, recovery of the known truth for the parameters and the reconstructed fields.

The heat examples are the Inverse Heat Lab's, which stays a separate app. On its plate, least squares on the finite-volume model gives h = 14.96 W/m²K for a true 15. The PINN gives 14.0 in 1500 steps, although its own temperature field reproduces the hot spot. The studio shows both.

docs.title: Automate it
docs.text:
curl https://inverse-studio.pinneapple.org/api/presets/rod_h_field > problem.json   # a complete request
curl -X POST https://inverse-studio.pinneapple.org/api/solve -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @request.json
curl https://inverse-studio.pinneapple.org/api/jobs/<id>

In Python: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.compare_methods(InverseProblem(...), methods). See the guide Identifiability, calibration and inverse problems.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: All methods fit the same model, so a missing physical effect can fool them all; read the held-out error. The adjoint needs a discretised model with an adjoint solver (the finite-volume fin, today), and the PINN needs one of the Inverse Heat Lab formulations. The 3D block is not run here. The app README lists every limit with the measured results.

docs.title: Meshless Method Lab (day 26)
docs.text:
Meshless or mesh-based: measure where each wins on your problem. Live at https://meshless.pinneapple.org. Source: apps/meshless_lab.

Describe a Poisson, Helmholtz or heat problem with a manufactured solution (or a source and boundary value), pick a domain (preset, polygon with holes, uploaded point cloud) and node spacings. Kansa, RBF-FD, finite differences on an embedded grid, linear finite elements and a PINN solve it on the same nodes; the lab reports error, cost, condition number, noise amplification and observed order, and names the winner of each criterion from the numbers.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
2-D scalar linear problems with Dirichlet conditions; no linear elasticity or Neumann conditions yet; R-OAMS is not in the library. See the app README.

Monetization: runs, problem size and reports.

docs.title: Physics AI Model Gateway
docs.text:
models.pinneapple.org · source apps/model_gateway

Physical models published as versioned endpoints behind one API. Every query is checked against the model's validity range, logged and metered.

Models served (pinneapple_registry.ModelGateway):

  • zoo models;
  • ONNX graphs with declared inputs, outputs and validity bounds;
  • Surrogate Studio models, as a model.zip, or by their ModelRef, in which case the gateway forwards to the studio and enforces the bounds itself;
  • any model behind the same /v1 API.

Per version. Each version has a stage and an OOD policy: warn predicts and flags, refuse gives no prediction. A caller can tighten the policy, never relax it.

Operations. Every call goes to the run log. Metrics per version: calls, rows, errors, OOD rows, refusals, latency p50 / p95. Each version can be downloaded as a contracts ModelRef.

Python: pinneapple_registry.gateway_client.GatewayClient(base_url, api_key=...) works against this gateway and the Surrogate Studio alike.

Library. pinneapple_registry.gateway, gateway_api, gateway_client; guide: Surrogates from simulation results.

Limits.

  • Publishing by URL and model.zip uploads are admin-only.
  • The OOD gate sees inputs only, and is a box for zoo, ONNX and remote models.
  • JAX models must be exported to ONNX.

docs.title: Reduced Order Model Lab (day 19)
docs.text:
Cheaper models of your simulations, with the error on held-out data in sight. Live at https://rom.pinneapple.org. Source: apps/rom_lab.

Upload snapshots of one mesh (OpenFOAM times, VTU/VTK/FRD series, NPZ/HDF5 arrays, a CSV/Parquet table). The lab fits POD + RBF, POD + GPR, DMD, Operator Inference and a neural surrogate at equal wall-clock budget, at several ranks, and scores each on snapshots it never saw: later times (a forecast), interleaved times, or unseen designs. It shows the energy of the singular values, error vs rank against the POD projection floor, error vs inference time with the Pareto front, the speed-up over the full-order model, and the reconstruction of any held-out snapshot.

docs.title: Export and chain
docs.text:
• .rom.npz: arrays and a JSON manifest, no pickle; ReducedModel.from_bytes(b).predict(times=...).
  • ONNX (POD + RBF, nearest, parametric neural, DMD) plus the spec for ModelGateway.publish(kind="onnx").
  • ModelRef per model (held-out metrics, split, training range, SHA-256) and a StudyResult for the study.

docs.title: The held-out design on its body (3-D)
docs.text:
When the snapshots carry a mesh (a VTU/VTK/FRD series, or arrays with cells_<type>), the result page shows the held-out snapshot on its own body: the full-order field, the ROM prediction and the pointwise error |ROM − FEM|, each with a colour bar, on the shape deformed by the FEM or the ROM displacement (scale factor, true scale, undeformed wire). The dataset's node sets are marked (the cantilever's clamp and loaded tip), with the error hotspots. A short text, computed from the two arrays only, says where the error concentrates and compares it with the study's number for that design and its mean over the held-out designs.

Library: pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom.views.reconstruction_view, built on pinneapple_analysis.validation.error_map and pp.viz.field_view; the page uses the shared viewer apps/_shared/static/shared/fieldview3d.js.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Snapshots must share one mesh; time steppers need a uniform step and are not validated outside the training window; no physics check runs on the reduced fields (ModelRef.trust_decision = UNCHECKED). See the app README.

Monetization: building, exporting and running reduced models.

docs.title: Surrogate Studio
docs.text:
surrogate.pinneapple.org · source apps/surrogate_studio

Turns simulation results into a fast predictive model, measured on runs it never saw, and serves it behind a versioned endpoint that enforces its validity range.

What it does. You upload a table of runs (CSV, Parquet, JSON, HDF5, NPZ, or a DatasetSpec) and pick the inputs and outputs. The studio then trains every applicable method on the same splits and compute budget:

  • polynomial ridge, a Gaussian process, gradient-boosted trees and an MLP;
  • FNO and DeepONet when the output is a field;
  • a PINN when a PDE is declared.

It measures each method on a random held-out split and on a distribution-shift split (new geometries, the edge of the design space), then picks the method with the lowest validation error. The chosen model is hosted at once at /v1/models/<name>/predict, the Model Gateway's API, and screens every query with an OOD gate.

Outputs.

  • A comparison table (error with spread over seeds, training and inference cost).
  • A trust decision with every check.
  • The limitations: validity bounds, where the errors concentrate, worst runs and, for fields, the error map and PDE residual.
  • The contracts (StudyResult, ModelRef, DatasetSpec), a Markdown report, and ONNX and TorchScript files.

docs.title: 3-D case: the solid FEM cantilever
docs.text:
The ROM Lab's 100 solid-FEM cantilevers become one field dataset: displacement and von Mises stress on the 31 × 4 × 7 node lattice. A surrogate is trained with the app's methods. The results page then shows:

  • the measured speed-up (FEM solve time on this machine against the surrogate's time per prediction);
  • the held-out errors per field and per zone (clamp, loaded tip, rest of the body), for the test and the extrapolated (smallest load angle) designs;
  • the errors on the tip displacement and on the largest stress;
  • any held-out design on its deformed body: surrogate, FEM reference and their difference, with a colour bar, and the verdict of the hosted endpoint's OOD gate (in range, warn or refuse) for that design.

The von Mises stress is declared non-negative: it is trained on its square root and predicted as its square, so no prediction can be negative. A line under the error table says why the pooled displacement error is larger than the tip error.

Library. pinneapple_analysis.surrogate (study, splits, methods, limits, contracts), pinneapple_analysis.cost.equal_budget, pinneapple_registry.ModelGateway and gateway_api; guide: Surrogates from simulation results.

Limits. These are measured on the same campaign, so other regimes are not covered. Methods run with their library defaults. The physics checks are only the declared PDE residual and constraints. FNO needs a uniform 1-D or 2-D grid. Hosted models are public unless the login or API keys are on.

docs.title: Digital Twin Runtime (day 20)
docs.text:
Put a validated model to work next to live data, and know when to stop trusting it. Live at https://twin.pinneapple.org. Source: apps/twin_runtime.

The runtime is deliberately small: one model type and one live data source per asset. The model is either the heated-tank lumped model (mass and energy balances) or a reduced-order surrogate given as a ModelRef. The source is MQTT (an embedded broker or yours), REST pushes, or OPC UA (experimental).

For every reading the twin:

  1. Estimates the state with an ensemble Kalman filter (level, temperature, and optionally a leak flow and the heater efficiency as parameters).
  2. Forecasts the next 10 minutes with a 5-95 % band. The band includes the uncertainty of the held inputs.
  3. Raises alerts from explicit rules:
  4. the estimate is outside its limits;
  5. the forecast band reaches a limit;
  6. a parameter is beyond 3σ of its limit;
  7. the normalised innovation stays above its χ² quantile, which means the data disagree with the model.
  8. Watches its own validity with pp.assess_drift on its one-step predictions: bias, coverage, trend, and inputs outside the model's training box. When the drift check says review or retrain, it requests revalidation, which re-scores the model open loop on the recent history.

Other systems read GET /api/assets/{asset}/state. The history is in SQLite or Postgres, and the run can be downloaded as a StudyResult.

docs.title: The series, end to end
docs.text: The Series flow tab chains the days 13-31 apps on one asset through the shared contracts. The campaign (ParameterSpace, DatasetSpec) feeds the surrogate (ModelRef with held-out metrics), then the uncertainty step (coverage on an unseen run), then the optimizer (checked against the closed-form physics optimum), then this twin. The twin requests revalidation once the inlet water leaves the surrogate's training range. The campaign and uncertainty steps call the library functions of the Campaign Planner and the Uncertainty Lab. The surrogate and optimizer steps run as library stand-ins until those apps are on main, and the page says which is which.

docs.title: Automate it
docs.text:
• POST /api/live/start with {"asset": "pump-7", "source": "rest"}, then POST /api/assets/pump-7/readings.
  • MQTT: publish JSON readings to pinneapple/<asset>/sensors.
  • POST /api/replay runs a twin over a CSV, Parquet or JSON record (upload it with POST /api/uploads first).
  • In Python, pinneapple_systems.operations.live.replay(table, model) and LiveTwin.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One model type and one source per asset. FMUs are not supported yet.
  • Alerts are screening rules, not a safety system. The twin sends no command to equipment.
  • The filter assumes Gaussian noise. Parameters move as random walks.
  • OPC UA is experimental and not in the default image.

Monetization: per monitored asset, data volume and inferences.

docs.title: Physics Validation Lab (day 24)
docs.text:
Is this model or result physically and numerically consistent? Live at https://validate.pinneapple.org. Source: apps/validation_lab.

Upload predictions or simulation results. Describe the equations, parameters, units, bounds, boundary conditions and reference data in a form, or upload a pinneapple check configuration, or reference a zoo model with query points. The lab runs the physics checks and reports them in three groups that answer different questions:

Group Question Numerical verification Were the equations solved right? Residuals, finite values, intact artefacts, method status Validation against data Does it match trusted data, inside the range the data covers? Reference error, QoIs, out-of-range queries Physical consistency Conservation, boundary and initial conditions, bounds and constraints, units

For each target, the report says which groups did not run (for example, no reference means no validation against data). Each check that ran has an evidence record: the SHA-256 of its inputs, its outputs, and start and finish times (evidence ledger). The report also holds the configuration and the hash of every input file, so pinneapple check --config pinneapple-check.toml reproduces it.

No single test guarantees that a model represents reality, and neither does this set of tests. A pass means only that the listed checks ran and held on these inputs, with these tolerances.

docs.title: On the mesh (3-D results)
docs.text:
When a result is 3-D and lives on a mesh (an OpenFOAM case zip, a VTU/VTK file with cells) and has a reference, the report adds a 3-D view of what the reference check (PC701) compared: the prediction, the reference and |prediction − reference| on the mesh, each with a colour bar. A displacement field deforms the body (scale factor, true scale). Declared boundary conditions are marked (OpenFOAM patches, planes such as x=min). A list gives the regions with the largest error: connected points in the top 10 % of the error, with their maximum and mean, size, share of the squared error and the faces of the domain they touch. Click a row to zoom to it. The relative L2 shown is the PC701 number. 2-D results, tables and models keep the current views. Library: pinneapple_veriphysics.mesh_views, pinneapple_analysis.validation.error_map, pp.viz.field_view.

The 3-D example is chosen to fail: the ROM Lab's POD + GPR model (4.4 % mean held-out error) at its worst held-out design, near the edge of its training box. It shows a failing reference check, not the ROM's typical quality.

docs.title: Automate it
docs.text:
• POST /api/validate takes files plus config (TOML) or spec (JSON) and returns the report. The interactive docs are at /docs.
  • In CI, the GitHub Action PINNeAPPle-Labs/PINNeAPPle@main runs the same checks on every pull request.
  • The report JSON, with its ledger, feeds the Engineering Evidence Report (day 30).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Python models and checkpoints are not run on the server. Upload their predictions, or use the Action.
  • The default tolerances of pinneapple check decide pass or fail unless you set them per target.
  • The report is pinneapple-validation-lab/v1. Export to validation-report/v1 (pp.validate) and its credibility levels will follow once those PRs are merged.

Monetization: validations per model, dataset or version, with private projects and CI history for teams.

docs.title: Execution Model
docs.text:
A run moves through the pipeline in this order. Each step is one or two concrete calls, all of which are covered in depth in Core Concepts; this page is the map between them.

  1. ProblemDefinition defines equations and constraints. A ProblemSpec — built directly, via ProblemBuilder, or via get_preset(name, **kwargs) — pins down the PDE kind, coordinates, fields, boundary/initial conditions, and domain bounds. (pinneapple_physics.pde_environment)

  2. Domain/Geometry produces sampling. build_domain(name) instantiates a PhysicsDomain2D/3D, and sample_domain(domain, n_interior, n_boundary) draws interior and boundary collocation point batches from it. (pinneapple_design.geometry)

  3. Model predicts fields from coords. build_model(name, **kwargs) instantiates a BaseModel subclass (SIREN, ModifiedMLP, AFNO, MeshGraphNet, ...) via the model registry; its only job is forward(x) -> fields. (pinneapple_neural.architectures)

  4. Physics/PINN computes residuals and builds loss terms. compile_physics(spec) (or compile_problem directly) turns the spec into a loss_fn(model, y_hat, batch) that differentiates the model's output with autograd (grad/jacobian/divergence/laplacian) to produce PDE-residual, boundary, and initial-condition loss terms, weighted by LossWeights. (pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver, pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde)

  5. Solver applies an optimization strategy. A Trainer (or TwoPhaseTrainer/TimeMarchingTrainer/ CausalPINNTrainer/DDPPINNTrainer for more specialized policies) runs the optimization loop against the compiled loss, producing a trained model and a training history. (pinneapple_neural.trainer)

  6. Backend executes the run. Tensor operations run through whichever backend is active (set_backend("torch" | "jax")); device placement, mixed precision, and distributed/HPC execution are handled by pinneapple_neural.trainer's parallel/HPC utilities beneath that abstraction. (pinneapple_tools.compute_backends)

  7. Researcher evaluates metrics and stores artifacts. The trained model is handed to Arena/PINNArenaBenchmark for comparison against other models or backends, RunLogger records a JSONL audit trail for reproducibility, and results can be checked against literature (hpo_experiments.reproduce) or a named benchmark (pinneapple_pdb.benchmarks). (pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite, pinneapple_tools.hpo_experiments, pinneapple_neural.trainer.audit, pinneapple_pdb)

docs.title: What's optional
docs.text: Steps 2 and 7 are the most commonly skipped or replaced in practice: a preset's own domain_bounds is often enough without an explicit PhysicsDomain2D (step 2), and a quick experiment may train and inspect a model without ever touching the Arena/benchmark layer (step 7). Steps 1, 3, 4, and 5 are the minimum needed to train anything.

docs.title: Package Layers
docs.text: This is the verified mapping from pipeline stage to package, replacing an earlier stub whose "Solver" row was inaccurate (it pointed at pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers, which is a classical-solver package, not the training-policy layer described in Solver).

docs.title: Core pipeline
docs.text:
Layer Package Notes Problem definition pinneapple_physics.pde_environment ProblemSpec, ProblemBuilder, presets, BC/IC types Geometry + sampling pinneapple_design.geometry SDF/CSG, PhysicsDomain2D/3D, mesh, MeshCollocator Data container pinneapple_data PhysicalSample, collation, collocation, active learning Model architectures pinneapple_neural.architectures BaseModel subclasses + ModelRegistry Physics / residuals + constraints pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver, pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde compile_problem, autograd ops, DoMINO; SymPy-based residuals Solver — training policy pinneapple_neural.trainer Trainer, TwoPhaseTrainer, TimeMarchingTrainer, CausalPINNTrainer, DDPPINNTrainer, loss-weight balancers Execution backend pinneapple_tools.compute_backends PyTorch (default) / JAX abstraction Benchmarking pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite Arena, PINNArenaBenchmark, transfer/meta benchmark pipelines Research pipeline pinneapple_tools.hpo_experiments literature discovery, knowledge base, reproduction Structured storage pinneapple_pdb Earth-observation-backed dataset builder + named-benchmark catalog

Classical numerical solvers (pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers — FEM/FDM/FVM/spectral/SPH/LBM, plus OpenFOAM/FEniCS bridges) are a distinct capability from the training-policy "Solver": they generate reference/ comparison data (or couple to external tools), rather than optimizing a neural network's weights. A pinneapple_neural.trainer.Trainer can train against data a numerical_solvers run produced, but the two are not the same layer.

docs.title: Extension packages
docs.text:
These sit on top of the core pipeline, consuming its outputs rather than being required by it:

Package Adds pinneapple_analysis Uncertainty quantification, physics validation, inverse problems pinneapple_adaptation Transfer learning and meta-learning across PDE families pinneapple_simulation Classical numerical solvers, particle dynamics, external-solver bridges pinneapple_systems Time series, co-simulation, digital twins pinneapple_design.design_optimizer Adjoint/Pareto/Bayesian/evolutionary shape optimization pinneapple_problemdesign Natural-language-to-PDE problem design agent pinneapple_arena YAML/JSON-driven multi-model benchmark runner and leaderboard pinneapple_quantum Quantum and quantum-inspired PINNs pinneapple_worldmodel Generalist physics foundation models pinneapple_hub Model hub client (push_to_hub/from_pretrained) pinneapple_registry Local, self-hosted artifact/experiment registry pinneapple_llm LLM-assisted pipeline drafting, gated by PhysicsGuardrail pinneapple_blender Field/trajectory export to .ply and Blender scene rendering pinneapple_perception Extracting physics observations from images/video/audio pinneapple_app FastAPI + frontend web app for browser-based benchmarking

docs.title: Compatibility shims
docs.text: pinneapple_models, pinneapple_solvers, and pinneapple_train are re-export shims (for pinneapple_neural.architectures, pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers, and pinneapple_neural.trainer respectively) kept only so older import paths keep working.

docs.title: System Overview
docs.text:
Problem → Data/Geometry → Model → Physics(PINN) → Solver → Backend → Research

PINNeAPPle is organized as a chain of independent packages, one per stage of this pipeline, connected by plain-data interfaces (ProblemSpec, sampled coordinate tensors, a loss-function callable, a trained model) rather than by inheritance or a shared runtime object. Each stage can be swapped without touching the others: change the preset without touching the network, change the network without touching the physics, change the training policy without touching the physics, change PyTorch for JAX without touching the training policy.

docs.title: The core packages
docs.text:
Stage Package Problem definition pinneapple_physics.pde_environment Data container pinneapple_data Geometry & sampling pinneapple_design.geometry Model architectures pinneapple_neural.architectures Physics / residual compiler pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver, pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde Training policy ("Solver") pinneapple_neural.trainer Execution backend pinneapple_tools.compute_backends Benchmarking / research pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite, pinneapple_tools.hpo_experiments

See Package Layers for the full mapping, including the packages that sit around this core pipeline (classical solvers, UQ, transfer/meta-learning, digital twins, design optimization, and more).

docs.title: A thin top-level convenience layer
docs.text: The pinneapple top-level package re-exports the pieces most needed to get started (get_preset, build_model, and similar) so a first experiment doesn't require knowing which sub-package each piece lives in. It is a convenience wrapper, not a separate implementation — every function it exposes delegates to one of the packages above.

docs.title: Compatibility shims
docs.text: Three packages exist purely to keep older import paths working while the "real" implementation lives elsewhere: pinneapple_models re-exports pinneapple_neural.architectures, pinneapple_solvers re-exports pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers, and pinneapple_train re-exports pinneapple_neural.trainer. New code should import from the non-shim location directly.

docs.title: Why the separation matters
docs.text: Because each stage only depends on the interface of the stage before it (a ProblemSpec, a batch of coordinates, a model's forward, a loss dict), you can, for example, benchmark the same trained model against a classical numerical solver's reference solution (pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers) without either package knowing the other exists — they only share PhysicalSample/tensor data, not code. This is also what makes the higher-layer packages (pinneapple_analysis for UQ/validation/inverse problems, pinneapple_adaptation for transfer/ meta-learning, pinneapple_systems for time series/co-simulation/digital twins, pinneapple_design.design_optimizer for shape optimization) additive rather than invasive: they consume the core pipeline's outputs and add capability on top, without the core pipeline needing to know they exist.

docs.title: No linear exceptional-point tuning in PT-symmetric tetramers
docs.text: Status: ASSUMED 4, PROVED 2, ARGUED 4, SUPPORTED 2

docs.title: [ASSUMED] assumption A1
docs.text: The couplings b_k(lam) are polynomials in a real control parameter lam (complex coefficients).

docs.title: [ASSUMED] assumption A2
docs.text: Target law: gamma_EP^2(lam) = l(lam) = J^2 + lam J G with J > 0 and G != 0 (a non-constant line).

docs.title: [ASSUMED] assumption A3
docs.text: The middle bond does not vanish identically (B = |b2|^2 is not the zero polynomial).

docs.title: [ASSUMED] definition D1
docs.text: gamma_EP(lam): the PT-breaking threshold, the smallest gamma > 0 at which the spectrum of H stops being real (an exceptional point).

docs.title: [PROVED] lemma L1
docs.text: PT symmetry P H* P = H holds iff b3 = b1 (b2 is free). - depends on: D1 - check (exact) residual vanishes when b3 = b1: passed, simplifies to 0 [0.00 s] - check (exact) residual entry (0,1) is b3 - b1: passed, simplifies to 0 [0.00 s] - status because: all checks exact and passed, dependencies proved

docs.title: [PROVED] lemma L2
docs.text: det(E - H) = E^4 + (gamma^2 - 2A - B) E^2 + (A^2 - B gamma^2), A = |b1|^2, B = |b2|^2: the spectrum depends on the couplings only through A and B. - depends on: L1 - check (exact) characteristic polynomial: passed, simplifies to 0 [0.00 s] - status because: all checks exact and passed, dependencies proved

docs.title: [ARGUED] lemma L3
docs.text: With x = E^2, the spectrum is real iff both roots of x^2 + p x + q (p = gamma^2 - 2A - B, q = A^2 - B gamma^2) are real and >= 0, so the threshold lies on branch I (q = 0: gamma^2 = A^2/B) or branch II (p^2 = 4q: (gamma^2 - 2A + B)^2 = 4A(A - 2B)). - depends on: L2, A3 - check (exact) discriminant p^2 - 4q: passed, simplifies to 0 [0.00 s] - check (exact) branch I: q = 0 at gamma^2 = A^2/B: passed, simplifies to 0 [0.00 s] - check (exact) on p = 0 the discriminant is -4q (a p = 0 exit is a q = 0 exit): passed, simplifies to 0 [0.00 s] - check (numerical) matrix threshold lies on a branch (random A, B): passed, holds on 300 random samples [0.57 s] - argument (not machine-checked): E = +/- sqrt(x) is real iff x is real and >= 0, i.e. iff p^2 - 4q >= 0, q >= 0 and p <= 0 (Vieta). These are continuous in gamma, so the first gamma where one fails has one of them at equality; p = 0 with p^2 - 4q >= 0 forces q = 0 (checked), leaving branch I or branch II. The continuity step is written, not machine-checked. - status because: checks passed; part of the argument is a written step not machine-checked

docs.title: [ARGUED] lemma L4
docs.text: Branch I cannot carry the target: A(lam)^2 = B(lam) l(lam) is impossible for polynomial couplings, since deg A^2 = 4 deg b1 is even and deg (B l) = 2 deg b2 + 1 is odd. - depends on: L3, A1, A2, A3 - check (exact) leading term of |b|^2 is |c|^2 lam^(2n) (degree 2 deg b, positive coefficient): passed, simplifies to 0 [0.00 s] - check (exact) 4p = 2q + 1 has no integer solution (even degree vs odd degree), all degrees: passed, no integer solution [0.01 s] - check (exact) degree parity on generic polynomials, deg b1, deg b2 <= 4: passed, holds for all 25 cases (generic coefficients, positive leading terms) [0.09 s] - argument: deg A^2 = 4 deg b1 (A = |b1|^2 has degree 2 deg b1) and deg (B l) = 2 deg b2 + 1; the two polynomials cannot be equal. - status because: a dependency is only argued

docs.title: [ARGUED] lemma L5
docs.text: Branch II cannot carry the target: gamma^2 = l on branch II squares to (B + l)^2 = 4A(l - B); when the degrees of the two sides match their leading coefficients have opposite signs (B_lead^2 > 0 against -4 A_lead B_lead < 0), otherwise one side dominates. - depends on: L3, A1, A2, A3 - check (exact) squaring branch II at gamma^2 = l: passed, simplifies to 0 [0.00 s] - check (exact) q >= 1: equal degrees 4q = 2p + 2q force p = q, all degrees: passed, 4q = 2p + 2q gives p = [q][0.00 s] - check (exact) p = q >= 1: leading coefficient B_l^2 + 4 A_l B_l of LHS - RHS is positive: passed, leading coefficient 4A_lB_l + B_l**2 is positive [0.00 s] - check (exact) q = 0: 2 = 2p + 1 has no integer solution, all degrees: passed, no integer solution [0.00 s] - check (exact) leading coefficient of (B + l)^2 - 4A(l - B) never vanishes, deg b1, deg b2 <= 4: passed, holds for all 25 cases (generic coefficients, positive leading terms) [1.05 s] - argument: deg A = 2p, deg B = 2q. If q >= 1, deg LHS = 4q and deg RHS = 2p + 2q: unequal degrees leave a nonzero leading term, equal degrees force p = q and a positive leading coefficient. If q = 0, deg LHS = 2 while deg RHS = 2p + 1 is odd. - status because: a dependency is only argued

docs.title: [SUPPORTED] lemma L6
docs.text: Numerical cross-check: no quadratic modulation of (b1, b2) makes the matrix threshold gamma_EP^2(lam) a non-constant straight line on [-1, 1]. - depends on: L2 - check (numerical) search over quadratic couplings: passed, no counterexample; smallest margin found 0.0001857 (2 searches) [176.43 s] - status because: numerical evidence only

docs.title: [ARGUED] theorem T1
docs.text: No PT-preserving polynomial modulation of the tetramer couplings realises exact linear exceptional-point tuning gamma_EP^2(lam) = J^2 + lam J G (G != 0). - depends on: L1, L3, L4, L5 - corroborated by: L6 [SUPPORTED] - status because: a dependency is only argued

docs.title: [SUPPORTED] conjecture C1
docs.text: The same restriction holds for PT chains with N >= 5 sites (paper's Conjecture 2). - depends on: T1 - check (numerical) pentamer: search over quadratic couplings (b1, b2, b2, b1): passed, no counterexample; smallest margin found 0.0007425 (1 searches) [39.50 s] - status because: numerical evidence only

docs.title: Adaptive forecasting: switching and combining models online
docs.text:
The same online-learning core (pinneapple_physics.online_learning) drives the adaptive ensembles of physics models (FNO, PINN, GNN, numerical solvers).

pinneapple_systems.time_series.AdaptiveForecaster keeps a pool of forecasting models (experts) and decides, at every step, how much to trust each one, using only the errors they made on data they had not seen. When the series changes regime (seasonal, then trending, then a random walk), the weights move to the model that fits the new regime within a few steps.

from pinneapple_systems.time_series import AdaptiveForecaster, LagRegressorExpert, default_experts
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor

experts = default_experts(season_length=12)                     # naive, drift, SES x3, Holt, Holt-Winters, Theta, AR...
experts["forest"] = LagRegressorExpert(RandomForestRegressor(100), n_lags=12, refit_every=50)

af = AdaptiveForecaster(experts, horizon=6)                      # mode="select" to switch instead of combining
run = af.run(y, start=48)                                         # backtest, one origin at a time
run.errors(h=1)                                                   # ensemble vs every expert vs best-in-hindsight
run.coverage(h=1), run.switches()                                 # interval coverage, model changes over time

af.update(new_value)                                              # online use
af.forecast()                                                     # forecast, interval, weights, active model

docs.title: Why it does not overfit
docs.text:
• Prequential: every weight update uses the error of a forecast issued before its target was observed; the experts are refitted only on past data. A test checks it: changing the data after time t leaves every forecast issued up to t unchanged.
  • No hyper-parameter fitted on the evaluation period: smoothing constants are separate experts (selected online), and the learning and switching rates of the aggregation are themselves chosen online by AdaHedge.
  • Guarantees, not tuning: Fixed-Share has a regret bound against the best sequence of experts with a limited number of switches (Herbster & Warmuth 1998); AdaHedge has a regret bound against the best (eta, alpha) without any parameter (de Rooij et al. 2014). The ensemble cannot be much worse than the best model, and it can be better when the best model changes over time.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Each expert issues forecasts for horizons 1..H at every origin.
  2. When the target arrives, each expert's error (absolute or squared, divided by the mean absolute one-step change of the series so far, clipped) updates, for that horizon, a grid of Fixed-Share aggregators with different learning rates eta and switching rates alpha.
  3. AdaHedge weights the aggregators; the forecast is the weighted average ("combine") or the forecast of the expert with the largest effective weight ("select").
  4. Adaptive conformal inference (Gibbs & Candes 2021) gives intervals whose coverage is corrected after every miss.

Failed experts (exceptions, non-finite forecasts) are left out of that step and scored with the worst loss.

docs.title: Results (tests/test_adaptive_forecasting.py)
docs.text:
Series Ensemble MAE (h = 1) Best single model in hindsight seasonal -> trend -> random walk 0.735 0.929 (AR) seasonal only 0.380 0.378 (AR)

The "best single model in hindsight" is not available online: it is the model you would have picked had you known the whole series. 90 % intervals cover 89 % of the outcomes on the regime-switching series.

docs.title: Positional astronomy and astrophysics (pinneapple_physics.astro)
docs.text:
An independent NumPy implementation of the apparent sky, validated against USNO NOVAS, JPL Horizons, the USNO almanac, NASA eclipse predictions and skyfield. It powers the Observatory app.

pip install "pinneapple[sky]"     # sgp4 + skyfield-data (bundles the public-domain JPL DE421 kernel)

from pinneapple_physics.astro import Observer, Time, apparent, rise_transit_set, moon_phase

here = Observer(-23.5505, -46.6333, 760)                  # latitude, longitude (east +), metres

docs.title: The orbit surrogate
docs.text:
from pinneapple_physics.astro.surrogate import train_orbit_pinn
rep = train_orbit_pinn("mars", jd_tdb=2461327.0, days=365, iters=800)   # ~30 s on one CPU core
rep["verdict"], rep["summary"]["max_angle_arcsec_test"], rep["checks"]

The network only learns the perturbation of the exact two-body solution, r = r_Kepler + s τ² g_θ(τ), so the initial position and velocity are hard constraints. Its loss is the residual of r'' = −μ r/|r|³ + Σ_j μ_j [(r_j − r)/|r_j − r|³ − r_j/|r_j|³] at collocation points (perturbers from the reference integration) plus a few anchor states. It is then scored on held-out integrator states: angular error, split-conformal coverage (pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.conformal), the error in two-body energy and angular momentum relative to their perturbation-driven variation, the equation-of-motion residual and the gain over Kepler. Mars passes every check (0.09″ over a year); the Earth fails them, because of the Moon, and the verdict says so.
