docs.title: astroML: periodograms, deconvolved densities and fits with errors
docs.text:
pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.presets.astroml_bridge wraps astroML (BSD-2-Clause), the code companion of Statistics, Data Mining, and Machine Learning in Astronomy. It sits next to the astropy bridge and returns NumPy arrays, small dataclasses and PhysicalSample objects. The module imports without astroML; calling a function that needs it raises an ImportError that says how to install it.

pip install astroML                # pulls astropy, scikit-learn, scipy, matplotlib
pip install "pinneapple[astroml]"  # same, through the extra

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.presets import astroml_bridge as ab

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
t = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 200, 150))                                   # days, irregular
y = 15 + 0.3 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 0.613) + rng.normal(0, 0.15, 150)   # mag

ab.best_period(t, y, 0.15, period_range=(0.2, 10))      # 0.61297 d
pg = ab.lomb_scargle_periodogram(t, y, 0.15, period_range=(0.2, 10))
pg.false_alarm_levels       # {0.01: 0.138, 0.001: 0.169}  power thresholds (Scargle 1982)
pg.peak_power, pg.peak_false_alarm   # 0.633, ~0
pg.to_upd()                  # PhysicalSample: power on a frequency coordinate
ab.light_curve_sample(t, y, 0.15, band="V")   # the light curve itself, point domain

xd = ab.xd_fit(X, Xerr, n_components=2)        # X (N, D); Xerr (N, D, D) covariances or (N, D) sigmas
xd.means, xd.covariances, xd.weights           # the intrinsic mixture, errors deconvolved

ab.bayesian_block_edges(t, x, sigma, fitness="measures", p0=0.001)   # change points of a time series
counts, edges, width = ab.knuth_histogram(data)

ab.fit_line_with_errors(x, y, dy)          # WLS: slope, intercept, covariance, chi2, dof
ab.fit_line_tls(x, y, dx, dy)              # errors on both axes (Hogg, Bovy & Lang 2010)

ab.validate()                              # the synthetic checks below

Units: astroML is unit-agnostic. Time is in the unit you pass (usually days); freq is in cycles per that unit, omega = 2π freq, periods in the unit of t. Periodogram power is the generalised Lomb-Scargle normalisation (Zechmeister & Kürster 2009), dimensionless in [0, 1].

function astroML piece lomb_scargle_periodogram, best_period time_series.lomb_scargle (generalised, with significance) multiterm_periodogram, best_period(n_terms=k) time_series.multiterm_periodogram bootstrap_peak_distribution time_series.lomb_scargle_bootstrap xd_fit density_estimation.XDGMM (extreme deconvolution) bayesian_block_edges, knuth_histogram density_estimation.bayesian_blocks, knuth_bin_width fit_line_with_errors, fit_line_tls linear_model.LinearRegression(y_error), linear_model.TLS_logL load_dataset(name) datasets.fetch_* (SDSS, LINEAR, RR Lyrae, ...; see DATASETS)

best_period searches a uniform grid with step 1 / (oversample · baseline) and then refines on 2001 points around the peak, so the answer is not limited by the coarse step.

load_dataset passes download_if_missing=False unless told otherwise (astroML's own default downloads). The datasets are a few MB to several hundred MB and are cached in ~/astroML_data.

docs.title: Check before trusting
docs.text:
validate() runs four synthetic checks offline. Measured with astroML 1.0.2, astropy 8.0.1, scikit-learn 1.9.1, seed 0, and over seeds 0-9:

check setup seed 0 seeds 0-9 tolerance period recovery 150 irregular points over 200 d, P = 0.613 d, amplitude 0.3, noise 0.15 0.612967 d, rel. error 5.4e-5 max 1.9e-4 1e-3 XD means 600 points, two 2-D Gaussians (sd 0.5) at (0, 0) and (4, 3), per-point errors 0.2-1.0 max mean error 0.072 (0.14 sd) max 0.19 sd 0.25 sd Bayesian-block step 300 points over 10 s, step 1 → 2 at t = 6.3 s, noise 0.2, p0 = 0.001 one edge at 6.316 s one edge each time, max error 0.025 s 0.05 s line fit, WLS and TLS y = 2.5 x − 1, 80 points, dx = 0.05, dy = 0.3 slopes 2.483 (WLS), 2.487 (TLS) max rel. error 1.0e-2 2e-2

All four pass on all ten seeds; validate() takes about 2 s on one CPU core.

XD deconvolves the width as well as the means: on the seed-0 data the intrinsic standard deviations come out 0.41-0.54 (true 0.5), while a plain scikit-learn GaussianMixture on the same noisy points gives 0.75-0.84.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Scargle false-alarm levels are optimistic on wide grids. astroML's significance assumes M = 2 N independent frequencies. For 150 points over 200 d searched over 0.1-5 cycles/day there are about 1000, and 12 of 200 pure-noise series (6 %) exceeded the nominal 1 % level. Use bootstrap_peak_distribution (or a narrower search) for a false-alarm probability you intend to quote.
  • Bayesian Blocks p0 on measured series. The p0 prior is calibrated for event data. On the step series above, p0 = 0.01 added a spurious edge in 2 of 10 noise seeds and the default p0 = 0.05 in more; p0 = 0.001 found only the step in all ten.
  • Aliases. A periodogram peak can be an alias (1-day alias for ground-based data, harmonics for non-sinusoidal shapes). best_period returns the highest peak; check multiterm_periodogram and the phase-folded light curve.
  • Deprecated upstream. In astroML 1.0 lomb_scargle, multiterm_periodogram, bayesian_blocks and knuth_bin_width delegate to astropy and emit deprecation warnings; the bridge silences them. If a future astroML removes them the bridge will raise, and the astropy equivalents are the replacement.
  • Not wrapped. LinearRegressionwithErrors needs the old PyMC3 (< 3.11); fit_line_tls maximises TLS_logL instead and returns no covariance. XD's mixing matrix R is not implemented in astroML.
  • XD costs O(N K D³) per EM step and converges to a local maximum; try a few random_state values for K > 2.

docs.title: Backend
docs.text: The Backend layer is the execution runtime abstraction: it decides which numerical library actually runs the tensor operations, and provides the lower-level device/parallelism utilities the Solver layer builds on. Everything above this layer (models, physics, training policy) is written against a common interface so it does not need to know whether it is ultimately running on PyTorch or JAX.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
pinneapple_tools.compute_backends (re-exported at pinneapple_tools, and via the legacy alias pinneapple_backend):

  • Backend — a namespace of backend-name constants (Backend.TORCH, Backend.JAX).
  • set_backend(name) / get_backend() — a simple global backend selector ("torch" is the default and requires no extra dependency; "jax" requires pip install jax jaxlib).
  • JAXBackend — jit_pinn(model_fn, residual_fn) JIT-compiles a PINN residual; vmap_residual(single_pt_residual) vectorizes a per-point residual over a batch; torch_to_jax/jax_to_torch convert tensors between the two libraries. jax_available() reports whether JAX is importable.
from pinneapple_tools.compute_backends import set_backend, get_backend, JAXBackend

set_backend("jax")
print(get_backend())  # "jax"

compiled = JAXBackend.jit_pinn(model_fn, residual_fn)
batched = JAXBackend.vmap_residual(single_pt_residual)

PyTorch is the default and by far the more complete path — every model, trainer, and benchmark task in the framework is written in PyTorch first; the JAX backend targets a narrower, PINN-residual-specific speedup.

docs.title: Device and parallelism utilities
docs.text: A related but separate set of helpers lives in pinneapple_neural.trainer and is used by Trainer/TwoPhaseTrainer/etc. to actually place work on hardware: best_device(), count_gpus(), gpu_info(), AMPContext (mixed precision), wrap_data_parallel/unwrap_model, CUDAPrefetcher, GradAccumTrainer (gradient accumulation), and HPC-scale utilities in trainer.hpc — FSDPConfig/wrap_fsdp, wrap_zero_optimizer, CUDAGraphModule, PowerSGD/Top-K gradient-compression hooks, build_torchrun_cmd/build_slurm_script, and PINNeAPPleProfiler. These are PyTorch-specific execution concerns (single-GPU vs. multi-GPU vs. cluster), one layer below compute_backends' torch-vs-JAX abstraction.

docs.title: What Backend does not do
docs.text: It has no notion of models, losses, or training loops — only of how tensor operations for a given backend name are dispatched and accelerated. Which loss to compute is PINN / Physics's job; when to step the optimizer is Solver's.

docs.title: PhysicsBackend: one array, derivative and solve API
docs.text:
pinneapple_core.backend defines PhysicsBackend, the interface the library's kernel code is written against, with torch and jax implementations. pp.set_backend("jax") (or with pp.use_backend("jax"):) selects the engine and pp.get_physics_backend() returns its object.

Group Operations arrays asarray, to_numpy, linspace, zeros, ones, eye, diag; elementwise math on bk.xp algebra matmul, solve, integrate (trapezoid) transforms grad, jacobian, vmap, jit (no-op on torch) 
def objective(bk, L):                       # no engine named here
    x = bk.linspace(0.0, L, 101)
    return bk.integrate(bk.xp.sin(x) ** 2, x)

for name in ("torch", "jax"):
    bk = pp.get_physics_backend(name)
    print(name, bk.grad(lambda L: objective(bk, L))(bk.asarray(2.0)))

Float64 is the default dtype on both, so the same code gives the same numbers: tests/pinneapple_core/test_backend.py solves a finite-difference Poisson problem and differentiates its objective with respect to the domain length on both engines (values agree to 1e-10 relative, gradients to 1e-8). Add an engine (CUDA kernels, an FEM or FVM code, an external solver) with register_backend("name", MyBackend), where MyBackend subclasses PhysicsBackend and implements the operations it supports; the rest raise NotImplementedError. jax is optional and enabled with x64 when first used. Existing PINN code paths are not yet ported to this interface: today it is the contract new kernel code uses.

docs.title: Black-hole weather: forecasting accretion flows with a trust horizon
docs.text: pinneapple_physics.blackhole reproduces and extends Duarte, Nemmen & Navarro (2022), Black hole weather forecasting with deep learning: a pilot study (MNRAS 512, 5848; arXiv:2102.06242; code, MIT: black-hole-group/DL_BH_fluids). The original work trained a U-Net on hydrodynamic simulations of the hot, radiatively inefficient gas around a black hole and forecast the flow about 10⁴ times faster than the fluid solver. This module adds what the weather work in PINNeAPPle asks of any forecast: for how long can it be trusted, and can we tell without the truth? Issue #399.

docs.title: Pieces
docs.text: module what it does hydro AccretionFlow: axisymmetric viscous hydrodynamics around a Schwarzschild black hole (Paczyński-Wiita potential, α-viscosity "SS" or "ST", equilibrium torus), finite volume (HLL, MUSCL, SSP-RK2) on a log-r grid; bondi_pw: exact transonic Bondi accretion for validation forecast DuarteUNet (layer-for-layer port of the original), DensityCodec, make_blocks, train_forecaster, rollout, lead_time_scores, trust_horizon, MassEnvelope twin accretion_scene: the flow revolved in 3D as a cutaway for PINNeAPPle-Twin3D, simulation and forecast side by side, trust signals as sensors capture capture_twin: records the Twin3D viewer (headless Chromium) to frames for GIFs

docs.title: The simulations
docs.text:
The paper's training data are PLUTO runs (Almeida & Nemmen 2020) that are not reachable from every environment, so examples/black_hole_weather/simulate.py regenerates the same kind of flow with the library's own solver:

  • units G = M = c = 1; potential Φ = −1/(r − 2), which places the innermost stable orbit at r = 6;
  • adiabatic gas (γ = 5/3) without cooling, total energy evolved so viscous heat stays in the gas;
  • viscosity only in the azimuthal stresses Trφ, Tθφ (Stone, Pringle & Begelman 1999), with ν = α cs²/ΩK ("SS") or ν = α r1/2 ("ST");
  • initial equilibrium torus with l(R) = lc(R/Rc)a (pressure maximum at Rc = 20, inner edge 12) in a cold atmosphere; r from 4 to 400 GM/c², 128 × 64 cells;
  • runs named like the paper's, PL{a}{SS|ST}{α}.

Validation (tests/test_blackhole_weather.py):

  • mass and angular momentum close to round-off (10⁻¹⁶) once the boundary fluxes are counted;
  • a uniform pressure at rest stays at rest (exact geometric source terms);
  • the inviscid torus holds its equilibrium;
  • exact Bondi accretion in the Paczyński-Wiita potential stays steady: accretion rate within 0.5 % and density within 0.2 % (median) over 2000 GM/c³.

As in other black-hole codes, the tenuous atmosphere has floors and a speed / temperature ceiling (v_max, t_cap); AccretionFlow.capped counts the cells where they act (≈1 % of the cells, next to the hole).

docs.title: The forecaster
docs.text: Five consecutive density snapshots go in as channels, the next five come out; the density is log-normalised and the outer atmosphere and polar cells are cropped, as in the original. The loss is MAE + α·MAE(pixels with y > 0.5) (the paper's multi-simulation loss; its one-simulation loss uses pixel boxes of its own grid, which do not transfer).

docs.title: Trust
docs.text:
• Trust horizon. Iterative rollouts from many start times; per lead time, the error of the forecast against persistence and against the time-mean flow, and the anomaly correlation (ACC) with the simulation. The horizon is where the ACC drops below 0.6 (the weather convention).
  • Mass check, no truth needed. The gas in the forecast window can only change by what crosses its edges, and the training simulations show how fast that ever happens (MassEnvelope). A rollout whose mass moves faster is creating or destroying gas — the "artificial mass injection" the original authors identify as the cause of drift — and the first lead where that happens is a trust limit available in operation.

docs.title: 3D digital twin
docs.text:
from pinneapple_physics.blackhole.twin import accretion_scene
sc = accretion_scene(grid, {"simulation": logrho_true, "forecast": logrho_pred}, times, r_view=60,
                     sensors=[{"id": "forecast error", "panel": "forecast", "series": err, "envelope": (0, err_max)}])
sc.export("out/bh_twin")            # pinneapple_twin3d.serve("out/bh_twin") -> browser

The axisymmetric flow is revolved into a 3/4 cutaway (two meridional planes and the equatorial sector) around a black sphere at the event horizon. The viewer accepts ?field=log10_density&cmap=inferno&view=1,0.75,-1&range=-6,0 to open on that view.

docs.title: Interstellar view (general-relativistic ray tracing)
docs.text:
raytrace.Camera.trace integrates the null geodesics of the Schwarzschild metric once per camera: each ray stays in a plane through the hole, and u = 1/r obeys u'' = 3u² − u, solved by RK4 with arc-length-limited steps. raytrace.render then integrates the emission of any (r, θ) density / temperature / velocity frame along those rays. It includes:

  • the gravitational and Doppler redshift (I ∝ g⁴);
  • optional grey absorption;
  • a colour temperature that follows g;
  • a procedural star field that is lensed with the flow;
  • a film-like bloom.

The tests check that the shadow edge sits at the critical impact parameter b = 3√3 M and that a thin disc shows its far side lensed above the shadow, as in Interstellar (James et al. 2015).

The twin also renders in Blender: Scene.render_blender / render_blender_frames (Cycles, pip install bpy).

docs.title: Resolution study, zoo dataset and retrained forecaster
docs.text:
The reference was checked on four grids (90 × 45 to 256 × 128, ratio √2, three seeds each, the same seeded perturbation on every grid). The tools are in the library:

  • convergence.resolution_study: conservative remap, Richardson order and GCI through pinneapple_analysis.verification, and statistical convergence;
  • dataset: the zoo dataset blackhole_riaf_density_256, whole trajectories per split;
  • forecast.train_on_trajectories: rollout loss, input noise, mass penalties, resumable;
  • skill.evaluate_skill: persistence, climatology and DMD baselines, moving-block bootstrap intervals, physics checks;
  • figures.

  • The means converge within their 95 % bands: the accretion rate is 2.18 ± 0.58 on 181 × 90 and 1.97 ± 0.63 on 256 × 128, and the mass in the window and the density slope also agree.
  • The profiles are not in the asymptotic range. From 181 to 256 they change by 4-11 %, against 0.5-2.5 % between the coarser grids, and l/l_K rises 3.8 % beyond its band. The likely cause is that the speed and temperature ceilings act on more cells as the resolution grows. These changes are the stated uncertainty band of the data.
  • The forecaster is not shipped. Retrained on 256 × 128 trajectories with replicate padding, a rollout loss and a mass penalty, it beats persistence with 95 % confidence from 60 to 2000 GM/c³ (skill 0.27 at 2000 M) and beats DMD. But it breaks the mass envelope of the training runs in 14-54 % of the frames.

Details and every number: examples/black_hole_weather/README.md, section "Zoo version".

docs.title: Results of the first version
docs.text: The port of the paper's U-Net does not beat persistence at the 20 GM/c³ frame spacing used here. It loses or gains 4-6 % of the gas per frame, which the mass check flags at the first frame. The residual variant (predicting the change) beats persistence over the whole 1200 GM/c³ test rollout: 45 % lower error in distribution and 21 % lower for an unseen α. Numbers, figures and GIFs are in examples/black_hole_weather/README.md.

docs.title: Core primitives: Domain, Geometry, Mesh, Field
docs.text:
pinneapple_core (also pp.core) is the shared vocabulary of tensors, geometry and topology. One object answers the four questions every physics workflow asks of a quantity: its derivative, its divergence, its value at an arbitrary point, and its integral.

Class What it is Domain A box in any dimension, or a 2D CSG shape. contains, sdf, sample_interior, sample_boundary(return_normals=True), volume. Geometry A Domain with named boundaries (x_min, x_max, ... for boxes) and mesh(h). Mesh Simplex mesh (interval, triangle, tetrahedron). Exact P1 gradient, integrate, interpolate, boundary_nodes. Field Values on a Grid, a Mesh or a PointCloud. FunctionField A torch callable with the same calls, derivatives by autograd. 
import numpy as np
from pinneapple_core import Field, Geometry

geom = Geometry.box([0, 0], [1, 1])
mesh = geom.mesh(h=0.05)

u = Field.on_mesh(mesh, lambda p: np.sin(np.pi * p[:, 0]) * p[:, 1])
u.gradient()                      # Field with values (N, 2)
u.integrate()                     # exact for the piecewise-linear interpolant
u.interpolate(np.array([[0.3, 0.4]]))

Values have shape (N, *components): (N,) scalar, (N, d) vector, (N, c, d) gradient of a vector. gradient() of a scalar gives (N, d); divergence() needs a vector with d components.

docs.title: How each support computes the four operations
docs.text: Support gradient interpolate integrate Grid central differences (second-order edges), non-uniform axes allowed multilinear trapezoid Mesh volume-weighted average of the exact cell gradients (exact for linear data) barycentric (NaN outside, or fill="nearest") exact for P1 PointCloud weighted local least-squares plane over the k nearest neighbours Delaunay-linear in d >= 2, np.interp in 1D weights, else Monte Carlo over a Domain FunctionField autograd, graph kept (create_graph=True) evaluation Monte Carlo over the Domain, or points + weights

docs.title: Notes and limits
docs.text:
• Mesh stores simplices only; surface meshes embedded in 3D (MeshData) are a different object.
  • Geometry.mesh is a structured mesh for boxes and a Delaunay mesh of a lattice plus boundary samples for 2D CSG shapes. Good for prototyping; use gmsh for production quality.
  • The point-cloud Monte Carlo integral assumes the points are uniform samples of the domain.

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
pinneapple_core.operators (also pp.grad, pp.div, ...) gives one function per operator, the torch.nn.functional of physics. The same call works on a grid, mesh or point-cloud Field (no point argument, returns a Field) and on a continuous field (a torch callable or FunctionField, takes the points x, returns a tensor that keeps the autograd graph).

Operator Result grad(f) (N, d) scalar, (N, c, d) vector div(f) scalar, from a vector field curl(f) (N, 3) in 3D, scalar dv/dx - du/dy in 2D laplacian(f) scalar, or one per component of a vector jacobian(f) (N, c, d), J[n, i, j] = d f_i / d x_j (c = 1 for a scalar) hessian(f) (N, d, d) of a scalar integrate(f) number; continuous fields take n= (Monte Carlo) or points=, weights= flux(f, where=None) outward flux integral f.n dS; where is a box face ("x_max") or a predicate 
import pinneapple as pp

u = Field.on_mesh(mesh, lambda p: p[:, 0] ** 2 + p[:, 1])
pp.laplacian(u)                    # Field of 2.0
v = Field.on_mesh(mesh, lambda p: p)
pp.flux(v) == pp.integrate(pp.div(v))   # divergence theorem, exact for P1 data

Accuracy against manufactured solutions (tests/pinneapple_core/test_operators.py, interior of the unit square, max error relative to the max of the exact value): grid 81x81 ~ 4e-4, mesh 40x40 ~ 3e-3, 4000 scattered points ~ 4e-2 for second derivatives and 3e-3 for first, continuous exact to round-off. On a mesh the second derivatives are two rounds of gradient recovery, so they are accurate in the interior and degrade at the boundary; a point cloud uses a local quadratic fit. flux is exact on a mesh for P1 fields, trapezoid on a grid, and Monte Carlo (error ~ 1/sqrt(n)) on a point cloud or a continuous field.

docs.title: Derivatives through solvers: pp.func
docs.text:
pinneapple_core.func (pp.func) wraps torch.func (grad, jacobian, jacrev, jacfwd, hessian, vmap) and adds wrt, the argument to differentiate by name or position:

from pinneapple_core import func
func.jacobian(model, wrt="geometry")(geometry, mu)     # d model / d geometry
  • func.implicit_solve(residual, x0, *params, solver=None) solves residual(x, *params) = 0 and differentiates the solution with the implicit function theorem, dx/dp = -(dF/dx)^-1 dF/dp. The backward pass is one adjoint solve, independent of the forward iterations, and solver= accepts any external code (never differentiated). The Jacobian dF/dx is dense; second derivatives through the solve ignore its dependence on params.
  • pinneapple_core.fem is a differentiable P1 finite-element Poisson solver (dense matrices, up to a few thousand nodes). Because the vertex coordinates are torch tensors, loss.backward() returns the gradient with respect to the geometry: write points = f(design_parameters) and differentiate. Tested against central finite differences of the same pipeline (relative agreement 1e-6 or better for a 1D length and for 2D width, height and bump parameters).

Examples: examples/core_primitives/01_poisson_pinn.py (PINN) and 02_operator_poisson_1d.py (neural operator).

docs.title: Animation-centred dashboards
docs.text:
pinneapple_tools.visualization.dashboard turns any time-dependent simulation into one view: - the animation in the middle; - charts around it, synchronised to its time cursor; - KPI tiles across the top; - a parameter panel and a colour bar.

The same dashboard exports as: - an interactive HTML page (one self-contained file, no server and no internet; scrubbing a chart moves the animation); - a static PNG; - a GIF/MP4 of the dashboard playing.

It uses the dark style of the studio renders (aircraft, Formula car).

Interactive page: rover-dashboard.html (≈ 6.3 MB, opens offline). Static: rover-dashboard.png. Video: rover-dashboard.mp4.

from pinneapple_tools.visualization.dashboard import Dashboard, Chart, Series, Marker, Tile, Param, ColorBar

db = Dashboard("Damped pendulum", t, frames,                 # frames: RGB arrays or image paths, one per t [s]
    charts=[Chart("Angle", "angle [rad]", "time [s]", [Series("theta", theta)], slot="left"),
            Chart("Phase portrait", "rate [rad/s]", "angle [rad]", [Series("orbit", rate, x=theta)],
                  [Marker("now", theta, rate)], kind="phase", slot="right"),
            Chart("Energy", "E [J/kg]", "time [s]", [Series("E", E)], slot="bottom")],
    tiles=[Tile("Energy", E, "J/kg")], params=[Param("Length", 1.0, "m")],
    colorbar=ColorBar("Speed [m/s]", "inferno", 0, 3))
db.to_html("pendulum.html")                                  # interactive, self-contained
db.to_png("pendulum.png", k=40)                              # the dashboard at frame 40
db.to_video(gif="pendulum.gif", mp4="pendulum.mp4", fps=12)  # GIF downscaled with gif_size / gif_every

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
Part What it is Dashboard(title, t, frames, ...) the frames of the animation and their times; subtitle, footer, colorbar Chart(title, ylabel, xlabel, series, markers, kind, slot) slot: "left", "right" or "bottom". Units go in the labels kind="series" one value per frame (x defaults to the times; any per-frame axis such as distance works). A cursor line follows the animation, and clicking or dragging the chart moves it kind="phase" fixed curves (Series(..., x=...)) plus Markers that move with the frames, e.g. a testbed curve and the operating point of each wheel Tile(label, value, unit, fmt) a KPI, either a scalar or one value per frame (the tile follows the cursor) Param(label, value, unit) a line of the parameter panel ColorBar(title, cmap, lo, hi) the colour scale of the field shown in the animation Dashboard.scene3d optional live three.js view (below)

Colour follows the entity: a label gets the same colour on every chart, taken in a fixed order from the categorical palette's dark-surface steps. The four-slot set was checked for colour-vision deficiency and contrast against the panel colour. A missing value (NaN) leaves a gap in a line.

docs.title: The interactive page
docs.text:
to_html(path) writes one file.

Animation. It is embedded as VP9 WebM plus H.264 MP4 sources with a keyframe every 4 frames, so seeking is exact and every browser engine finds a format it plays. Without ffmpeg it falls back to JPEG frames.

Charts: - drawn on canvases at the screen's pixel density; - hovering shows a crosshair and the values; - clicking or dragging a time chart moves the animation to that instant; - play/pause, a speed selector, a time slider and the arrow keys step through the frames; - the tiles follow the cursor.

Reuse of the studio viewer. The colour bar and the number formatting come from the studio viewer's studio-core.js, inlined, so they match the viewer and the renders.

Live 3D. With scene3d set, a Live 3D tab draws the vehicle parts moving with the frames over the terrain. It uses the studio's vendored three.js, inlined through an import map, and a studio.lighting preset (black lunar sky, low Sun). The view orbits freely and follows the scrubbed time. html.scene3d_payload(bodies, poses, terrain, lighting) builds the data for any rigid-body animation.

Size depends on the frames. The rover page, with 150 frames at 1024 px plus the 3D data, is 6.1 MB.

docs.title: Static PNG and videos
docs.text: to_png and to_video draw the same layout with matplotlib (1920 × 1080 by default). The figure is drawn once; each frame only changes the image, the cursors, the moving markers and the tiles. The MP4 keeps every frame. The GIF is downscaled (gif_size) and can skip frames (gif_every) at the same playback speed; its 256-colour palette shifts the series colours a little, so the MP4 and the HTML page are the reference versions.

docs.title: The rover dashboard
docs.text:
pinneapple_simulation.vehicle.dashboard builds the dashboard of any vehicle run:

import pinneapple as pp
from pinneapple_simulation.vehicle import dashboard as vdash
frames, ks, clim = vdash.render_frames(run, terrain, n=150,      # planetary renders, 3-D ruts
                                       field="normal_stress", field_alpha=0.45, field_glow=0.05,
                                       field_saturation=0.6, clim_percentiles=(5, 95))
db = vdash.vehicle_dashboard(run, frames, ks, model=wong_reece, surrogate=pp.zoo.load("rover_contact_grc1_viper"),
                             clim=clim, field_label="Peak normal stress in the ruts [kPa]", field_saturation=0.6,
                             scene3d=True, terrain=terrain)

The animation shows: - a hard, low Sun (lunar_low_sun, 12°) under a black sky, with long shadows; - regolith with small craters and rocks; - wheels that roll with the joint angles and leave ruts deformed into the terrain mesh: a floor at the computed sinkage, walls at the angle of repose, berms of displaced soil and grouser marks spaced by the pitch and the slip, all shaded and shadowed by the low Sun; - the ruts coloured by the peak normal stress they carried [kPa], with its colour bar. The map is muted and semi-transparent (field_alpha=0.45, field_glow=0.05, field_saturation=0.6): it tints the regolith's albedo before the photometry, so the rut walls, the grouser marks and the Sun's shading and shadows dominate; its range spans the 5-95 % percentiles of the stress the ruts carry (≈ 14-21 kPa), so the variation along the ruts shows; - the ground running out to the real lunar horizon, so no mesh edge shows in any frame (checked for the frames by studio.planetary.border_visibility).

Around it: - left: drawbar pull, driving torque and sinkage versus slip. The grey line is the single-wheel testbed curve at the static wheel load; the dots are the four wheels' live operating points; - right: speed against the command; slip per wheel; the PINN against the run's Wong-Reece model for the front-left wheel (same inputs; gaps where a wheel leaves the PINN's training box). The PINN is the pre-trained model of the model zoo, pp.zoo.load("rover_contact_grc1_viper"); a zoo model is wrapped in terramechanics.surrogate.ZooContactSurrogate; - bottom: sinkage and normal load per wheel along the traverse; the PINN's error for every wheel; - tiles: distance [m], mean slip, maximum sinkage [mm], drive energy [J] and the PINN's RMS error [N], all up to the cursor; - parameters: the vehicle, the wheel, the soil (with units), gravity, the command, the time step, the PINN model, its held-out error (from its model card) and its error along this run.

examples/studio/07_lunar_rover_dashboard.py regenerates every file: - docs/assets/studio/rover-dashboard.{html,png,gif,mp4}: the MP4 at 1920 × 1080; the GIF at 1280 × 720, laid out natively at that size (to_video(gif_font_scale=1.0)) so the chart text stays readable, with one shared octree palette and frame differencing to stay under 6 MB (dashboard.static.write_gif); - rover-frame.png, one rendered frame.

The run behind it is the crater crossing of the lunar rover page: NASA VIPER (450 kg) on GRC-1 at lunar gravity, a 0.2 m/s command, 45 s, 2 ms steps. The rover covers 8.63 m with a mean slip of 0.018 and a maximum sinkage of 36.6 mm (the rear-left wheel digging in while it pushes against the rock), uses 794 J (92 J/m), and reaches 10.5° of pitch and 3.8° of roll; the front-left wheel leaves the soil for a moment near 1.3 m (its sinkage and load drop to zero).

The zoo PINN along the run. rover_contact_grc1_viper v1.1.0 is trained on the physics of this run (GRC-1 with slip-sinkage, n1 = 0.8; the dashboard checks it with ZooContactSurrogate.check_physics and shows "PINN physics vs run: same"). Its model card gives a held-out drawbar-pull RMSE of 0.22 N; along this run, at the states the wheels met, its drawbar-pull RMSE over all wheels is 0.33 N, with no error above 1 N. v1.0.0, trained before slip-sinkage was added (n1 = 0), erred by 11.3 N RMS on the same run and by up to ≈ 190 N near the rock; it stays loadable as a superseded release (see the model zoo guide).

docs.title: Earth-system building blocks and data assimilation
docs.text: Four verified pieces for climate, weather, hydrology and digital-twin work. Each is checked against an exact solution or a standard test case (tests/test_geophysics.py, tests/test_data_assimilation_conservation.py). Shortcuts: pp.geophysics and pp.assimilation.

docs.title: Shallow water on the sphere (pinneapple_simulation.geophysics.sphere_shallow_water)
docs.text:
Spectral-transform model in vorticity-divergence form on a Gaussian grid (triangular truncation T_N, RK4, optional del^4 hyper-diffusion), with the test suite of Williamson et al. (1992, J. Comput. Phys. 102:211):

from pinneapple_simulation.geophysics import SphericalHarmonics, williamson_case6, stable_dt

sh = SphericalHarmonics(42)                      # T42: 64 x 128 Gaussian grid
model = williamson_case6(sh)                      # Rossby-Haurwitz wave, wavenumber 4
model.run(14 * 86400, dt=600.0, diagnostics_every=86400)
fields = model.fields()                           # u, v, h, zeta, delta, hs on the grid
model.history                                     # mass, total energy, potential enstrophy per day
Case What it checks Result at T42 2, steady geostrophic flow (alpha = 0, pi/4, ~pi/2) exact steady state, flow over the poles normalised l2 height error ~1e-13 after 5 days 5, flow over a mountain topography, nonlinear flow stable for 15 days; mass exact, energy drift 2e-8 6, Rossby-Haurwitz wave long-time stability, wave propagation eastward at ~11 deg/day (barotropic theory 12.2); energy drift 2e-8 in 14 days

Mass is conserved to round-off by construction (the divergence of the mass flux is analysed directly).

docs.title: Richards equation (pinneapple_simulation.geophysics.richards)
docs.text:
1-D unsaturated flow in mixed form with the modified Picard iteration of Celia et al. (1990), mass-conservative. Soils: van Genuchten-Mualem, Brooks-Corey, Clapp-Hornberger / Campbell, Gardner. Boundary conditions: head, flux, free drainage; optional sink (root uptake).

from pinneapple_simulation.geophysics import CELIA_1990_SOIL, Boundary, solve_richards

r = solve_richards(CELIA_1990_SOIL, depth=100.0, n_cells=100, h0=-1000.0, t_end=86400.0,
                   top=Boundary("head", -75.0), bottom=Boundary("free_drainage"))
r.h[-1], r.theta[-1], r.mass_balance_ratio        # profiles after one day; ratio = 1.000000

Verified against the exact steady infiltration profile of the Gardner soil (second-order convergence).

docs.title: Two-layer energy-balance model (pinneapple_simulation.geophysics.energy_balance)
docs.text: Upper ocean and deep ocean (Held et al. 2010; Geoffroy et al. 2013), with efficacy of deep-ocean heat uptake: exact integration of annual forcing, closed-form step response, ECS and TCR, and fit_two_layer for estimating the parameters from a warming series and its forcing. An abrupt-forcing run identifies every parameter. A historical ramp identifies the transient response (TCR) but not lambda and the deep-ocean capacity separately; the fit returns their correlation (about -1) so this is visible.

docs.title: 4D-Var through autograd (pinneapple_analysis.data_assimilation)
docs.text:
Strong-constraint 4D-Var where the model is any PyTorch function (a solver written in torch, a neural surrogate or a hybrid), so the adjoint comes from autograd. Control variable B^{-1/2}(x0 - xb), L-BFGS, observation operators and covariances per observation time, gradient_check (the adjoint test) and a Lorenz-96 identical-twin experiment.

from pinneapple_analysis.data_assimilation import Observation, Var4D, lorenz96_step

var = Var4D(model=lorenz96_step, B_sqrt=1.0)
result = var.analyse(x_background, [Observation(step=k, y=y_k, H=lambda x: x[::2], R=1.0) for k, y_k in obs])
result.x0, result.trajectory

docs.title: Exact conservation for surrogates (pinneapple_physics.conservation)
docs.text:
project_integral corrects a predicted field so that its weighted integral (mass, energy, water) equals a target exactly: additive (smallest correction), multiplicative (keeps the pattern) or positive (clip then rescale, the global mass fixer). ConservationProjection(model, weights) wraps a network so that a rollout keeps the total of its input; it stays differentiable and can be used during training.

These methods are implemented from the cited papers.

docs.title: From a problem description to checked CAD, fit-for-purpose meshes and one report
docs.text:
pinneapple_design.fitmesh turns a problem written in words (English or Portuguese) into reference geometries, checked CAD variants, meshes sized for what the result will be used for, and a single report that ties every decision to its evidence. The goal is the mesh and CAD quality the problem needs: not so fine that it wastes days, not so coarse that nothing in the result can be trusted.

from pinneapple_design.fitmesh import FitMeshSession

s = FitMeshSession("Erosion and pressure drop in a 3 inch pneumatic pipe bend, air at 20 m/s", "study/")
s.step()                         # the open questions and the geometry options, with references
s.answer(accuracy="design")      # screening / design / verification
s.choose_geometry("pipe_bend_90")
s.choose_parameters(n=4)         # the suggested parameters and ranges, or vary={"bend_ratio": [1, 3]}
s.generate_cad()                 # STEP + STL per variant, each with its checks
s.plan_meshes()                  # mesh plan per variant, with the rules and sources used
s.generate_meshes(procs=4)       # meshes + quality (and the coarser family for design / verification)
s.add_results("pressure drop", [f_fine, f_medium, f_coarse])   # optional: grid-convergence index
s.report()                       # study/report.html and study/report.json

FitMeshSession.run(text, out_dir, answers=..., geometry=..., vary=...) does it all in one call, and pinneapple_design.fitmesh.api.create_app() exposes the same steps over HTTP (one call per step, files and report downloadable).

docs.title: The steps
docs.text: Step What happens What is checked Problem physics, fluid, speed, size, Reynolds number, purpose, quantities, material and load are read from the text; anything missing becomes a question; every fact keeps its source (text, answer, default, model) unanswered facts are listed in the report Geometry templates ranked by physics and keywords: NACA 4-digit wing, Ahmed body, cylinder, sphere, 90° pipe bend, backward-facing step, plate with a hole, cantilever beam, plate-fin heat sink each template cites the published references it can be compared with Parameters high-influence parameters proposed for variation over their usual range (sizes within a factor 2 of the base), the rest kept; dependent sizes follow (development lengths in diameters); Latin hypercube, reference design first validity limits of every parameter CAD STEP and STL per variant valid solid (OpenCascade), volume against the exact formula, watertight STL, STL/solid volume within the tessellation tolerance for the purpose, dimensions against each reference object (same / inside the studied range / extrapolated) Mesh plan method, sizes, prism layers, domain, cell and cost estimate, and the mesh family every rule is written into the rationale with its source Meshes Gmsh (solids: quadratic tetrahedra, .msh and CalculiX .inp; 2-D sections with a boundary layer), snappyHexMesh (3-D external with far field and ground, internal with inlet and outlet from the CAD faces) pinneapple_data.cae quality (non-orthogonality, skewness, aspect ratio, scaled Jacobian, disconnected regions), checkMesh, prism-layer coverage Report one JSON and one HTML page, a verdict per stage grid-convergence index when the results of the three meshes are given

docs.title: The rules behind the mesh plan
docs.text:
Purpose Surface cells Wall treatment Prism growth Meshes screening (~10 %) L/40, 4 across the smallest feature wall functions, y+ ≈ 50 (30-300) 1.3 one design (a few %) L/80, 8 across the smallest feature y+ ≈ 1 where separation or wall quantities matter (k-ω SST without wall functions) 1.2 the mesh and one 1.5× coarser verification L/120, 12 across the smallest feature y+ ≈ 1 1.15 three, ratio 1.5, for the GCI
  • First-cell height from the skin friction at the reference length: Cf = 0.026 Re^-1/7 (White) turbulent, 0.664 Re^-1/2 laminar, and the pipe friction factor 0.316 Re^-1/4 for internal flows. y+ between 5 and 30 (the buffer layer) is never used.
  • External domains: 5 L upstream, 10-20 L downstream, 5 body sizes to the sides; the blockage is reported. Extruded sections (wing, cylinder, step) are meshed as 2-D unless a 3-D wake is asked for.
  • Solids: quadratic tetrahedra; 2-4 elements through the thinnest wall; 16-48 elements around holes, where the stress peaks; the closed-form check (Kt from Peterson's, beam formulas) is printed next to the plan.
  • Grid convergence: observed order, Richardson extrapolation and GCI with a safety factor of 1.25 for three grids (Roache; Celik et al., J. Fluids Eng. 130:078001, 2008). Oscillatory convergence is reported as a range, not forced through the formula, and the asymptotic range is checked.

docs.title: Language models, local or hosted
docs.text:
from pinneapple_design.fitmesh import FitMeshSession, LLMAssist
llm = LLMAssist(provider="ollama", model="qwen2.5:7b")          # or "anthropic" / "openai"
s = FitMeshSession("a bracket that holds a 2 kg motor on a wall", "study/", llm=llm)

The model can read the problem, rank the geometries, propose parameters and ranges, write a CadQuery part when no template fits, and review the mesh plan. It proposes; PINNeAPPle checks:

  • unknown template or parameter names are dropped and ranges are clipped to the validity limits (the report says so);
  • model-written CadQuery is parsed first (imports limited to cadquery, math and numpy; no file, system or dunder access), then runs in a separate isolated Python process with a timeout, and the part goes through the same CAD checks, marked "no published reference";
  • the mesh review may change only the y+ target, the growth ratio and the layer count, inside the rule limits; refused changes are written into the rationale.

Calls can be logged with pinneapple_llm.ConversationStore. Without a model everything runs on the rules.

docs.title: How this compares with the tools in use today
docs.text:
Commercial meshers (Fluent watertight and fault-tolerant workflows, STAR-CCM+ automated meshing, Fidelity Pointwise, ANSA batch meshing) and open ones (Gmsh, snappyHexMesh, cfMesh, Netgen) size meshes from curvature, proximity and gaps, but the first-layer height still comes from a y+ target the user supplies, and none checks the resolution against the quantity of interest before solving. Design-space tools (CAESES, optiSLang, HEEDS, Dakota, SALib) sample the ranges the engineer sets; none says where a range came from. Text-to-CAD (Zoo, Text2CAD, CAD-Coder, CADCodeVerify) now produces running CadQuery for simple parts, but dimensional accuracy is weak and failures can be silent. LLM simulation agents (MetaOpenFOAM, Foam-Agent, ChatCFD) report how often a case runs, not whether it is fit for purpose, and none runs a grid-convergence study.

This module's aim is the missing piece: references and ranges with their source, CAD checked against exact formulas and published objects, a mesh sized from the physics and the purpose, and one report with a verdict per stage. Template parts are not free-form CAD and the rules are not adjoint-based adaptation; when the stakes are high, the verification purpose and the GCI are what make a number quotable.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Nine templates today; any other part goes through the language model (no published reference) or a STEP file.
  • snappyHexMesh prism layers collapse at sharp edges and thin gaps; the coverage is measured and reported, and a low coverage is a warning, not hidden.
  • Cell, cost and degree-of-freedom estimates are order-of-magnitude.
  • Gmsh (GPL) and OpenFOAM (GPL) are optional external tools; install them separately (pip install gmsh).

docs.title: Free-surface flow: runners, channels, launders
docs.text:
pp.cfd.FreeSurfaceFlow (pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.free_surface) writes and runs OpenFOAM interFoam cases with two phases separated by a free surface (volume of fluid). It covers:

  • melt runners and launders;
  • spillways and open channels;
  • tanks filled by a jet.
from pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.free_surface import FreeSurfaceFlow, Phase, SampleLine

flow = FreeSurfaceFlow(
    mesh="cases/runner/mesh",                                   # or regions={name: (V, F)} for snappyHexMesh
    roles={"jet": "inlet", "top": "atmosphere", "exit": "outlet"},       # every other patch is a wall
    inlet_velocity={"jet": (0.0, 9.85, 1.74)},                  # the full vector, m/s
    level=-2.04,                                                 # initial liquid level, height along -gravity
    liquid=Phase("metal", rho=7200, nu=8.472e-6), gas=Phase("air", rho=1.2, nu=1.5e-5), sigma=1.8,
    gravity=(0, 0, -9.8), end_time=30.0, sample_every=0.1, keep_every=1.0,
    lines=[SampleLine("L1", (-1.8, -7.429, -2.2), (-1.8, 15.305, -2.2), 101)])
flow.write("cases/runner/run", procs=4)
flow.run("cases/runner/run", procs=4)                           # setFields, decomposePar, interFoam
prof = flow.profiles("cases/runner/run", t_start=2.0)["L1"]    # times x points, and the time mean

docs.title: Boundary conditions
docs.text:
Role Velocity Liquid fraction Pressure k, ω inlet the given vector 1 fixed flux from intensity (1 %) and mixing length (0.1 m) outlet, atmosphere pressure inlet-outlet inlet-outlet; reverse flow is gas total pressure p_ref (prghTotalPressure) inlet-outlet wall no slip zero gradient fixed flux wall functions

Initial state. The liquid fills everything below level. level is a height along −gravity, so gravity may be tilted, as for a sloped channel meshed in its own frame. hRef is set at the level, so the initial hydrostatic state is in balance. The turbulence model is k-ω SST, or laminar.

docs.title: Lines sampled while the solver runs
docs.text:
LiveLineSampler reads each time the solver writes and records the nearest cell's value at every point of every line. There is no spatial interpolation, and points outside the fluid are dropped. It then writes postProcessing/lines/<t>/<line>.csv.

  • No function objects. It does not use OpenFOAM function objects. Their sets and probes types abort in parallel on OpenFOAM v1912.
  • Bounded disk. With keep_every, the times it has sampled are deleted, except one every keep_every seconds and the last. This bounds the disk use of a long transient. In a 30 s run of 180 000 cells, the 300 field writes would otherwise take more than 10 GB.
  • Serial and decomposed cases. It reads both. It also takes a callable instead of a directory, for runners that retry in new directories.

docs.title: Example: floor slope of a melt runner
docs.text:
examples/free_surface/01_runner_slope_study.py uses TroughSection (pinneapple_design.geometry.trough): a 2-D section of an 8 m runner with a 0.5 m weir at the downstream end.

Setup. - A jet enters through an 8 cm slot and reaches the bath at about 5 m/s. - The floor pivots about the weir end, so only the depth under the jet changes: 0.26 m at +2° (floor descending toward the weir), 0.50 m at 0° and 0.74 m at −2°. - The mesh is rectangular in the runner's frame, and the slope enters through tilted gravity. A sloped mesh with vertical gravity diverged in the shallow upstream corner. The tests check that the tilted frame keeps the weir crest, the bath level and the vertical jet speed.

Results. k is taken 5 cm above the floor and averaged over 4–12 s:

Slope Metal under the jet Mean k, impact zone 0.5–3 m Relative to 0° Peak k +2° 0.26 m 1.40 m²/s² ×2.9 5.0 m²/s² 0° 0.50 m 0.49 m²/s² ×1 1.6 m²/s² −2° 0.74 m 0.20 m²/s² ×0.41 0.40 m²/s²

A deep pool at impact damps the jet before it reaches the floor, and a shallow one lets it hit the floor almost undamped. The ranking is clear.

The magnitudes are for screening only: - the section is 2-D, so a slot replaces the round jet; - the turbulence model is RANS with wall functions, on 4 cm cells; - after 12 s the bath is still filling, about 25–35 % more liquid than at the start.

The study ranks the slopes but does not give a wear rate.

Tests: tests/test_free_surface.py. They check the region split, the tilted frame, the written case (patch roles, the empty front and back skipped, inlet k from the intensity, a rotated box for setFields, hRef), and a short OpenFOAM run that keeps the floor line in the bath and deletes the sampled times.

docs.title: Geomechanics with the material point method
docs.text:
pinneapple_simulation.particle_dynamics.geo_mpm simulates granular flows, landslides, dam breaks and soft bodies with the material point method (MPM), in physical units, in 2-D or 3-D. It is written in PyTorch from the published algorithms: - MLS-MPM with APIC transfer, Hu et al. (2018); - Drucker–Prager return mapping in Hencky strain, Klár et al. (2016).

Material Model Sand(friction_deg, E, nu, rho) Cohesionless Drucker–Prager without dilation. In 2-D the default is plane strain: the out-of-plane elastic stretch is tracked, so the total out-of-plane strain stays zero, as in a laboratory flume, and the cone is matched to Mohr–Coulomb in plane strain. In 3-D it is matched in triaxial compression Fluid(K, rho, gamma) Weakly compressible fluid: pressure from J (Tait-like), no shear memory Elastic(E, nu, rho) Fixed-corotated hyperelastic solid

Boundaries. The walls are the faces of the domain: "slip", "sticky", or "friction" with a Coulomb coefficient.

Bodies. Each body is seeded with ppc particles per cell along each axis. A run can hold several bodies of different materials.

Output. Frames are written in GeoTaichi's layout (<out>/particles/MPMParticle<NNNNNN>.npz, with position, velocity, volume, stress and body).

from pinneapple_simulation.particle_dynamics.geo_mpm import GeoMPM, Sand, box, runout
sim = GeoMPM(domain=(1.4, 0.3), dx=0.01, floor="sticky", walls="slip")
sim.add_body(box((0, 0), (0.2, 0.2)), Sand(friction_deg=30.0))
frames = sim.run(t_end=1.0, save_every=0.05, out="runs/collapse")
runout(frames[-1]["position"])

docs.title: GeoTaichi
docs.text:
GeoTaichi (Zhejiang University, GPL-3.0) is a much larger Taichi framework. It covers: - MPM, including two-phase porous media and incompressible fluids; - DEM and level-set DEM, affine bodies; - FEM and IGA; - MPM–DEM, FEM–MPM and IGA–MPM couplings, with incremental potential contact.

pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.geotaichi uses it as an external program. PINNeAPPle never imports or ships its code: - run_geotaichi(script, workdir) runs one of its scripts in a separate process, with GEOTAICHI_HOME pointing at a checkout. - read_geotaichi(path) reads the MPM or DEM particle frames. Pickled entries are skipped unless allow_pickle=True, which should be used only for files you trust. - frames_to_samples(frames) turns them into PhysicalSamples, the format the rest of the library trains on.

read_geotaichi also reads geo_mpm frames, so a GeoTaichi run and a PINNeAPPle run of the same problem can be compared directly. The GeoTaichi features not yet in geo_mpm are listed in issue #471: μ(I) rheology, porous media, DEM coupling, GPU, and a learned simulator on MPM data.

docs.title: Example: granular column collapse
docs.text:
examples/geomechanics/01_granular_column_collapse.py collapses sand columns with φ = 30°, width L0 = 0.2 m and aspect ratios a = H0/L0 of 0.5 to 3. Each column stands against a back wall, on a rough floor, with 1 cm cells. The runout is compared with the fits Lube et al. (2005) measured in two-dimensional collapses: (L∞ − L0)/L0 = 1.2 a for a < 1.8, and 1.9 a^(2/3) for a > 2.8.

a MPM (L∞ − L0)/L0 Lube et al. (2005) MPM / experiment Final height / L0 0.5 0.44 0.60 0.73 0.47 (H0 = 0.5) 1 1.32 1.20 1.10 0.77 2 3.71 2.4–3.0 (transition) 1.2–1.5 1.03 3 6.20 3.95 1.57 1.07

Agreement. The deposits come to rest (final speeds of a few mm/s). For a ≤ 1 the runout is within about 27 % of the experiments, and the short column keeps its top: final height close to H0 for a = 0.5, as observed.

Limit. Tall columns run out too far, and the 2/3 power regime is not reproduced. This is the known limit of rate-independent plasticity, which has no rate- or inertia-dependent friction. The μ(I) rheology that captures it is the first item of issue #471.

Choosing the yield cone. The cone matching matters as much as φ. Measured on the same columns (a = 0.5, 1 and 2): - with pure 2-D strains (no plane-strain constraint) and the triaxial cone, the runout was 4–10 % longer than with the default; - with plane strain but the triaxial-compression cone, it was 36–48 % shorter.

Tests: tests/test_geo_mpm.py checks: - free fall of an elastic block at g, mass conserved; - a hydrostatic pressure gradient of ρg within 5 % (fit over 0.1–0.4 s, while the weakly compressible column oscillates); - a sand column that spreads within bounds and comes to rest; - the frame reader on GeoTaichi-style files, pickled entries included.

docs.title: Geometry & Domain
docs.text: The Geometry & Domain layer turns a domain description into two things a training loop needs: a way to test "is this point inside/on the boundary?" and a way to sample interior and boundary collocation points from it.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
pinneapple_design.geometry (re-exported at pinneapple_design), organized into:

  • SDF primitives — 2D (sdf2d_circle, sdf2d_rectangle, sdf2d_ellipse, sdf2d_annulus, sdf2d_capsule, sdf2d_triangle, sdf2d_convex_polygon) and 3D (sdf3d_sphere, sdf3d_box, sdf3d_cylinder, sdf3d_torus, sdf3d_capsule), plus combinators (sdf_union, sdf_intersection, sdf_difference, sdf_smooth_union/intersection/difference, sdf_translate, sdf_scale, sdf_rotate_2d, sdf_onion, sdf_repeat_2d).
  • CSG (pinneapple_design.geometry.csg) — an object-oriented layer over the same idea: CSGRectangle, CSGCircle, CSGEllipse, CSGPolygon, combined with CSGUnion, CSGIntersection, CSGDifference.
  • Physics domains (pinneapple_design.geometry.gen.domains / domains3d) — PhysicsDomain2D / PhysicsDomain3D base classes that wrap an SDF with named boundary regions and give you sample_interior(n), sample_boundary_region(name, n), and get_pinn_batch(...) directly. Built-ins include channel, channel-with- obstacle, lid-driven-cavity, L-shape, annular, and multi-obstacle domains in 2D, with analogous 3D domains.
  • Mesh — structured/SDF-based mesh generation, MeshCollocator for sampling collocation points from a 3D mesh, and STL/STEP import.

docs.title: Building and sampling a domain
docs.text:
from pinneapple_design import build_domain, sample_domain

domain = build_domain("lid_driven_cavity_2d")   # dim=2 by default
x_int, x_bnd = sample_domain(domain, n_interior=4096, n_boundary=512)

build_domain dispatches to the registry lookups get_domain (2D) or get_domain_3d (3D) depending on dim; sample_domain is a thin wrapper that calls domain.sample_interior(n_interior) and domain.sample_boundary(n_boundary). Use list_domains() / list_domains_3d() to see every registered built-in name.

docs.title: Custom geometry
docs.text: Any PhysicsDomain2D/3D subclass only needs to implement sdf(p) and sample_boundary_region(region_name, n, seed); the base class handles interior sampling via rejection against the SDF and assembles PINN-ready batches for you. For irregular or imported shapes, build a GeometryAsset via build_geometry_asset/load_geometry_asset and drive collocation with MeshCollocator instead of an analytic SDF.

docs.title: Relationship to the rest of the pipeline
docs.text: A domain produces coordinate batches with no notion of which fields live on them or which PDE governs them — that pairing happens when ProblemDefinition's conditions are matched against the domain's named boundary regions, and residuals are compiled in PINN / Physics.

docs.title: PINNeAPPle Lab: experiments at scale, and a database of results and datasets
docs.text:
Open the experiment catalogue: every experiment with its figures, movies, checks, tiers and trust card, generated by python -m pinneapple_lab site docs/lab.

pinneapple_lab runs experiments reproducibly and stores everything they produce in one place. The goal is a growing database of physics experiments that can be used as demonstrations and use cases, and as training data for future PINNeAPPle models.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
An experiment is a class with parameters and a run(ctx) method. A run is one execution with one set of parameters. Its id is a hash of the experiment, its version and the parameters, so:

  • the same run is never computed twice; an existing result is returned as cached:...;
  • changing the experiment's code meaning means bumping version, which keeps the old results apart.

Through the RunContext, an experiment records:

what how where inputs and outputs ctx.input(name, value), ctx.output(name, value): arrays → .npy, dicts / numbers → .json, files → copied inputs/, outputs/ metrics ctx.metric(name, value, step=None); final values plus a curve log metrics.json, metrics_log.jsonl validation ctx.check(name, passed) or ctx.check(name, value=..., reference=..., rtol=..., max=...); a failed check ends the run as failed_validation validation.json status and stages with ctx.stage("train"):; statuses running, completed, failed_validation, failed (with traceback) run.json, progress.json figures and animations ctx.figure(name, fig), ctx.image(name, array), ctx.gif(name, frames) figures/ datasets ds = ctx.dataset(name, units=...), then ds.add(**sample); samples are written in shards, with a card (schema, shapes, value ranges, units, provenance, checksum) datasets/<name>/ provenance parameters, git commit, Python and package versions, timings run.json

Runs live in lab/runs/<experiment>/<run_id>/ and are indexed in lab/index.sqlite. Set the location with --root or $PINNEAPPLE_LAB.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
from pinneapple_lab import Experiment, register, run, sweep, LabStore

@register
class MyExperiment(Experiment):
    name = "my_experiment"
    version = "1"
    params = {"Re": 100.0, "seed": 0}
    space = {"Re": ("log", 10.0, 1000.0)}           # for random / Latin-hypercube sweeps

    def run(self, ctx):
        with ctx.stage("simulate"):
            field, cd = simulate(ctx.params["Re"])
        ctx.metric("drag_coefficient", cd)
        ctx.check("drag_positive", value=cd, min=0.0)
        ctx.dataset("fields").add(u=field, Re=ctx.params["Re"])
        ctx.figure("field", plot(field))

run("my_experiment", {"Re": 200.0})
sweep("my_experiment", grid={"Re": [50, 100, 200]}, n_jobs=3)
sweep("my_experiment", samples=100)                 # Latin hypercube over `space`

store = LabStore()
store.table("my_experiment")                        # pandas: params and metrics per run
store.export_dataset("my_experiment", "fields", "train.npz")   # completed runs only
store.catalog()                                     # lab/CATALOG.md

From the command line:

python -m pinneapple_lab list
python -m pinneapple_lab sweep cylinder_lbm -g Re=20,40,60,80,120,160,200 -j 4
python -m pinneapple_lab sweep oscillator -n 200
python -m pinneapple_lab status
python -m pinneapple_lab report
python -m pinneapple_lab export cylinder_lbm vorticity data/cylinder_vorticity.npz

An experiment defined outside the package is addressed as package.module:ClassName.
