docs.text: Module What it does mission Mission (variables, objectives, Limits absolute or relative to the baseline, Budget, acceptance tolerances, fixed conditions, hypotheses) simulator Simulator interface: check(params) -> issues, run(params, workdir) -> SimOutcome(outputs, ok, cost_s, fields, meta); FunctionSimulator ledger Ledger of RunRecords (purpose, reason, prediction before the run, outputs, cost), budget, environment (CPU, versions, commit), events.jsonl surrogates GPModel, MLPEnsemble, QuadraticRSM; compare_models (k-fold RMSE, relative error, R², 95 % coverage, fit time); FieldSurrogate (POD + per-mode model) and field_errors per region domain ValidatedDomain: distance to the nearest simulated design in units of their typical spacing, and the simulated range of every variable, with the reasons in words trust assess_candidates (P(feasible), constrained expected improvement, a TrustReport per candidate, labels), choose_next (the written rule below), verification_checks qualification solver_qualification: the same design on several meshes / iteration counts, outside the budget report figures from the snapshot (Pareto, models, learning, field triptych, trust cards) and the Markdown report domains.racecar RaceCarAero (OpenFOAM, FormulaCar) and flagship_mission()

docs.title: The triage
docs.text: Label Meaning What the lab does with it favourable inside the validated domain, P(meets every limit) ≥ 0.9, 95 % intervals within the acceptance tolerances confirms the most promising one by simulation uncertain inside the domain, but the prediction cannot settle the decision: P(feasible) between 0.05 and 0.9, an interval wider than the tolerance, or a large expected field error in the critical region (e.g. the diffuser) simulates it when its constrained expected improvement is at least the best favourable one's: that is where the decision changes out of domain the model is extrapolating (too far from every simulated design, or outside the simulated range of a variable) if the model's best design is here, simulates it before believing it unlikely P(feasible) < 0.05 not pursued

docs.title: Adding a physical domain
docs.text: Write a Simulator with honest check and run (a failed run returns ok=False and its reason, never made-up outputs), and a mission factory; the lab, the triage, the report and the dashboard work unchanged. A field on a fixed set of points (field_names, regions, field_points) enables the field surrogate and the critical-region check. pinneapple_autolab/domains/racecar.py is the reference.

docs.title: The AI Aerodynamicist
docs.text:
examples/autolab_aero/autolab_aero.py: "Find a lower-drag aerodynamic design at 70 m/s. Preserve the required downforce, stay within the geometry constraints, and validate the final design using CFD." on a parametric open-wheel car (front and rear wing angles, diffuser angle, ride height), OpenFOAM simpleFoam k-ω SST on snappyHexMesh, half model over a moving road. Full report, ledger and figures: examples/autolab_aero/_out/report.md. Measured on this repository's 4-core container (OpenFOAM v1912), 2026-10-24:

Solver qualification (baseline, forces averaged over iterations 400-800 because the steady RANS forces keep oscillating by about 2 % after 500 iterations):

mesh cells drag vs fine downforce vs fine balance vs fine medium 0.21 M -8.8 % -43.7 % (wing elements one or two cells thick) -3.4 % campaign (wings and floor at the fine levels) 0.42 M -0.2 % -8.4 % +9.6 % fine 0.82 M 0 0 0

Campaign: 20 CFD runs (1 baseline, 10 space-filling, 6 chosen one at a time, 3 final verifications), 3.3 h of solver time, no failed run.

judged before its CFD CFD said run012, run013 out of domain (the model's optimum, extrapolating) verified; drag predicted within 0.8 % and 1.2 % run014 - run017 uncertain (P(feasible) 0.73 - 0.84) 1 verified, 3 rejected (downforce or balance limit violated; run016's drag 3036 N against 2849 ± 46 N predicted) run018 - run020 favourable 3 verified

Recommendation: run019 (simulated), drag 2795 N against 3315 N (-15.7 %), downforce 7319 N (limit 7038 N), balance 1.073 (limit 0.913 - 1.116). On the fine mesh (outside the budget): drag -13.95 % (5.5 x the iteration noise), downforce +0.8 % (within the noise), balance 1.029 against a fine-mesh limit of 1.018: outside by 1 %, within 1.4 x the noise. The drag reduction is resolved by the solver on both meshes; the balance limit is not resolved on the campaign mesh (+9.6 % bias), which the report flags.

Surrogates (5-fold cross-validation, 20 runs): MLP ensemble chosen for every output, held-out mean relative error drag 2.4 %, downforce 10.2 %, balance 4.3 %; the quadratic response surface needs more runs than its 28 coefficients and is skipped. Surface Cp (POD + GP): held-out RMSE 0.07 on the body, 0.12 on the diffuser, 0.21-0.24 on the wings (the wings have vertices only at their span ends).

docs.title: The agent (stage 2)
docs.text:
pinneapple_autolab.agent puts an agent in front of the same lab:

mission in words ─► interpret_mission ─► Mission (+ what was read from which words, what was assumed)
                         │  refuses: an operating point the solver is not set up for, a request with no objective
                         ▼
              act(planner, lab_toolbox) ─► one controlled tool call at a time ─► evidence
                         │  LabPlanner (deterministic) or LLMStepPlanner (a language model), same tools
                         ▼
              answer ─► audit_claims: every number must come from a tool result; the recommended run must be a
                         successful simulation that meets every limit
  • Tools (lab_toolbox): read_mission, plan, simulate_baseline, space_filling, check_design, learn, optimize_and_assess, recommend_next, simulate_candidate, verify_best, status, answer. None changes the operating conditions, the bounds, the limits or the solver settings; a step with an argument a tool does not declare (simulate_baseline(speed=90)) or a tool that does not exist is refused and recorded.
  • Planners share :func:pinneapple_autolab.core.act (decide, check, run, record, repeat), added next to the plan-then-execute loop of the other missions: LabPlanner needs no network; LLMStepPlanner asks a model (pinneapple_llm.call_llm: Anthropic, OpenAI or any OpenAI-compatible server, Ollama) for each next step and sees the evidence so far.
  • Plugging in a real model: python examples/autolab_aero_agent/agent_mission.py --provider anthropic with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set (needs the anthropic package), or --provider ollama --model <name> with an Ollama server on the machine, or --provider openai_compatible for vLLM / llama.cpp / LM Studio. The container these results come from has no key and no route to model downloads, so the session below used LabPlanner.
  • Replay (pinneapple_autolab.replay.ReplaySimulator): a design already simulated is answered from its recorded measurement (exact parameter match, labelled replayed_from in the new ledger); any other design is simulated for real. Nothing is interpolated.

Measured (examples/autolab_aero_agent/_out/): the mission text was read into drag minimised, downforce >= baseline (from "Preserve the required downforce"), 20 simulations (from "at most 20 CFD runs"), 3 kept for verification (from "validate the final design using CFD"); the balance limit was added and stated as an assumption. The agent took 31 tool calls and reproduced the stage-1 campaign decision for decision (all 20 designs answered from the stage-1 ledger, 0 new runs), and answered run019 (drag 2795.5 N against 3314.8 N); the audit found every number in the answer in a tool result. "Lower drag at 80 m/s" and "Make the car look fast" were refused with their reasons. A scripted careless planner (rogue_session.json, not a real model) had its speed change and its invented tool refused before anything ran, and the "40 %" and "1990 N" of its answer flagged.

docs.title: Autonomous Physics Lab
docs.text:
The scientific cycle on a costly reference simulator (surrogates compared on held-out data, triage, the next simulation chosen by what is unknown, verification) is in the AI Aerodynamicist guide.

A mission in plain language becomes a plan of controlled library calls; every call leaves evidence (arguments, a summary of the result, wall time, error) and the mission ends in a decision with its trust report. The agent never runs code of its own: it can only order the tools registered for its kind of mission, with the arguments each tool declares.

from pinneapple_autolab import Tool, Toolbox, Step, TemplatePlanner, LLMPlanner, execute

box = Toolbox("demo", [Tool("add", lambda state, a=1, b=2: {"sum": a + b}, "add two numbers", {"a": "x", "b": "y"})])
plan = TemplatePlanner([Step("add", {"a": 3}, "why this step")]).plan("add three", box)
run = execute(plan, box)                 # run.state["add"] == {"sum": 5}; run.evidence[0].seconds, .summary
Piece What it does Tool(name, fn, description, inputs, summary) a library call fn(state, **args) -> dict; only the arguments in inputs are accepted Toolbox(kind, tools) the controlled set of tools of one mission kind; check(step) says why a step cannot run TemplatePlanner(steps) deterministic: the steps a mission kind always needs (no network, no API key) LLMPlanner(fallback, provider=..., llm=..., required=...) a language model orders the same tools as JSON; an unknown tool or argument, a missing required step or any failure falls back to the template plan and the reason goes into plan.notes execute(plan, toolbox) runs the steps in order through the toolbox only, Run(plan, state, evidence)

Language model. LLMPlanner uses pinneapple_llm.call_llm (Anthropic, OpenAI or a local Ollama model). With no API key and no local model, as in the runs below, it falls back to the template plan and says so. To plan with a model: set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (or OPENAI_API_KEY, or run Ollama) and pass planner="llm". The model only orders and parameterises the tools; the numbers in the report still come from the solvers.

docs.title: Demo 2: the self-optimizing engineer (board cooling)
docs.text:
pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling: a board with an overheating part, a junction limit, the room for a heat sink and a fan budget.

from pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling import DEFAULT_TEXT, run_mission

run = run_mission(DEFAULT_TEXT, out_dir="out")        # planner="llm" to let a model order the tools
print(run.state["verify"]["decision"], run.state["deliver"]["report"])

The plan (template planner):

Step Tool Library 1 read_mission parse_mission: numbers from the text with the words they came from, defaults listed as such 2 baseline simulate(mission, None): bare board in still air 3 screen_natural the largest heat sink the envelope allows, still air, several fin gaps 4 sample simulate_many: Latin-hypercube designs (base, fins, height, air speed), coupled reference solves 5 learn holdout: POD + Gaussian-process surrogate of the junction temperatures and the board-top map, measured on held-out designs; more solves until max error <= 3 K and the +-2 std band covers >= 90 % 6 optimize design_loop: lightest heat sink that meets every limit with pessimistic cooling at mean + 2 std, fan air power and fin gap constraints (differential evolution); the optimum is solved on the reference, added to the snapshots and the search repeated until the reference confirms it 7 verify verify: the design on finer grids (board cells x2 per direction, heat-sink base grid x2) and the trust report 8 deliver figures, glTF / USD, the self-contained three.js viewer, Blender Cycles stills and the animation (GIF / MP4), report.md, summary.json, trust_report.json

Reference (simulate): pinneapple_physics.pcb.solve (layered 3-D finite volumes, JEDEC two-resistor packages, convection + radiation) coupled to pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.evaluate_design (3-D finite-volume base, fin correlations, pressure drop) through the case-top resistance (Component.r_top_k_w), iterated to a fixed point of the heat that goes up through the sink. Pessimistic repeats the solve with each engine's convection band (board x 0.8, heat sink x 0.85).

Trust report (verify): every junction under its limit (pessimistic, fine grids), fan budget and envelope (critical); board and heat-sink energy balance, coupling convergence, the heat-sink engine's own checks, grid convergence; the surrogate within its band on the verified design, hold-out error, coverage and the nearest-snapshot baseline, and applicability (inside the design space, no farther from a snapshot than the held-out designs).

Needs scikit-learn (the Gaussian processes) and, for the renders, pip install bpy. Run it: python examples/autolab/self_optimizing_engineer.py (--smoke for 24 solves without renders, --no-render without Blender). The measured results of the run in the repository are in examples/autolab/_out/self_optimizing_engineer/report.md. Flow Studio node: autolab.board_cooling.

Scope. Engineering models with published correlations, not CFD: uniform air temperature in the enclosure, ducted flow through the fins (no bypass), typical package data. The air paths in the 3-D scene are an energy balance per strip of air, drawn to show where the heat goes. No conjugate CFD (OpenFOAM) run is part of this demo.

docs.title: Demo 3: the digital twin that knows when it is wrong (pipe loop)
docs.text:
pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.pipe_loop: a pumped, heated water loop (pump, heater, pipe A with a 90° elbow, a T junction, branches B and C with valves to two tanks) with ten sensors (four pressures, three flow meters, three temperatures) and five inputs (pump speed, two valve openings, inlet temperature, heater duty).

from pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.pipe_loop import run_mission

run = run_mission(out_dir="out")                     # planner="llm" to let a model order the tools
b = run.state["benchmark"]["benchmark"]
print(b["confusion"], b["accuracy"], run.state["trust"]["decision"])
Step Tool What it does 1 read_mission what to watch and which answers are asked for 2 build_twin the fast model: POD + Gaussian processes of the ten readings over the operating envelope (NORMAL_BOX), measured on held-out operating points 3 calibrate alarm thresholds from healthy runs (not guessed) 4 monitor three events and a healthy hour: an obstruction in branch B, a drifting flow meter on B, the pump driven above the envelope 5 request_simulation where the model is out of its domain: the reference at the new operating point vs the readings (does the plant still obey the physics?), then reference solves in the widened envelope, refit, monitor again 6 benchmark controlled cases with known answers (random kind, size, location, onset, operating history): confusion matrix, location accuracy, Kalman size error, false alarms, detection delay 7 trust the twin's trust report 8 deliver control-room figures, confusion matrix, GIF, 3-D scene (pressure on the walls, transparent elbow with its velocity profile, sensors coloured by the verdict), viewer, Blender animation, report

How it tells the causes apart. Ten physics residuals are computed from the readings alone: mass balance at the tee, Darcy-Weisbach / Colebrook flow of each pipe from its pressure drop, the pump curve, both valve laws, the heater energy balance and both branch heat losses. Each fault moves the residual vector in its own direction (a biased sensor moves every residual it enters; an obstruction in pipe B moves only the Darcy residual of B, mass and energy still balance), so the window mean of the residuals is matched to the fault directions by least squares; a noisy sensor shows as variance excess along its squared direction. An extended Kalman filter tracks an extra loss coefficient per pipe, so an obstruction comes with its size and uncertainty. The model is out of its domain when the inputs leave the training envelope, or when the fast model disagrees with readings that satisfy every physics residual; then the twin asks for a reference simulation instead of trusting its fast model.

Run it: python examples/autolab_digital_twin/twin_knows_when_wrong.py (--smoke: 3 cases per kind, no renders). Measured results of the run in the repository: examples/autolab_digital_twin/_out/report.md. Flow Studio node: autolab.pipe_twin.

Scope. The plant is simulated and its faults injected, so every answer is known; a real plant adds unmodelled effects and sensor behaviour. The quasi-steady model holds for valve moves slower than ten acoustic round trips (quasi_steady_valid); faster ones need the water-hammer solver. The elbow streamlines are the 1/7 power-law profile, not CFD.

docs.title: Simulation Campaign Planner: which simulations need to run
docs.text: The Simulation Campaign Planner (day 13 of the app program) decides which cases of a simulation campaign are worth their compute. You describe the parameter space and the budget. It returns a design of experiments, its coverage, the planned cases that repeat runs you already have, a run order, and the case files for OpenFOAM, CalculiX or your own Python code.

docs.title: In the library
docs.text:
Everything the app does is a library call:

from pinneapple_data.contracts import Parameter, ParameterSpace
from pinneapple_data.doe import plan_campaign
from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.campaign_cases import write_campaign

space = ParameterSpace(name="cantilever", budget=30, parameters=[
    Parameter(name="length", low=0.2, high=1.0, unit="m", group="geometry"),
    Parameter(name="height", low=0.02, high=0.08, unit="m", group="geometry"),
    Parameter(name="material", kind="categorical", values=["steel_S355", "aluminium_6061_T6"], group="material"),
    Parameter(name="tip_load", low=100, high=5000, unit="N", log=True, group="boundary")],
    constraints=["length >= 8 * height"])
plan = plan_campaign(space, method="maximin", existing=runs_done, existing_id_column="run_id")
plan.summary()            # coverage of the plan, of the existing runs and of both; repeats dropped
plan.study_result()       # StudyResult: metrics, checks with their values, limits
write_campaign(plan, "campaign/", outputs=["tip_deflection"])
Module What pinneapple_data.doe.design lhs, maximin, sobol, halton, random, full_factorial, fractional_factorial (minimum-aberration generators, resolution reported), infill (greedy maximin around existing runs; adaptive with outputs) pinneapple_data.doe.coverage discrepancy (centred L2), minimum / mean nearest-neighbour / fill distance, 1-D and 2-D projection coverage pinneapple_data.doe.redundancy planned cases within a tolerance of an existing run or of each other; near-duplicate pairs in the existing data pinneapple_data.doe.prioritize greedy-maximin run order: every prefix is spread out pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.campaign_cases case tables, run_cases.py, OpenFOAM airfoil cases, OpenFOAM base-case copies with dictionary edits plus the openfoam.campaign plan, CalculiX cantilever decks, .inp templates

docs.title: What to trust
docs.text: The fractional factorials match the minimum-aberration designs of the literature, and the space-filling designs are tested against random sampling. The generated CalculiX decks run with CalculiX 2.21 within 1 % of beam theory. The coverage is measured in the unit cube of the parameters, so it shows where you have no data, not where the response is difficult. Read the limits in the app README.

docs.title: Next steps in the chain
docs.text: The plan exports dataset.skeleton.json, a DatasetSpec whose outputs are still to come. The Workflow Runner (day 27) runs the cases and fills it. The Surrogate Studio (day 14) trains on the finished dataset.

docs.title: Chain of whys: why each element of a design exists, computed
docs.text:
Why does a roof slope? A flat tiled roof lets the rain through: water climbs the gap of each lap by capillarity, the wind pushes it further and, with nothing to drain it, the storm ponds on top. Why a ceiling? On a clear night the tile radiates to the sky, its underside drops below the dew point of the room air and drips. pinneapple_reason turns that way of explaining a design into a computation that works for any project and any scale:

requirement -> naive concept -> physical check (numbers) -> failure mode (mechanism + the number that proves it)
            -> countermeasure (new element, cost, expected effect) -> check every requirement again -> ... -> all pass

Every claim in a chain comes from a computed check: a closed-form model with its source, or a solver of the library (finite-difference beam, 3-D board finite volumes, plate-fin heat-sink correlations, method of characteristics). An LLM can propose candidates; it never supplies a number.

from pinneapple_reason import cases, reason, write_report

chain = reason(*cases.roof())          # requirements, the naive concept, a title
print(chain.explain("en"))             # version 0 -> version N, and why
write_report(chain, "roof_report")     # chain.json, report.md / .html, figures, trust.json

python -m pinneapple_reason run roof --out roof_report does the same from a terminal; python -m pinneapple_reason modes lists the library.

docs.title: The data model (pinneapple_reason.chain)
docs.text: Object What it holds Requirement what the design must do (text, both languages), the failure modes that would stop it (modes), limit overrides Concept one version of the design: parameters in SI units, elements, and the source of every value (sources: a premise, a cited standard value, or the countermeasure that set it) Verification one failure mode on one concept: demand vs capacity (the two numbers that decide), margin, mechanism in words built from the numbers, every measured quantity, method, assumptions, sources, applicability range (validity) and internal checks (self_checks); .check() is its pinneapple_analysis.trust.Check Finding the first failing verification and its proof Option a countermeasure tried: changes, cost (quantity x unit cost), target margin before / after, whether it fixes the failure, what it breaks, who proposed it Step / Chain every version with all its checks, the options and the one chosen, and why; to_dict / from_dict / save / load round-trip through JSON

docs.title: The library of failure modes (pinneapple_reason.library, pinneapple_reason.modes)
docs.text:
Domain Failure mode Check Countermeasures hydraulics / capillarity lap_water_ingress capillary rise between plates + wind head + run-off film (Nusselt) or ponded storm vs lap rise L sin(alpha) (Garden, CBD-40) increase_slope (sized to the material's minimum slope), longer_lap hygrothermal underside_condensation steady roof network on a clear night (Swinbank sky, Watmuff wind, ISO 6946 surfaces, grey plates) vs Magnus dew point ceiling_ventilated_attic, ceiling_insulation thermal comfort radiant_heat_gain same network on a sunny day: ceiling surface - air vs 5 K warm-ceiling asymmetry (ASHRAE 55) ceiling_ventilated_attic, radiant_barrier, ceiling_insulation electrothermal joule_heating I^2 R_on(T) coupled to the 3-D board model (pinneapple_physics.pcb) or the plate-fin heat sink (pinneapple_physics.closed_form.plate_fin_heatsink) until T_j is consistent; loop gain >= 1 is runaway thermal_vias, heatsink_natural (best fins in the envelope), forced_air (sized air speed) structures bending_strength, deflection, lateral_torsional_buckling, flexural_buckling, fatigue EN 1990 / EN 1991-2 loads, 5qL^4/384EI checked by the FD beam solver, EN 1993-1-1 6.3 with Timoshenko's M_cr, Basquin deepen_girders, lateral_bracing, wider_flanges, column_midheight_brace, thicker_section structural dynamics pedestrian_resonance first vertical mode (checked by Rayleigh's method on the FD deflection), steady response to one walker, harmonics 1-3 (Bachmann & Ammann), 0.7 m/s^2 (EN 1990 A2) tuned_mass_damper (Den Hartog), deepen_girders wind wind_uplift |Cp| 1/2 rho V^2 vs weight + fixings tile_clips hydraulics / cavitation pump_cavitation NPSH available (ISO 2533 atmosphere, Magnus vapour pressure, Colebrook suction loss) vs required + margin lower_pump, larger_suction_pipe hydraulic transients water_hammer, column_separation method of characteristics (pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.water_hammer_moc), Korteweg wave speed; Joukowsky / Michaud as references slow_valve_closure, higher_pressure_class corrosion galvanic_corrosion O2-diffusion-limited cathode x area ratio, Faraday's law vs corrosion allowance insulating_kit, coat_cathode

A new mode is a function evaluate(params, limits) -> Verification registered with register_mode(FailureMode(...)); it declares the parameters it needs (Need), its sources, the premises whose spread the uncertainty check moves (uncertain) and known-answer cases (known_answers, run by the tests and by the trust card). A countermeasure is register_countermeasure(Countermeasure(name, element, title, effect, addresses, apply, cost, ...)); apply may size itself from the failing verification (modes._util.size_to_pass tries values until the mode passes with the case's design_margin), requires / excludes name elements, and cost returns the physical quantity the change costs (extra area, steel mass, excavation, a fan). The cost index is that quantity times a relative unit cost declared as a premise (override per case with the parameter cost.<countermeasure>).

docs.title: The engine (pinneapple_reason.engine)
docs.text:
At each step: run every failure mode of every requirement (in the order given) and take the first that fails; apply every countermeasure for it (plus the advisor's proposals) to a copy of the concept and re-run every check on the copy; keep the cheapest option that fixes the failure without breaking anything that passed (ties within 1 %: most checks passing, then largest margin). If none fixes it alone, keep the one that improves the margin most and go on; an option that returns to an earlier version is refused. The chain ends resolved, unresolved (nothing in the library improves the failure) or at max_steps.

With an LLM (pinneapple_reason.llm.LLMAdvisor(pinneapple_design.intent.CallLLM(...)), or any object with extract(text, schema)), the advisor proposes countermeasures from the library and a first concept; unknown names and parameters no mode reads are dropped, and proposals are tried and judged like any other option (Option.proposed_by == "llm").

docs.title: The four worked cases (pinneapple_reason.cases, examples/chain_of_whys/)
docs.text:
Numbers below are what the library computes for the premises listed in each report.

Case Version 0 Chain roof clay tiles laid flat, no ceiling rain: capillarity 14 mm + wind 6.2 mm + ponded storm 25 mm against a 0 mm lap rise -> pitch to 22° (lap rises 28.1 mm vs 20.7 mm head) -> clear night: tile underside 14.9 °C below the 16.4 °C dew point -> ventilated ceiling (ceiling underside 18.1 °C) -> sunny day: ceiling 12 K above the air, 78.7 W/m^2 into the room -> radiant barrier (2.6 K) footbridge 30 m, two welded girders sized for strength deflection 133 mm > L/360 = 83.3 mm -> girders 1.05 m deep -> lateral-torsional buckling: 123 kN m resistance vs 1660 kN m -> 10 cross-frames (1786 kN m) -> first mode 2.05 Hz in the walking band, 1.70 m/s^2 > 0.7 -> tuned mass damper, mu = 1 %, 164 kg (0.24 m/s^2); deepening the girders again also fixed it, with 1606 kg more steel power_board 20 A D2PAK MOSFET on a 4-layer board board alone: 15.9 K/W, loop gain 0.76, T_j 626 °C -> best heat sink in a 40 x 40 x 20 mm envelope, natural convection: 218 °C -> forced air at 0.5 m/s: 109 °C < 125 °C pumped_main pump 5 m above the sump; valve closing in 2 s NPSH available 2.41 m < 4.5 m -> pump lowered to 2.2 m lift (5.2 m) -> MOC peak 1.81 MPa > PN10 -> 15 s closure: 0.80 MPa, no column separation

Run all four with python examples/chain_of_whys/chain_of_whys.py (reports in examples/chain_of_whys/_out/; the .html reports are self-contained, so they are regenerated rather than committed).

docs.title: Reports and trust
docs.text:
write_report(chain, out_dir, lang="pt" | "en") writes:

  • figures/timeline.png: version cards; each arrow names the countermeasure and its cost, each card the failure and its numbers and the state of every requirement;
  • figures/margins.png (PASS / FAIL with demand / capacity per check and version), figures/demand_capacity.png (one panel per failure mode) and domain figures: minimum pitch by covering, natural frequency against the walking bands, head at the valve after the closure starts;
  • report.md and a self-contained report.html (light and dark), chain.json, trust.json.

The trust report (pinneapple_reason.trust.trust_report) is a TrustReport over the final version: every requirement's check (critical), the known-answer cases of the modes used, the internal checks (energy-balance closure, equilibrium, fixed-point convergence, MOC surge decay), the solver-vs-closed-form agreements, the applicability ranges and the worst margin when each uncertain premise moves by its spread. trust_card answers the six questions of pinneapple_lab.curation.trust_stages from those checks. A chain whose margins do not cover the spread of its premises gets REVIEW, not APPROVED.

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
• Flow Studio: node types reason.requirement, reason.concept, reason.verify, reason.failure_mode, reason.countermeasure, reason.chain, reason.report (palette section Optimization & control), port types requirement, concept, chain; example flow pinneapple_flow/flows/reason_roof.json.
  • MCP server: reason (job), reason_library, reason_check (MCP server).
  • Agent workbench: reason_chain, reason_library, reason_check for the physics agent (agent workbench).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The checks are engineering models with stated ranges, not code sign-off: one-dimensional steady roof network with a clear-sky model, single-pedestrian steady resonance (an upper bound), no cavity model after column separation, a linear R_on(T). Case inputs are premises written in each report; replace them with your data. Costs are relative indices meant to rank options for the same finding, not estimates.

docs.title: Check power: how often each check catches a known defect
docs.text:
A check that says PASS carries no stated power until it has been run against defects of known size. The fault-injection suite (pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_injection, issue #697) does that: it takes correct cases from a verified reference solver, injects controlled faults into the model output or into the dataset, and records every check's response. The result is a detection matrix (check × fault × magnitude) with the false-alarm rate of each check on clean cases and the minimal magnitude each check detects.

from pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_injection import run_fault_injection

rep = run_fault_injection("darcy_2d", n_cases=50)       # or "burgers_1d"
print(rep.to_markdown())          # detection matrix, false alarms, minimal detectable magnitude, ROC AUC
assert rep.passed, rep.failures() # every fault caught at its documented magnitude, <= 1 % false alarms per check
rep.check_power()                 # the "check power" section of a validation report (dict)

The current matrix, regenerated by python scripts/fault_injection_matrix.py --out docs/guides, is in the detection matrix. CI runs the same script at a small size (--small) through tests/test_fault_injection.py.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
Both wrap the verified solvers of pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.operator_benchmarks (tests/test_operator_benchmarks.py: Cole-Hopf for Burgers, a manufactured solution with second-order convergence for Darcy).

problem equation output checked clean variation (inside the training envelope) darcy_2d -div(a grad u) = 1, u = 0 on the unit square, a a thresholded Gaussian random field (Li et al. 2021) u on 32 × 32 cells coefficient contrast, feature size, fraction of high-permeability cells, reference solved 1-3× finer and averaged burgers_1d u_t + (u²/2)_x = ν u_xx, periodic u(t, x) at 21 times × 128 points amplitude, feature size, ν (0.8-1.25×), reference solved 1-3× finer

Every case is regenerated from its seed and its variation, so a case found in a report is a few numbers.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
Each check is a pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.monitor.ValidityCheck returning a continuous value (larger = more suspicious) and rejecting above its tolerance. They reuse the library: the finite-difference provider and relative residual of pinneapple_check.numerics, the solver's own conservative Darcy stencil (operator_benchmarks.darcy_operator) and Burgers integrator, the spectral shells of validation.field_metrics, the Darcy consistency and the duplicate and leakage detectors of the dataset audit (pinneapple_data.audit), and the bounds and training-envelope checks of the physics monitor.

problem check what it measures both residual (finite differences) PDE residual with second-order differences, relative to the terms that balance Darcy residual (conservative, solver stencil) |A⁻¹(A u - f)| / |A⁻¹ f| with the two-point-flux operator of the solver Darcy boundary condition (u = 0) u extrapolated to the faces Darcy bounds 0 ≤ u ≤ 0.0737 max f / min a (minimum principle, comparison with the torsion function of the square) Darcy conservation net finite-volume outflow against the integral of the source Burgers residual (one-step re-integration) each snapshot advanced to the next with the verified integrator Burgers initial condition, periodicity, bounds (max principle), mass conservation, energy decay both spectral content energy above a quarter (Darcy) or the 2/3-rule cutoff (Burgers) of the grid wavenumbers both training envelope physics_audit.Envelope of the input features (amplitude, spectral centroid, range)

default_checks(problem) is the set a user runs today (finite-difference residual, boundary or initial condition, bounds, training envelope); check_library(problem) has all of them. Dataset checks (dataset_checks) add near-duplicate inputs, train/test leakage and the worst sample of every case check.

docs.title: Faults
docs.text:
fault level what it does bias, scale model output + m max|u|, output × (1 + m) noise model white noise of m std(u) (high frequency) smoothing model Gaussian smoothing over m cells (spectral bias) wrong_boundary model Darcy: u = m max|u| on x = 0; Burgers: a ramp that breaks periodicity source_sign_flip model Darcy: f → -f on x < m; Burgers: advection sign flipped for the last fraction m of time out_of_range model inputs beyond the training range; the model saturates (Darcy) or scales linearly (Burgers) stale_model model trained on an older configuration (Darcy: low permeability × (1 + m); Burgers: ν × (1 + m)) coefficient_drift data every sample solved with a coefficient off by (1 + m), modelled on NVIDIA/physicsnemo#2036 duplicates, low_diversity data training samples replaced by copies or near-copies (NVIDIA/physicsnemo#2035) leakage data test samples copied from training unit_mixup data outputs in mm instead of m swapped_channels data Darcy: input and output swapped; Burgers: snapshots in reverse time order

Each fault has a ladder of magnitudes and a documented magnitude (per problem where they differ) at which at least one check must catch it in 90 % of the trials; the acceptance of #697 also requires at most 1 % false alarms per check on the clean cases.

docs.title: Reading the matrix
docs.text:
• min. detectable: the smallest magnitude a check detects in at least 90 % of the trials; "—" means not at any magnitude of the ladder. Some checks are blind to some faults by construction (the training envelope never sees a smoothed output); the matrix says which.
  • rate / AUC: detection rate at the check's tolerance, and the ROC AUC of the check's value between clean and faulty cases (0.5 = blind, 1 = perfect separation, below 0.5 = the fault makes the case look cleaner, e.g. smoothing lowers the spectral content).
  • true error: median relative L2 error of the faulty output against the correct field; it tells which detections matter.

The tolerances here are hand-set: the matrix measures them, it does not tune them. The validation arena attacks them, calibrates them with a stated false-alarm rate and hardens the set of checks.

docs.title: Check power: the detection matrix
docs.text: Generated by python scripts/fault_injection_matrix.py (full size, seed 0); do not edit by hand. The method is described in Check power.

docs.title: Check power: darcy_2d
docs.text: 200 clean cases (seed 0), 40 datasets of [16, 8] samples; detected = flagged in at least 90% of the trials.

docs.title: Check power: burgers_1d
docs.text: 200 clean cases (seed 0), 40 datasets of [16, 8] samples; detected = flagged in at least 90% of the trials.

docs.title: Choosing a method: PINN, neural operator, graph network or the solver
docs.text:
PINNeAPPle covers the whole Physics-AI workflow: geometry, simulation campaigns, data-driven surrogates (neural operators, graph networks, MLPs), physics-informed networks, optimisation on top, and verification of the result. Which learned method to use depends on the problem, not on the library. This page gives the decision table, the evidence behind it, and the entry point for each choice.

The evidence is an equal-budget benchmark: every method gets the same training compute, the same number of hyper-parameter trials and the same hardware, and the cost of the simulation data is counted separately (PINNeAPPle-Benchmark, experiment 09). Its budgets are small (one CPU core per run, no GPU), so read its numbers as directions, not as the best each method can do.

docs.title: Decision table
docs.text:
Your situation Use Why (benchmark evidence below) Entry point One forward problem, a solver exists for it The numerical solver Faster than training any model for one instance (63 ms to 56 s here against 120-900 s of training) and exact to its discretisation Solvers and pp.cfd No solver or mesh for the equations or the geometry, one instance, a smooth solution PINN Needs only the equations; expect percent-level errors at best in modest budgets (16-25 % on Burgers and Navier-Stokes here, 87 % on Darcy) PINN factory Coefficients with jumps, shocks, turbulence, no data The numerical solver The PINNs barely learned or did not converge on these (Darcy rel. L2 0.87; the RANS airfoil 0.96, no better than predicting zero, at any budget up to 4 h) Solvers and pp.cfd Simulation data available (or affordable), many new inputs on a grid Neural operator: FNO first, DeepONet second FNO: 24-150x more accurate than the PINN at the same training compute, also at equal FLOPs and out of distribution; milliseconds per query; the data repays itself after 1-14 queries Neural operators Many geometries with a low-dimensional parametrisation (CST, a few design variables), fields needed POD + MLP on the parameters 0.4 % velocity error on held-out airfoils (MeshGraphNet 17 %), 55 µs per design MLP surrogates Many geometries without a shared parametrisation, fields on a mesh Graph network (MeshGraphNet; #293 for Transolver, GINO, point clouds) Works on any mesh from one model; on a parametrised family it was beaten by POD + MLP MeshGraphNet Many geometries, only integrals needed (Cl, Cd, peak stress) MLP on the shape parameters Cd within 0.3 % in distribution, 0.7 % outside the design space; a scalar regressor beats field models on scalars MLP surrogates Inverse problem (a coefficient from sparse sensors), few cases Calibration through the solver; a PINN only without a solver Classical calibration: 0.9 % error in h; the PINN: 11 % in range, 39 % out of range Inverse problems Inverse problem, many cases inside a known range, answers in a fraction of a second Surrogate + calibration The classical calibration's accuracy (1 %) at 1-7 % of its cost per case; it held 2-4.5 % outside its training range Inverse problems Fields versus integrals Fields: operator, POD + MLP or a graph network. Integrals only: MLP on the parameters Integral targets are low-dimensional and easier - Regime: turbulent (RANS/LES), separated flow Solver for the data, then a data-driven surrogate The data-free RANS PINN collapsed to the zero-flow solution of its own equations; a closure without data cannot place the boundary layer Solvers and campaigns

Two costs decide between "train once on data" and "solve each instance":

  • Amortisation. A surrogate pays for its data and training once, then answers each query in milliseconds. A per-instance PINN pays its training for every new instance. pinneapple_analysis.cost.AmortizedCost gives the cost per query and the break-even number of queries.
  • Extrapolation. A surrogate is only as good as its training range; a PINN or the solver has no training range. Check the out-of-distribution rows below before trusting a surrogate outside its data.

docs.title: The evidence
docs.text:
Equal-budget benchmark, PINNeAPPle-Benchmark experiment 09, run with pp.benchmark (Running a benchmark). CPU only: one core per training run, 300 s (Burgers, Darcy, Navier-Stokes), 900 s (airfoil), 120 s (inverse heat); the same 4-trial search for every method; 3 seeds; n = instances in each cell.

Problem (n test / n OOD) Best data-driven, error in / out of distribution PINN, same instances Reference solver per instance Burgers 1-D, rel. L2 (3 / 2) FNO 0.00168 / 0.0393 0.246 / 0.592 1 s Darcy 2-D, rel. L2 (3 / 2) FNO 0.0167 / 0.0138 0.873 / 0.891 63 ms Navier-Stokes 2-D, rel. L2 (3 / 2) FNO 0.0068 / 0.0107 0.16 / 0.507 3 s Airfoil, Cd rel. error (4 / 12; PINN 4 / 4) MLP 0.295 % / 0.739 % RANS PINN 89.8 % / 87.7 % OpenFOAM 56 s Airfoil, velocity rel. L2 (4 / 12; PINN 4 / 4) POD + MLP 0.00383 / 0.0179 potential flow 0.833 / 0.856; RANS 0.96 / 0.98 OpenFOAM 56 s Inverse heat, h rel. error (3 / 2) surrogate + calibration 1.01 % / 2.06-4.48 % 11.4 % / 39.3 % FV + calibration 9 s: 0.946 % / 3.31 %

What it does not show: GPU budgets (several methods were still improving), a wider search (the airfoil setup audit shows the potential-flow PINN gains from other loss weights and a lower learning rate), PINNs with data, and a Darcy OOD set that is really out of distribution (the library's data gate flagged it). The experiment's README lists every limitation and every check the library ran.

docs.title: PINN factory
docs.text: pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.factory.pinn_factory: PINNProblemSpec (equations as strings, conditions, inverse parameters, exogenous signals), PINNFactory(spec).generate_loss_function(), PINN and NeuralNetwork. Hard initial conditions from gridded data: pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.operator_benchmarks.FourierInterpolant. See PINN / Physics.

docs.title: Neural operators
docs.text: pinneapple_neural.architectures.neural_operators: fno.FourierNeuralOperator (1-D), fno.FNO2d, fno.FNO3d, deeponet.DeepONet. Reference data for the standard problems: operator_benchmarks.burgers_1d, navier_stokes_2d_vorticity, darcy_2d, periodic_grf.

docs.title: MeshGraphNet and geometry surrogates
docs.text: pinneapple_neural.architectures.graphnn.mesh_graph_net.MeshGraphNet; the aero app's field-and-coefficient model pinneapple_design.aero.surrogate.AeroGNN. Geometry-agnostic surrogates (Transolver, GINO, point-cloud baselines behind one interface): issue #293.

docs.title: MLP surrogates
docs.text:
pinneapple_design.aero.surrogate.MLPEnsemble (shape parameters + angle → Cl, Cd, Cm, with an ensemble spread); pinneapple_neural.architectures.neural_operators.deeponet.mlp for a plain MLP.

POD + MLP for fields over a parametrised family: pinneapple_analysis.benchmark.builtin.airfoil_impl.train_mlp_fields (POD of the training fields, an MLP from the parameters to the POD coefficients), the benchmark's mlp_fields method.

docs.title: Inverse problems
docs.text: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.heat_transfer: run_fin, run_plate (PINN with h as an inverse parameter; run_plate(budget=...) trains under a compute budget). Calibration through a solver or a surrogate: pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.heat_fv_reference.plate_2d plus any 1-D search.

docs.title: Solvers, pp.cfd and campaigns
docs.text: pp.cfd (pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.external_flow): OpenFOAM around any body, FlowResult. The campaign runner pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.openfoam.campaign runs one verified case many times and returns results a surrogate can train on (OpenFOAM parameter campaigns). The 2-D airfoil campaign of the benchmark is apps/aero_optimizer/tools/generate_dataset.py.

docs.title: Comparing methods yourself
docs.text:
pinneapple_analysis.cost: ComputeBudget, train_within_budget (stops at the budget, budget-aware schedules), count_flops (works around torch.autograd.grad), equal_budget_search (the same number of trials per method), AmortizedCost, relative_l2, time_per_query, hardware_record.

from pinneapple_analysis.cost import ComputeBudget, train_within_budget, cosine_lr, set_lr

budget = ComputeBudget(wall_s=300)            # or flops=..., steps=...

def step(progress):                           # progress in [0, 1]: the fraction of the budget used
    set_lr(opt, cosine_lr(progress, 1e-3))
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = loss_fn(model, next_batch())
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()
    return loss.detach()

run = train_within_budget(step, budget)       # run.steps, run.wall_s, run.flops, run.history

docs.title: Colab notebooks
docs.text:
Five self-contained notebooks that run top to bottom on a free Google Colab GPU runtime (Runtime > Change runtime type > T4 GPU), or on a CPU (slower). The first cell installs PINNeAPPle from PyPI (pinneapple>=0.7.0) and picks the GPU when there is one; the parameter cell (SMOKE, epochs, grid sizes) sets how big each run is.

Notebook What it shows Open 01 First PINN: heat in a plate a Laplace problem solved with pp.solve by a PINN and by FEM, then its trust card: PDE residual, boundary conditions, conservation, maximum principle, reference 02 Airfoil: geometry, surrogate, validation CST airfoil geometry, Cl / Cd / Cm from a trained ensemble with its spread, validated against stored OpenFOAM runs, XFOIL and thin-airfoil theory 03 Equal-budget benchmark three PINN architectures and FEM with the same epochs, points and seeds; error against budget; trust card of the winners; pp.benchmark when installed 04 Lunar rover terramechanics + dashboard NASA VIPER on lunar regolith (Wong-Reece wheels, multibody, deformable terrain), the testbed validation, a PINN of the wheel-soil contact and the animated dashboard as a GIF 05 Verify a model the trust card catching an under-trained PINN, a harmonic field with the wrong boundary, and extrapolation, without a reference solution

Files the notebooks read (the airfoil model and CFD results, the trust-card module on releases older than the one that ships pp.trust_card) come from a local checkout when there is one, otherwise from the repository on GitHub.

docs.title: Running them headless
docs.text:
python scripts/run_colab_notebooks.py --smoke            # every notebook with tiny sizes (what CI runs)
python scripts/run_colab_notebooks.py 02                 # one notebook at full size
python scripts/run_colab_notebooks.py --check-clean      # committed notebooks must carry no outputs

The committed notebooks have their outputs cleared; --clear strips them after editing.
