The equal-budget benchmark API (pp.benchmark) and the geometry library (pp.geometries) are being merged: the benchmark notebook already has the cell that switches to pp.benchmark (marked Switch to pp.benchmark) and runs it only when the API is installed.

docs.title: Dataset physics audit: does the data solve its PDE?
docs.text:
A model trained on wrong data inherits the error, and model-level checks may never see it. Two open bugs of a widely used Physics AI library show how training data can be silently wrong: generated Darcy data that did not solve the documented equation (NVIDIA/physicsnemo#2036) and permeability samples with far less diversity than documented (NVIDIA/physicsnemo#2035). pinneapple_data.audit checks the data itself, before anyone trains on it.

import pinneapple as pp

card = pp.datasets.audit("heatsink_forced_convection")      # a zoo dataset, with the constraints its card states
print(card)                                                 # one line per check: PASS / WARN / FAIL / NOT-APPLICABLE

from pinneapple_data.audit import audit_dataset
card = audit_dataset({"train": {"a": a_train, "u": u_train}, "test": {"a": a_test, "u": u_test}},
                     physics="darcy", generator=my_permeability_sampler, units={"a": "-", "u": "-"})
card.to_json("audit_card.json")

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
Check What it measures Fails when finite infinities and missing values any infinity (NaN is a warning, marked "documented" when the metadata says the value was not recorded) physics.solve per sample: ||u - A^-1 f|| / ||A^-1 f||, the distance to the solution of its own discrete problem (the residual in the A^-1 norm) above 2 % physics.bc, physics.flux boundary values against the exact discrete solution's; net boundary flux against the source integral above 2 % constraint: ... declared relations between columns ("r_base_k_w > 0", "source_width_mm == source_frac_w * base_width_mm") any row breaks one diversity.duplicates exact and near copies inside the train, validation and test splits (closer than 1e-3 x the median nearest-neighbour distance) any diversity.effective effective number of distinct samples: participation ratio of the principal-component spectrum, against freshly drawn samples of the stated generator when there is one below half the generator's (without a generator: below 2) diversity.spectrum mean radial spectrum of the inputs against the generator's off by more than a factor 2 in a shell leakage nearest training sample of each test sample any test sample closer than 1e-3 x the median training spacing units units in the metadata parse, and match the problem's when stated otherwise

The physics check is built in for "darcy" (-div(a grad u) = f, u = 0 on the unit square, cell-centred, the discretisation of operator_benchmarks.darcy_2d and of darcy_2d_li2021); any other problem passes a DatasetPhysics(name, columns, check, tolerances). Each solve check runs on up to 64 random samples per split by default (max_physics_samples).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Zoo datasets (cards stored in pinneapple_hub/zoo/audit_cards/ and shown in each dataset's Hub card):

Dataset Decision Notes heatsink_forced_convection PASS 4 constraints on 6000 rows, no duplicates or leakage heatsink_natural_convection PASS 3 constraints on 5000 rows rover_contact_grc1_viper PASS airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6 WARN Cm is NaN in the 340 training rows: documented ("Cm not recorded in the campaign table") single_wheel_tests WARN 5 torque values NaN: documented ("NaN = not reported"); one split, so no leakage check burgers_1d_li2021, darcy_2d_li2021 not audited yet Hub-only; the test downloads and audits them where the network allows

Defects (tests/test_dataset_audit.py, Darcy on 32 x 32 cells, coefficient from the Li et al. 2021 generator):

  • data generated by an independent finite-difference solver of the expanded equation -a lap u - grad a . grad u = f pass (physics.solve below 1 %: the two discretisations differ by their truncation error); the same solver with the cross term scaled by 0.5 (the #2036 defect) fails on every sample (solve above 10 %, flux imbalance too);
  • permeability samples whose Fourier coefficients share one value per sample (the #2035 defect) fail diversity.effective (below 0.1 of the generator's) and diversity.duplicates, while still solving the PDE;
  • one test sample of 20 copied from the training set (5 %) fails leakage, with the pair listed.

docs.title: In pinneapple check
docs.text:
[[dataset]]
path = "datasets/darcy.npz"          # <split>__<column> arrays (the zoo layout); or zoo = "darcy_2d_li2021"
physics = "darcy"
constraints = ["u > 0", "u < 1 / 24"]

Rules: PC451 (physics and constraints), PC452 (diversity), PC453 (leakage); infinities report as PC403, units as PC501.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Without a stated generator, diversity can only flag a collapse (an effective sample count below 2); a set that is merely narrower than documented needs the generator.
  • Leakage and duplicates are measured in the space of the declared inputs (standardised for tabular data). A copy that was transformed (shifted, rotated, resampled) is not a near copy in that space.
  • The physics check is as good as the stated discretisation: data generated by another consistent scheme differ by its truncation error, so the tolerance must be above it (0.5 % at 32 x 32 for a contrast-20 coefficient).

docs.title: Design from intent
docs.text:
pinneapple_design.intent turns a goal written in plain language into a design you can build: geometry, materials and operating conditions, with the margin to every failure mode, a trust report and the limits of what was checked. It never fills a gap with an invented number: a value it needs and cannot read becomes a question, a value it defaults says where the default comes from, and a request no template covers is refused with what would be needed.

import pinneapple as pp

pp.design("a heat sink for a 40 W chip in still air")
# NeedsInput: What is the highest allowed temperature of the chip's case (or source)? [°C]

pkg = pp.design("a heat sink for a 40 W chip in still air", answers={"t_limit": (85, "°C")}, out_dir="hs")
print(pkg.summary())        # design, verdict with probability, trust decision, model calls
pkg.files["html"]           # hs/report.html; also report.pdf, design.json, geometry/*.step|stl|glb, check/

pp.design("an electric motor for my drone")
# OutOfScope (needs): needs an electromagnetics design template: the interior-PM machine FEA and drive ...

The same call from a shell and from an agent:

pinneapple design "a bracket that holds 2 kN" --answer arm_length=100mm --out bracket
pinneapple design --templates

and the MCP tool design (pinneapple-mcp), which answers questions and refusals at once and runs the design as a job (poll job_status).

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
Each stage is a typed object you can inspect, test and replace.

Stage Object What it does intent -> requirements formulate(text) -> RequirementSpec picks a template by keywords, reads every number unit pair, checks the unit's dimension and the template's range with pinneapple_data.physical_units, fills the template's slots; each value is stated (with the quote), answered, defaulted (with its source) or missing; missing critical values become Questions requirements -> physics plan(spec, template) -> PhysicsPlan governing physics, assumptions, design variables, the models at each fidelity with their availability on this machine, failure modes multi-fidelity optimisation optimise(...) -> OptimisationResult Latin-hypercube screening on the closed form, then the design-study core (pinneapple_design.design_optimizer: NSGA-II on the reduced model, or the GP surrogate-assisted loop when the reduced model costs seconds), distinct candidates (the knee of the Pareto front for several objectives) robustness robustness(...) -> Robustness Monte-Carlo propagation (pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.tolerance.propagate) of the uncertain inputs to the probability that every margin stays >= 0, with a Wilson interval, the 5th percentile of each margin and the rank correlation of each input with the smallest margin verification verify(...) -> Verification the full solver on the chosen design, its own checks, and the comparison with the reduced and closed-form models output by output assessment assess(...) -> Assessment the trust report (pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport) and the verdict: will work, likely to work (not verified by the full solver), marginal, will not work, unverified package DesignPackage geometry (STEP, STL, glTF, renders), bill of materials with cited properties, operating window, build instructions, every number with the model it comes from, model calls per fidelity, limits; report.html / report.pdf, design.json, check/ for pinneapple check

Every template designs at the worst corner of its own uncertainty (the optimum is robust, not on the nominal edge), then the Monte Carlo measures the probability of success around it. When the full solver measures something the cheap models assumed (the bracket's stress-concentration factor), the design is re-checked with the measured value and re-optimised if it no longer meets its margins.

An LLM is optional. Anything with extract(text, schema) -> dict (for example CallLLM("anthropic"), which wraps pinneapple_llm.call_llm) can propose the template and values; a value is used only if its quote is in the request and contains the number, and its unit has the slot's dimension. The deterministic parser always runs and wins on conflicts, so the pipeline works offline.

docs.title: The five demos
docs.text:
python examples/design_from_intent/design_from_intent.py runs all five through the same pipeline; the outputs are in examples/design_from_intent/_out/. The numbers below are copied from _out/summary.json of that run.

request first reply design verdict (P, 95 % interval) full solver check model calls (closed form / reduced / full) (a) "I want a toy car that does a loop" complete (every value defaulted with a source) R = 8.4 cm, clothoids 2.5 R = 21.0 cm, launch 2.47 m/s, car 31 g, 1.5 mm PLA strip will work (1.000, 0.998-1.000) Newton: goes round at both time steps, v_top 1.507 m/s >= worst-case envelope 1.023 m/s 2000 / 6600 / 1 (b) "a bracket that holds 2 kN" asks for the arm length (answered: 100 mm) Al 6061-T6, t = 17 mm, w = 36 mm, mounting leg 72 mm, two M6 8.8 will work (0.9985, 0.9956-0.9995) CalculiX: peak 94.3 vs 96.8 MPa (hex FE), deflection 0.380 vs 0.380 mm 12000 / 19 / 1 (c) "a heat sink for a 40 W chip in still air" asks for the temperature limit (answered: 85 °C) copper C110, base 100 x 100 x 6.5 mm, 14 fins 1.1 x 47 mm will work (1.000, 0.998-1.000) finite volume: source (case) temperature 77.7 vs 77.6 °C (network), energy balance 1e-12 2000 / 2600 / 1 (d) "a wing for a 1.2 kg model glider, at most 2 m span" complete span 2.0 m, AR 7.69, taper 0.33, NACA 2412 will work (1.000, 0.998-1.000) fine lattice: sink 0.4409 vs 0.4406 m/s, e 0.989 vs 0.990 2000 / 6600 / 1 (e) "an electric motor for my drone" out of scope: needs an electromagnetics design template (current-density, thermal, demagnetisation limits) - - - -

The closed-form call counts include the Monte-Carlo samples when a template runs its robustness study on the calibrated closed form (the bracket). Each report also gives an estimate, not a measurement, of the time the full solver would have needed for every evaluation: the measured seconds of its one full call times the number of evaluations (about 650 h for the loop and 130 h for the bracket on the machine of this run; the measured call time varies between runs).

docs.title: (a) Loop-the-loop car
docs.text:
Nothing in the request is a number, so every value is a default with its source: the rolling-resistance coefficient and the launcher scatter are design envelopes, not measurements (the design must work for any rolling resistance up to 0.05 and a launcher 5 % slow), the drag coefficient's worst case is the bluff-body end of the range (a cube is about 1.05, Hoerner), the strip material is the printable PLA with its datasheet yield strength.

  • Closed form: v_top^2 = v0^2 - 2 g z_top - losses with the losses at the mean speed, the top condition v_top^2 >= g (R - h), the peak load at the end of the entry clothoid.
  • Reduced: the 1-D along-track ODE (d(v^2)/ds with N = m (v^2 kappa + g cos theta), rolling resistance on N, drag, the wheels' inertia), RK4, vectorised: 6600 designs in 6.6 s. The car is a point on its centre-of-mass path, the track offset inwards by the centre-of-mass height h (12.5 mm for the car, 6 mm for Newton's sphere), so kappa = 1 / (R - h) on the top arc and N / (m g) = v_top^2 / (g (R - h)) - 1 at the top: 0.49 at the worst case (1.023 m/s, R - h = 7.14 cm), not the 0.27 a radius of R would give. Without losses it conserves energy to 0.3 % and reproduces the v0^2 = 5 g R threshold of a circular loop (tests).
  • Full: NVIDIA Newton (XPBD) on the 3-D track mesh with its side rails and the helical exit, at two time steps. Newton's contact dissipates energy on the curved mesh (5.7 % of the launch energy by the top here, with no friction at all, and it does not go away with a smaller step or a finer mesh), and its Coulomb friction, correct on its flat analytic case (stopping distance 0.5087 vs 0.5097 m), takes most of the energy of a rolling sphere on the curved mesh. So the Newton run is frictionless and judged against the worst-case envelope: the car must stay on the track (largest gap to the surface 0.1 mm) and keep at least the envelope's speed at the top (1.507 >= 1.023 m/s).

The optimiser minimised the launch speed and the peak load on the car together; the knee of the front uses the longest clothoid allowed (2.5 R), which cuts the peak load to 5.0 g at the worst case, with a loop 8.4 cm in radius. Operating window (1-D model): launch 2.24 to 7.02 m/s (the upper end is the strip's yield / 2), any car from 10 g up, rolling resistance up to 0.0695 at the design speed minus the scatter.

docs.title: (b) Bracket, verified with CalculiX
docs.text:
pp.design("a bracket that holds 2 kN") asks how far from the mounting face the load acts: the bending moment depends on it and there is no safe default. With 100 mm:

  • Closed form: cantilever beam theory (M c / I, P L^3 / 3 E I).
  • Reduced: an in-house hexahedral FE model of the L (C3D8I, the fillet as a staircase), 0.53 s per design, so the optimiser fits a GP surrogate of it and checks 19 designs with the FE model.
  • Full: CalculiX on a gmsh C3D10 mesh of the exact part (filleted corner, two M6 clearance holes, ISO 273), two mesh sizes. Checks: support reaction = load (1e-7), the arm's bending stress against M c / I at mid-arm (0.05 %), mesh convergence of the peak (1.2 %). The measured stress-concentration factor of the R = t fillet is 0.97 of the nominal stress (the peak is not at the fillet for this proportion), fed back into the reduced model.

The bracket is sized at the worst corner of its stated uncertainty (load +10 %, plate -0.2 mm, yield 90 % of the datasheet value; all three labelled as assumptions in the report). The two M6 8.8 bolts (proof load from ISO 898-1) set the mounting-leg length: they are the limiting failure mode (5th-percentile margin 0.017). The STEP file is the OpenCASCADE B-rep from the gmsh script, with the exact holes and fillet.

docs.title: (c) Passive heat sink
docs.text: The request gives the power and "still air" (read as 0 m/s, quoted in the report); the allowed temperature has no safe default, so it is asked for. With 85 °C the template reuses the heat-sink sizer physics: the closed form is the hand calculation (Elenbaas / Bar-Cohen coefficient evaluated once with the fin root at the limit), the reduced model the converged resistance network, the full model the 3-D finite-volume solve of the base with its energy balance, spreading cross-check and grid convergence. The design is sized with the convection coefficient 15 % low and the interface resistance 50 % high (the engine's stated band and the paste's spread). In still air within the default 100 x 100 x 50 mm envelope only copper meets the limit at that corner: 1.23 kg, source (case) temperature 77.7 °C nominal, 83.9 °C with the coefficient 15 % low (the base underside peaks at 77.2 °C under the source; the paste's 10 K·mm²/W over 30 x 30 mm adds 0.44 K at 40 W). Operating window: up to 47.2 W at 25 °C, or 31.3 °C ambient at 40 W.

docs.title: (d) Glider wing
docs.text: The lift comes from the vortex-lattice code of pinneapple_design.aero (closed form: elliptic lifting line; reduced: a 3 x 10 lattice per half span; full: 8 x 32, with the lattice convergence of the span efficiency, Munk's e <= 1 and the lift slope below Helmbold's estimate as checks), the profile drag from turbulent flat-plate friction and Hoerner's thickness form factor. The wing is chosen for the lowest sink rate with the design speed taken at the heavy (+5 %), thin-air (-6 % density) and draggy (+25 % profile drag) corner, so the lift coefficient stays below the 0.8 design cap in every Monte-Carlo sample: span 2.0 m (the stated limit), aspect ratio 7.7, taper 0.33, NACA 2412, sink 0.44 m/s at 7.2 m/s (wing alone). No viscous solver ran: the report says so, and that a RANS check is the next level.

docs.title: (e) Out of scope
docs.text: pp.design("an electric motor for my drone") returns OutOfScope(kind="needs"): needs an electromagnetics design template: the interior-PM machine FEA and drive models exist (pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines), but no template sizes a machine from a request yet, and it would also need winding current-density, thermal and demagnetisation limits, which those models do not check. A motor template is the natural next one to write with the guide below. Weapons are refused outright (kind="refused"); a request no template matches lists the installed templates; a request a template matches but cannot honestly design (a loop for a roller coaster that carries people, a bracket under fatigue loading, a liquid-cooled heat sink) is refused by that template's check_scope with what it would need.

docs.title: Writing a template
docs.text:
A new domain plugs in with one class and one register call. The worked example is pinneapple_design/intent/templates/example_spring.py, a helical compression spring (Shigley, ch. 10):

import pinneapple_design.intent as I
from pinneapple_design.intent.templates.example_spring import CoilSpringTemplate

I.register(CoilSpringTemplate())
pkg = I.design("a steel compression spring that takes 50 N with 10 mm travel", verify=False)
print(pkg.summary())

What a template declares, in the order the pipeline uses it:

  1. Selection and reading. keywords (word -> weight; the best total selects the template) and slots: each Slot has an SI unit (its dimension is what the parser matches), the words that point to it in a sentence, its valid range, and either critical=True (asked for when missing) or a default with a default_source. Phrases can set values through cues (("still air", 0.0)). check_scope(spec) refuses requests the physics does not cover; extra_questions(spec) asks for "one of these two" values.
  2. Physics. physics and assumptions (shown in the plan and the report), objectives (ObjectiveChoice with the words that select each one), failure_modes (each names an output that is a margin, >= 0 when the mode does not occur, typically capacity / demand - 1).
  3. Variables. variables(spec) -> [DesignVariable]; integers and choices (materials) are integer variables, and a value the user stated is fixed rather than optimised.
  4. Models. fidelities (closed form, reduced, full; each with the modules or programs it needs) and evaluate(level, X, spec, **options), which returns every margin and objective for a batch of designs. The full solver runs through verify(design, spec) -> FullResult with its own checks (equilibrium, energy balance, mesh convergence, a closed-form reference) and the outputs to compare with the reduced model (compare; compare_kind "at_least" / "at_most" for a solver known to be biased one way). reduced_is_expensive = True makes the optimiser fit a GP surrogate of the reduced model.
  5. Robustness. uncertainties(spec, design) -> [Uncertain] (nominal, spread, distribution and why this range), design_options(spec) (the worst corner the optimiser designs at), robust_level (a closed form calibrated to the best model that ran on the design, when the reduced model is too slow for thousands of samples).
  6. Package. geometry (closed Body meshes in metres), bill_of_materials (with the cited properties from pinneapple_design.intent.materials), operating_window, build_instructions, limits, figures.

Rules that keep templates honest: every material property comes from materials.MATERIALS (each value carries its source) or from the user; every default has a default_source; an envelope that is assumed rather than measured says so in its source and in limits; a model that has no stall, fatigue, buckling or radiation says so in limits.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: tests/test_design_intent.py: parsing offline, units and ranges, template selection, refusal, the LLM quote check, cited materials, each demo's models against closed forms (energy conservation and v_top^2 = g R for the loop, beam theory for the bracket, the finite-volume energy balance for the heat sink, Munk's e <= 1 for the wing), the CalculiX bracket when ccx and gmsh are installed, determinism with a fixed seed, the package files passing pinneapple check, the CLI, the MCP tool and a new template plugged in. The Newton loop check takes minutes and runs with PINNEAPPLE_SLOW=1.

docs.title: Design studies: one problem, many optimisers, verified candidates
docs.text:
pinneapple_design.design_optimizer describes a design optimisation problem once and runs any method on it under the same evaluation budget. Every evaluated design is recorded, so the Pareto front, the convergence history, the feasibility report and the cost are computed the same way whatever produced them. Candidates found on a surrogate are re-evaluated with a reference model or solver before anyone calls them optimal.

It is the engine behind two apps: the Engineering Design Optimizer (black-box, surrogate + high-fidelity verification) and the Physics Design Optimizer (gradient-aware, method comparison, design files).

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
from pinneapple_design.design_optimizer import (Constraint, DesignProblem, DesignSpace, FunctionEvaluator,
                                                Objective, Variable, run)

space = DesignSpace([Variable("x", -1.0, 3.0), Variable("y", -1.0, 1.0)])
f = lambda X: {"f1": X[:, 0] ** 2 + X[:, 1] ** 2, "f2": (X[:, 0] - 2) ** 2 + X[:, 1] ** 2, "g": X[:, 0] + X[:, 1]}
problem = DesignProblem("demo", space, [Objective("f1"), Objective("f2")], [Constraint("g", upper=1.5)],
                        FunctionEvaluator(f, ["f1", "f2", "g"], torch_fn=f))   # torch_fn: gradients via autograd
result = run(problem, "nsga2", budget=400, seed=0)
print(result.summary(), result.evaluations.rows(space, result.pareto())[:3])
  • Variable(kind="integer") rounds a variable (fin counts, ply counts). Gradient methods relax it when the evaluator accepts fractional values (relaxable=True), mark those iterates relaxed and evaluate the rounded end point; relaxed designs never enter a Pareto set.
  • Constraint(kind=...) labels a limit as physical, manufacturing or validity; feasibility_report lists each constraint's value, margin and status (active within 5 % of the bound, inactive, violated).
  • An evaluator may return "_valid"; False (a surrogate outside its training range, a geometry that does not exist) makes the design infeasible with that reason.

docs.title: Evaluators
docs.text: Evaluator Use FunctionEvaluator(fn, outputs, torch_fn=None) any vectorised Python model; torch_fn makes it differentiable ZooEvaluator(name, space, fixed=...) a pp.zoo model; its validity range marks designs invalid TorchModuleEvaluator(module, outputs, ...) an MLP, PINN, neural operator or differentiable physics model CommandEvaluator(command, space, outputs) an external solver: designs in a CSV, outputs back in a CSV from_model_ref(ref, space) zoo:<name>, a TorchScript file or cmd:<command> from a model reference GPSurrogate(problem, outputs) Gaussian-process surrogate trained on your evaluated designs

docs.title: Methods and budget
docs.text: run(problem, method, budget=..., seed=...) with random (Latin hypercube), nsga2, pymoo-nsga2 (optional pymoo), scipy-de, scipy-slsqp (finite-difference gradients), bayesian (GP, ParEGO) and gradient (Adam through autograd). One evaluation is one design passed to the evaluator: a finite-difference gradient costs d + 1, an autograd step costs one (and its wall time is reported). compare_methods runs several on the same budget and seeds and reports the hypervolume (normalised over all runs), the evaluations needed to reach 95 % of the best, and whether each run converged (hypervolume grew less than 1 % over its last quarter).

docs.title: Verification and active learning
docs.text:
from pinneapple_design.design_optimizer import presets, run, select_candidates, verify_candidates

problem = presets.heatsink_problem("surrogate")                 # zoo MLP of the heat-sink FVM engine
res = run(problem, "nsga2", budget=600, initial=problem.space.from_dicts([presets.heatsink_baseline()]))
chosen = select_candidates(res.evaluations, res.pareto(), 5)
report = verify_candidates(problem, res.evaluations, chosen, presets.HeatsinkEvaluator("fvm"))
print([r["status"] for r in report.rows], report.errors["t_source_c"])

Statuses: verified (the reference ran and the design is feasible under it), rejected by reference, reference failed, only surrogate. surrogate_assisted(problem, reference) fits a GP on reference runs, optimises on it with each constraint applied to a pessimistic value (mean plus or minus 2 standard deviations), verifies designs along the front and adds them to the data; the error it reports per round is measured at designs the GP had not been trained on.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
• heatsink_problem(fidelity): plate-fin heat sink in ducted air, minimise mass and cost (or pressure drop) within source temperature, pressure drop, fin stress and extrusion limits. Fidelities surrogate (zoo MLP, differentiable), closed_form (resistance network) and fvm (3-D finite-volume base, the reference). The cost model is an assumption the user sets (CostModel).
  • airfoil_problem(): CST airfoil at Re 4e6, minimise drag and maximise spar depth at a lift target, on the zoo ensemble airfoil_cst_rans_mlp (differentiable). No reference solver ships with it, so its candidates stay "only surrogate" until verified with OpenFOAM.
  • plate_fin_bodies, airfoil_bodies and design_file(bodies, "stl" | "step") write the chosen design as a binary STL or an AP214 faceted STEP file through the geometry library's writers; preset_bodies(preset, design) picks the right one.
  • preset_info(preset): what a form needs (variables, operating point, limits, cost model, objectives, baseline design and the reference that verifies candidates).

docs.title: After a run: what an app shows and exports
docs.text:
The design apps are built on these calls, so a run gives the same files and tables from Python:

  • verify_front(problem, ev, front, n, reference) returns the candidates spread along the front, the verification report (None without a reference) and the status of each candidate;
  • write_design_files(folder, problem, ev, candidates, status, labels=...) writes evaluations.csv, candidates.csv (with the verification status and, from a comparison, the run that found each one), candidates_to_run.csv (the variables only, to run in your solver) and parameter_space.json;
  • chart_points(problem, ev, front) thins the evaluations for a trade-off plot and keeps the front;
  • verify_uploaded_results(space, candidates, results, objectives, constraints) verifies the exported candidates against the solver results you ran offline, matching rows by their variable values;
  • MethodComparison.union_result() and .fronts(seed) give a comparison as one result (for study_result) and each method's front.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The heat-sink model assumes ducted laminar/developing flow without radiation; the fin stress is root bending of a cantilever fin under a uniform lateral load. The hypervolume above two objectives is a seeded Monte Carlo estimate. Bayesian optimisation refits a GP at every proposal, so it is meant for budgets of a few hundred evaluations at most.

docs.title: Electromagnetics and electrodynamics
docs.text: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics (pp.em) solves electromagnetic problems in SI units and checks the results against independent references; pinneapple_physics.maxwell_checks (pp.maxwell) checks any electromagnetic field, from a solver or a neural network, against Maxwell's equations without a reference solution. This page gives the theory the code implements, what is verified and to which order, and the limits.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• SI units throughout. Constants are CODATA 2022 (pp.em.constants): mu0 = 1.25663706127e-6 N/A² (measured since the 2019 SI redefinition), eps0 = 1 / (mu0 c²), eta0 = mu0 c.
  • Phasors are Re[X exp(+j omega t)] (engineering convention, as in Taflove & Hagness, Pozar, scikit-rf). A lossy medium has Im(eps_r) < 0; a wave travelling to +z is exp(-j k z). Physics texts (Jackson, Bohren & Huffman) use exp(-i omega t); their eps is the complex conjugate of the one here. pp.em.mie takes the index in this package's convention (m = n - j k, the same as miepython).
  • pp.em.units.check_equations() verifies that every term of every law below has the same SI dimension (pinneapple_data.physical_units, now with T, Wb, coulomb, farad, henry and siemens), and check_units({"B": "mT", ...}) flags fields declared in the wrong unit or scale before residuals are computed.

docs.title: Maxwell's equations
docs.text:
Differential form (Jackson, Classical Electrodynamics, 3rd ed., sec. 6.1; Griffiths, Introduction to Electrodynamics, 4th ed., ch. 7):

Law Differential Integral Gauss div D = rho oint_S D . dA = Q_enc Gauss (magnetic) div B = 0 oint_S B . dA = 0 Faraday curl E = -dB/dt oint_C E . dl = -d/dt int_S B . dA Ampere-Maxwell curl H = J + dD/dt oint_C H . dl = I_enc + d/dt int_S D . dA

with D = eps E, B = mu H, J = sigma E + J_s. Charge continuity d rho/dt + div J = 0 follows from the divergence of Ampere-Maxwell plus Gauss; Poynting's theorem du/dt + div S + J . E = 0, S = E x H, u = (E . D + B . H) / 2, from the curl equations (Jackson sec. 6.7).

Interface conditions (Jackson sec. I.5): n x (E1 - E2) = 0, n x (H1 - H2) = K, n . (D1 - D2) = sigma_s, n . (B1 - B2) = 0. A perfect electric conductor (PEC) has n x E = 0.

docs.title: Formulations
docs.text:
Regime Unknown Equation Where Electrostatics phi, E = -grad phi -div(eps grad phi) = rho solve_electrostatic (P1 FEM), kinds electrostatics, electrostatics_integral Magnetostatics (2-D) A_z, B = curl(A_z e_z) -div(nu grad A) = J + curl(nu Br) solve_magnetostatic (P1 FEM, Newton for nonlinear B-H), kind magnetostatics_az Magneto-quasistatics phasor A_z -div(nu grad A) + j omega sigma A = J_s + sigma u_c solve_time_harmonic (solid conductors with imposed currents), eddy_current_fdm (axisymmetric), kind eddy_current_az Full wave, time domain E, H curl equations kinds maxwell_tm, maxwell_te, maxwell_3d, maxwell_tm_integral Full wave, frequency domain phasor E_z lap E + k0^2 eps_r E = f kind maxwell_tm_frequency

The A-formulation in a solid conductor carries the voltage per metre u_c as an extra unknown fixed by its net current (Jin, The Finite Element Method in Electromagnetics, 3rd ed., ch. 4 and 8), which is the 2-D A-V formulation.

docs.title: Integral form as a PINN loss
docs.text: The compiler kinds electrostatics_integral and maxwell_tm_integral impose the integral laws on a square control volume around each collocation point (Gauss-Legendre quadrature on its edges). They need only first derivatives and they see material interfaces: with eps jumping from 1 to 4 across a capacitor, phi = y satisfies eps lap(phi) = 0 on both sides, so the differential residual is exactly zero for this wrong field, while the flux of D through the squares that straddle the interface is not (tests/test_maxwell_checks.py::test_integral_gauss_sees_the_dielectric_interface_the_differential_form_misses).

docs.title: Presets with closed-form solutions
docs.text:
pp.PhysicalProblem.from_preset(name); pp.solve(problem, "analytic") returns the exact field, so pp.compare(problem, [...], reference="analytic") scores any method:

Preset Physics Exact solution em_two_dielectric_capacitor (_differential) Gauss across a dielectric interface D uniform, E_i = D / eps_i (Griffiths ex. 4.7) em_wire_az magnetostatics of a round conductor Ampere's law em_tm_cavity (_integral) TMz standing wave in a PEC square Ez = sin sin cos, Pozar sec. 6.3 em_skin_effect eddy currents into a conductor A0 exp(-(1 + j) x / delta) em_cylinder_scattering plane wave on a dielectric cylinder, TMz series of cylinder functions (Harrington sec. 5-9)

docs.title: Materials
docs.text:
• Medium(eps_inf, mu_r, sigma, poles=...) with Drude(omega_p, gamma), Lorentz(delta_eps, omega0, delta) and Debye(delta_eps, tau) poles (Taflove & Hagness, Computational Electrodynamics, 3rd ed., ch. 9). Each pole carries the coefficients of its auxiliary differential equation for time-domain solvers; the trapezoidal recursions reproduce chi(omega) at second order in dt (table below). is_passive checks Im(eps_r) <= 0.
  • Anisotropic(eps_r, mu_r, sigma) tensors, uniaxial(n_o, n_e, axis), rotations, and the two refractive indices of a plane wave along any direction from Fresnel's equation of wave normals. is_reciprocal is the symmetry of the tensors (a gyrotropic medium is not reciprocal).
  • Magnetic: linear LinearMaterial, Magnet (B = mu0 mu_r H + Br), measured BHCurve (monotone PCHIP), BrauerCurve, and FrohlichKennelly (B = mu0 H + H / (alpha + beta |H|), every quantity of the Newton solver in closed form). JilesAtherton(Ms, a, k, c, alpha) integrates the hysteresis model of Jiles & Atherton (J. Magn. Magn. Mater. 61, 1986) along an applied-field path; its dM/dH is derived from the model's own definitions (M = Mrev + Mirr), and c = 1 reproduces the anhysteretic curve.

docs.title: References in closed form
docs.text: pp.em.statics: capacitors (parallel plate, coax, spheres), point and line charges, infinite wire, exact Biot-Savart of straight segments (biot_savart, with the cancellation-free form beside long segments), circles, helices, the off-axis loop field in elliptic integrals, finite solenoid, Helmholtz pair, Maxwell's mutual inductance of coaxial loops, loop self-inductance. pp.em.waves: Fresnel coefficients, Brewster and critical angles, planar multilayers by characteristic matrices (Born & Wolf), skin depth and surface impedance, rectangular and circular waveguide cut-offs and modes, rectangular and cylindrical cavity resonances and the TE101 conductor Q (Pozar), Hertzian dipole fields and power, thin-dipole patterns, half-wave dipole resistance and directivity (Balanis), TMz scattering by a cylinder, surface-plasmon and plasma dispersion. pp.em.mie: Mie series for dielectric and perfectly conducting spheres (Bohren & Huffman; Wiscombe's series length), efficiencies, asymmetry parameter, amplitude functions.

docs.title: Physics checks of any field
docs.text:
pp.maxwell.maxwell_checks(grid, fields, eps=..., mu=..., sigma=..., omega=None) judges a field without a reference, like the Darcy checks: Gauss's laws, Faraday, Ampere-Maxwell and continuity as relative residuals (||sum of terms|| / sum of ||term||, second-order differences), Poynting's energy balance over the grid box, PEC faces, and optionally a reference. Every residual is also computed on the grid with every other point: the ratio r(2h) / r(h) is about 4 when the residual is discretisation error (the field obeys the law) and about 1 when the field violates it, and the message says which. A law whose terms all vanish for the given components is reported as not informative instead of passed. tangential_continuity, pec_boundary, reciprocity and passivity cover interfaces and S-parameters. maxwell_trust_report gives the deploy decision.

In CI:

[[result]]
path = "fields.npz"           # x, y, (z), (t) axes; Ex..Hz / Bx.., Dx.., Jx.., rho; phasors as Ez_re / Ez_im
physics = "maxwell"
parameters = { eps_r = 1.0, mu_r = 1.0, sigma = 0.0 }   # omega = <rad/s> for phasors

pinneapple check reports Gauss's laws under PC102, Faraday / Ampere-Maxwell / continuity under PC301 and Poynting's theorem under PC103 (tolerances maxwell-gauss, maxwell-faraday, maxwell-ampere, maxwell-continuity, maxwell-energy). save_maxwell_npz writes the file with SI units and check_config_entry the configuration block. It runs without torch.

docs.title: Time domain: FDTD on the Yee grid
docs.text:
pp.em.fdtd solves the curl equations by the leapfrog scheme of Yee (1966): E at integer, H at half time steps, components staggered by half a cell (Taflove & Hagness, Computational Electrodynamics, 3rd ed., ch. 3). One code path covers 1-D, 2-D and 3-D: an axis with one node is a direction of invariance.

import numpy as np
from pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics import fdtd, media

grid = fdtd.YeeGrid((200, 200, 1), (1.5e-2, 1.5e-2, 1.5e-2))     # dt = 0.99 x the Courant limit
sim = fdtd.FDTD(grid, {"x": "cpml", "y": "cpml"}, npml=10)
sim.set_material(fdtd.fill_fraction(grid, lambda x, y, z: np.hypot(x - 1.5, y - 1.5) < 0.3), media.Medium(3.0))
sim.add_plane_wave(fdtd.PlaneWaveTFSF("x", "Ez", fdtd.modulated_gaussian(1e9, 0.6e9), ((30, 170), (30, 170), (0, 1))))
dft = sim.add_dft(["Ez", "Hx", "Hy"], [1e9])
sim.run_until(40e-9)
  • Stability. dt <= 1 / (c sqrt(sum 1/dx_i^2)) (TH eq. 4.65). YeeGrid refuses a larger step; the test shows grid-scale noise growing by 1e6 in 400 steps at 1.02 times the limit and staying bounded at 0.999.
  • Numerical dispersion. The scheme's waves obey (sin(omega dt/2) / (c dt))^2 = sum_i (sin(k_i dx_i/2) / dx_i)^2 (TH eq. 4.12, numerical_dispersion). The FDTD resonances match this relation to 1e-7 and the continuum at second order.
  • Energy. The scheme conserves (1/2) sum eps E^{n-1} . E^n + (1/2) sum mu |H^{n-1/2}|^2 exactly in a lossless cavity (energy(); constant to 1e-12 in the test).
  • Boundaries. pec, pmc, periodic, bloch (Floquet phase exp(-j k_b L), complex fields) and cpml, the convolutional PML of Roden & Gedney (2000) with polynomial sigma, kappa and linear alpha grading (TH sec. 7.9). Measured reflection 5 cells from the PML: -51 dB (5 cells), -87 dB (10), -106 dB (20).
  • Dispersive media by auxiliary differential equations solved with the E update: Drude (polarisation current, trapezoidal), Debye (polarisation, trapezoidal), Lorentz (polarisation, central), TH sec. 9.4-9.6.
  • Sources and plane waves. Soft and hard E sources, impressed currents (a Hertzian dipole is one cell of J). PlaneWaveTFSF is a total-field / scattered-field box driven by an auxiliary 1-D line with the same dx and dt. The masked-curl form works for any box in 1-D, 2-D and 3-D, and the leakage into the scattered-field region is 1e-16.
  • Sub-cell averaging. fill_fraction gives the fraction of each cell inside a shape, and set_material mixes eps arithmetically with it at the nodes. Each E component then takes the harmonic mean of its two nodes (the series rule for E normal to an interface; harmonic_eps=False switches it off). For E tangential to the surface this is the exact first-order correction (Farjadpour et al., Opt. Lett. 31, 2006):
  • the TMz cylinder converges at order 2, where the staircased one jumped between 1.2 % and 3.4 %;
  • on a sphere (E normal to part of the surface) harmonic averaging cuts the Q_sca error from 9.7 % to 2 %, but the error then plateaus near 2 % instead of converging. Full anisotropic (Kottke) smoothing is not implemented.
  • Monitors and output.
  • Probes and running DFTs (phasors in this package's exp(+j omega t) convention, E and H stamped at their own times).
  • poynting_flux_dft gives the power through a plane.
  • NearToFarField gives far-field patterns and radiated power from equivalent currents on a closed box (Balanis, Advanced Engineering Electromagnetics, eq. 6-122).
  • snapshot() returns node- and time-centred fields in the layout of maxwell_checks, so an FDTD run can be checked like any other field.

Figures and animations: pinneapple_tools.visualization.electromagnetics (field_movie writes GIF with Pillow or MP4 with ffmpeg, field_map adds a material outline and Poynting arrows, radiation_pattern draws polar patterns). examples/electrodynamics/08_fdtd_gallery.py writes results/fdtd_cylinder_scattering.gif / .mp4, results/fdtd_cylinder_field_map.png and results/fdtd_dipole_pattern.png. Each figure comes with its check: the cylinder's field against the series of cylinder functions (1.7 % at 30 cells per wavelength), the snapshots through maxwell_trust_report (APPROVED), and the dipole pattern and power against the closed forms.

docs.title: Electric machines
docs.text: The A_z solver includes a polar ring mesher with a moving band, magnets, coils, (anti-)periodic constraints, Maxwell-stress (Arkkio) and co-energy torque, flux linkage, back-EMF, cogging, Steinmetz/Bertotti iron loss, resistance-limited magnet eddy loss, and an SPMMachine model with adjoint torque sensitivities used by the rotor topology optimisation (pinneapple_design.topology, guide). tests/test_motor_magnetics.py asserts: slotless SPM torque within 1e-3 of the exact subdomain solution by both Maxwell stress and co-energy (360 angular steps, rotor off the grid); Maxwell-stress and co-energy torque of the slotted 24-slot machine within 0.3 %; skin-effect impedance of a round wire within 0.3 % of the Bessel solution (the table below measures 8.55e-4); adjoint rotor-torque sensitivities within 1e-5 of finite differences, for linear and nonlinear iron. examples/topology_optimization/03_reluctance_rotor.py (run 2026-10-17) optimises a reluctance rotor to a mean torque of 38.10 N m with linear iron; re-evaluated with the nonlinear B-H curve the same rotor gives 13.44 N m, so saturation must be in the optimisation loop for thin-featured designs.

docs.title: Interior-PM traction motor: the 2004 Toyota Prius
docs.text:
pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines models interior-magnet machines on conforming meshes:

  • geometry: parametric V-magnet rotors (VRotor: V opening and depth, magnet width and thickness, bridges, ribs, centre post, magnet segments) and round-bottom slots (RoundBottomSlots), the parametrisations of pyleecan's HoleM50 and SlotW11; prius_2004() holds the dimensions of pyleecan's Toyota_Prius.json (48 slots, 8 poles, 0.75 mm gap, 83.82 mm stack, stacking factor 0.95).
  • mesher: every polygon edge is a mesh edge (conforming Delaunay with Gabriel-edge recovery, concentric-shell splitting at small angles). Half a pole and half a slot pitch are meshed, mirrored and copied around, so all poles and slots have identical, symmetric elements: the no-load torque of the aligned rotor is 6e-13 N m and the cogging curve is antisymmetric with zero mean. The air gap holds three ring layers; only the middle one (moving band) is re-triangulated as the rotor turns.
  • steel: M400-50A (EN 10106) B-H curve and specific-loss table (50 Hz to 2.5 kHz), the data of pyleecan's material library (Apache-2.0), and the Prius magnet grade (Br 1.24 T at 20 degC, -0.1 %/K); stacked applies the stacking factor; TableIronLoss interpolates the catalogue table; fit_iron_loss fits k_h f^alpha B^beta + k_c (f B)^2 + k_e (f B)^1.5 with the classical term from resistivity and thickness.
  • pmsm.IPMMachine: Newton solution with the nonlinear B-H curve, Arkkio and co-energy torque, flux linkage, back-EMF, the dq frame (d-axis on the magnet flux), torque ripple, frozen-permeability flux split and L_d / L_q, MTPA by golden-section search on the FEA torque, iron loss per element in its own frame (table or fit) and resistance-limited magnet eddy loss.

The FEA is checked against a published benchmark here and against a second, independent code (gmsh + GetDP) in the next section. FEMM (Windows-only) and pyleecan (its wheel needs a git-only dependency) do not run in this environment. The published reference is the torque against current angle of the Prius motor at 250 A peak computed by Yang, Krishnamurthy and Brown (IEEE IEMDC 2013), as tabulated in pyleecan's test suite. Their model and pyleecan's geometry are not the same file (centre post, magnet temperature, steel data), so agreement within a few per cent is the expectation, not a mesh error.

python examples/electrodynamics/10_pmsm_prius.py --write-docs (run on 2026-10-17, 960 gap nodes, 29 936 elements) wrote the table below and examples/electrodynamics/results/10_pmsm_prius.json; figures: 10_pmsm_field.png (|B| and flux lines at MTPA, 250 A), 10_pmsm_curves.png (torque against current angle with the published curve, cogging, back-EMF), 10_pmsm_mtpa.png (MTPA locus, L_d and L_q).

Results of that run (magnets at 20 degC, 1.24 T):

Peak current (A) MTPA angle (deg from q) Mean torque (N m) Ripple pk-pk L_d (mH) L_q (mH) 50 27.6 70.4 24.9 % 1.945 4.871 100 37.1 147.8 25.5 % 1.741 3.697 150 43.1 221.3 22.5 % 1.623 3.101 200 47.1 287.9 22.8 % 1.511 2.729 250 50.3 345.6 22.9 % 1.386 2.435

L_d and L_q are the apparent frozen-permeability values at each MTPA point (saturation lowers L_q from 4.87 to 2.44 mH). The d-axis is the fundamental of the magnet flux linkage, from the winding layout (pm_flux_angle): a single no-load solution's flux vector carries the slot harmonics and sits 0.79 electrical degrees off, which shifted the torque at pure negative d-axis current by -12 N m; with the fundamental the mean torque at Phi0 = 180 deg is 0.0 N m, as the rotor's mirror symmetry requires.

Torque against current angle at 250 A, against Yang et al. (2013):

Phi0 (deg) 60 70 80 90 100 110 120 130 140 150 160 170 180 this FEA (N m) 92.0 133.6 175.8 217.3 256.0 289.9 318.2 338.1 345.6 330.1 267.1 151.4 0.0 published (N m) 79 125 160 192 237 281 319 343 353 332 266 164 22 difference +13.0 +8.6 +15.8 +25.3 +19.0 +8.9 -0.8 -4.9 -7.4 -1.9 +1.1 -12.6 -22.0

The peak agrees within 2.1 %; the largest deviation is +25.3 N m (+13 %) at 90 deg (pure q-axis current), the rms deviation 13.3 N m. Shifting the curve in angle does not remove it: the best-fitting offset (-1.32 deg) lowers the rms over 70 to 170 deg only from 12.2 to 9.7 N m. The differences are in magnitude where the magnet torque dominates (low Phi0, more torque here) and at 180 deg, where a machine symmetric about its d-axis has no mean torque but the published curve gives 22 N m (an angle convention or an asymmetry of their model). Plausible causes, not resolved here: magnet remanence or temperature of the published model, its steel curve, the centre post (W1 = 0 in pyleecan's file).

No load: cogging 1.38 N m peak to peak (antisymmetric, zero mean), magnet flux linkage 0.209 Wb peak per phase. Back-EMF from the flux linkage at 120 rotor angles per electrical period (spectral derivative): 87.6 V phase peak fundamental at 1000 rpm (107.3 V line-to-line rms fundamental, 0.1073 V/rpm), THD 9.3 % phase and 8.5 % line; largest harmonics 11th 6.5 %, 5th 4.2 %, 7th 3.6 %, 3rd 2.4 % of the fundamental (the 3rd cancels between phases). No published Prius back-EMF constant could be retrieved here to compare with. Losses at 1500 rpm (100 Hz), 250 A MTPA: stator iron 391 W, rotor iron 29 W with the catalogue table (332 W and 32 W with the Bertotti fit), magnet eddy loss 37.9 W (resistance limited, one piece per magnet). The Bertotti fit to the M400-50A table up to 1 kHz has 8.2 % rms and 22 % maximum relative error; the table model is the default. Mesh convergence of the torque is not monotone (480, 960, 1920 gap nodes: 343.42, 345.65, 344.22 N m): treat the FEA torque as converged to about 0.4 %.

Case Quantity Reference Error (finest) Observed order Status Magnetised ring, sector mesher + P1 FEM relative L2 error of A_z, h halved closed form (two magnetised cylinders + harmonic) 1.91e-04 1.89, 1.91, 1.99 (expected 2) pass Machine sector geometry (Prius slot and magnet areas) slot area, gap nodes doubled exact area (trapezoid + half disc) 5.70e-05 1.99, 1.81, 1.90 (expected 2) pass Prius IPM: Maxwell stress vs co-energy torque Arkkio torque at 250 A, 3 rotor angles virtual work dW'/dtheta (4th-order differences) 1.96e-03 - pass Prius IPM: dq power balance and frozen permeability mean Maxwell-stress torque over 60 el. deg 1.5 p (psi_d i_q - psi_q i_d) 1.96e-04 - pass Prius IPM: torque vs current angle (Yang et al. 2013) mean torque, 250 A, Phi0 = 60..180 deg published FEA (IEMDC 2013), 13 angles 2.08e-02 - pass Prius IPM: mesh convergence of the peak torque mean torque at 250 A, 50 deg, gap nodes doubled successive differences 4.15e-03 - pass

Notes from the same run:

  • Magnetised ring, sector mesher + P1 FEM: 8 sector copies, magnet edges on mesh edges
  • Machine sector geometry (Prius slot and magnet areas): magnet area (straight edges) exact to 4.4e-16
  • Prius IPM: Maxwell stress vs co-energy torque: max relative difference over the angles
  • Prius IPM: dq power balance and frozen permeability: frozen-permeability superposition error 4.1e-11; L_d = 1.386 mH, L_q = 2.420 mH, psi_pm = 0.2140 Wb at this point
  • Prius IPM: torque vs current angle (Yang et al. 2013): peak 345.6 N m at Phi0 = 140 deg (published 353 N m at 140 deg); largest deviation +25.3 N m at 90 deg; rms 13.3 N m; an angle offset of -1.32 deg fits best (rms 12.2 -> 9.7 N m over 70..170 deg)
  • Prius IPM: mesh convergence of the peak torque: 480: 343.42 N m, 960: 345.65 N m, 1920: 344.22 N m; difference ratio 1.56

docs.title: Second code: gmsh + GetDP, and interoperability
docs.text:
pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.getdp solves the same machine with gmsh 4.12 and GetDP 3.2, external GPL programs called as executables (apt install gmsh getdp):

  • write_geo writes the same polygons as the mesher;
  • write_pro writes a 2-D A-formulation with the M400-50A curve as an Akima table of nu(|B|^2) and Newton-Raphson (JacNL, tolerance 1e-9), a moving air gap, and the Arkkio torque and phase flux linkages computed in GetDP;
  • solve runs both programs.

Mesh, nonlinear solver and torque integral are GetDP's own; only the geometry, the materials and the currents are shared.

python examples/electrodynamics/14_prius_getdp_crosscheck.py (run on 2026-10-18) uses 960 gap nodes in both codes: 29 936 elements here, 58 309 in GetDP. Two further runs add their results to results/14_prius_getdp_crosscheck.json: --cogging-convergence and --cogging-diagnosis. Figures: 14_prius_getdp_crosscheck.png and 14_prius_cogging_convergence.png. Mean torque at 250 A against current angle, over 12 rotor angles:

Phi0 (deg) PINNeAPPle (N m) GetDP (N m) Difference Yang 2013 (N m) 60 91.97 90.94 -1.03 79 70 133.64 132.56 -1.09 125 80 175.84 174.76 -1.09 160 90 217.26 216.19 -1.07 192 100 255.97 254.94 -1.03 237 110 289.94 289.03 -0.90 281 120 318.15 317.34 -0.81 319 130 338.14 337.38 -0.76 343 140 345.65 344.98 -0.66 353 150 330.14 329.58 -0.55 332 160 267.13 267.29 +0.16 266 170 151.40 151.25 -0.15 164 180 0.00 -0.24 -0.24 22

Per quantity:

Quantity PINNeAPPle GetDP Difference Published Torque vs angle, max / rms difference 1.09 / 0.81 N m (0.19 % at the peak) Torque vs Yang 2013, rms / max 13.3 / 25.3 N m 12.9 / 24.2 N m Yang 2013 Back-EMF fundamental, 1000 rpm (60 positions) 87.60 V 87.64 V +0.04 % Phase back-EMF THD 9.35 % 9.04 % -0.31 points No-load d-axis flux linkage psi_d0 0.20914 Wb 0.20921 Wb +0.03 % Apparent L_d at 250 A, 50 deg 1.370 mH 1.385 mH +1.1 % Apparent L_q at 250 A, 50 deg 1.856 mH 1.864 mH +0.4 % Cogging pk-pk, 1920 gap nodes 1.341 N m 1.004 N m -25 %

The apparent inductances are (psi_d - psi_d0) / i_d and psi_q / i_q at the same point in both codes. They differ from the differential values in the MTPA table above.

The two codes agree on everything except cogging. Cogging is the small difference of large forces, 0.4 % of the peak torque here. The cogging study:

Gap nodes PINNeAPPle (elements) GetDP (elements) 480 1.698 N m (13 120) 1.538 N m (28 777) 960 1.353 N m (29 936) 1.046 N m (58 309) 1920 1.341 N m (77 904) 1.004 N m (153 737)
  • Both codes converge under mesh refinement (0.9 % and 4 % change in the last step), but to values 25 % apart.
  • With linear iron (mu_r 2500, no saturation) at 960 nodes they agree: 1.2225 against 1.2111 N m, 0.9 %.
  • A 10 times denser GetDP B-H table changes its cogging by 1e-5 N m.

So the difference lies in the saturated iron: the 1.5 mm bridges carry about 2.4 T at no load. A symmetric machine has odd cogging. PINNeAPPle's mirrored mesh gives exactly odd cogging. GetDP's mesh is not symmetric, and its cogging carries an even part of up to 0.089 N m with nonlinear iron and 0.020 N m with linear iron, a measure of its discretisation error. Even comparing odd parts only, the codes differ by 23 %. Which value is closer to the real machine is not settled here: that needs a measurement or a third code. Cogging from either code carries this uncertainty.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.interop:

  • pyleecan: from_pyleecan reads pyleecan's Toyota_Prius.json, included under tests/data/pyleecan (Apache-2.0). The test checks that it gives exactly prius_2004(). to_pyleecan writes the parameters back, and the round trip is exact.
  • FEMM: femm_lua writes a Lua script for FEMM's magnetics module: geometry, B-H curve, magnets, circuits and the analysis. It is checked by re-reading its nodes against the mesher's polygons, not by running FEMM.
  • ElmerFEM: elmer_case writes the gmsh geometry and a MagnetoDynamics2D .sif. It is not run here.
  • MATLAB: to_mat / from_mat. DXF: to_dxf / read_dxf_polylines, with one layer per region. Both round trips are tested.
  • Data contracts: rotor_parameter_space gives a ParameterSpace of the rotor variables. fluxmap_dataset gives a flux map as a DatasetSpec table, written to CSV, Parquet or HDF5 by pinneapple_data.contracts.tables.

docs.title: Drive model: MTPA, flux weakening, efficiency map, WLTC energy
docs.text:
pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.drive turns a machine into a drive under inverter limits:

  • FluxMap.from_fea(machine, I_max): mean torque and dq flux linkages of the FEA on an (i_d, i_q) grid (saturation and cross-saturation included, odd/even symmetry in i_q), and per grid point the speed-free iron-loss sums and magnet-loss coefficient (IPMMachine.loss_components), so the core loss at any speed is k_h f^alpha S_h + k_c f^2 S_c + k_e f^1.5 S_e + c_m f^2 without new field solutions. LinearDQ is the constant-inductance model with closed-form MTPA and flux-weakening torque.
  • Drive(machine, R, I_max, V_max): steady state v_d = R i_d - w psi_q, v_q = R i_q + w psi_d, current and voltage amplitude limits (v_max_svpwm(V_dc) = V_dc / sqrt 3). max_torque(speed) searches the outer boundary of the feasible current set (current circle, voltage ellipse, so maximum-torque-per-volt operation is included); operating_point(T, speed) returns the currents of least copper + core loss for a torque (MTPA at low speed, flux weakening at high speed); efficiency_map evaluates a speed x torque grid.
  • Vehicle and cycle_energy: road load and inertia over a speed trace, a single gear, regeneration up to the braking envelope (the rest goes to the friction brakes), battery-side energy of the drive. wltc_class3b() is the WLTC class 3b trace of UN GTR No. 15, Annex 1 (1800 s, 23.266 km, 131.3 km/h).

python examples/electrodynamics/11_prius_drive.py --write-docs (run on 2026-10-17) builds the flux map of the Prius model (9 x 9 currents up to 250 A, 480 gap nodes, 12 rotor angles; loss data on 5 x 5 points, 24 angles per electrical period) and evaluates the drive with stated assumptions: 250 A peak, 500 V DC link with SVPWM (288.7 V phase peak), phase resistance 93.6 mOhm at 100 degC from the winding data (72 series turns, 8.49 mm^2 conductors, end turn 0.16 m per side estimated), and an illustrative compact car (1450 kg, C_rr 0.009, C_d A 0.58 m^2, wheel 0.30 m, gear 4.113, 97 %). Results (results/11_prius_drive.json, 11_prius_drive.png):

  • envelope: 343.6 N m up to 2000 rpm, then flux weakening (181.0 N m at 3750 rpm, 104.4 N m at 6000 rpm); peak electromagnetic power 77.7 kW at 2500 rpm under these limits. The Prius's published rating (50 kW, 400 N m, quoted in pyleecan's test suite) comes from its own inverter current and thermal limits, which are not modelled;
  • peak efficiency 96.2 % at 2750 rpm, 70.7 N m (copper + iron + magnet loss; no inverter or mechanical loss; the map is evaluated up to the motoring and braking envelopes at every speed from 100 to 6000 rpm);
  • WLTC class 3b: motoring 11.52 MJ, regenerated 2.97 MJ, drive losses 0.98 MJ, no friction braking needed within the braking envelope, battery-side 102.1 Wh/km for this car.

The optimiser is checked against the closed forms of the linear machine and against energy bookkeeping:

Case Quantity Reference Error (finest) Observed order Status Drive: torque envelope vs closed form (linear dq) max torque, 500..10000 rpm, both signs MTPA / circle-ellipse intersection (R = 0) 1.31e-14 - pass Drive: least-loss currents vs MTPA closed form currents of least copper loss, 4 torques i_d = (psi - sqrt(psi^2 + 8 (L_q - L_d)^2 I^2)) / (4 (L_q - L_d)) 1.97e-08 - pass Drive cycle: WLTC class 3b energy balance battery energy of a lossless drive road-load work (kinetic energy returns to zero) 0.00e+00 - pass Prius flux map: interpolation vs direct FEA torque at 3 off-grid currents (7 x 7 grid) FEA at the same currents 2.72e-04 - pass

Notes from the same run:

  • Drive: torque envelope vs closed form (linear dq): L_d = 0.6 mH, L_q = 2.4 mH, psi_m = 0.2 Wb, 250 A, 500 V SVPWM
  • Drive cycle: WLTC class 3b energy balance: trace: 23266.3 m (GTR 15: 23 266 m), max 131.3 km/h, sum 83758.6 km/h s
  • Prius flux map: interpolation vs direct FEA: error relative to 300 N m

docs.title: Step skew, tolerances and a 3-D view
docs.text:
pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.robustness:

  • Step skew by multi-slice 2-D FEA. A rotor of K axial segments, with segment k turned by delta_k = s (k - (K-1)/2). Each segment is a 2-D slice with the same stator and phase currents. The torque and flux linkage are the means over the slices. skewed_torque gives load torque and ripple, skewed_no_load gives cogging and flux linkage. Inter-segment axial flux and end effects are neglected, as in every multi-slice model. For a harmonic of order h per period lam, the slice mean multiplies the straight rotor's harmonic by the step-skew factor |sin(K h pi s / lam) / (K sin(h pi s / lam))| (step_skew_factor).
  • tolerance_model(geometry): the FEA mean torque and ripple as a function of remanence scale, magnet thickness, magnet width and air gap, for pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.tolerance.propagate (JCGM 101 Monte Carlo).
  • skewed_field_3d extrudes each segment's 2-D solution into prisms turned by its skew angle. export.write_vtu and export.solution_to_vtu write VTK unstructured grids for ParaView.

python examples/electrodynamics/15_prius_skew.py (run on 2026-10-18; 960 gap nodes, 12 rotor angles per period, 250 A at 50.3 deg) gives results/15_prius_skew.json, 15_prius_skew.png, 15_prius_skew_3d.png and 15_prius_skew_3d.vtu. The skew is the total (K - 1) s; the slot pitch, which is also the cogging period, is 7.5 deg:

Total skew (deg) Cogging pk-pk, K = 2 (N m) K = 3 (N m) Torque, K = 2 (N m) K = 3 (N m) Ripple, K = 2 K = 3 0 1.353 1.353 345.6 345.6 22.9 % 22.9 % 1.875 0.639 0.877 343.9 344.5 18.7 % 20.1 % 3.75 0.624 0.472 338.8 341.1 8.8 % 13.3 % 5.625 0.639 0.420 330.1 335.3 11.2 % 7.9 % 7.5 1.353 0.846 317.0 326.6 16.2 % 7.3 %

At the classic step-skew optimum, a total skew of (K-1)/K of the cogging period, the cogging falls:

  • two steps at 3.75 deg: 1.35 to 0.62 N m, with the load ripple down from 22.9 to 8.8 % for 2.0 % less torque;
  • three steps, near 5 deg (5.625 deg computed): 1.35 to 0.42 N m, ripple 7.9 %, torque -3.0 %.

Two steps over a full slot pitch reproduce the straight rotor's cogging exactly, because the two slices are a whole cogging period apart.

With the same two-step skew over one slot pitch, the back-EMF (120 positions per electrical period) shows:

  • the fundamental falls by 0.96593, against the closed-form factor cos 15 deg = 0.96593;
  • every harmonic of the skewed rotor equals the straight harmonic times the factor, to within 1.5e-9 of the fundamental;
  • the phase THD drops from 9.3 to 7.2 %.

The verification case below checks the same identity on the cogging harmonics of 2- and 3-step skews (1.0e-8).

Case Quantity Reference Error (finest) Observed order Status Step skew: multi-slice cogging vs skew factor cogging harmonics, 2 and 3 steps sin(K h pi s / lam) / (K sin(h pi s / lam)) x straight rotor 1.01e-08 - pass

The identity is exact because the slice offsets are multiples of the moving-band step, so every slice uses the same band triangles. It verifies the multi-slice composition, not the 2-D field itself.

python examples/electrodynamics/17_prius_tolerances.py (run on 2026-10-18) propagates manufacturing tolerances through the FEA by Monte Carlo (JCGM 101, propagate): 200 samples, one nonlinear FEA each, with 480 gap nodes and 12 rotor angles at 250 A and 50.3 deg. The tolerances are normal inputs and are stated assumptions, not measured data. One standard deviation of each:

  • remanence 1 % (a +-2 % batch spread at two sigma);
  • magnet thickness 0.025 mm;
  • magnet width 0.05 mm;
  • air gap 0.025 mm, on a 0.75 mm gap (the rotor radius moves).

Results are in results/17_prius_tolerances.json and 17_prius_tolerances.png:

Output Nominal Mean Std 1 % / 99 % Standardised regression coefficients (remanence, thickness, width, air gap) R^2 Mean torque (N m) 343.35 343.31 1.96 338.9 / 347.4 0.82, 0.15, 0.24, -0.54 0.999 Ripple (pk-pk) 20.1 % 20.2 % 0.47 % 19.1 / 21.2 % -0.19, -0.07, -0.02, -0.95 0.983

The torque spread (0.57 % of nominal) is set by the remanence first and the air gap second. The ripple spread is set almost entirely by the air gap: a larger gap smooths the slot harmonics. Both outputs are close to linear in these inputs (R^2 >= 0.98), so a linear surrogate fitted to a few FEA solutions would reproduce this study. All 200 samples met the stated specification: torque >= 98 % of nominal and ripple <= 25 %. The yield is therefore 1.000, with a Wilson 95 % interval of 0.981 to 1.000. The nominal torque differs from the 960-node value (345.6 N m) by the mesh; the spread is a difference between samples on the same mesh.

docs.title: Magnet temperature, thermal network and demagnetisation
docs.text:
pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.thermal:

  • ThermalNetwork: isothermal nodes with heat capacities, conductances between nodes and to fixed-temperature boundaries, time-dependent sources; steady state and transients (backward Euler or trapezoidal rule). machine_network(geometry) builds the seven-node model of a water-jacketed machine (stator yoke, teeth, winding in the slots, end windings, rotor, magnets, shaft path) from the cross-section: cylindrical-shell conduction 2 pi k L / ln(r2/r1), slot insulation, axial conduction to the end windings, convection across the gap and at the end windings. The material, contact and heat-transfer data are the stated defaults of MachineThermalData (coolant 65 degC). They are inputs, not correlations fitted here, and illustrative: none is measured on a Prius.
  • IPMMachine(..., magnet_temperature=T): remanence Br(T) = Br20 (1 + alpha_Br (T - 20)), with alpha_Br = -0.1 %/K (the pyleecan Prius magnet). magnet_temperature_sweep evaluates MTPA torque, back-EMF and L_d, L_q with the FEA at each temperature.
  • demagnetisation_margin(machine, solution, Hcj): in every magnet element, the field opposing the magnetisation H_rev = -(B . m - Br) / (mu0 mu_r) against the intrinsic coercivity (the knee of a square-loop sintered NdFeB magnet). It returns the per-element ratio H_rev / Hcj and the demagnetised area fraction (ratio > 1). intrinsic_coercivity(Hcj20, T, beta) = Hcj20 (1 + beta (T - 20)). NDFEB_HCJ_MIN_KAM holds the minimum Hcj at 20 degC of each grade letter (N 12, M 14, H 17, SH 20, UH 25, EH 30, AH 35 kOe), the manufacturers' grade convention. beta = -0.55 %/K is a typical datasheet value for sintered NdFeB and an assumption here: use the grade's datasheet.

python examples/electrodynamics/13_prius_thermal.py (run on 2026-10-18, 960 gap nodes) gives results/13_prius_thermal.json, 13_prius_thermal.png and 13_prius_demag.png.

Performance against the magnet temperature (MTPA at 250 A; EMF is the phase fundamental, peak, at 1000 rpm):

Magnets (degC) Br (T) Torque (N m) MTPA angle (deg) EMF (V) L_d (mH) L_q (mH) 20 1.240 345.6 50.3 87.6 1.386 2.435 60 1.190 338.7 50.6 84.0 1.386 2.443 100 1.141 331.6 51.0 80.2 1.388 2.458 150 1.079 322.6 51.4 75.4 1.389 2.474

From 20 to 150 degC, Br falls by 13.0 % and the EMF by 13.9 %. The torque at 250 A falls by only 6.7 %, because the reluctance torque does not depend on the magnets. L_q rises by 1.6 % as the weaker magnets saturate the q-axis iron less.

The thermal network takes the drive model's per-second losses over four WLTC class 3b cycles. Copper loss is split between the slots and the end windings by length. Iron loss is split by the FEA loss density at 250 A: yoke 26 %, teeth 63 %, rotor 10 %. The magnet loss goes to the magnets. Mean losses are copper 298 W, iron 247 W and magnet 0.2 W. The peak temperatures are:

  • teeth 82.5 degC;
  • winding 80.3 degC;
  • magnets 78.5 degC;
  • end winding 75.1 degC;
  • yoke 71.9 degC.

The network then runs at peak load from the end-of-cycle state: 343.2 N m at 1500 rpm, with copper 8.75 kW, iron 382 W and magnet 30 W. The hotter winding node reaches 180 degC (class H) after 237 s. The magnets settle at 127.4 degC.

Demagnetisation at that magnet temperature, at the full d-axis current (i_d = -250 A) and at the peak of a three-phase short circuit estimated as 2 psi_pm / L_d = -165 A (demagnetised area fraction of the magnets; H_rev is the worst element):

Grade Hcj at 127 degC (kA/m) -250 A, H_rev 719 kA/m -165 A, H_rev 517 kA/m N 391 99.4 % 31.8 % M 456 93.3 % 3.2 % H 554 18.6 % 0 SH 651 2.4 % 0 UH 814 0 0

The worst elements sit at the outer magnet corners and at the V tip. 13_prius_demag.png shows the per-element ratio for grades H and SH in both cases.

The table above uses the default mesh: 784 magnet elements, 2.2 mm mean size. To test how much the fractions depend on the magnet mesh, demagnetisation_refinement refines the magnets over four levels. It lowers the element-size growth away from the gap, keeping the gap mesh fixed (13_prius_demag_mesh.png). Each cell gives the demagnetised area, the area above 0.9 Hcj and the worst-element ratio H_rev / Hcj:

Magnet elements (size) H, -250 A SH, -250 A UH, -250 A M, -165 A H, -165 A 784 (2.24 mm) 18.6 / 83.4 % / 1.30 2.4 / 7.6 % / 1.10 0 / 0 % / 0.88 3.2 / 10.9 % / 1.13 0 / 2.0 % / 0.93 1920 (1.43 mm) 19.4 / 85.5 % / 1.43 2.6 / 8.3 % / 1.21 0 / 0.7 % / 0.97 3.3 / 12.3 % / 1.25 0.2 / 1.0 % / 1.03 4224 (0.96 mm) 18.6 / 85.5 % / 1.46 2.0 / 7.5 % / 1.24 0 / 0.7 % / 0.99 4.1 / 14.0 % / 1.28 0.4 / 1.1 % / 1.06 7216 (0.74 mm) 18.8 / 85.1 % / 1.52 2.3 / 8.6 % / 1.29 0.2 / 0.5 % / 1.03 3.6 / 14.0 % / 1.33 0.3 / 1.0 % / 1.10

The area fractions settle. The demagnetised fraction stays within 0.9 percentage points across the four levels, and within 0.6 between the two finest. The area above 0.9 Hcj stays within 3.1 points across the levels (M at -165 A rises from 10.9 to 14.0 %) and within 1.1 between the two finest. The worst-element ratio does not converge. It grows by 4 to 6 % at each level because the field is singular at the sharp corners where the magnet meets the pocket. A demagnetised fraction of a few tenths of a percent at the finest mesh is a corner effect of the same kind, as for UH at -250 A and H at the short circuit.

The conclusions therefore rest on the area fractions, not on the worst element. When hot, grade H loses about 19 % of the magnet area at the full d-axis current, and about 85 % of the area lies within 10 % of the knee. Grade SH loses about 2 %, with 8 % within 10 % of the knee. In UH, only the corners reach the knee. Corner-level demagnetisation is not resolved by this model: the real corners are rounded and their field is not singular.

The grade rows are a comparison of candidate grades, not a statement about the real car. We found no accessible public source that states the grade of the 2004 Prius magnets. Neither does the pyleecan model this geometry comes from: it gives Br and mu_r only. So the "N demagnetises" row says nothing about the production motor, whose magnets were chosen by Toyota for its own current and temperature limits.

The network and the demagnetisation field are checked against closed forms (machines.verification):

Case Quantity Reference Error (finest) Observed order Status Thermal network: first-order transient node temperature at t = tau, dt halved T_b + P/G (1 - e^-1) (closed form) 4.79e-06 2.00, 2.00, 2.00 (expected 2) pass Thermal network: cylindrical conduction series of thin flat shells, n doubled 2 pi k L / ln(r2/r1) 5.08e-06 2.00, 2.00, 2.00 (expected 2) pass Demagnetisation field in a magnetised ring reverse field in the magnet, h halved closed form of the magnetised ring 5.99e-03 1.02, 0.89, 0.95 (expected 1) pass

The element-wise B of P1 elements is first order, hence the observed order of the demagnetisation field.

docs.title: Rotor design: FEA + Gaussian-process surrogate + NSGA-II
docs.text:
pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.design puts the FEA behind the design-study core of pinneapple_design.design_optimizer:

  • rotor_evaluator maps five rotor variables (magnet width W4 and thickness H3, V depth H0 and opening W0, bridge H1) to the FEA mean torque and ripple at a fixed current, plus the exact magnet mass. Invalid geometries are rejected without a solve.
  • rotor_design_problem maximises torque and minimises magnet mass, with ripple at most 30 %.
  • hybrid_vs_fea_only compares two studies:
  • surrogate-assisted NSGA-II (surrogate_assisted): a Latin-hypercube start, then rounds of GP fit, NSGA-II on the GP, and FEA on points along the predicted front (adaptive sampling);
  • NSGA-II that calls the FEA for every individual.

It compares them at equal quality, the hypervolume of the feasible FEA-evaluated designs, and re-evaluates every design of the hybrid front with a finer FEA (verify_candidates).

python examples/electrodynamics/12_prius_rotor_design.py (run on 2026-10-18) uses three seeds. The study FEA has 288 gap nodes and 6 rotor angles at 250 A, 50 deg. The hybrid starts from 24 Latin-hypercube points and runs 4 rounds of 8 FEA verifications. The FEA-only NSGA-II has a budget of 2000 designs. Results are in results/12_prius_rotor_design.json and 12_prius_rotor_design.png:

Seed Hybrid FEA calls Hybrid hypervolume FEA calls for NSGA-II to reach it Saving NSGA-II final (FEA calls) 0 53 0.8938 711 92.5 % 0.9194 (1582) 1 52 0.8893 601 91.3 % 0.9067 (1600) 2 51 0.9379 605 91.6 % 0.9598 (1554)

At equal quality the hybrid needs 51 to 53 FEA solutions where NSGA-II on the FEA needs 601 to 711, a saving of 91 to 93 %. Given enough calls, the FEA-only GA ends higher: 0.907 to 0.960 after about 1600 calls. The hypervolume is normalised per seed by the ideal and nadir points of both runs, so it compares the two runs of one seed, not seeds with each other.

The GP's held-out error on the 8 FEA points of each round, in the last round:

  • torque: mean 0.07 to 0.14 %, max 0.35 %;
  • magnet mass: 0.01 % or less;
  • ripple: mean 2.5 to 4.6 %, max 11 %. In the first round it was up to 46 %, so ripple is the weak output.

All 83 designs of the three hybrid fronts were re-evaluated with the finer FEA (480 gap nodes, 12 angles):

  • all remain feasible;
  • torque changes by at most 1.1 % (mean 0.8 %);
  • ripple rises by 15 to 19 % on average and by up to 30 %, because 6 rotor angles under-sample it.

A design study should therefore apply its ripple limit with that margin or evaluate ripple with 12 angles.

Against the Prius rotor through the same finer FEA (343.4 N m, 1.236 kg, ripple 20.3 %), each front has 6 to 8 designs with more torque and less magnet: about 364 N m (+6 %) at 1.21 kg, with ripple 24 to 25 %. These designs sit at the lower bound of the bridge, 1.0 mm against the Prius's 1.5 mm. A thinner bridge leaks less magnet flux, but the bridge carries the centrifugal load. Mechanical stress, demagnetisation and the torque-speed envelope are not constraints of this study, so it does not claim a better rotor. It shows the method and its FEA-call saving.

docs.title: End effects: end windings and magnet end leakage
docs.text:
Two effects outside the 2-D cross-section:

  • End windings. machines.endwinding models each coil end as a thin conductor on the cylinder at the mean slot radius: axially out of the stack by the overhang, a half circle over the coil span, then back.
  • The same path gives the end-turn length of the phase resistance (prius_phase_resistance, 0.16 m per coil end), so resistance and inductance share one geometry.
  • end_winding_inductance integrates the phase inductances with Neumann's double integral, using the thin-wire kernel 1 / sqrt(r^2 + g^2) with the wire's geometric mean distance g = a e^-1/4 (statics.filament_inductance). The coil bundle is a round conductor of the slot's copper area. Both ends are included, in air and with the stator end face as an infinitely permeable mirror (image currents); the two cases bound the laminated face.
  • The dq leakage L_end = L_aa - M_ab adds to both axes in the voltage equations (Drive(..., L_end=...)). It cancels in the torque 1.5 p (psi_d i_q - psi_q i_d).
  • Magnet end leakage. getdp.end_leakage_3d builds a 3-D magnetostatic model of half the stack, from the mid-plane to the end face, with an air region beyond the face: the cross-section extruded into prisms. The solver is GetDP, using a magnetic scalar potential and Picard iteration on the secant permeability. The model is compared with the same mesh without the end air, which is the extruded 2-D field. The ratio of the no-load air-gap flux under a pole corrects the 2-D magnet flux.

The filament inductance is verified against closed forms (tests/test_emachine_ends.py):

  • a circular loop against Rosa's mu0 R (ln(8R/a) - 7/4), within 2e-3;
  • two coaxial loops against Maxwell's elliptic-integral mutual inductance, below 1e-3 and second order in the polygon;
  • a loop above the iron mirror against the same loop plus the mutual of its image, within 2e-3.

python examples/electrodynamics/16_prius_end_effects.py (run on 2026-10-18) gives results/16_prius_end_effects.json and 16_prius_end_effects.png.

End windings, 24 coils of 9 turns, overhang 19.4 mm:

  • L_aa 148.2 uH, M_ab 13.0 uH, so L_end = 135.2 uH in air;
  • 115.3 uH with the iron face;
  • 150 and 300 pieces per metre agree to 1.4e-4.

In air, L_end is 9.8 % of L_d (1.386 mH) and 5.6 % of L_q at 250 A. With the drive model and the FEA flux map (250 A, 500 V), the maximum torque is:

Speed (rpm) 1000 2000 3000 4000 5000 6000 2-D model (N m) 343.6 343.6 239.3 167.4 128.5 104.4 + end windings in air 343.6 338.1 213.3 150.1 115.7 94.2 + end windings, iron face 343.6 339.9 216.8 152.4 117.4 95.6

The end-winding reactance takes voltage, so the corner speed moves down. Above it the envelope falls by 10 to 11 % in air: 239.3 to 213.3 N m at 3000 rpm and 104.4 to 94.2 N m at 6000 rpm. At part load in flux weakening, the efficiency rises slightly because less negative i_d is needed:

  • 4000 rpm, 100 N m: 94.27 to 94.36 %;
  • 6000 rpm, 60 N m: 90.86 to 91.29 %.

The 3-D/2-D ratio of the magnet flux on three meshes:

  • 0.9345 with 116 856 prisms;
  • 0.9463 with 198 336 prisms;
  • 0.9482 with 342 832 prisms.

The steps are 0.0118 then 0.0019. Lengthening the end air from 40 to 60 mm changes the ratio by 1e-4 (0.9462). The half stack has one end and the full stack two, so the ratio applies to the whole 83.8 mm machine: the end leakage removes 5.2 % of the 2-D magnet flux.

The correction scales the remanence in the 2-D FEA by that ratio, from 1.24 to 1.176 T, so saturation and reluctance torque follow:

  • the MTPA torque at 250 A falls from 345.7 to 336.7 N m (-2.6 %), with the MTPA angle moving from 49.5 to 50.1 deg;
  • the back-EMF fundamental at 1000 rpm falls from 87.6 to 82.9 V (-5.4 %).

The torque falls less than the flux because the reluctance torque does not depend on the magnets.
