docs.title: Fixed while building this
docs.text:
• eddy_current_fdm.annular_current_source normalised the coil current density by the nominal band area, so the injected current depended on how the band fell on the grid (0.75 N I in one case); it now injects exactly N I. axial_flux_density returned half the field on the axis (A / r with A = 0 there instead of its limit dA/dr), and eddy_current_density returned +j omega sigma A, the eddy current with the wrong sign for the solver's exp(+j omega t) convention. Together these explain the coil field "about 0.20 times" the loop formula recorded in the validation gallery.
  • The Newton solver of solve_magnetostatic could stall at a residual of 1e-7 because its Armijo test compared energy differences below round-off; near convergence it now takes the full Newton step (6 iterations to 3e-13 on the saturated iron ring).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The FEM solvers are 2-D (planar or axisymmetric for eddy_current_fdm), first order (P1), and resolve geometry on the mesh (polar grids are staircased in angle).
  • FDTD: uniform grids only. The sub-cell averaging is not the full anisotropic smoothing: curved surfaces with E normal to them keep an error of a few percent that does not converge (2 % on the Mie sphere below). The CPML is tuned for vacuum; inside dispersive or negative-permittivity media its reflection is not measured. Surface plasmon polaritons are verified only in closed form: an FDTD SPP run on a lossless Drude interface did not converge cleanly at affordable resolutions (4.9 % at 80 cells per wavelength), so no FDTD SPP number is claimed. NumPy, single thread: a 60^3 grid takes 19 ms per step with PEC walls and 38 ms with CPML on all sides (measured in the development container).
  • The differential compiler kinds do not differentiate material maps: jumps of eps, mu or nu are only seen by the integral kinds.
  • maxwell_checks uses central differences on tensor grids: fields with discontinuities (material interfaces, PEC edges) leave residuals there that are not errors of the field; crop them or check each region separately.
  • Machines: 2-D FEA; end effects as corrections (end-winding inductance from thin filaments, magnet end leakage as one 3-D no-load ratio applied through the remanence, not a coupled 3-D solution at load); skew by multi-slice, without inter-segment axial flux; magnets at a uniform temperature, iron loss from B waveforms with the elliptic-to-alternating split (no minor loops, no rotational-loss data), magnet eddy loss resistance-limited (valid while the skin depth exceeds the magnet size). The Bertotti fit to the M400-50A table has measured errors (see the notes above); the table model is exact at the catalogue points only.
  • Thermal: a lumped network whose material, contact and heat-transfer data are illustrative defaults, not measured or fitted to a Prius; one temperature per node (no hot spot inside the slot, magnets uniform). Hcj(T) is the grade minimum with an assumed -0.55 %/K coefficient. The demagnetisation check is static, a square-loop knee test on the 2-D field (no recoil-line modelling, no partial demagnetisation of later operation). The worst-element ratio does not converge under mesh refinement (field singular at the sharp magnet corners), so only area fractions are reported as results. The short-circuit peak 2 psi_pm / L_d is an estimate, not a transient simulation.
  • Drive: steady state only (no current-controller dynamics, no PWM ripple or harmonics losses), no inverter, mechanical or battery losses; the voltage limit is that of linear space-vector modulation.
  • JilesAtherton is the scalar model; its parameters must be fitted to measured loops of the material. illustrative_steel is a formula, not a measured grade.

docs.title: Engineering Design Optimizer (app, day 17)
docs.text:
Black-box design optimisation within physical and manufacturing limits, with the chosen candidates confirmed by a high-fidelity model. Live at https://optimize.pinneapple.org; source and deployment notes in apps/engineering_optimizer.

Input design variables (or a ParameterSpace), objectives, constraints, and an evaluation model: the heat-sink example (zoo surrogate or closed form), a table of designs you evaluated (GP surrogate with held-out error), a pp.zoo model (ModelRef URI zoo:<name>), or an operator-configured solver Methods NSGA-II (library and pymoo), SciPy differential evolution, Bayesian optimisation, Latin-hypercube baseline; optional active learning against the reference Output candidates along the Pareto front with a verification status, trade-off and convergence plots, feasibility report (active constraints, margins), surrogate vs reference errors, CSV / ParameterSpace / ModelRef / StudyResult files

The engine is the library: Design studies. The same problem through Python:

from pinneapple_design.design_optimizer import problem_from_spec, reference_for_spec, run, verify_candidates
from pinneapple_design.design_optimizer import select_candidates

spec = {"source": "preset", "preset": "heatsink", "objectives": [{"name": "mass_g"}, {"name": "cost"}]}
problem, _ = problem_from_spec(spec)
res = run(problem, "nsga2", budget=600)
report = verify_candidates(problem, res.evaluations, select_candidates(res.evaluations, res.pareto(), 5),
                           reference_for_spec(spec))

Limits. Candidates are optimal for the search model; only those the reference re-evaluated are "verified". The heat-sink example assumes ducted laminar flow and no radiation, and its cost model is a placeholder for your numbers. A surrogate from your data is valid inside the range of the data only.

docs.title: Engineering GUI agent: run engineering software and keep the evidence
docs.text: pinneapple_tools.automation runs a task in engineering software (FreeCAD, CfdOF, OpenFOAM, ParaView) and delivers the files plus a record of what happened: every command, log, screenshot, produced file (with its SHA-256) and check, in an HTML evidence report and a StudyResult (the data contract the apps share). Think of it as Selenium for computational engineering: the application's own API first, the GUI only when there is no API, and a screenshot of each GUI step either way.

docs.title: The committed example: channel with an obstacle
docs.text:
pinneapple_tools/automation/examples/channel_obstacle/ holds a parametric FreeCAD project (a 400 mm long, 100 mm high, 50 mm wide air channel with an obstacle on its floor, every dimension an alias of a spreadsheet), a macro that changes a parameter, and the workflow:

# Step Action How 1 Open the FreeCAD project freecad.open FreeCAD Python inside the FreeCAD GUI on a virtual display; window found with xdotool, screen captured 2 Set the obstacle height freecad.macro the committed .FCMacro sets the alias, recomputes, checks the volume against the parameters, saves a new file 3 Prepare the CFD case cfdof.setup CfdOF's Python API: laminar steady incompressible air, velocity inlet, pressure outlet, walls, gmsh mesh 4 Mesh openfoam.mesh CfdOF's Allmesh (gmsh, gmshToFoam), then checkMesh; checks "Mesh OK" and that the mesh is in metres 5 Solve openfoam.solve simpleFoam via CfdOF's Allrun; asks for confirmation (expensive); checks end reached and convergence 6 Post-process paraview.export pvpython: velocity and pressure of every cell to CSV, |U| on the mid-plane to PNG 7 Verify verify.criteria the acceptance criteria below, computed from the result files

Acceptance criteria, each computed from the OpenFOAM files with pinneapple_check's finite-volume reader: converged (residual control 1e-4), outlet flow equals inlet flow within 1 %, inflow equals the prescribed velocity times the inlet area within 1 %, pressure drop below an illustrative 0.01 Pa design limit, velocity exported.

Measured on FreeCAD 1.0.2, CfdOF 1.37.3, OpenFOAM v1912, gmsh 4.13.1, ParaView 5.11.2 (4 CPU cores), inlet 20 mm/s:

Obstacle height Cells Iterations Inflow (m³/s) Mass imbalance Pressure drop Decision 25 mm 20 193 119 1.000e-4 1e-8 1.9 mPa ACCEPTED 55 mm (default) 19 370 162 1.000e-4 5e-9 3.5 mPa ACCEPTED 80 mm 18 618 223 1.000e-4 7e-9 14.1 mPa (14.3 in the Docker run) REJECTED by the 0.01 Pa limit

The whole workflow takes about 30 s (FreeCAD start-up included). gmsh meshes with several threads, so the cell count changes by a few hundred between runs of the same input (19 370 and 19 588 for 55 mm); the decisions did not.

from pinneapple_tools.automation import Runner, Workflow, example_workflow

wf = Workflow.load(example_workflow("channel_obstacle"))
run = Runner(wf, "runs/r1", inputs={"obstacle_height_mm": 55}).run()
print(run.state)                     # awaiting_confirmation: the solver step is "expensive"
run = Runner(wf, "runs/r1").run(approve=["solve"], approver="j.doe")
print(run.state, run.message)        # passed / rejected, with the criteria that failed
# runs/r1/report.html, runs/r1/study_result.json, runs/r1/run.json, and every step's files and logs

docs.title: What the agent found while building the example
docs.text:
These are the reasons the checks exist; each was found by a real run and is now handled and recorded.

  • The mesh stayed in millimetres. CfdOF picks the transformPoints syntax from FOAM_API, which OpenFOAM v1912 does not set. The mesh step edits the test in Allmesh and records the edit; the "mesh is in metres" check compares the checkMesh bounding box with the expected size.
  • The solver diverged after potential-flow initialisation. On v1912, potentialFoam -initialiseUBCs wrote outlet velocities of hundreds of m/s and simpleFoam stopped with a floating-point exception. The run stopped at the solve step with the solver's stack trace in the report. The example now starts from a uniform field.
  • The inflow was 6 % lower than prescribed. CfdOF's velocity inlet (fixedNormalInletOutletVelocity) did not hold the prescribed flux on v1912: the outlet balanced the inlet perfectly, so a mass-balance check alone passed, but the inflow was 9.41e-5 m³/s instead of 1.00e-4. The inflow criterion rejected the run; the solve step now writes the inlet as fixedValue on ESI releases before v2006 and records the edit.
  • A bug in pinneapple check's per-patch fluxes. FV.patch_sums read past the end of the boundary arrays the balances pass it, so every patch total was 0 (only the net balance was right). Fixed, with a test.

docs.title: The app: guiagent.pinneapple.org
docs.text:
apps/guiagent (port 8115) puts the library behind a web page and a REST API. You:

  1. type a task, or pick the workflow and its inputs;
  2. watch the step timeline fill with checks and screenshots;
  3. approve or decline the solver step;
  4. download the evidence report, the StudyResult and the run as a zip.

Runs execute in the shared job queue of apps/_shared (one at a time; others wait), belong to the caller and are metered in runs, compute seconds and storage. The public server runs only the committed workflows. Uploading your own workflows, projects and macros is for self-hosted mode (GUIAGENT_MODE=selfhosted), because a macro is code. The Docker image is separate and optional (FreeCAD, CfdOF, OpenFOAM, ParaView, Xvfb); see apps/deploy/README.md.

Waiting for approval before the solver A finished run (80 mm obstacle, rejected by the pressure-drop limit)

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text:
Module What it does workflow Workflow (YAML/JSON): inputs with bounds, steps (action, params, after, requires, expects, confirm), criteria, limits. Templates {inputs.x}, {steps.id.output}, {example}, {workdir}. validate() lists every problem. interpret interpret(task, catalog(), llm=None): a sentence ("obstacle height 5.5 cm at 3 cm/s") picks a committed workflow and sets its inputs (units converted, bounds checked); a dict or JSON/YAML is validated as is. An OllamaClient (pinneapple_data.formfill.llm) is optional and goes through the same validation. A sentence can never add steps or run code. adapters freecad.open, freecad.macro, cfdof.setup (FreeCAD GUI on Xvfb), openfoam.mesh, openfoam.solve (command line), paraview.export (pvpython), verify.criteria, web.capture (Playwright). register() adds your own. display VirtualDisplay (Xvfb, screenshots with Pillow), XdotoolDriver, PlaywrightDriver, and PywinautoDriver: the interface for Windows GUIs (Ansys Workbench, Abaqus/CAE), documented but not runnable in a Linux container. runner Runner(workflow, folder, inputs).run(approve=[...]): stops on the first failure, on a missing application (blocked) and before any step that needs confirmation (expensive, overwrite, destructive, external). A step whose expected files already exist counts as an overwrite. Runs resume from run.json. plan() says what a run would need without running it. verify mass_balance, inflow, pressure_drop, patch_fluxes, patch_mean on OpenFOAM results (pinneapple_check.fv); criteria converged, artifact, physics_lint (pinneapple check). report write_report (one HTML file with images embedded), to_study_result: a pinneapple_data.contracts.StudyResult (study_type="runs", checks and criteria as CheckRecord, files as FileRef with SHA-256, limits, provenance), the contract the Evidence Report app reads. runner_step register() adds the step kind guiagent to the Simulation Workflow Runner (pinneapple_core.workflows): one runner step runs a committed workflow with inputs and the confirmations it is given in approve, and outputs its verdict, criteria and metrics. available() names the missing applications.

A step is passed only if its action returned, every check it produced held and every file it was expected to leave exists. Images are labelled with what they are: screen (the virtual display), window (one window or the 3D view cut from the screen), render (exported by the application), plot (drawn from a log).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: FreeCAD 1.0 (the AppImage, extracted), the CfdOF workbench (~/.local/share/FreeCAD/Mod/CfdOF), OpenFOAM (the Ubuntu openfoam package), ParaView with pvpython, Xvfb and xdotool. Toolchain.discover() finds them, or set PINNEAPPLE_FREECAD, PINNEAPPLE_CFDOF, FOAM_BASHRC, PINNEAPPLE_GMSH, PINNEAPPLE_PVPYTHON. Without them the workflow model, interpretation, runner, criteria and report still work (and are tested); the application steps report blocked.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One application chain and one workflow so far. SALOME (scriptable geometry and meshing, GUI actions recorded as Python) is the next adapter; ParaView-only post-processing workflows (a .foam or .vtu in, fields and images out) need only paraview.export and are the cheapest to add.
  • Laminar, steady, one mesh, no mesh-independence study: the pressure drop is a mesh-dependent estimate.
  • The GUI is driven through FreeCAD's Python inside its GUI; xdotool finds and observes windows. Pixel-level clicking is supported by XdotoolDriver but not used by the example, because an API exists.
  • pywinauto workflows (Windows applications) are an interface only here.

docs.title: Predicting El Niño: physical, physics-informed, data-driven and hybrid models under one protocol
docs.text:
This guide compares families of forecasts of the Niño-3.4 sea-surface-temperature (SST) anomaly at leads of 1 to 24 months:

  • conceptual physics: the recharge oscillator and the delayed oscillator;
  • an intermediate coupled ocean–atmosphere model: an equatorial shallow-water ocean, a Gill atmosphere and an SST equation;
  • physics-informed networks (PINNs);
  • data-driven models, including a CNN on SST maps in the spirit of Ham et al. (2019);
  • hybrids: physics plus learned correction, data assimilation with an ensemble Kalman filter, and ensembles.

Every model runs under one protocol, and the guide reports how much skill each one has, measured against the baselines. Every number below is read from the committed results.

Everything comes from one script, examples/enso_forecasting/run_study.py. * Its results are in examples/enso_forecasting/results/: * study.json: the merged zoo, the ENSO scores and the case studies; * tables.md: generated from the JSON, the source of every table below; * data.json, solver_checks.json, spring_barrier.json, phase.json and shallow_water_pinn.json; * manifests/: the URL and SHA-256 of every downloaded source file. * The figures are in examples/enso_forecasting/figures/. * The library code is pinneapple_systems.time_series.enso, tested in tests/test_enso.py. The protocol, baselines, tests and generic forecasters are the ones of forecast_lab; see the near-random forecasting guide.

In short (test period: origins 2012–2022, targets to 2024-12; every number from results/):

  • Best at short leads. At 1–6 months the best models are close together. They are:
  • the recharge oscillator with seasonal coefficients and multiplicative noise (15 fitted numbers);
  • the LIM;
  • the SST-map CNN, with and without pre-training;
  • the multi-model ensemble. At lead 6 their anomaly correlation (ACC) is 0.58–0.70, against 0.36 for persistence and 0.42 for ARIMA.
  • Significance.
  • Against climatology (one-sided DM, Holm across the 23 non-baseline models), every model is significantly better at leads 1–2 only. From lead 3 on, no model is distinguishable from climatology on this test period.
  • Against the best baseline chosen on validation, after Holm correction across the 30-model zoo, only three models are significantly better: the ensemble and the pre-trained CNN (leads 1–3) and the CNN (lead 1).
  • Against persistence, many models have positive RMSE skill at every lead (up to 0.31 at lead 6). The one-sided Diebold–Mariano tests on 132 overlapping monthly forecasts have little power beyond a few months.
  • Beyond about 9 months. No model keeps ACC above 0.5. At 12–24 months the best ACC is 0.30–0.42. The forecasts are close to climatology: CRPS skill against climatology is below 0.07 for every family representative beyond lead 9.
  • Spring barrier. The ACC of forecasts that target June–August collapses at lead 6, to 0.06 for persistence (cross-validated hindcasts 1985–2009). The seasonal recharge oscillator keeps 0.64 there; the constant one keeps 0.50.
  • PINNs.
  • The PINN that identifies the recharge oscillator fails on the observations: F2 ≈ 100 instead of 1.3, and lead-3 ACC −0.69.
  • Fitting a PINN per origin and extrapolating matches integrating the same equations. It adds nothing.
  • The equatorial shallow-water PINN recovers the wave speed from synthetic data (2.76 vs 2.7 m/s) but not the damping or the boundary reflection, and leaves large PDE residuals.
  • The physical intermediate model. It reproduces the observed thermocline tilt when forced by observed winds (r = 0.85). But its fitted coupled version is too damped: Niño-3.4 standard deviation 0.12 K in a free stochastic run, against 0.87 K observed. As a forecaster it is no better than ARIMA. Its EnKF ensemble is badly under-dispersed: 17 % of the targets fall inside the central 95 % interval at lead 6.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from pinneapple_systems.time_series.enso import dataset, forecasters as F, study
from pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab.study import evaluate

ds = dataset.build_dataset()                     # first call streams ~92 GB of source files, keeps ~0.2 GB
data = dataset.to_series(ds)                     # columns: nino34, wwv, h_west, h_east, nino4, nino3, nino12
prot = study.protocol(ds.months)                 # test period from 2012-01, leads 1-12, 15, 18, 21, 24
split = prot.final_split(len(data))
ro = F.RechargeOscillatorForecaster(seasonal=("R", "F1", "F2", "eps"), multiplicative=True)
ro.fit(data, split["train"], split["val"], prot.horizons)
print(evaluate(ro, data, split["test"])["rmse"])
res = study.run_model("lim", data, prot)         # tuning by purged walk-forward CV, test scores, DM tests

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
All sources are public, openly licensed and need no credentials.

The NOAA servers that publish the usual index files cannot be reached from the environment where this study ran: * CPC: sstoi.indices, ONI, SOI; * PSL; * PMEL's WWV file.

The same NOAA data were taken instead from NOAA's open-data buckets on AWS. ERA5 came from WeatherBench 2 on Google Cloud.

Every file is hashed. Its SHA-256 and URL are in a manifest, committed as results/manifests/*.json.gz. Passing those manifests (the script does) makes a download that does not reproduce a recorded hash fail. Raw files are reduced and deleted; their hashes stay.

quantity source how it is used SST, Niño 3.4 / 3 / 4 / 1+2 NOAA OISST v2.1 AVHRR-only daily 0.25° (Huang et al. 2021, J. Climate 34:2923; DOI 10.25921/RE9P-PT57), bucket noaa-cdr-sea-surface-temp-optimum-interpolation-pds, public domain every final (not preliminary) daily file of 1981-09 to 2026-09 (16 466 files), averaged per month into 1° cells over 30S–30N, 100E–60W; indices are cos-latitude-weighted box means; maps on the model grid (2° × 1°, 20S–20N, 120E–80W) thermocline (20 °C isotherm depth, D20) World Ocean Database (Boyer et al. 2018, NOAA Atlas NESDIS 87), bucket noaa-wod-pds, public domain: moored buoys (TAO/TRITON), XBT and Argo profiles D20 of every quality-controlled cast (flags 0) in 8S–8N, binned into 10° longitude bins (130E–80W) per month for 5S–5N and 2S–2N; anomalies; empty bins filled month by month from the observed bins with the 4 leading EOFs of the base period WWV proxy, tilt the 5S–5N D20 bins wwv = zonal mean D20 anomaly (the region of Meinen & McPhaden 2000, J. Climate 13:3551); h_west / h_east = means west / east of 155W wind stress, SOI proxy ERA5 (Hersbach et al. 2020, QJRMS 146:1999) 6-hourly on the 64 × 32 grid of WeatherBench 2 (Rasp et al. 2024, JAMES 16:e2023MS004019), gs://weatherbench2, Copernicus licence (free use and redistribution with attribution; contains modified Copernicus Climate Change Service information) bulk stress τ = ρ C_D |U| U (C_D = 1.3e-3) from every 6-hourly 10 m wind, monthly means 1959-01 to 2022-12; Tahiti–Darwin pressure index at the nearest cells cross-checks NCEI 0–700 m heat content, 3-month means 1955–2020 (Levitus et al. 2012, GRL 39:L10603; bucket noaa-cdr-ocean-heat-content-pds); the statsmodels El Niño data set (Niño 1+2 SST 1950–2010, NOAA CPC) correlations below

Not used, and why: * GODAS / ORAS5 thermocline fields. No credential-free route was reachable from here (PSL is blocked; the ORAS5 files on AWS are model initial conditions only). The thermocline comes from the in-situ casts instead. * The station SOI. The CPC file cannot be reached; the ERA5 pressure index is a proxy of it. * ERA5 after 2022-12. WeatherBench 2 stops at 2023-01-10. ERA5 enters only the fitting of the intermediate model (training years) and the analyses below, never a forecast input.

The record is 1982-01 to 2024-12 (516 months). It is limited by the World Ocean Database, whose 2024 files are the latest. Anomalies use the calendar-month climatology of 1982–2011, inside the development period, so the test period does not inform them.

Checks against independent sources (results/data.json): * Niño-3.4. OISST against ERA5 SST: r = 0.983, RMSE 0.17 K (492 months, 1982–2022). * Niño 1+2. OISST against the statsmodels CPC series: r = 0.994 (1982–2010), mean difference −0.22 K. The difference is in absolute SST: the two products differ in their analysis. * WWV proxy. Against the NCEI 0–700 m heat content of 5S–5N, 120E–80W (3-month means): r = 0.84 (156 seasons). * Pressure index. Niño-3.4 against the ERA5 Tahiti–Darwin index: r = −0.63. * Casts. 562 280 moored-buoy, 79 730 XBT and 197 197 Argo casts give D20. * On average 96 % of the 10° bins have a cast in a month. * Coverage is 69–82 % in 1982–1984 and 83 % in 2024 (the WOD 2024 files are incomplete). * In 2 months fewer than 4 bins were observed, and the previous month's values were carried forward. * Trend. Over 1982–2024 Niño-3.4 has a linear trend of +0.05 K per decade. The anomalies keep it, so the test period is slightly warm relative to the 1982–2011 base. Every model sees the same anomalies.

docs.title: The protocol
docs.text:
The protocol is forecast_lab's, unchanged (enso.study.protocol):

  • Test period: origins 2012-01 to 2022-12.
  • There are 132 origins, one per month, for leads 1–12, 15, 18, 21 and 24 months.
  • The test period is fixed before any tuning.
  • Its targets reach 2024-12, so they include the 2015/16 and 2023/24 El Niños.
  • Development period: 1982-01 to 2011-12.
  • It ends with a validation block of 30 origins, which is used for early stopping, for spread calibration and for choosing each family's representative.
  • Training labels stop 24 months (the largest lead) before that block. That leaves 247 training origins.
  • Every input needs 36 months of history.
  • Tuning. Each tuned model gets 4 configurations drawn from its grid. Each configuration is scored by purged walk-forward cross-validation on 3 folds.
  • Scores.
  • Anomaly correlation (ACC) per lead.
  • RMSE skill against persistence and against the best baseline: at each lead, the baseline with the lowest validation RMSE among persistence, climatology, AR, ARIMA, exponential smoothing, seasonal naive and the phase-aligned mean cycle.
  • CRPS skill against climatology, central-interval coverage and PIT.
  • One-sided Diebold–Mariano tests (HLN correction, long-run variance over the h-step overlap) against persistence and against the best baseline, Holm-adjusted across the zoo at each lead.
  • Skill by target calendar month.
  • Categorical scores: El Niño ≥ +0.5 K, La Niña ≤ −0.5 K, monthly Niño-3.4.
  • One process per model. forecast_lab.study.merge_zoo pools the per-model results. It recomputes every comparison over the whole zoo, so the Holm adjustment covers all models together (tested to equal a single run in tests/test_enso.py).

docs.title: The models
docs.text:
family model (enso.study.zoo) what it is baseline persistence, climatology, AR (AIC), ARIMA, exponential smoothing, seasonal naive, phase-aligned mean cycle forecast_lab data GBM, MLP, LSTM, TCN, transformer forecast_lab lag models on all seven indices data lim linear inverse model (Penland & Sardeshmukh 1995, J. Climate 8:1999) on 6, 10 or 15 SST EOFs plus WWV or the west/east D20, analytic Gaussian forecast data cnn CNN on the last 3 or 6 SST anomaly maps (pooled to 4° × 2°) plus the D20 indices and the season, 5 seeds averaged; the design of Ham et al. (2019), much smaller data + physics cnn_pretrained the same CNN, first trained on a 300-year stochastic run of the intermediate model fitted to the training years only, then fine-tuned on the observations data + physics pinn_ro, pinn_ro_closure recharge oscillator identified by a PINN on the training years (pinn.identify_recharge, via pinneapple_neural's InversePINN), without / with a learned closure g(h) of the thermocline feedback; forecasts integrate the identified equations data + physics pinn_extrapolation for every origin, a PINN fitted to the last 24 months and to the recharge-oscillator residual up to 24 months ahead; the forecast is the network beyond the data (one grouped network for all origins) data + physics mlp_physics_loss, gbm_physics_features forecast_lab's physics-residual MLP and physics-feature GBM on (T, h) with the recharge oscillator physical ro, ro_stochastic, ro_seasonal_multiplicative Jin's (1997) recharge oscillator on (Niño-3.4, WWV), deterministic, stochastic (200-member Euler–Maruyama), and with annual cycles in all four coefficients plus multiplicative noise σ(1 + B T) physical ro_multiple_shooting the same equations fitted by forecast_lab's ODE forecaster (multiple shooting) physical delayed_oscillator Battisti–Hirst dT/dt = aT − bT(t − τ) − cT³ on Niño-3.4, τ tuned in {3, 6, 9, 12} months physical im_nudged the intermediate coupled model (below), initialised by nudging its SST to the observed maps (5-day time scale) along the whole record hybrid ro+gbm, ude_ro recharge oscillator + GBM residual correction; universal differential equation (recharge oscillator + neural closure trained through the integrator) hybrid im_enkf the intermediate model with a localised stochastic EnKF (24 members, Gaspari–Cohn localisation 25° × 8°) assimilating the monthly SST maps and the observed D20 bins; 10-member forecasts with stochastic winds hybrid ensemble equal-weight mixture of the seasonal recharge oscillator, the LIM and a GBM

Prior knowledge given to the physical models: * the form of the equations; * starting guesses that are not the answer; * the ocean's wave speed c = 2.7 m/s and damping 1/(900 days). These are fixed, not fitted, in the intermediate model.

Every coefficient that is estimated, is estimated from the training years only.

docs.title: The intermediate coupled model
docs.text:
enso.intermediate is a model in the spirit of Zebiak & Cane (1987, Mon. Wea. Rev. 115:2262), simplified:

  • Ocean.
  • A linear reduced-gravity shallow-water ocean on the equatorial β-plane, on an Arakawa C-grid of 2° × 1°.
  • The domain is 120E–80W, 20S–20N, with walls east and west and 5° sponges north and south.
  • Time stepping is RK4 with an 8-hour step.
  • Atmosphere. Gill's (1980) steady damped long-wave response to a heating proportional to the SST anomaly, solved exactly per meridional mode by FFT on the whole longitude circle (ε = 0.1, c_a = 60 m/s). The linear map SST → stress is stored as a truncated SVD.
  • Coupling. μ, the stress per unit Gill wind, is fitted by least squares of the ERA5 zonal stress anomalies on the Gill winds of the observed SST.
  • SST equation. dT/dt = −ε_T T + γ(x) S(y) h + κ(x) S(y) τ_x, with S(y) = exp(−(y/6°)²). ε_T, γ and κ are regressed per longitude on the observed equatorial SST, the observed D20 and the model's own stress.
  • Amplitude factor. h_scale converts model h to D20. It comes from the ocean forced by ERA5 stress over the training years.

What the fit gives on the training years (study.json, model_info.im_nudged): * Coupling. μ = 0.0055 N m⁻² per unit Gill wind. The Gill winds of the observed SST explain 28 % of the ERA5 zonal-stress variance over 10S–10N. * Stochastic forcing. The standard deviation of the residual stress is 0.011 N m⁻². * Ocean alone, forced by ERA5 stress (the ocean hindcast): * its equatorial h correlates with the observed 2S–2N D20 at 0.49–0.79 per 10° bin; * the east-minus-west tilt correlates at 0.85 and the zonal mean (WWV) at 0.65; * the fitted amplitude factor is 1.22. * SST equation. * The damping ε_T is 0.29–0.48 per month (2–3.5 months). * The thermocline feedback γ rises from about 0 in the west to 0.026 K m⁻¹ per month in the east. * The wind feedback κ is 10–28 K per (N m⁻²) per month. * The coupled model with these coefficients is strongly damped. A 300-year stochastic run (6 members × 50 years) has a Niño-3.4 standard deviation of 0.12 K, against 0.87 K observed. The intermediate model is therefore a weak oscillator. The CNN pre-trained on its run learns from far too little ENSO variability (see section 2).

docs.title: 1. The solvers are right
docs.text:
pipeline.solver_checks, results/solver_checks.json, figure figures/solver_checks.png:

check measured theory Kelvin wave speed (2.5° × 1°, 6 h) 2.689 m/s c = 2.7 m/s −0.42 % Kelvin crossing time 120E–80W 76.6 days 76.3 days Kelvin speed error, dlon 5 → 2.5 → 1.25° (dlat, dt with it) −1.60 %, −0.42 %, −0.11 % observed order 1.93, 1.98 long Rossby (n = 1) speed −0.863 m/s −c/3 = −0.9 m/s −4.1 % (a finite-width packet is slower than the long-wave limit) Gill response vs closed form (ε = 0.1, heating half-width 2 L_a), relative L2 of u / v / p 72 points: 1.5e-3 / 3.7e-2 / 1.1e-3; 576 points: 5.2e-5 / 1.4e-3 / 3.2e-5 0 easterlies east (u = −0.98) and westerlies west (u = +1.27) of the heating, off-equatorial Rossby lows recharge oscillator (R = −0.05, F1 = 0.02, F2 = 1.5, ε = 0.03 per month), RK4 1 step per month period 36.3367, growth −0.040000 36.3366 months, −0.04 per month relative errors 1.8e-6 and 3.4e-5 delayed oscillator (a = 1/6, b = 1/3, τ = 6 months), RK4 with dt = 1 → 0.1 month period error 1.7e-4 → 1.6e-6, growth error −7.6e-3 → −7.6e-5 Lambert-W root 0.0782 ± 0.1888i per month (period 33.28 months) second order

The v error of the Gill check converges more slowly than u and p. The closed-form v needs the x-derivative of the Rossby amplitude, which is taken by finite differences of the quadrature result, and it has kinks at the edges of the heating.

docs.title: 2. Skill against lead
docs.text:
Anomaly correlation (ACC) of the family representatives on the test period:

lead (months) 1 3 6 9 12 18 24 persistence 0.93 0.73 0.36 0.08 0.01 −0.14 −0.36 ARIMA (best baseline on validation, leads 2–6) 0.93 0.76 0.42 0.06 0.02 0.12 0.21 recharge oscillator, seasonal + multiplicative noise (physical) 0.95 0.84 0.63 0.39 0.30 0.35 0.42 LIM 0.95 0.88 0.67 0.44 0.29 0.02 −0.00 CNN (data) 0.95 0.87 0.70 0.50 0.26 0.41 0.30 CNN pre-trained on the intermediate model 0.95 0.85 0.66 0.45 0.30 0.35 0.08 ensemble (RO seasonal + LIM + GBM; hybrid) 0.95 0.84 0.58 0.36 0.20 0.01 0.02 intermediate model + EnKF 0.93 0.78 0.48 0.24 0.16 0.02 0.14 intermediate model, SST-nudged 0.93 0.73 0.36 −0.00 0.09 0.23 0.20

What the zoo shows:

  • The ranking is close at short leads. The two CNNs have the best RMSE skill against persistence at leads 1–3 (0.16–0.30). The seasonal recharge oscillator and the LIM are within 0.06 of them. At lead 6 the seasonal recharge oscillator is best (0.31), with the LIM and the pre-trained CNN at 0.30.
  • Only three models pass the strict test. Against the best baseline chosen on validation, Holm-adjusted over the zoo, they are:
  • the ensemble, leads 1–3;
  • the pre-trained CNN, leads 1–3;
  • the CNN, lead 1. The seasonal recharge oscillator has positive skill against the best baseline at every lead (0.09 to 0.50), but no DM test reaches significance.
  • "Best baseline" is misleading beyond lead 6.
  • From lead 7 on, the baseline with the lowest validation RMSE was the seasonal naive forecast: the value one dominant period before, with the period estimated from the training periodogram.
  • The validation block (30 origins, 2007–2010) happens to suit it. On the test period it is the worst baseline, with RMSE skill −0.23 at lead 9 and −0.05 at lead 18.
  • Every model therefore shows a jump of RMSE skill "against the best baseline" at lead 7 in the figure. That jump says nothing about the models.
  • Against ARIMA and climatology (both in the zoo table), skill beyond lead 9 is small. The best models' RMSE skill against persistence at 12–24 months (0.29–0.38) is mostly that of climatology (0.25–0.34): damping towards zero.
  • The protocol is kept as it was fixed. A longer validation block would have chosen ARIMA or climatology. This is the main caveat of the comparison.
  • Data-hungry models stay at baseline level. With 247 training origins, GBM, MLP, LSTM, TCN and transformer have ACC 0.26–0.36 at lead 6, the level of persistence. The CNN does better because its inputs are the SST maps and the D20 indices, and the LIM does well for the same reason. Both are regularised: the CNN by weight decay and early stopping on 5 seeds, the LIM by being linear.
  • The physics feature does not help. GBM with recharge-oscillator features (the data + physics representative on validation) is no better than the plain GBM: ACC 0.27 vs 0.26 at lead 6, 0.00 vs 0.11 at lead 9. Its validation score (0.700, the best of its family) did not carry over.
  • The recharge-oscillator variants agree.
  • Least squares of integrated one-month predictions, forecast_lab's multiple-shooting ODE fit, the stochastic 200-member version and the UDE give the same scores to ±0.01.
  • The constant-coefficient fit has growth −0.066 per month and period 44 months.
  • The seasonal fit with multiplicative noise has period 50 months and B = −0.03 K⁻¹. That B is negligible: no measurable state dependence of the noise.
  • Probabilistic scores.
  • The ensemble has the flattest PIT (deviation 0.12) and 95 % coverage 0.95.
  • The seasonal recharge oscillator's own 200-member ensemble covers 0.88 (mean over leads).
  • The EnKF intermediate model's 10-member forecasts are far too narrow (0.17 at lead 6).
  • At lead 1, CRPS skill against climatology is 0.64–0.69 for all representatives. Beyond lead 9 it is below 0.07.

Representatives of each family (chosen on the validation block) and three baselines (persistence, climatology, ARIMA). Left: anomaly correlation (dotted line: 0.5). Middle: RMSE skill against climatology on the test period; filled markers where the one-sided DM test against climatology, Holm-adjusted across the non-baseline models at that lead, is significant at 5 % (pipeline.skill_against). The skill against the validation-chosen "best baseline" is not plotted, because that reference switches to the seasonal naive forecast at lead 7 (see below). It stays in the zoo table. Right: CRPS skill against climatology.

docs.title: 3. The spring predictability barrier
docs.text:
The test period has only 11 forecasts per (target month, lead) cell, too few to map the barrier. So the cheap models were also run as blocked, purged cross-validated hindcasts over the development period: * origins 1985–2009, 300 of them, 25 per cell; * each 4-year block is forecast by a model fitted on the other years; * 24 months are purged on both sides of each block; * the test period is never used.

The result: * Persistence collapses through the boreal spring. Its lead-6 ACC is 0.83 for January–March targets but 0.06 for June–August targets (origins in December–February). That is the barrier. * The recharge oscillator carries the thermocline memory across it. With constant coefficients it keeps 0.50 for June–August targets. With seasonal coefficients it keeps 0.64, and the LIM keeps 0.55. * The seasonal fit's barrier. Its growth rate R(s) is most negative in late boreal spring (around March–April): −0.077 − 0.031 cos(2πs/12) − 0.165 sin(2πs/12) per month, with s = 0 in January. The annual harmonics of F1, F2 and ε are fitted too. * The test period shows the same pattern, but noisily. For the test-period representatives, the 0.5 contour bends towards short leads for targets in May–August.

docs.title: 5. Case studies: 1997/98, 2015/16, 2023/24
docs.text:
The plume figure shows observed Niño-3.4 and the forecasts of the representatives (median of their predictive distributions).

1997/98 (peak 2.38 K, November 1997). The models were refitted on data whose labels end in 1993-06: the development data before 1997-01, with the last 15 % as validation and a 24-month purge. Median forecasts: * From February 1997 (before the onset; the spring barrier), every model predicted at most +0.52 K at lead 6 (August, observed +1.84 K) and at most +0.94 K at lead 9 (November, observed +2.38 K). The recharge oscillator and the ensemble were the highest. * From May 1997, for November the recharge oscillator gave +1.42 K, the ensemble +1.22 K, the GBM with physics features +1.19 K and the CNN +0.61 K. Observed: +2.38 K. * From August 1997 (already at +1.96 K), the median forecasts for November were +1.8 to +2.3 K. Only the recharge oscillator and the ensemble then turned the forecast towards La Niña, at leads 9–12 (+0.74 / +0.82 K at lead 9, observed +0.63 K). The CNN, the GBM and persistence stayed warm.

2015/16 (monthly peak 3.00 K, November 2015). * From May 2015, for November (lead 6): the CNN gave +2.05 K, the recharge oscillator +1.60 K, the ensemble +0.92 K and the physics-feature GBM +0.73 K. * From February 2015, all medians were at most +1.5 K at leads 3–9.

2023/24 (monthly peak 2.11 K, December 2023; 2.10 K in November). These origins lie after the test period; the models are those of the main test. * From May 2023, for November: the recharge oscillator +1.48 K, the CNN +1.21 K, the ensemble +0.91 K. * From February 2023: +0.09 to +0.85 K at lead 6 (observed +1.42 K).

In all three events the median forecasts underestimated the peak, from February origins by more than 1 K.

*Forecasts at leads 1, 3, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 24 months from the origin (dotted line), one colour per family representative: median marker, 50 % (thick) and 90 % (thin) intervals; observed Niño-3.4 in black; grey band ±0.5 K. Each panel title says whether its forecasts are out of sample: * 1997/98: "out-of-sample: refit, data to 1996-12". The models were refitted on data up to 1996-12 only (training labels to 1993-06, the rest as the validation block). No year from 1997 on entered the fit. * 2015/16: "out-of-sample: test period". * 2023/24: "out-of-sample: after the test period". These are the models fitted for the main test (training labels end in 2007).

No panel is in-sample.*

docs.title: 6. The recharge oscillator in phase space
docs.text:
• Observed phase relation. Over 1982–2024, h (the WWV proxy) leads T (Niño-3.4) by about 6 months:
  • corr(T(t + 6), h(t)) = 0.53;
  • corr(T(t − 9), h(t)) = −0.51, the discharge after the event.
  • Mean paths. Started from the observed state at four El Niño onsets (1997-04, 2009-06, 2015-03, 2023-04), both fitted oscillators turn clockwise in the (h, T) plane, as the observed loops do. But they decay: growth rate −0.066 / −0.076 per month, an e-folding time of 13–15 months. Their mean paths stay well inside the observed orbits.
  • Stochastic runs. One noise realisation of the record's length has a T standard deviation of 0.89 K (constant) and 0.80 K (seasonal), against 0.87 K observed. The h standard deviation is 9.0 and 8.7 m, against 7.7 m observed. In these fits ENSO is a damped oscillator sustained by noise: the noise amplitudes and the damping together reproduce the observed variance.

docs.title: 7. PINNs: what they learn and where they fail
docs.text:
Recharge-oscillator identification. pinn.identify_recharge trained a network X(t) on the 305 training months. The residual of the recharge-oscillator equations was penalised at 2048 random collocation points per step, for 4000 steps, with R, F1, F2 and ε learned. * The residual became small: RMS 0.045 / 0.038 of each variable's standard deviation per month. * The parameters are far from the least-squares estimates (R = −0.08, F1 = 0.015, F2 = 1.38, ε = 0.06). The PINN found R = −0.40, F1 = 0.003, F2 = 101, ε = −0.38. * The network fitted h (RMSE 0.67 m, against a standard deviation of about 9 m) but not T: RMSE 0.85 K, against a standard deviation of 0.87 K. The data are a noise-driven series, and a single smooth trajectory that satisfies a deterministic ODE cannot pass through them. * With the learned thermocline-feedback closure (pinn_ro_closure) the outcome is the same (F2 = 98). * As forecasters these identified equations are the worst models in the zoo: ACC −0.69 at lead 3. * An honest fit would need a weak-constraint formulation (a noise term in the residual, weighted by its variance) or multiple shooting. The least-squares fit of integrated one-month predictions is the latter, and it is what the physical models use.

PINN extrapolation (pinn_extrapolation): one PINN per origin, fitted to the last 24 months and to the recharge-oscillator residual up to 24 months ahead. * The residual in the forecast part is small: RMS 0.045–0.054 of the standard deviations, in the first chunks of origins. * The forecast is the integral of the same equations from a smoothed initial state. Its RMSE skill against persistence is within 0.03 of the recharge oscillator integrated by RK4 at every reported lead (ACC 0.54 vs 0.54 at lead 6). * It costs 114 s of training against well under a second of integration, and adds nothing.

Equatorial shallow-water PINN (shallow_water_pinn.json). This is the two-mode (Kelvin + first Rossby) long-wave ocean plus an equatorial SST equation with a learned thermocline-feedback closure g(x, h), over 1996–1999. It was trained with ERA5 forcing and a PDE weight of 100 (6000 steps, 4096 collocation points). * Synthetic data (the 2-D model forced by ERA5, true c = 2.7 m/s, damping 900 days, closed west wall): * the PINN recovered c = 2.76 m/s; * it did not recover the damping (43 days) or the west-wall reflection (a_W = 0.004 instead of the two-mode value 2); * the Kelvin-equation residual stayed at 2.6 times the typical tendency. The PINN fitted the data (r = 0.82) with a leaky, strongly damped basin instead of satisfying the wave equations. * Observations (D20 and SST at the 15 bins): * it fits the D20 with r = 0.70 (RMSE 15.8 m) and the SST with r = 0.97 (0.37 K); * c = 1.90 m/s (the first baroclinic mode is about 2.5–2.9 m/s); * damping 51 days and a_W = 0.02; * the Kelvin residual is 1.4 times the typical tendency. The SST part is well constrained: ε_T = 0.20 per month, κ = −1.8 K per (N m⁻²) per month. The learned closure g(x = 210E, h) is positive for deep thermocline anomalies (+0.66 K per month at h = +20 m) and for shallow ones (+0.68 K per month at h = −40 m). That is not physical for a thermocline feedback; the closure absorbs whatever the linear terms miss. * The 2-D model forced by the same ERA5 stress reproduces the observed D20 better than the PINN: r = 0.79 after a fitted amplitude factor of 1.46.

In short: * PINNs identified one parameter (the Kelvin speed, on synthetic data). * They did not identify the damping, the reflection or the recharge-oscillator coefficients from these data. * They forecast no better than the equations they encode. * Where they "fit", they did so by leaving the physics residual large.

Equatorial (2S–2N) anomalies against longitude and time, 1996–1999: * the observed D20 (TAO / XBT / Argo bins); * the 2-D shallow-water model forced by ERA5 stress, scaled by its fitted amplitude factor; * the equatorial-wave PINN's D20; * the observed SST; * the PINN's SST, with its learned thermocline-feedback closure.

docs.title: 8. 1997/98 in 3-D
docs.text: figures/enso_1997_98_slab.mp4 is the clip, 47 frames, January 1997 to December 1998, one interpolated frame between months. It was rendered with Blender Cycles through pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.render (enso.render, pipeline.slab_frames). * The slab covers 120E–80W and 20S–20N, with depths exaggerated (1 scene unit per 100 m). * Top surface (2S–20N): the observed monthly OISST SST. * Wall along 2S: the SST of that row, from the surface down to the thermocline. It is the southern face of a 4°-wide equatorial band, so the warm layer's thickness is visible. * Lower surface: the 20 °C isotherm, coloured by its depth anomaly. The scale is diverging, ±40 m, red = deeper, with its own colour bar at the bottom left. The surface is built from two parts: * the mean D20 of the casts over 1982–2011, in 2° × 10° bins; * plus the anomaly of the 2-D shallow-water model forced by ERA5 stress, scaled by its fitted amplitude factor. So the 3-D thermocline is model-assisted, not observed. * What it shows: compare January 1997 with December 1997. * The warm water spreads east along the equator. * In December 1997 the rendered thermocline at 2S–2N is 30–53 m deeper than normal east of 130W (red) and 21–34 m shallower west of 170W (blue): the tilt has flattened. The observed 2S–2N D20 anomalies that month are +34 to +44 m at 125W–95W and −32 to −48 m at 135E–175W. * The still above is December 1997. figures/enso_1997_01_slab.png is January 1997.

docs.title: Comparison with published systems
docs.text: No published skill number is quoted as checked here. * The study could not open the source of any of them from this environment: Nature, the IRI web site, NOAA CPC and PSL do not resolve or are refused by the network policy. * Ham et al. (2019, Nature 573:568) report an all-season Niño-3.4 correlation above 0.5 up to a lead of about 17 months, for a CNN pre-trained on CMIP5 runs and reanalysis. We could only read this claim in search-engine summaries, not in the paper, so the number, its validation period (said to be 1984–2017) and its definition of lead are not verified. * The study's own CNN, trained on 247 monthly samples of observations, drops below ACC 0.5 after lead 9. The pre-trained one does too: it was pre-trained on a weakly varying intermediate model, not on CMIP. * The IRI multi-model plume skill could not be checked.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One short test period. It has 132 monthly origins from 2012–2022: two strong El Niños and one long La Niña.
  • Consecutive forecasts overlap; the DM tests correct for that, but their power is low beyond a few months.
  • The target-month cells of the test period hold 11 forecasts each.
  • The best-baseline choice at leads ≥ 7 fell on the seasonal naive forecast, a validation-block accident (see section 2). Read skill against ARIMA, climatology and persistence there.
  • Thermocline data. The thermocline is the in-situ D20 binned along the equator, not an ocean reanalysis. Coverage is thin in 1982–1984 and in 2024, and the WWV proxy is not the PMEL product: no PMEL file could be reached.
  • The intermediate model is linear and strongly damped as fitted. It has no nonlinear advection, no mixed-layer physics and only one baroclinic mode. Its coupling and SST coefficients come from regressions on 1982–2007 data. A model tuned for self-sustained oscillation (as Zebiak and Cane did) might forecast differently. This study reports the regression-fitted one.
  • One seed and one configuration draw per model. The CNN averages 5 seeds; the others use one.
  • The ensemble is a fixed equal-weight mixture, not tuned.
  • ERA5 only to 2022-12. It is used only for fitting and for diagnostics, never as a forecast input.
  • No CMIP pre-training. The pre-training data come from the study's own fitted intermediate model.
  • Persistence and the anomaly base. Anomalies use a fixed 1982–2011 base. The +0.05 K per decade trend is not removed.

docs.title: Evidence ledger: a test passed only if it ran
docs.text:
A report that says "all checks passed" is only as good as the record behind it. pinneapple_veriphysics.ledger keeps that record. Each entry holds:

  • the check that ran;
  • the SHA-256 of its exact inputs;
  • its outputs;
  • start and finish times (UTC);
  • the verdict.

The entry is sealed with the SHA-256 of its own content. EvidenceLedger.status(check) returns "passed" or "failed" only for a complete entry that is still intact. Every other case returns "not run": no entry, a missing input hash, outputs or time, a crash, or an entry edited after it was sealed.

from pinneapple_veriphysics.ledger import EvidenceLedger, sha256_bytes

ledger = EvidenceLedger()
with ledger.run("energy-balance", inputs_sha256=sha256_bytes(b"field bytes"), tool="my-check") as rec:
    rec.outputs = {"imbalance": 2e-4}
    rec.passed = 2e-4 < 1e-3
assert ledger.status("energy-balance") == "passed"
assert ledger.status("mass-balance") == "not run"

docs.title: Validation Lab: three groups, one record per check
docs.text:
pinneapple_veriphysics.validation_lab.run_validation(folder) runs pinneapple check on the inputs of a folder. It reports the outcomes in three separate groups:

Group Question Rules Numerical verification Were the equations solved right? PC3xx residuals, PC403 finite values, PC8xx artefact integrity, PC901 method status, PC001 readable inputs Validation against data Does it match trusted reference data, inside the range the data covers? PC7xx reference regression and QoIs, PC6xx out-of-range use, PC452/PC453 dataset diversity and leakage Physical consistency Conservation, boundary and initial conditions, constraints, units PC1xx, PC2xx, PC401/PC402 bounds, PC5xx units, PC451 dataset physics

The report lists, per target, the groups in which no check ran. Each outcome becomes a ledger entry. The inputs hash of an entry combines the target's files, its reference and the configuration. The report also holds the manifest of every input file with its hash, and the configuration itself, so pinneapple check --config pinneapple-check.toml reproduces the run.

config_from_spec writes that configuration from a plain description of predictions, physics, units, bounds, boundary conditions, reference and tolerances. assert_no_code refuses models that would import or unpickle uploaded code; zoo models are allowed.

No single test guarantees that a model represents reality, and neither does this set of tests. The report says so.

docs.title: Evidence report and package
docs.text:
pinneapple_veriphysics.evidence_package reads other tools' outputs and builds a report:

  • Validation Lab reports;
  • ledgers;
  • pinneapple check --json;
  • Simulation Comparator results;
  • StudyResult / ModelRef / DatasetSpec JSON;
  • metrics tables;
  • any other file, by hash.

The report has a methodology, conditions, a baseline comparison, tests, limitations and references to every artifact by SHA-256. It renders as HTML or PDF (with pinneapple_tools.reporting.paperkit), and build_package writes a zip whose MANIFEST.json holds the hash of every file. verify_package checks the zip against that manifest.

Records are matched per source. A test from a source that only claims a pass (a pinneapple check JSON, a StudyResult with tests but no evidence) is printed as "not run", with the claim beside it. The same holds when another run used the same check id. The tests in tests/pinneapple_veriphysics/test_evidence_ledger.py enforce this.

The Engineering Evidence Report (day 30) is built on these modules. The Physics Validation Lab (day 24) is built on these modules.

docs.title: Flight dynamics, turbulence and take-off
docs.text:
pinneapple_simulation.flight flies a rigid aircraft in six degrees of freedom. The wing and tail loads come from the library's vortex lattice (pinneapple_design.aero.vlm), solved again at every step with the local air velocity at each panel. The other parts are thrust, gravity, landing-gear contact with the runway, MIL-F-8785C / MIL-HDBK-1797 turbulence and gusts, trim, a simple pilot / autopilot, and animated 3-D scenes for the browser viewer and Blender.

from pinneapple_simulation import flight

ac = flight.catalog.build("a320")                  # light_ga, regional_turboprop, a320, motor_glider
tr = flight.trim(ac, V=128.0, altitude=3000.0)     # alpha, elevator, throttle for steady level flight
d = flight.stability_derivatives(ac, tr)           # CL_alpha, Cm_q, Cl_p, Cn_beta, ... and the static margin

hist = flight.simulate_takeoff(ac)                 # brake release -> V_R -> lift-off -> 400 ft
m = flight.takeoff_metrics(ac, hist)               # ground roll, V_LOF, theta, distance to 35 ft, climb gradient
cf = flight.raymer_takeoff(ac)                     # closed-form estimate with the same aircraft model

spec = flight.turbulence_spec(3000.0, "severe")    # von Karman, MIL-F-8785C intensities and scale lengths
hist, metrics, *_ = flight.turbulence_encounter(ac, 128.0, 3000.0, spec, duration=60.0)

from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.web import web_viewer
web_viewer(flight.visuals.flight_scene(ac, hist), "viewer/")   # time slider, gust arrows, wing loading, HUD

Every number on this page was produced by the scripts in examples/flight_dynamics/ and is stored in examples/flight_dynamics/results/*.json. The tables are filled from those files by 06_tables.py. Where an input is an assumption, it is listed as one in Aircraft.info["assumptions"] and below.

The component masses are the wing (the Raymer general-aviation or transport equation, as the aero optimizer uses them), the tails, engines, fuel, payload or occupants, and the fuselage and systems. Assumptions, per aircraft, are in results/stability.json (info.assumptions). The main ones:

  • Take-off CLmax is 1.6 (GA, flaps 10°), 2.1 (turboprop, flaps 15°), 2.0 (A320 class, CONF 1+F) and 1.45 (glider). These values set V_R and the stall margin and are not computed.
  • Flaps are modelled as a rotation of the panel normals by tau·delta on the flapped strips. Tau is the thin-airfoil flap effectiveness × 0.85. Slats are not modelled.
  • The gear positions are taken from the geometry where it has gear (ATR 72 entry). On the A320 class they are chosen so the nose gear carries ~7 % of the weight. On the light aircraft the mains sit at a 15° tip-back angle.
  • Tyre rolling friction is 0.02.
  • Propellers have efficiency 0.80 (0.75 on the glider) and a static figure of merit of 0.70.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Rigid body. - Axes: earth NED, body x forward / y right / z down. - State: position, body velocity, a unit quaternion for the attitude, and body rates. Euler angles are only an output, and quat_to_euler stays finite at θ = ±90°. - Equations: x' = C v, v' = F/m − ω × v, ω' = I⁻¹(M − ω × Iω). - Integration: RK4 with the quaternion renormalised after each step.

Aerodynamics (quasi-steady vortex lattice in the loop). - At every evaluation, the relative air velocity at each control point (flight velocity, ω × r, and the wind sampled per spanwise strip) sets the right-hand side of the lattice. - The influence matrix depends only on the geometry, so it is LU-factorised once. - Forces come from Kutta-Joukowski on the bound legs with the local velocity. Lift, pitching moment, pitch and roll damping, downwash at the tail and the dihedral effect therefore all come from one model. So does the rolling moment of a gust that differs from one wing to the other. - Control surfaces rotate their panels' normals (elevator, ailerons, flaps). - Added by build-up: - the fin as a lifting line, with the Helmbold lift slope at 1.55 × its aspect ratio and the rudder through tau; - the fuselage Munk moments in pitch and yaw (Raymer eqs. 16.25, 16.47); - zero-lift drag, gear and flap drag; - induced drag, with McCormick's ground-effect factor at the wing height.

Engines. - Turbofan: Mattingly's high-bypass lapse T/T_SL = δ₀(1 − 0.49 √M). - Propeller: T = ηP/√(V² + V₀²), so T equals the momentum-theory static thrust at rest and ηP/V in flight.

Gear. Each leg is a vertical spring-damper with a rolling resistance μN and a tyre side force that saturates at the friction limit. The nose wheel steers. Springs and dampers are sized for a 0.25 m static compression and a damping ratio of 0.6.

Trim and derivatives. - trim zeroes u̇, ẇ and q̇ for given speed, altitude and flight-path angle. - stability_derivatives takes central differences of the full model. - modes gives the eigenvalues of the 12-state linearisation.

Pilot and autopilot. - The pitch, roll and yaw loops are designed per aircraft from its own Cm_δe, Cl_δa, Cn_δr and inertias, for a target natural frequency and damping, and scheduled with the dynamic pressure. - Outer loops: altitude through pitch attitude, heading through bank, airspeed through the throttle, and a washed-out yaw damper. - Take-off schedule (an assumed technique, not a certified one): - full throttle and the take-off flap; - nose wheel and rudder hold the centreline, ailerons hold the wings level; - at V_R the pitch attitude goes up at 3°/s to 12° (transports) or at 6°/s to 11° (light aircraft); - V_R is 1.05 V_s (transports) or 1.10 V_s (light aircraft), with V_s the take-off-flap stall speed; - after lift-off the pitch attitude is trimmed to fly 1.25 V_s (1.30 V_s for light aircraft), and bank holds the track along the runway.

Turbulence (flight.turbulence, MIL-F-8785C §3.7 and MIL-HDBK-1797 §4.9):

  • Intensities and scale lengths:
  • Low altitude (h < 1000 ft): σ_w = 0.1 W₂₀ with W₂₀ = 15 / 30 / 45 kt. σ_u = σ_v = σ_w / (0.177 + 0.000823 h)^0.4. L_w = h and L_u = L_v = h / (0.177 + 0.000823 h)^1.2.
  • Medium and high altitude (h > 2000 ft): isotropic. σ comes from the exceedance-probability chart: light 1e-2, moderate 1e-3, severe 1e-5. L is 1750 ft (Dryden) or 2500 ft (von Kármán).
  • Between 1000 and 2000 ft, values are interpolated linearly.
  • Spectra:
  • Dryden: Φ_u = σ²(2L/π)/(1 + (LΩ)²), Φ_w = σ²(L/π)(1 + 3(LΩ)²)/(1 + (LΩ)²)².
  • von Kármán: the same with exponents 5/6 and 11/6 and the 1.339 factor.
  • Generators:
  • FrozenLine: spectral synthesis along the path, with exact amplitudes and random phases.
  • DrydenFilter: the forming filters with white noise, discretised exactly (Van Loan).
  • FrozenField3D: isotropic, divergence-free 3-D von Kármán turbulence from random Fourier modes (Kraichnan 1970). Its energy spectrum E(k) projects exactly onto the MIL 1-D spectra (checked by quadrature).
  • DiscreteGust: the 1-cosine gust, as the MIL ramp or the full shape.
  • ShearWind: the logarithmic wind profile.
  • The high-altitude intensity table is the MIL-F-8785C Figure 7 table as used by common implementations of the specification. It is reproduced in HIGH_ALTITUDE_SIGMA_FT_S.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Turbulence against the target spectra. Each generator, component and spectral form is checked. The PSD ratio is the band-averaged Welch PSD divided by the target, in eight log bands between 4/L and the resolution.

The frozen line has exact amplitudes, so its variance is the band-limited integral of the target spectrum. The forming filter is a stochastic process, so 200,000 samples leave a few per cent of scatter.

The 3-D field is one realisation of 96 × 32 random modes with dx_min = 2 m: the band is k ≤ k_max = π/(2 dx_min) = 0.785 rad/m, marked on the right-hand plot. Its isotropic energy spectrum matches the MIL forms to 1e-3 by quadrature (tests/test_flight_turbulence.py).

Along a line, the band-averaged w spectrum follows the target between 5/L and 0.2 rad/m (the band ratios in the table). Above that it falls off: from 0.2 rad/m to 0.95 k_max the ratios are 0.12–0.62 (u), 0.52–1.0 (v) and 0.30–0.85 (w) (psd_ratio_high_band in results/verification.json). The reason is that a line spectrum at k₁ needs modes with |k| > k₁, and there are none beyond k_max. The field therefore represents wavelengths down to about 4 × 2π/k_max = 16 dx_min, and the line spectrum at high k is spiky because the modes are discrete.

The encounters use dx_min = MAC/4 (128 log-spaced shells, so the mode count does not grow with k_max). They therefore resolve gusts down to wavelengths of about 4 MAC. 4 MAC / span is 0.47 for the A320 class (MAC 4.04 m, span 34.13 m), 0.54 for the light GA (1.48 m, 11.02 m), 0.34 for the ATR class (2.30 m, 27.05 m) and 0.15 for the glider (0.86 m, 23.0 m), from results/stability.json. Shorter gusts, which would add rolling and pitching moments of their own, are filtered out.

docs.title: Turbulence encounters
docs.text:
The turbulence is the same for all four aircraft: von Kármán, MIL-F-8785C severe (exceedance probability 1e-5) at 3000 m, σ = 7.05 m/s, L = 762 m. It is a frozen 3-D field, so the two wings meet different gusts.

Each aircraft flies at its own speed for 120 s: 55, 120 and 128 m/s, and the glider at 40 m/s. Glider pilots speed up in rough air, and at 30 m/s its trim leaves little α margin to the clean CLmax (an assumption of the study). Each case is run stick-fixed and with the autopilot (altitude, heading and speed hold), in three realisations of the field. The first 5 s are discarded.

Cabin accelerations are the specific force at the passenger stations: a_cg + ω̇ × r + ω × (ω × r). Load factors are in body axes, so steady level flight gives n_z = cos θ.

aircraft controls V [m/s] W/S [Pa] A = ρVCLα/2(W/S) [g per m/s] A·σ_w [g] RMS Δn_z CG [g] spread over seeds max Δn_z min Δn_z RMS bank [deg] peak bank [deg] RMS pitch [deg] RMS n_y CG [g] worst cabin station: RMS / peak Δn_z [g] max α [deg] α at clean CLmax [deg] model validity Light GA (C172 class) stick fixed 55 666 0.1919 1.328 0.586 0.078 2.47 -1.42 22.6 63.1 13.1 0.050 rear seat: 0.609 / 2.59 12.7 14.1 valid Light GA (C172 class) autopilot 55 666 0.1919 1.091 0.368 0.045 1.46 -1.23 7.0 18.8 4.4 0.032 rear seat: 0.389 / 1.52 16.4 14.1 beyond stall Turboprop (ATR 72 class) stick fixed 120 3698 0.0846 0.626 0.566 0.072 2.18 -1.08 14.9 39.0 12.7 0.067 aft row: 0.590 / 2.26 10.1 11.8 beyond stall Turboprop (ATR 72 class) autopilot 120 3698 0.0846 0.616 0.314 0.028 0.98 -1.01 4.5 12.5 2.9 0.034 aft row: 0.338 / 1.14 8.6 11.8 valid Airliner (A320 class) stick fixed 128 5879 0.0520 0.358 0.287 0.072 1.16 -0.80 14.7 39.4 6.4 0.040 aft row: 0.331 / 1.32 14.1 14.1 beyond stall Airliner (A320 class) autopilot 128 5879 0.0520 0.353 0.214 0.047 0.69 -0.71 3.1 8.6 2.7 0.026 aft row: 0.246 / 0.84 13.1 14.1 valid Motor glider (AR 28) stick fixed 40 446 0.2471 1.522 – – – – – – – – – – 7.4 departed Motor glider (AR 28) autopilot 40 446 0.2471 1.510 – – – – – – – – – – 7.4 departed

"Model validity" compares each run with the model's limits, using the stall angle of attack (α at the assumed clean CLmax, from the trim) as the limit of the linear lattice. A run is "beyond stall" if any realisation spends time above it. It is "departed" if the bank passes 90° or α goes 10° past stall. A departed run describes a loss of control the quasi-steady linear model cannot represent, so its numbers are not a gust response.

  • Motor glider in severe turbulence: at 40 m/s, atan(σ_w/V) = 10.0° of RMS gust angle meets 6.5° of α margin from the trim. All three autopilot realisations depart, and one of the three stick-fixed ones does. Their numbers are blanked in the tables. Only the glider's light-turbulence row stays valid. In moderate turbulence it spends 7.0 % of the time past the stall angle, without departing; its clip and trace show that moderate run.
  • Light GA with the autopilot (severe): 0.01–1.5 % of the time past the stall angle, depending on the realisation.
  • Turboprop and A320 class, stick fixed: at most 0.2 % of the time past it in one realisation.
  • Turboprop and A320 class with the autopilot: never reach the stall angle.

These fractions are time_above_stall_frac in results/turbulence.json. - Stick-fixed runs: over 120 s they include the unattended spiral and phugoid excursions (large bank angles), so their RMS values are not gust response alone. The autopilot rows are the comparison between aircraft.

Wing loading and lift-curve slope. A rigid wing held fixed in a vertical gust w would see Δn = A·w with A = ρ V CL_α / (2 W/S). A·σ_w is therefore an upper bound for the RMS increment: plunge and pitch relieve it. The Pratt-Walker formula adds the alleviation factor K_g = 0.88 μ / (5.3 + μ), with the mass ratio μ = 2(W/S) / (ρ c̄ CL_α g), for a 1-cosine gust of half-length 12.5 c̄. Here U_de = 25 ft/s EAS, the same for every aircraft.

The simulation is quasi-steady, without Küssner / Wagner lift lag. Its discrete-gust peak should therefore lie between Pratt and the unalleviated value.

The same gust for all four. One physical gust: a vertical 1-cosine up-gust of 7.62 m/s over 100 m (H = 50 m) at 3000 m, stick fixed, each aircraft at its cruise speed (07_same_gust.py). The slow, lightly loaded aircraft meet it for longer, so they have time to plunge and pitch into it. Pratt's K_g was derived for H = 12.5 MAC and is shown only for reference.
