docs.title: 3-D visualisation
docs.text:
flight.visuals.flight_scene(ac, hist, wind=...) builds a studio Scene with an Animation. It contains:

  • the aircraft mesh (the parametric airframe, or the geometry-library mesh for the ATR class) moved by the recorded attitude and position;
  • the runway with its markings;
  • the trajectory trail;
  • the vertical gust w as vertical arrows on a heading-aligned grid around the aircraft, coloured blue (down) to red (up), and as wisps along the flown track;
  • the lattice loading ΔCp on a sheet just above the wing and tail skins;
  • a HUD with airspeed, height, n_z, pitch and bank.

web_viewer writes the browser viewer, which has play / pause, a time slider, playback speed, a follow camera and a vectors toggle. blender.render_animation renders Cycles frames with the HUD burnt in and encodes MP4 / GIF.

The viewers are written by 03_takeoff.py and 04_turbulence_encounters.py into examples/flight_dynamics/_out/ (not committed). Open one with python -m http.server -d examples/flight_dynamics/_out/a320_takeoff/viewer.

The "Streamlines" button shows the gust wisps; "Vectors" toggles the arrows.

Clips are rendered by 05_render_clips.py from the saved runs. They are 720 × 405, 12 Cycles samples and 96 frames at 12 fps, kept small enough to commit, in docs/assets/flight_dynamics/clips/. Raise --size, --samples and --frames (with --keep-in-out) for full-resolution renders.

Clips: see the gallery at the top of this page.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
python examples/flight_dynamics/01_verification.py          # PSD, trim, conservation, lattice checks (~2 min)
python examples/flight_dynamics/02_trim_and_stability.py    # trim, derivatives, modes, mass properties (<1 min)
python examples/flight_dynamics/03_takeoff.py               # take-offs, crosswind, gust, viewers (~10 min)
python examples/flight_dynamics/04_turbulence_encounters.py # encounters, Pratt (~25 min on 4 cores)
python examples/flight_dynamics/07_same_gust.py             # the four aircraft through one gust (~1 min)
python examples/flight_dynamics/04_turbulence_encounters.py --moderate-visuals motor_glider
python examples/flight_dynamics/05_render_clips.py          # Blender clips (needs bpy; ~3 h on 4 cores with haze)
python examples/flight_dynamics/06_tables.py                # the tables and turbulence figures on this page
python examples/flight_dynamics/08_viewers.py               # rebuild the viewers and screenshots
pytest tests/test_flight_turbulence.py tests/test_flight_dynamics.py tests/test_studio_animation.py

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Quasi-steady aerodynamics.
  • Lift follows the angle of attack instantly: there is no Wagner or Küssner lift build-up and no downwash lag (Cm_α̇).
  • Short gusts are therefore felt fully. This is why the discrete-gust peaks exceed Pratt's.
  • Linear lattice.
  • The lattice has no stall and no section-drag polar. Only the stall margin (maximum CL reached against the assumed take-off CLmax) is reported.
  • Thickness, compressibility and viscous effects on lift are absent. The aero optimizer's Prandtl-Glauert stretch is not used here, because all runs are at M ≤ 0.43.
  • No aeroelasticity. The wing is rigid. On the high-aspect-ratio glider and the airliner, wing bending would change both the gust loads and the cabin accelerations.
  • Ground effect acts on the induced drag only (McCormick factor). The lift increase near the ground is not modelled.
  • Turbulence fields.
  • The 3-D field is isotropic, with one scale length (L_w). At low altitude it keeps the MIL intensities but not their different scale lengths.
  • The frozen-field (Taylor) hypothesis is used throughout.
  • Propeller and engine effects. Slipstream, torque, P-factor and gyroscopic moments are not modelled, and the engines respond instantly to the throttle.
  • Aircraft data. The aircraft are "class" models, not the real types. Planforms, masses, inertias, take-off CLmax, gear stiffness and the pilot technique are estimates or assumptions (listed above and in Aircraft.info). Only the published figures quoted with their source are data.
  • One-engine-out take-off and braking are not simulated. The certified field length therefore cannot be reproduced; only the all-engines distance is compared.

docs.title: The flow schema (pinneapple-flow/1) and how another app reuses it
docs.text:
pinneapple_flow is the library behind Flow Studio. Its document format, port types, node registry, runtime and store are independent of the GUI, so another application (for example the PINNeAPPle-CFD app) can depend on the package, register its own node types and run or store the same documents.

pip install "pinneapple[flow]"            # or: pip install -e ".[flow]" from a checkout
python -m pinneapple_flow schema          # the JSON Schema below, generated from the code
python -m pinneapple_flow catalog --json  # every node type: ports, parameter schema, availability

docs.title: The document
docs.text:
{
  "schema": "pinneapple-flow/1",
  "id": "heat-rod",
  "name": "Heat in a rod",
  "description": "free text",
  "nodes": [
    {"id": "geo", "type": "geometry.domain", "params": {"dimension": 1}, "position": {"x": 0, "y": 0}, "label": "Rod"},
    {"id": "eq",  "type": "equations.system", "params": {"template": "heat"}}
  ],
  "edges": [
    {"id": "geo.geometry->eq.geometry", "source": "geo", "source_port": "geometry", "target": "eq", "target_port": "geometry"}
  ],
  "meta": {"planner": "heuristic", "prompt": "heat in a rod"}
}
Field Rules schema exactly pinneapple-flow/1; other versions are refused (FlowError) nodes[].id a letter or _, then letters, digits, _, - (at most 64); unique; at most 200 nodes nodes[].type a registered node type; nothing else runs: the document never carries code nodes[].params checked against the type's parameter schema (params_schema()); unknown names are errors edges[] source.source_port (an output) to target.target_port (an input) of compatible port types meta free: the planner that produced the flow, the prompt, the stored version

pinneapple_flow.validate_flow(doc) returns every problem (Issue(level, message, node, edge, param)): unknown types or parameters, values out of range, edges between unknown ports or incompatible types, a second edge into a single-valued input, missing required inputs, cycles. check_flow raises when there is an error. flow_json_schema() is the JSON Schema of the document (draft 2020-12).

docs.title: Port types
docs.text:
Type Value geometry {"dimension", "shape", "bounds": {"x": [lo, hi], ...}, "time": [t0, t1] or null, "coords": [...]} mesh {"geometry", "n": {"x": 64, ...}, "n_t"} equations {"fields", "pdes", "conditions", "coefficients", "unknowns", "exact", "family", "classification"} problem {"geometry", "equations", "mesh"?} solution artifact .npz with values (shape (*axis lengths, n_fields)) and axis_<c>; the port value carries coords, fields, method, label model artifact (.pt): a surrogate (pinneapple_flow.learn.load) or PINN weights dataset artifact .npz: X, Y (point observations) or A, Y, grid, grid_shape (operator learning) series artifact .npz: t, values; the port value carries channels metrics, params JSON figure, scene, report artifacts (PNG; glTF + pinneapple-field-view/v1 meta; HTML / Markdown / JSON) twin artifact JSON: snapshot, alerts, forecast requirement, concept JSON: pinneapple_reason.Requirement list / Concept (to_dict) chain artifact JSON: pinneapple_reason.Chain (chain.json, schema pinneapple.reason.chain/1) any accepts every type

An artifact value is {"$artifact": "<absolute path in the run folder>", "kind": "npz" | "json" | "pt" | "png" | ...}; pinneapple_flow.runtime.load_artifact(value) reads it. An output may feed an input of the same type, an input of type any, or one of the conversions in pinneapple_flow.types.CONVERSIONS (a problem carries its geometry and equations, a solution is a dataset, ...).

docs.title: Equations
docs.text: Equations are text in the grammar of pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde.text: numbers, + - * / ** ^, coordinates (single letters, t is time), fields, coefficient names, sin cos tan exp log sqrt abs sinh cosh tanh atan asin acos sign heaviside, derivative shorthand (u_t, u_xx, T_xy), d(f, x, ...) and lap(f) (over the spatial coordinates, so one text works in 1-D, 2-D and 3-D). The text is translated node by node from Python's ast; it is never passed to eval or sympify. Conditions are {"kind": "dirichlet" | "neumann" | "robin" | "initial" | "periodic", "on": "x_min" | "x_max" | ... | "boundary" | "t_min", "equation": "u = 0"}.

docs.title: Extending the library from another package
docs.text:
Another application registers what it adds through the public API, never by editing the module dictionaries:

import pinneapple_flow as pf

pf.register_port_type("cfd_case", "an OpenFOAM case folder", converts_to=["dataset"])
pf.register_references("my_app/references.yaml")        # or a dict key -> entry; checked like the curated file
pf.register_rule(pf.Rule("cfd.k_omega_sst", "k-omega SST for wall-bounded turbulence", cites=("menter1994sst",),
                         topic="method"))
store = pf.FlowStore("postgresql+psycopg://...", table_prefix="flow_")   # flow_flows, flow_runs, ...

A port type, reference or rule that is already registered with different content is refused, so documents and decision records stay portable. FlowStore.save_flow returns the current version unchanged when the document is the same as the latest one. python -m pinneapple_flow references --verify resolves every DOI of the registry online through doi.org and Crossref, and compares the registered title. check() on an LLM or user reference does the same when PINNEAPPLE_FLOW_VERIFY_REFS=1.

docs.title: Adding node types from another package
docs.text:
from pinneapple_flow import Param, Port, node

@node("cfd.simple_foam", "simpleFoam case", category="CFD",
      inputs=[Port("mesh", "mesh")], outputs=[Port("solution", "solution"), Port("metrics", "metrics")],
      params=[Param("iterations", "int", 500, minimum=1)],
      calls="pinneapple_cfd.solvers.simple_foam")
def simple_foam(ctx, inputs, params):
    ...                                   # ctx.workdir, ctx.log, ctx.metric, ctx.figure, ctx.save_npz, ctx.view
    return {"solution": ctx.save_npz("solution", values=..., axis_x=...), "metrics": {...}}

Import the module that defines the nodes before running or serving (for example in the app's start-up); the catalog, the validator, the planner's repair step and the GUI pick the new types up from REGISTRY. A new port type is registered with register_port_type (see above).

docs.title: Where a node appears in the palette
docs.text:
pinneapple_flow.palette describes the palette every front end shows: thirteen sections in workflow order (palette.sections(): Problem & geometry, Equations, Classical solvers, Physics AI, Surrogates & ROMs, Data, Inverse & calibration, Validation & UQ, Optimization & control, Digital twin, Visualization, Export & report, and Library calls (advanced), which holds the generated auto.* nodes grouped by package and starts collapsed). Each catalog row carries a palette object: section, a human title, a one-line summary (the first sentence of the description), tags, package, curated, group and, for an unavailable node, an install hint (pip install fmpy). A node registered by another package chooses its section with a tag:

@node("cfd.simple_foam", "simpleFoam case", category="CFD", tags=("section:solvers", "rans", "openfoam"), ...)

without one it falls back on its category, then on the advanced section. palette.search(text) ranks the catalog (every query word must match; title, then tags, type, description and package; curated nodes above generated library calls), and FlowService.palette(user) / set_palette_prefs(user, ...) keep each user's favourites and recent node types in the store (user_prefs table).

docs.title: Running and storing
docs.text:
• pinneapple_flow.run(flow, workdir=..., from_node=..., store=...) compiles the flow into a pinneapple_core.workflows.Workflow (one step of kind pinneapple_flow.node per node) and runs it with WorkflowRunner: per-node logs and states (queued, running, done, degraded, not_run, failed, cached, cancelled), retries, cancel, and skip-done by content hash (a node whose type, parameters and upstream are unchanged reuses its outputs).
  • not_run: the node did not run, and report["not_run_reason"] says why. This happens when its library or tool is missing (available() is false: the step is not refused, it finishes not_run), when the node calls ctx.not_run(reason), or when a required input comes from a node that did not run. An optional input from such a node is just absent.
  • degraded: the node ran on a declared fallback (ctx.degrade(reason)); report["degraded"] lists the reasons.
  • Every finished run passes through pinneapple_flow.runtime.on_run_finished(result, flow), for headless, service and GUI runs alike. A run that finished done is written as a PINNeAPPle Lab experiment manifest (experiment.json in the run folder) by pinneapple_lab.manifest.from_flow_run. The manifest holds the nodes, the library modules they call, the parameters, every measured metric with how it was measured, the checks, the figures and videos, and decisions.json with the decision records and their references. Other packages append to RUN_FINISHED_HOOKS. What each hook did is in result.hooks; a failing hook never fails the run.
  • pinneapple_flow.store.FlowStore(url) keeps flows with versions, runs and per-node outputs (metrics, report, artifact paths) in SQLite (default) or any SQLAlchemy URL (postgresql+psycopg://...). Tables: flows, flow_versions, runs, node_results.
  • pinneapple_flow.service.FlowService is what an HTTP layer exposes (plan, validate, previews, flows, runs, node results, artifacts); Flow Studio's routes are one call each.

docs.title: Decision records
docs.text:
Every choice a flow makes carries a record (pinneapple_flow.decisions.Decision, JSON):

{
  "id": "3f2a9c1d0e", "node": "eq", "topic": "equations",
  "what": "equations: u_t = alpha*lap(u)",
  "decided_by": {"kind": "rule", "id": "family.heat"},
  "rationale": "keyword scores heat (4.5), ...; highest score wins",
  "value": ["u_t = alpha*lap(u)"],
  "references": [{"key": "carslaw1959heat", "title": "Conduction of Heat in Solids (2nd ed.)",
                  "authors": ["H. S. Carslaw", "J. C. Jaeger"], "year": 1959, "status": "registry", "link": ""}],
  "evidence": [{"kind": "example", "ref": "examples/flow_studio/results/heat_1d/summary.json",
                "detail": "heat 1D: FD and PINN vs exact, Lab tier"}],
  "uncited_reason": "", "confidence": 0.85, "label": "high", "no_reference": false, "suggestion": "",
  "notes": "", "created": 1760817600.0
}
Field Meaning topic equations, dimension, bcs, coefficients, method, architecture, hyperparameters, hpo, twin, validation, route, data, other decided_by {"kind": "rule", "id": <rule id in pinneapple_flow.rules>}, {"kind": "llm", "id": "<provider>/<model>"} or {"kind": "user", "id": ...} references entries of the curated registry (pinneapple_flow/references.yaml, status: "registry"), or DOIs / URLs given by an LLM or a user: verified when they resolved (only with PINNEAPPLE_FLOW_VERIFY_REFS=1), not found, or unverified evidence what in the repository backs the decision: a test, an example result, a library constant confidence, label 0-1 and high / medium / low; a decision with neither a usable reference nor evidence is no_reference: true, capped at 0.35 (0.5 for a user's own choice) and carries a suggestion (run a validation node or a benchmark) uncited_reason why a rule has no literature reference (reading the user's words, a project convention, a rule of thumb) raise_with for a no reference or low-confidence decision: registered node types that would back it with evidence (pinneapple_flow.decisions.RAISE_NODES, by topic); the GUI inserts them wired into the flow

Where they live: planner and LLM decisions in flow.meta["decisions"]; user edits in flow.meta["user_edits"] ({"node", "param", "value", "notes"?, "references"?}, turned into user decisions by pinneapple_flow.decisions.collect); decisions a node takes while running in its report (report["decisions"]). The store keeps all of them per flow version and per run (table decisions); export.report prints a "Decisions and references" section. tests/test_flow_decisions.py checks that every rule cites the registry or says why not.

docs.title: Lab seal and what would raise it
docs.text:
pinneapple_flow.lab_status reads, never computes, the quality letter of a validated item:

  • seal_status(item, lab) gives {"letter", "name", "scale", "reason", "failing_check", "hint", "sealed", "source"}. The letter comes from the Lab curation (pinneapple_lab.curation.TIERS, A-F) through pinneapple_lab.seal.seal_for, which also gives the failing check for E and F and the next step. letter: null means the item was never curated.
  • next_steps(item, lab) calls pinneapple_lab.curation.next_steps. Each gap keeps the Lab's actions (id, kind, target, command, text). Each action's nodes holds the registered node types that carry it out: the action's dotted target is a library call a registered node declares in its calls. Command-line actions have none. Without that API (an older Lab) the result is available: false with the curation's plain gaps.
  • insert_nodes(flow, anchor, [{"type", "params"}]) adds registered node types and wires each input by port type: from the anchor first, then its upstream nodes, then any other node. One output feeds at most one input of a new node.

validate.lab stores the first two under report["lab"]. The service attaches the run's seals to every node result (lab). HTTP: GET /api/lab/seal?item=, GET /api/lab/next-steps?item=, POST /api/flows/insert-nodes.

docs.title: Library-call nodes and user-defined node types
docs.text:
lib.<key> nodes come from the curated allowlist in pinneapple_flow/libcalls_catalog.py: a callable (module:function or module:Class.method), its palette category, references, which inputs come from ports, and parameters generated from its signature. A user-defined type is data, never code:

{"type": "custom.soft_soil", "base": "solver.terramechanics", "title": "Wheel on JSC-1A", "category": "Custom",
 "params": {"soil": {"default": "JSC-1A", "hidden": true}, "slip": {"default": 0.3}}}

auto.<module>.<function> nodes are generated from the public API by pinneapple_flow.autocalls and committed as pinneapple_flow/autocalls.json, so the catalog loads without importing those modules. A function qualifies when a form can fill every required argument, no argument names a path, URL, host, command, expression or credential, and its body neither evaluates text, starts processes nor writes files. Each entry records whether it ran with its default values in a fresh interpreter. python -m pinneapple_flow autocalls regenerates the file.

base must be an allowlisted key and every parameter must exist on it and pass its check. Definitions are stored (custom_nodes table) or carried in flow.meta["custom_nodes"] so a flow that uses them stays portable. python -m pinneapple_flow coverage lists which library packages and modules are reached by nodes, and why the others are not (docs/flow_studio/COVERAGE.md).

docs.title: FMI import compatibility
docs.text: PINNeAPPle imports FMUs to generate training and validation data for Physics AI models (pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.modelica: simulate_fmu, fmu_to_upd, sweeps). This page lists the FMUs that import has been tested with. It is generated by examples/modelica/fmi_compatibility.py, which runs every FMU through simulate_fmu in each interface it offers (check_fmus in fmi_compat.py).

docs.title: Importing tool
docs.text:
• PINNeAPPle with fmpy 0.3.32, Python 3.11.15, platform x86_64-linux, run on 2026-10-16.
  • CS = Co-Simulation, ME = Model Exchange.
  • A run passes when it reaches the stop time of the FMU's default experiment with finite outputs. For Dahlquist (x' = -k x) the trajectory is also compared with exp(-k t): within 1e-3 through Model Exchange and within 0.1 through Co-Simulation, where the FMU integrates with its own fixed-step explicit Euler.
  • Result: 38 of 38 runs passed.

docs.title: Geometry library
docs.text:
Realistic parametric 3-D geometries for Physics-AI, each with the code that regenerates it and ready-made files you can just import. Every entry is in metres in a documented frame, made of closed, outward-oriented bodies (watertight, no self-intersections, checked by tests/test_geometry_library.py), at two levels of detail: light (committed in data/geometries/, at most a few tens of thousands of triangles) and fine (on the Hugging Face Hub, dataset PINNeAPPle-Labs/geometry-library). Real-world dimensions come from the published sources listed by info(); values chosen by engineering judgement are flagged as estimates.

import pinneapple as pp

pp.geometries.list()                                  # names (also pp.geometries.categories())
pp.geometries.info("wind_turbine_nrel5mw")            # dimensions, parameters with ranges, sources, physics uses
g = pp.geometries.build("wind_turbine_nrel5mw", pitch_deg=8.0, rotor_azimuth_deg=30.0)
g.check()                                             # watertight / outward per body, bounding box
g.export("turbine.stl"); g.export("turbine.glb"); g.export("turbine.step"); g.export("turbine.usda")
g.solid()                                             # one fused watertight surface for meshing (manifold3d)
g.scene()                                             # pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio Scene: Blender, web viewer
g.render("turbine.png")                               # thumbnail (software renderer, no GPU)
pp.geometries.load("airliner_a320", format="glb")     # path of the pre-generated file
pp.geometries.load("airliner_a320", format="stl", lod="fine")   # downloaded from the Hub, SHA-256 checked, cached

docs.title: Files and the loader
docs.text:
level triangles where formats light <= 20 000 (36 000 for the airliner and the two-stage launcher) repository (data/geometries/<name>/) and Hub STL, glTF (in git); OBJ, USD, STEP (Hub) fine up to 400 000 Hub STL, glTF, OBJ, USD

load(name, format, lod) looks in the repository copy, then the cache (~/.cache/pinneapple/geometries, $PINNEAPPLE_GEOMETRY_CACHE), then the Hub, verifies the SHA-256 recorded in pinneapple_design/geometry_library/manifest.json, and falls back to build() with the default parameters when offline (PINNEAPPLE_OFFLINE=1) or when the file is not published yet. The defaults reproduce the stored files (the test compares the rebuilt light STL with the committed one). STEP is a faceted B-rep (one solid per body, planar triangular faces) that OpenCASCADE, FreeCAD and the usual CAD tools import as solids; it is published for the light level (the fine one would be about 100 MB, export it locally with g.export("x.step") if needed).

The geometries job of .github/workflows/publish-zoo.yml rebuilds every file, checks it against the manifest and uploads it to the Hub when the repository secret HF_TOKEN is set (it skips the upload with a warning otherwise), then verifies the published files by anonymous download. Regenerate after changing an entry:

python scripts/geometry_library.py light       # light STL + glTF, thumbnails
python scripts/geometry_library.py hub         # all files of both levels in dist/geometries
python scripts/geometry_library.py manifest    # SHA-256 of everything
python scripts/geometry_library.py sheet       # contact sheet + turntable GIF
python scripts/geometry_library.py docs        # this page

docs.title: Reference frames
docs.text: Vehicles: right-handed, x aft from the nose (the free-stream direction), y to starboard, z up, z = 0 on the ground for ground vehicles. Other entries state their own frame in info(name)["frame"] (e.g. the wind turbine: x downwind, z up from the tower base; the aorta: patient axes). Every geometry is in metres, including the heat sink and the aorta.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• examples/geometry_library/01_caarc_building_wind_openfoam.py: the CAARC tall building in an atmospheric boundary layer with OpenFOAM through the generic STL path of pp.cfd.ExternalFlow (writes the case when OpenFOAM is not installed).
  • examples/geometry_library/02_wind_turbine_bem.py: blade-element momentum on the NREL 5-MW blade of the library: power and thrust curve, compared with the published rated power.
  • examples/geometry_library/03_airliner_vlm.py: vortex-lattice lift slope, neutral point and induced drag of the airliner, plus a wetted-area friction-drag estimate from the library mesh.

docs.title: Single-aisle airliner (A320 class) (airliner_a320)
docs.text:
Circular fuselage with cabin and cockpit windows and a livery, low swept wing with dihedral, washout and sharklets, two under-wing turbofans on pylons, swept tails sized by volume coefficient; in cruise (gear up). Wraps pinneapple_design.aero.airliner.Airliner.

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 38.75 x 35.43 x 10.23 m. Frame: right-handed, metres: x aft from the nose (the free-stream direction), y to starboard (right), z up; origin on the centre plane at the nose, z = 0 on the fuselage axis.
  • Parameters: length [m], wing_area [m^2], aspect_ratio, taper, sweep_le [deg], dihedral [deg], twist [deg], fan_diameter [m], engine_station, sharklets.
  • Physics: external aerodynamics (RANS, cruise lift/drag, high-lift studies); vortex-lattice / panel methods; wake-vortex and contrail studies; aero-structural wing optimisation.
  • Sources: length 37.57 m, span 35.80 m with sharklets (34.10 m without), fuselage width 3.95 m, wing area 122.6 m^2, height 11.76 m on the gear: Airbus (2023). A320 Aircraft Characteristics - Airport and Maintenance Planning, Rev. 41, section 2-2 (general dimensions). https://aircraft.airbus.com/en/customer-care/fleet-wide-care/airport-operations-and-technical-data/aircraft-characteristics; (estimate) LE sweep, dihedral, washout, tail volume coefficients, airfoil (NACA 2412 stand-in for the supercritical section): engineering estimates from public three-views; (estimate) bounding box of the model: 38.75 m long (the swept horizontal-tail tips end 1.2 m behind the 37.57 m tail cone), 35.43 m span over the sharklets, 10.2 m high in cruise with the gear retracted (11.76 m on the gear): model geometry
  • Wraps pinneapple_design.aero.airliner.Airliner (still importable from there).
  • Known: wing_right: sub-millimetre crossings of the sharp trailing edge (legacy loft); wing_left: sub-millimetre crossings of the sharp trailing edge (legacy loft); sharklet_r: sub-millimetre crossings of the sharp trailing edge (legacy loft); sharklet_l: sub-millimetre crossings of the sharp trailing edge (legacy loft).

docs.title: Quadcopter drone (F450 frame class) (quadrotor_drone)
docs.text:
X-configuration quadcopter on its landing legs: 450 mm diagonal frame with PCB centre plates, red front / white rear arms, 2212-class outrunner motors, four counter-rotating two-blade 10 x 4.5 in propellers (constant geometric pitch, cambered sections, swept tips), canopy, GPS mast, battery and a two-axis camera gimbal.

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 0.559 x 0.498 x 0.27 m. Frame: right-handed, metres: x aft (the nose is between the two red arms, at -x), y to starboard, z up; origin on the ground below the frame centre (feet on z = 0).
  • Parameters: arm_diagonal [m], prop_diameter [m], prop_pitch [m], rotor_azimuth_deg [deg].
  • Physics: multirotor aerodynamics (rotor-rotor and rotor-frame interaction, hover / forward flight); propeller noise; ground effect and downwash; flight-dynamics / control surrogates.
  • Sources: 450 mm diagonal wheelbase, 10 x 4.5 in propellers, 2212-class motors: DJI (2013). Flame Wheel F450 user manual / specifications: diagonal wheelbase 450 mm, frame weight 282 g, recommended 10 x 4.5 in propellers and 2212 motors. https://www.dji.com/flame-wheel-arf; constant geometric pitch: blade angle atan(P / (2 pi r)): standard propeller nomenclature (e.g. McCormick, B.W. (1995). Aerodynamics, Aeronautics and Flight Mechanics, 2nd ed., Wiley); (estimate) plate size, arm section, motor 28 x 26 mm, blade chord / thickness distribution, landing legs, 3S battery 135 x 43 x 26 mm, gimbal and camera sizes: estimates from hobby-grade parts

docs.title: Regional twin turboprop (ATR 72-600 class) (turboprop_atr72)
docs.text:
High-wing regional twin turboprop on its gear: fuselage with cabin windows, cockpit glazing and a livery, untapered inner / tapered outer wing with a morphing plain flap and leading-edge de-icing boots, two nacelles with chin intakes and spinners, six-blade propellers lofted with constant geometric pitch, T-tail with dorsal fin, main-gear sponsons with twin wheels and a twin nose wheel.

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 27.17 x 27.05 x 7.65 m. Frame: right-handed, metres: x aft from the nose (the free-stream direction), y to starboard (right), z up; origin on the centre plane at the nose, z = 0 on the ground (aircraft on its gear, tyres touching z = 0).
  • Parameters: wing_span [m], wing_area [m^2], flap_deg [deg], prop_diameter [m], blade_pitch_deg [deg], prop_azimuth_deg [deg], htail_span [m].
  • Physics: external aerodynamics of a high-wing turboprop (RANS, take-off / landing flap settings); propeller-wing interaction and slipstream (actuator disc / sliding-mesh blades); propeller aero-acoustics and cabin noise sources; icing on the wing and tail leading edges; ground effect and crosswind on the gear.
  • Sources: overall length 27.17 m, span 27.05 m, height 7.65 m, wing area 61.0 m^2, wheel track 4.10 m, wheelbase 10.77 m, six-blade propellers of 3.93 m: ATR (2014). ATR 72-600 Aircraft Characteristics for Airport Planning (ATR 72 AC/AP), section 2 general dimensions; and ATR, 'ATR 72-600' product data sheet. https://www.atr-aircraft.com/our-aircraft/atr-72-600/; propeller diameter 3.93 m, six composite blades: Collins Aerospace (Hamilton Sundstrand) 568F six-blade composite propeller, diameter 3.93 m, as fitted to the ATR 72-600 (EASA Type-Certificate Data Sheet P.009 for 568F propellers; ATR 72 TCDS EASA.A.084); (estimate) fuselage maximum width 2.77 m and height 2.62 m (published external diameter quoted 2.77-2.87 m; 2.77 m used): estimate from ATR 72 airport-planning cross-section; (estimate) wing planform: constant chord to 4.6 m, taper 0.55 outboard, 3.1 deg LE sweep, 2 deg outer dihedral, NACA 3418 -> 3413 stand-ins for the ATR sections, 1 deg -> -2 deg twist: engineering estimates from public three-views; (estimate) nacelle, sponson, fin / dorsal fillet, tailplane chords, blade chord / thickness / sweep, main tyre 0.82 m and nose tyre 0.45 m diameters, gear position: estimates from photographs and three-views; (estimate) tailplane span 7.31 m: ATR 72 three-view dimension (published in Jane's All the World's Aircraft; treated as approximate)

docs.title: Human thoracic aorta (arch) (aortic_arch)
docs.text:
Adult human thoracic aorta lumen: aortic root with three-lobed sinus of Valsalva, ascending aorta, arch and descending thoracic aorta with the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, fused (manifold3d union) into one watertight lumen with flat-capped inlet and outlets.

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 0.1134 x 0.0766 x 0.3114 m. Frame: right-handed patient frame, metres: x towards the patient's left, y posterior, z cranial; origin at the centre of the aortic-root inlet (annulus plane).
  • Parameters: ascending_diameter [m], sinus_diameter [m], arch_diameter [m], descending_diameter [m], arch_radius [m], ascending_length [m], descending_length [m], arch_plane_deg [deg], bct_diameter [m], lcca_diameter [m], lsa_diameter [m], bct_angle_deg [deg], lcca_angle_deg [deg], lsa_angle_deg [deg], bct_bifurcation, rsa_diameter [m], rcca_diameter [m], fused.
  • Physics: hemodynamics: pulsatile blood flow, wall shear stress, secondary flow in the arch; aneurysm / coarctation and stent-graft planning studies; fluid-structure interaction of the aortic wall; particle (embolus) transport into the supra-aortic branches.
  • Sources: thoracic aortic diameters by segment (sinus ~33-36 mm, ascending ~29-32 mm, arch ~26-28 mm, descending ~23-26 mm in adults): Hager, A., Kaemmerer, H., Rapp-Bernhardt, U., Bluecher, S., Rapp, K., Bernhardt, T.M., Galanski, M., Hess, J. (2002). Diameters of the thoracic aorta throughout life as measured with helical computed tomography. J. Thorac. Cardiovasc. Surg. 123(6), 1060-1066. https://doi.org/10.1067/mtc.2002.122310; arch geometry (arch width / height, curvature radius ~30-35 mm): Redheuil, A., Yu, W.C., Mousseaux, E., et al. (2011). Age-related changes in aortic arch geometry: relationship with proximal aortic function and left ventricular mass and remodeling. J. Am. Coll. Cardiol. 58(12), 1262-1270. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2011.06.012; (estimate) chosen defaults within the published ranges, branch diameters 12 / 8 / 10 mm, branch take-off angles, lengths, sinus lobing, arch plane rotation and the centreline shape: anatomical estimate

docs.title: CAARC standard tall building (caarc_building)
docs.text:
The CAARC standard tall building for wind-loading comparisons: a 30.48 x 45.72 x 182.88 m (100 x 150 x 600 ft) prism with a 50-storey curtain-wall facade, in a deterministic urban block of lower buildings on a 300 m-radius turntable ground (top at z = 0).

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 600 x 600 x 183.9 m. Frame: right-handed, metres, full scale: x the wind direction at 0 deg incidence (normal to the 45.72 m wide face), y across, z up; origin at the tower base centre on the ground (z = 0 is the ground top; the ground disc is 1 m thick).
  • Parameters: height [m], width [m], depth [m], orientation_deg [deg], surroundings, density, seed, ground_radius [m].
  • Physics: mean and fluctuating wind pressures on a tall building (CAARC benchmark); along / across-wind base moments and vortex shedding; LES of the atmospheric boundary layer with urban roughness; pedestrian-level wind comfort around the tower.
  • Sources: 100 x 150 x 600 ft (30.48 x 45.72 x 182.88 m) CAARC tall-building model, wind normal to the wide face at 0 deg: Melbourne, W.H. (1980). Comparison of measurements on the CAARC standard tall building model in simulated model wind flows. J. Wind Eng. Ind. Aerodyn. 6(1-2), 73-88. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-6105(80)90023-9; (estimate) 50 storeys of 12 ft, curtain-wall bays, spandrel bands (visual facade only): engineering estimate; (estimate) surrounding urban block (55 m street grid, 12-45 m buildings, density 0.7), 300 m ground disc: generic, generated (not a published configuration)

docs.title: Closed centrifugal pump impeller (centrifugal_impeller)
docs.text:
Closed (shrouded) centrifugal pump impeller of the ERCOFTAC test-case size: D2 = 420 mm, 7 backward-curved log-spiral blades between inlet angle beta1 and outlet angle beta2, hub with keyed bore, back shroud and front shroud with suction eye and wear-ring neck. Blades are separate bodies penetrating both shrouds.

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 0.42 x 0.42 x 0.166 m. Frame: right-handed, metres: z the rotation axis pointing into the suction eye (upstream), origin on the axis in the hub-side plane of the outlet (back-shroud inner face); the impeller rotates in +theta about +z, blades are backward-curved.
  • Parameters: outlet_diameter [m], outlet_width [m], eye_diameter [m], blade_count, beta1_deg [deg], beta2_deg [deg], blade_thickness [m], bore_diameter [m], keyway, keyway_width [m], keyway_depth [m], front_shroud.
  • Physics: pump performance (head, efficiency) with frozen-rotor / sliding-mesh CFD; impeller-diffuser interaction and unsteady blade loading; cavitation at the blade leading edge; rotordynamic and structural (FEA) analysis of the impeller.
  • Sources: (estimate) outlet diameter D2 = 420 mm and 7 blades of the ERCOFTAC centrifugal-pump test impeller (recalled from the published description; check against the paper before quantitative use): Ubaldi, M., Zunino, P., Barigozzi, G., Cattanei, A. (1996). An experimental investigation of stator induced unsteadiness on centrifugal impeller outflow. J. Turbomach. 118(1), 41-54. https://doi.org/10.1115/1.2836604 (ERCOFTAC centrifugal pump test case); (estimate) b2 = 40 mm, eye 200 mm, beta1 = 20 deg, beta2 = 22.5 deg, blade thickness 6 mm, shroud / hub contours, wrap angle: generic design within the usual ranges: Gulich, J.F. (2014). Centrifugal Pumps, 3rd ed. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-40114-5 (impeller design: blade angles, log-spiral blades, shroud / hub contours); keyway 14 mm wide, 3.8 mm deep in the hub for a 50 mm shaft: DIN 6885-1 (1968). Parallel keys, keyways, deep pattern (shaft 44-50 mm: key 14 x 9, hub depth 3.8 mm)

docs.title: KRISO Container Ship (KCS), full scale (container_ship_kcs)
docs.text:
3600-TEU class container ship at full scale (Lpp 230 m, B 32.2 m, T 10.8 m, Cb ~0.65) with bulbous bow, transom stern, skeg, 5-blade propeller and rudder, aft deckhouse with bridge windows and wings, funnel, hatch covers and stacked containers. The hull form is a parametric approximation of the KCS lines (the official offsets are not reproduced); draft, trim and container tiers are parameters.

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 241.1 x 32.2 x 47 m. Frame: right-handed, metres: x aft from the forward perpendicular (FP at x = 0, AP at x = 230), y to starboard, z up; z = 0 on the calm waterline (the keel at midships is at z = -draft).
  • Parameters: draft [m], trim [m], container_tiers.
  • Physics: calm-water resistance and nominal / effective wake (RANS, free surface); self-propulsion with the 5-blade propeller and rudder (SIMMAN / Tokyo 2015 cases); seakeeping and added resistance in waves; trim optimisation; wind loads on the superstructure and container stacks.
  • Sources: KCS: Lpp 230 m, B 32.2 m, T 10.8 m, D 19.0 m, Cb 0.651, bulbous bow and transom stern: Kim, W.J., Van, S.H., Kim, D.H. (2001). Measurement of flows around modern commercial ship models. Experiments in Fluids 31(5), 567-578. https://doi.org/10.1007/s003480100332; KCS full-scale data and propeller (D = 7.9 m, 5 blades, P/D ~ 1.0): Hino, T., Stern, F., Larsson, L., Visonneau, M., Hirata, N., Kim, J. (eds.) (2021). Numerical Ship Hydrodynamics: An Assessment of the Tokyo 2015 Workshop. Lecture Notes in Applied and Computational Mechanics 94, Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-47572-7 (KCS: Lpp 230 m, B 32.2 m, T 10.8 m, D 19.0 m, Cb 0.6505, propeller D 7.9 m, 5 blades, scale 1:31.6); KCS manoeuvring definition (rudder, propeller): SIMMAN 2008 / 2014 workshop on verification and validation of ship manoeuvring simulation methods: KCS geometry and conditions. http://www.simman2014.dk/ship-data/moeri-container-ship-kcs/; (estimate) hull form: super-ellipse sections on parametric waterlines tuned to Cb ~ 0.65, stem rake, forefoot, skeg and counter; the official KCS offsets are NOT reproduced: parametric approximation; (estimate) bulb, rudder (5.3-6.0 m chord, NACA 0018), propeller blade outline and skew, deckhouse, bridge, funnel, lifeboats, hatch covers, 13-row container stowage (40-ft ISO boxes 12.19 x 2.44 x 2.59 m), propeller centre 4.4 m above the keel: estimates for a 3600-TEU class ship (the KCS was conceived without superstructure)

docs.title: Wigley parabolic hull (wigley_hull)
docs.text:
The analytic Wigley hull y = (B/2)(1 - (2x/L)^2)(1 - (z/T)^2) below the waterline, continued wall-sided up to a flat deck at the freeboard: a closed solid (Cb = 4/9). The classic ITTC benchmark for wave resistance, sinkage / trim and potential-flow / RANS free-surface codes.

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 1 x 0.1 x 0.1025 m. Frame: right-handed, metres: x aft, y to starboard, z up; origin at midships on the centre plane in the calm waterline (bow at x = -L/2, stern at x = +L/2, keel at z = -T).
  • Parameters: length [m], beam [m], draft [m], freeboard [m].
  • Physics: wave resistance and wave pattern (Michell thin-ship theory, Rankine panels); RANS / VOF free-surface CFD validation (resistance, sinkage and trim); seakeeping: heave / pitch response in head waves; mesh-convergence benchmark for hull CFD.
  • Sources: parabolic waterlines and frames y = (B/2)(1-(2x/L)^2)(1-(z/T)^2): Wigley, W.C.S. (1934). A comparison of experiment and calculated wave-profiles and wave-resistances for a form having parabolic waterlines. Proc. Royal Society of London A 144(851), 144-159. https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1934.0040; benchmark proportions L/B = 10, B/T = 1.6: Kajitani, H., Miyata, H., Ikehata, M., Tanaka, H., Adachi, H., Namimatsu, M., Ogiwara, S. (1983). The summary of the cooperative experiment on Wigley parabolic model in Japan. Proc. 2nd DTNSRDC Workshop on Ship Wave-Resistance Computations, Bethesda, 5-35 (ITTC Resistance Committee benchmark, L/B = 10, B/T = 1.6); (estimate) default L = 1 m (non-dimensional reference) and freeboard 0.04 L, wall-sided above the waterline: choice for a normalised closed solid

docs.title: Open-wheel racing car (Formula 1 style) (f1_car)
docs.text:
Monocoque with sidepods and engine cover, floor with diffuser, two-element front and rear wings with endplates (DRS open or closed), driver helmet, halo and four exposed wheels. In the spirit of the 2022+ regulations, not any team's car. Wraps pinneapple_design.geometry.vehicles3d.FormulaCar.

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 5.57 x 1.97 x 1.03 m. Frame: right-handed, metres: x aft from the nose (the free-stream direction), y to starboard (right), z up; origin on the centre plane at the front-wing leading edge, z = 0 on the ground for ground vehicles.
  • Parameters: wheelbase [m], ride_height [m], front_wing_aoa [deg], front_flap_aoa [deg], rear_wing_aoa [deg], rear_flap_aoa [deg], drs_open, diffuser_angle [deg].
  • Physics: ground-effect aerodynamics (downforce, floor and diffuser); wake / dirty-air studies for following; DRS open / closed drag delta; tyre-wake interaction.
  • Sources: max wheelbase 3.6 m, width 2.0 m, height 0.95 m above the reference plane, 18-inch wheels (tyre diameter ~0.72 m): FIA (2022). Formula 1 Technical Regulations, articles 3 and 10; (estimate) wing chords, sidepod and engine-cover shapes: estimates from broadcast imagery
  • Wraps pinneapple_design.geometry.vehicles3d.FormulaCar (still importable from there).

docs.title: Four-door road car (fastback / notchback) (road_car)
docs.text:
Mid-size four-door saloon: super-elliptic body with glazing, lights, trim and wheel arches, four tyres with rims, slant / rear-window angle as the main aerodynamic parameter (Ahmed-body physics on a realistic shape). Wraps pinneapple_design.geometry.vehicles3d.RoadCar.

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 4.6 x 1.86 x 1.39 m. Frame: right-handed, metres: x aft from the nose (the free-stream direction), y to starboard (right), z up; origin on the centre plane at the nose, z = 0 on the ground for ground vehicles.
  • Parameters: length [m], width [m], roof_height [m], clearance [m], windshield_deg [deg], slant_deg [deg], style, wheelbase [m], wheel_radius [m].
  • Physics: external aerodynamics with moving ground (drag, lift, wake); slant-angle / rear-wake studies; aero-acoustics around the A-pillar; vehicle soiling and cooling-drag surrogates.
  • Sources: (estimate) D-segment saloon envelope (length 4.6-4.9 m, width 1.82-1.87 m, height 1.40-1.45 m): manufacturer data of mid-size saloons; generic shape, not a specific model; slant-angle drag physics: Ahmed, S.R., Ramm, G., Faltin, G. (1984), SAE 840300
  • Wraps pinneapple_design.geometry.vehicles3d.RoadCar (still importable from there).

docs.title: Two-stage launcher (Falcon 9 Block 5 class) (falcon9_booster)
docs.text:
Two-stage medium-lift launcher: 3.7 m core with a white first stage, black interstage carrying four titanium lattice grid fins, white second stage and a 5.2 m x 13.1 m ogive payload fairing; nine Merlin-class bells in an octaweb and four folding carbon landing legs. Grid-fin angle, leg deployment and fairing on / off for ascent and booster-return aerodynamics.

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 5.2 x 5.2 x 70 m. Frame: right-handed, metres: z up along the vehicle axis, x / y lateral; origin on the axis in the plane of the first-stage nozzle exits; legs and grid fins at 45 / 135 / 225 / 315 deg azimuth.
  • Parameters: grid_fin_angle [deg], legs_deployed, fairing.
  • Physics: ascent aerodynamics (axial force, transonic buffet on the fairing / boattail); booster re-entry and landing burn: grid-fin control authority, base heating of the octaweb; supersonic retro-propulsion plume-body interaction; structural loads: wind / max-q bending.
  • Sources: height 70 m, core diameter 3.7 m, nine first-stage engines, black interstage, grid fins and four landing legs: SpaceX (2024). Falcon 9 vehicle overview (height 70 m, diameter 3.7 m, nine Merlin engines on the first stage, one Merlin Vacuum on the second). https://www.spacex.com/vehicles/falcon-9/; payload fairing outer diameter 5.2 m, height 13.1 m: SpaceX (2021). Falcon User's Guide, sections 1-3 and 5 (fairing 5.2 m outer diameter, 13.1 m height; vehicle configuration). https://www.spacex.com/media/falcon-users-guide-2021-09.pdf; (estimate) stage break-down (first stage to 42.6 m, interstage to 47.3 m, second stage to 56.9 m), ogive shape, bell contour (exit diameter 0.86 m), octaweb ring radius 1.2 m: estimates from published photographs and the overall dimensions; (estimate) grid fin 1.5 x 1.3 x 0.22 m with a 45-deg lattice, leg length 9.6 m, deployed leg angle 115 deg, leg / fin azimuths: estimates from photographs

docs.title: Two-stage launch vehicle with fins (launch_vehicle_two_stage)
docs.text:
Two-stage launcher with a tangent-ogive payload fairing, interstage, four tail fins in + configuration and a cluster of engine bells (plume off). Wraps pinneapple_design.geometry.vehicles3d.LaunchVehicle (Barrowman stability included there).

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 43.5 x 7.8 x 7.8 m. Frame: metres; x along the axis from the nose tip toward the engines (the free-stream direction in ascent), y and z across, fins in the x-y and x-z planes.
  • Parameters: length [m], diameter [m], fin_span [m], n_engines.
  • Physics: ascent aerodynamics (transonic / supersonic drag, Cp); static stability (Barrowman); fin flutter / aeroelastic surrogates.
  • Sources: (estimate) proportions of medium-lift launchers (fineness 12-15, fairing 1.2 x core): generic; not a specific vehicle; fin aerodynamics: Barrowman, J. (1967). The practical calculation of the aerodynamic characteristics of slender finned vehicles. NASA Goddard
  • Wraps pinneapple_design.geometry.vehicles3d.LaunchVehicle (still importable from there).

docs.title: NASA VIPER lunar rover (viper_rover)
docs.text:
Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover from public NASA figures: chassis with side and aft solar arrays, deck radiator, mast with camera head, high- and low-gain antennas, TRIDENT drill, four active-suspension corner modules with spoked, grousered wheels. Wraps pinneapple_simulation.vehicle.viper.viper().cad.

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 1.692 x 1.539 x 2.5 m. Frame: right-handed, metres: x forward, y to the left, z up; origin on the ground below the chassis centre.
  • Parameters: wheel_radius [m], wheel_width [m], grouser_count, grouser_height [m].
  • Physics: terramechanics (wheel-soil, slip, sinkage); multibody dynamics; thermal (lunar night, radiator); lighting / perception at the lunar south pole.
  • Sources: 1.5 m x 1.5 m x 2.5 m (mast up), ~450 kg, wheels ~0.5 m diameter, active suspension: NASA VIPER fact sheets and NTRS papers listed in pinneapple_simulation.vehicle.viper.VIPER_SOURCES; (estimate) detail placement (antennas, hazcams, instruments): estimates from NASA imagery; bounding box of the model: 1.69 m long (the front instruments and bumpers stand proud of the 1.5 m chassis), 1.54 m wide over the wheels, 2.50 m to the top of the mast: model geometry
  • Wraps pinneapple_simulation.vehicle.viper.viper_cad (still importable from there).

docs.title: Light twin helicopter (H145 class) (helicopter_h145)
docs.text:
Light twin-engine helicopter: pod-and-boom fuselage with wrap-around glazing and a livery, engine cowling with exhausts, four-blade bearingless main rotor (NACA 0012/1312-type sections, -10 deg linear twist, collective, coning, azimuth), ducted Fenestron-type tail rotor with ten unevenly spaced blades in a shroud with fin and ventral fin, horizontal stabiliser with endplates and a skid landing gear; standing on the skids.

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 13.64 x 11 x 3.95 m. Frame: right-handed, metres: x aft from the nose (the free-stream direction), y to starboard (right), z up; origin on the centre plane at the nose, z = 0 on the ground under the skids; length includes the main rotor turning (blade 1 over the nose at azimuth 0).
  • Parameters: rotor_diameter [m], collective_deg [deg], rotor_azimuth_deg [deg], coning_deg [deg].
  • Physics: rotor aerodynamics in hover and forward flight (BEM, actuator disc, blade-resolved CFD); rotor-fuselage interaction and download on the stabiliser; ducted tail-rotor (Fenestron) performance and acoustics; brown-out / downwash near the ground; ground resonance on skids.
  • Sources: main-rotor diameter 11.00 m, length rotors turning 13.64 m, fuselage length 11.64 m, height 3.95 m: Airbus Helicopters (2023). H145 technical data / H145 Technical Information brochure: main rotor diameter 11.00 m, length (rotors turning) 13.64 m, fuselage length 11.64 m, height 3.95 m. https://www.airbus.com/en/products-services/helicopters/civil-helicopters/h145; four-blade bearingless main rotor, Fenestron tail rotor: EASA (2023). Type-Certificate Data Sheet R.010 (MBB-BK 117 / H145): four-blade bearingless main rotor, ducted (Fenestron) tail rotor on the D-3 / H145 variants; (estimate) blade chord 0.31 m, -10 deg twist, NACA 0012/1312 stand-ins (the actual DM-H3/H4 sections are not reproduced), Fenestron ~1.1 m duct with 10 blades, rotor-hub height 3.28 m, cabin width 1.74 m, skid track 2.2 m, stabiliser span 2.76 m: estimates from photographs and three-views

docs.title: High-speed train (ICE 3 / CRH3 class) (high_speed_train)
docs.text:
Streamlined head car with a long nose, wrap-around windscreen and headlights, passenger window band and red livery stripe, bogies with 920 mm wheelsets behind fairings, gangway in the inter-car gap, a lowered pantograph on the roof and a trailing end car, on two rails and sleepers (top of rail z = 0). Nose length and number of cars (1-3) as parameters, zero yaw.

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 51.95 x 2.95 x 5.07 m. Frame: right-handed, metres: x aft from the nose (the free-stream direction), y to starboard (right), z up; origin on the centre plane at the nose, z = 0 at the top of rail (EN 14067 reference plane); rails and sleepers lie below z = 0.
  • Parameters: nose_length [m], n_cars.
  • Physics: train aerodynamics: drag, slipstream and the nose pressure pulse (EN 14067); crosswind stability (side force and roll moment; yaw by rotating the inflow); tunnel entry micro-pressure waves and passing-train loads; pantograph aero-acoustics and under-body / ballast flow.
  • Sources: car width 2.95 m, height 3.89 m above top of rail, end car 25.675 m, intermediate car 24.775 m, bogie-centre distance 17.375 m, wheel diameter 0.92 m: Siemens Mobility (2018). Velaro D / ICE 3 (BR 407) and Velaro China (CRH3) technical data: car body width 2,950 mm, height above top of rail 3,890 mm, end-car length 25,675 mm, intermediate-car length 24,775 mm, bogie-centre distance 17,375 mm, wheel diameter 920 mm (new). Velaro product data sheets, https://www.mobility.siemens.com/global/en/portfolio/rail/rolling-stock/high-speed-and-intercity-trains/velaro.html; top of rail as the aerodynamic reference plane, standard gauge 1.435 m: CEN (2018). EN 14067-4: Railway applications - Aerodynamics - Part 4: Requirements and test procedures for aerodynamics on open track (top of rail as the reference plane, standard gauge 1435 mm); rail profile (60E1-like, 172 mm high, 72 mm head, 150 mm foot): CEN (2017). EN 13674-1: Railway applications - Track - Rail - Vignole railway rails 46 kg/m and above (60E1); (estimate) nose profile and plan-form curves, windscreen extent, window pitch 1.45 m, inter-car gap 0.6 m, bogie wheelbase 2.5 m, pantograph geometry, sleeper 2.6 x 0.26 x 0.22 m at 0.6 m: estimates from photographs of ICE 3 / CRH3 trains

docs.title: Pin-fin heat sink (pin_fin_heatsink)
docs.text:
Electronics pin-fin heat sink: a 60 x 60 x 5 mm aluminium base plate carrying an in-line (or staggered) array of circular, square or elliptic pin fins set by diameter, height and pitch, with a copper heat-source pad under the base. Flow along x for forced-convection studies.

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 0.06 x 0.06 x 0.0265 m. Frame: right-handed, metres: x along the base length (cooling-air flow direction), y across, z up along the pins; origin at the centre of the base plate's underside (the heat-source pad lies below, z < 0).
  • Parameters: base_length [m], base_width [m], base_thickness [m], pin_diameter [m], pin_height [m], pitch [m], pin_shape, pin_aspect, layout, heat_source, source_size [m], source_thickness [m].
  • Physics: conjugate heat transfer (pins + base, heat source); forced convection and pressure drop across pin arrays (inline vs staggered); flow bypass and fin-efficiency studies; thermal design optimisation (pin diameter / pitch / height).
  • Sources: pin-fin heat-sink family and test configuration (square base with in-line pin arrays, bypass flow, pin diameter / height / pitch as the design variables): Jonsson, H., Moshfegh, B. (2001). Modeling of the thermal and hydraulic performance of plate fin, strip fin, and pin fin heat sinks - influence of flow bypass. IEEE Trans. Compon. Packag. Technol. 24(2), 142-149. https://doi.org/10.1109/6144.926376; in-line versus staggered pin-fin array arrangement: Sparrow, E.M., Ramsey, J.W., Altemani, C.A.C. (1980). Experiments on in-line pin fin arrays and performance comparisons with staggered arrays. J. Heat Transfer 102(1), 44-50. https://doi.org/10.1115/1.3244247; (estimate) base 60 x 60 x 5 mm, pins d = 3 mm, h = 20 mm, pitch 6 mm (10 x 10), 25 mm heat-source pad: representative of the tested heat sinks, not the exact published specimens: engineering estimate

docs.title: NREL 5-MW reference wind turbine (wind_turbine_nrel5mw)
docs.text:
Three-bladed upwind 5-MW turbine: blades lofted through the published chord / twist table with a cylinder-to-airfoil root transition, 2.5 deg precone, 5 deg shaft tilt, hub with spinner, nacelle and tapered tower (onshore, base at z = 0). Rotor azimuth, blade pitch and yaw-free geometry for rotor CFD (actuator line / sliding mesh), wake and loads studies.

  • Bounding box (default build, L x W x H): 24.49 x 109.3 x 152.5 m. Frame: right-handed, metres: x downwind, y lateral, z up; origin at the tower base on the ground; rotor upwind of the tower (x < 0).
  • Parameters: rotor_diameter [m], hub_diameter [m], hub_height [m], pitch_deg [deg], rotor_azimuth_deg [deg], precone_deg [deg], shaft_tilt_deg [deg], overhang [m], nacelle_length [m].
  • Physics: rotor aerodynamics (BEM, actuator line, blade-resolved CFD); wake and wind-farm interaction; aeroelastic blade loads; tower shadow, icing, erosion of the leading edge.
  • Sources: rotor 126 m, hub 3 m, hub height 90 m, precone 2.5 deg, shaft tilt 5 deg, overhang 5 m, blade chord / twist / airfoil table, tower 6 m -> 3.87 m over 87.6 m: Jonkman, J., Butterfield, S., Musial, W., Scott, G. (2009). Definition of a 5-MW Reference Wind Turbine for Offshore System Development. NREL/TP-500-38060. https://doi.org/10.2172/947422; (estimate) airfoil shapes: the DU 40/35/30/25/21 and NACA 64-618 sections are approximated by NACA 4-digit sections with the same thickness ratio and 2-4 % camber: approximation (coordinates of the DU sections are not reproduced); bounding box: 109.3 m wide because at azimuth 0 the blades point up and at +-120 deg (2 R sin 120 deg), 152.5 m high (hub 90 m + R cos(precone)): model geometry; (estimate) nacelle 14 x 3.8 x 3.9 m and spinner shape: estimates from 5-MW-class nacelles

docs.title: Identifiability, calibration and inverse problems
docs.text:
One core in pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems answers three questions in order:

  1. Can these parameters be recovered from these measurements? analyze_identifiability. Run it before the experiment, when only the sensor positions and the noise are known.
  2. What are the parameters, and how sure are we? calibrate. It fits the measurements, gives confidence intervals only where the data determine the parameter, and checks the fit on held-out measurements.
  3. Which inversion method should I trust for this problem? compare_methods. It runs least squares, an adjoint gradient, automatic differentiation, Bayesian regularisation and a PINN on the same data, and ranks them by held-out error.

The Parameter Identifiability Lab, the Model Calibration Lab and the Inverse Model Studio apps are built on these calls.

docs.title: Models, parameters, measurements
docs.text:
Object What it holds Parameter(name, value, lower, upper, unit, log=None, fixed=False, truth=None) One unknown. Positive parameters are analysed in ln (a sensitivity is then per 100 % change). truth is used only to check synthetic studies. Observations(inputs, sigma, values=None, observable=None) One row per measurement: inputs such as position or time, the noise sigma, the measured value (or none yet), and which observable the row measures ("T", "q_base", ...). Observations.from_frame(df, ...) reads a table loaded by pinneapple_data.data_health.load_table (CSV, Excel, Parquet, JSON, sensor exports, decimal commas). ForwardModel predict(theta, inputs, observable). Ready-made models: PinFinModel (analytic fin), RodModel (finite-volume fin with h(x) zones: exact sensitivities, one-solve adjoint, torch twin), PlateModel (the Inverse Heat Lab's 2D plate), LumpedCoolingModel, ArrheniusModel. Your own model: ExpressionModel("T_air + (T0 - T_air)*exp(-k*t)", ...) (parsed safely, nothing is passed to eval), CallableModel(fn, ...) (any Python function or solver interface), or TabulatedModel(table, ...) (simulated runs interpolated over the parameters).

model_from_spec({...}) builds any of these from JSON. get_preset(name) returns ten problems with known answers, for example fin_h, fin_h_k, fin_h_k_flux, rod_h_field, rod_base_bc, plate_h, cooling_h, cooling_h_C and arrhenius_one_T / _two_T. Their measurements are synthetic: the model at the stated truth plus Gaussian noise from a fixed seed.

docs.title: 1. Identifiability before the experiment
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems as inv

fin = inv.PinFinModel(d_mm=5, length_mm=50)
params = fin.default_parameters()
params[1].fixed = False                                   # k unknown as well as h
sensors = inv.Observations({"x_mm": [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]}, sigma=0.5,
                           observable=np.array(["T"] * 5, dtype=object))
report = inv.analyze_identifiability(fin, sensors, params)
print(report.summary)

The output: 0 of 2 parameters identifiable. Moving h up and k up together leaves the predictions unchanged: the data fix h/k, not h and k separately. Most informative extra measurement: q_base at x_mm=0. The fin temperatures depend on h and k only through h/k. The base heat flow scales with sqrt(h k), so a heat-flux meter makes both identifiable.

The report combines four methods:

  • Fisher information (rank, condition number, Cramér-Rao bounds, expected correlations). The eigen-directions with zero or small eigenvalues are reported as ambiguities, with the combination the data do fix.
  • Local sensitivity of every measurement to every parameter, and the leverage of each measurement (its share of the identifiable information).
  • Profile likelihood (Raue et al., 2009) with 95 % intervals. A profile that rises only because another parameter reaches its bound is reported as such, not as a closed interval.
  • Posterior by adaptive Metropolis (flat priors inside the bounds) for cheap models.

It then gives a D-optimal design: from candidate measurements (other positions, times, temperatures or another observable), the greedy picks that most increase log det F, with the rank and the bounds each pick would give.

Limits: the Fisher rank is a local numerical test at one point, not a symbolic proof of global identifiability. The profile and the posterior are only as good as the bounds you give.

docs.title: 2. Calibration
docs.text:
b = inv.get_preset("fin_h_k_flux").build()
cal = inv.calibrate(b["model"], b["observations"], b["parameters"], holdout=b["validation"])

With the heat-flux meter, the run above gives h = 25.17 W/m²K (Jacobian 95 % interval 23.74 to 26.68, bootstrap 24.81 to 25.49) and k = 16.13 W/m·K (15.16 to 17.16, bootstrap 15.88 to 16.38). The truth is 25 and 16. The held-out RMSE is 0.41 °C for a sensor noise of 0.5 °C. Without the meter (fin_h_k), both parameters come back not estimable, with no interval and the reason.

  • Identifiability is checked at the calibrated values. A non-identifiable parameter gets no interval.
  • Jacobian intervals use the stated sigma (absolute_sigma=True, a sensor specification). They are widened by sqrt(chi2/dof) when the residuals are larger than the stated noise, and never narrowed. Pass absolute_sigma=False when sigma is only a weight.
  • Bootstrap intervals come from residual resampling and refitting.
  • Held-out measurements are never fitted. They can be given explicitly, as a random fraction, or as the last rows by an input (holdout_by="t_s", an extrapolation test).
  • warnings lists a parameter on its bound, a reduced chi-square far from 1, a held-out error much larger than the fit error, and a missing validation set.

docs.title: 3. Comparing inversion methods
docs.text:
out = inv.compare_methods(inv.get_preset("rod_h_field").problem(),
                          ["least_squares", "adjoint", "autodiff", "bayesian"])

This preset reconstructs a convection field h(x) in four zones and the temperature field T(x) from twelve thermocouples. Every method recovers the truth inside its 95 % interval. Held-out RMSE: 0.176 °C for least squares, adjoint and autodiff, and 0.180 °C for the Bayesian MAP, whose smoothness prior pulls the zones together. Forward model evaluations: 11 (least squares, exact sensitivities), 39 (adjoint, one extra solve per gradient whatever the number of zones), 48 (autodiff) and 3012 (Bayesian, of which 3000 are the MCMC chain).

Method Needs Uncertainty least_squares any model Gauss-Newton interval adjoint adjoint_gradient (e.g. RodModel) Gauss-Newton interval autodiff predict_torch Gauss-Newton interval bayesian any model (MCMC if cheap) posterior interval, flagged as set by the prior for non-identifiable parameters pinn pinn (the Inverse Heat Lab fin and plate; h only) none from one run

available_methods(problem) says which methods apply and why the others do not. With a known truth, every solution reports its parameter and field errors and truth_recovered. That flag is true when the truth lies inside the interval of every identifiable parameter, or within 5 % when the method gives no interval.

Measured on the presets (synthetic data, same seeds): the Inverse Heat Lab plate PINN (plate_h, 1500 steps, 56 s on one CPU core) gave h = 14.0 W/m²K for a true 15. Least squares on the finite-volume model gave 14.96.

docs.title: Industrial presets
docs.text:
A preset is an engineering problem already set up, solved and validated with PINNeAPPle. You open it, replace the defaults with your own values and run it. Each preset carries:

  • a data sheet: the sector, the question it answers, every input in SI units with a realistic default and the source of that default, the outputs and the validity domain;
  • the pipeline: geometry, then the model, then the solver (and optionally the surrogate), then post-processing, then a decision;
  • checks on every run: a trust report with conservation, convergence, correlation ranges and the applicability domain;
  • references: comparisons against citable values with the error measured (standards, published benchmarks, analytic solutions, independent solvers). A preset with no independent reference says so on its data sheet;
  • optional capabilities, where the physics allows them: a 3-D scene of the result, a surrogate, an inversion, an optimisation checked with the solver, and design variants run side by side.
import pinneapple as pp

pp.presets.names()                                     # the catalogue
p = pp.presets.load("water_distribution_network")
p.card()                                               # data sheet (JSON-ready; the Hub shows it)
r = p.run(demand_factor=1.3, hw_c=100)                 # your values, SI units
print(r)                                               # outputs, decision, trust report
p.validate()                                           # reference cases with the measured error
p.optimize()                                           # e.g. least-cost diameters, re-solved and checked
p.invert()                                             # e.g. Hazen-Williams C from logged pressures
pp.presets.load("water_hammer_valve_closure").run(fidelity="surrogate", t_close=6.0)

Command line:

python -m pinneapple_presets list
python -m pinneapple_presets card power_pcb_junction
python -m pinneapple_presets run power_pcb_junction vias=16 t_ambient=45
python -m pinneapple_presets validate steel_footbridge_pedestrian
python -m pinneapple_presets report all            # rewrites examples/industrial_presets/ and the Hub index

In the Flow Studio, the preset.run node takes the preset name, a dictionary of overrides and the fidelity (solver or surrogate). The preset.validate node runs the references.

docs.title: Catalogue
docs.text: The table is in examples/industrial_presets/README.md. It is regenerated from the stored results, so every number in it was measured. Each preset folder holds its README: the data sheet, the measured outputs, the validation table, the surrogate hold-out error, the inversion, the optimisation, the variants and the figures.

docs.title: Surrogates
docs.text:
SurrogateSpec(inputs, outputs, n_train, n_test, bounds, log, log_outputs) declares the surrogate. python -m pinneapple_presets surrogate <name> then builds it in five steps:

  1. It draws a Latin hypercube over the inputs.
  2. It runs the real solver at every point.
  3. It fits one anisotropic Gaussian process per output.
  4. It measures the error on an independent hold-out set.
  5. It stores everything as a few-kB JSON file in pinneapple_presets/data/surrogates/.

A run(fidelity="surrogate") call returns each output with its standard deviation. When the inputs fall outside the training box, or when a parameter differs from the value the surrogate was trained at, the call raises a warning, the trust report marks the check "contradicts", and nothing is extrapolated silently. pinneapple_presets.surrogate.serve_spec(name) describes the surrogate for a model server: its inputs with bounds and units, its outputs, its error and the call that runs it.

docs.title: Adding a preset
docs.text:
1. Subclass pinneapple_presets.Preset.
  2. Set the data-sheet attributes: params as Param(name, unit, default, source, lo, hi), and outputs.
  3. Implement solve(p) -> dict, checks(p, out) -> [Check], decide(p, out) and references(). Add the optional scene, figures, invert, optimize and variants methods where the physics allows them.
  4. Register the class in pinneapple_presets/registry.py.
  5. Run python -m pinneapple_presets report <name>.
  6. Add a test.

Every default needs its source. Every reference needs its citation, plus the tolerance it must meet.

docs.title: Self-modifying brick builds
docs.text:
pinneapple_design.bricks builds structures from interlocking toy bricks, judges every build with physics and redesigns it until it meets a goal: the longest cantilever past a table edge, a bridge that carries a load with the fewest parts, the tallest tower that survives a push. The geometry follows the LDraw unit system, so builds open in LDraw-compatible editors and real part shapes can be loaded from the LDraw parts library.

from pinneapple_design.bricks import Assembly, Ground, analyse_assembly

a = Assembly(ground=Ground("table", [(-1000, 0, -1000, 1000)]))   # a table that ends at x = 0
a.add("brick_1x8", -4, 0, 0, colour="blue")                         # half of it past the edge
a.add("brick_1x8", 0, 0, 3, colour="yellow")                        # on top, reaching 64 mm further
r = analyse_assembly(a)
print(r.status, r.explanation)                                      # mechanism: where the centre of mass left

docs.title: The parts
docs.text:
quantity value source stud pitch 8.0 mm (20 LDU) LDraw unit system plate / brick height 3.2 mm / 9.6 mm (8 / 24 LDU) LDraw unit system stud 4.8 mm diameter, 1.6 mm high LDraw stud.dat primitive part width 8 n - 0.2 mm (0.1 mm clearance per side) StableLego configuration (7.8 mm unit) brick masses e.g. 2x4: 2.16 g, 1x8: 3.03 g StableLego brick library (Liu et al. 2024) plate masses shell model fitted to the brick masses (worst residual +28 % on the 1x1 brick) parts.fit_mass_model

The catalogue (parts.CATALOG) holds rectangular bricks and plates with their LDraw part numbers. Assemblies live on the stud grid (x, y in stud pitches, z in plate heights). Two parts are joined where the top of one overlaps the bottom of the other: each overlapping cell is one stud-tube contact. Assembly.validate() reports overlaps and parts with no contact path to the ground; the ground is a table (smooth) or a baseplate (studs), optionally limited to regions such as a table edge or two banks.

docs.title: The physics
docs.text:
Statics (statics.analyse). Every part is a rigid body. Every contact patch carries compression at its four corners, and a stud joint also carries a clutch tension at each stud (at most JointModel.clutch_n) and a horizontal force at each stud; smooth contacts carry Coulomb friction. A linear programme finds the force distribution with the smallest peak stud utilisation. If one exists within the clutch, the build stands (the lower-bound theorem of plasticity); if none exists even with unbreakable studs, the build is a mechanism and the report says which support polygon the resultant left and by how much. capacity gives the largest factor on the external loads, and progressive_failure releases the critical joints round by round.

Joint model. The clutch is 0.98 N per stud, the friction capacity reported for the StableLego analysis (Liu, Deng, Wang, Liu, IEEE RA-L 9(11) 2024) and reused by BrickGPT (Pun et al., arXiv:2505.05469). No uncertainty is published, so the sensitivity study scales it by an assumed 0.5x to 1.5x. Limits of the model:

  • tension only: a joint fails when its pull-out force exceeds the clutch;
  • horizontal stud forces are unbounded by default (as in StableLego); JointModel(shear_n=...) caps them;
  • a single stud is a pivot about the vertical (no torsion);
  • rigid parts and no joint compliance: the force distribution is the most favourable one, so the verdict is optimistic for brittle clutch;
  • side-by-side parts do not push on each other (there is a 0.2 mm gap);
  • contact forces act at least edge_inset_mm (0.5 mm, assumed) inside a patch edge. Without it the search drives builds onto a knife edge (centre of mass exactly over a table edge), which the statics accepts with zero margin and Newton tips; the closed-form checks use sharp edges (edge_inset_mm=0).

Dynamics (dynamics.replay). NVIDIA Newton replays a build: every cluster held together by intact studs is one rigid body made of its boxes, released joints become box-box contacts with friction, tables have edges and a floor below, and vertical loads are dead weights. Newton has no breakable joints, so the statics decides which joints let go and Newton shows what happens next.

FEA (fea.solve). The voxelised build as one Hex8 solid (incompatible modes), for load paths and stresses in the plastic. It is an upper bound on stiffness: joint compliance is not modelled.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text: search.evolve and search.surrogate_search mutate builds with plain edits (add, remove, move, swap, rotate, recolour) and grammar rules that read the last evaluation (extend toward the goal, add a counterweight, brace the joint that failed, widen the base, mirror a half of a span). Every candidate is simulated; duplicates are looked up. Evolution selects survivors with NSGA-II and Deb's constraint handling on the goal's objectives (for example reach and part count). The surrogate search proposes eight times more children than it can afford, ranks them with a Gaussian process trained on every build simulated so far (upper confidence bound on a penalised score) and simulates only the best. search.compare runs both with the same evaluation budget and seeds.

docs.title: Visuals
docs.text:
• visuals.evolution_timeline + timeline_scene(...).export(folder): the twin3d three.js viewer plays the evolution generation by generation. Build frames are coloured by stud utilisation (the load path); rejected candidates are replayed by Newton with the joints that let go in red. Serve the folder over http.
  • visuals.render_frames, write_gif, write_mp4: the same frames from the software renderer.
  • visuals.render_blender, turntable_blender: Blender Cycles renders (pip install bpy).
  • visuals.write_instructions: step images per layer, a part list and an LDraw file with one STEP per layer.

docs.title: LDraw files and the parts library
docs.text: ldraw.write_ldr / write_mpd write builds; ldraw.read_ldr reads .ldr and .mpd files (sub-models expanded, quarter-turn rotations; parts off the grid or outside the catalogue are listed in skipped). ldraw.fetch_parts_library() downloads the LDraw parts library at run time into a cache folder; it is licensed CC BY 2.0 ("LDraw.org Parts Library") and is not copied into this repository. ldraw.PartsLibrary(root) triangulates real parts for renders.

docs.title: The experiment
docs.text:
python examples/bricks/self_modifying_bricks.py --full       # 5 seeds x 400 evaluations per strategy and goal
python -m pinneapple_lab sweep bricks -g case=cantilever,bridge,tower

docs.title: Results of the full run
docs.text:
5 seeds, 400 physics evaluations per run and strategy (examples/bricks/_out/report.md has every number, summary.json the raw values).

Closed forms. All nine checks pass (trust report APPROVED): the LP reproduces the harmonic stacking limit and the single-block limit exactly, the stud-cantilever tension and the tower tipping push to 1e-16, the beam reactions to 1e-15; the voxel FEA beam deflection is within 0.4 % of Timoshenko (1.4 % above Euler-Bernoulli alone, which leaves out shear). Newton agrees with harmonic stacking at 0.9x to 0.99x (stands) and 1.01x to 1.05x (falls). It disagrees at exactly 1.00x, the neutral equilibrium of the closed form, where it tips the stack.

Statistic: the median of the best score over the 5 seeds, a seed that found no feasible build counted as the worst, and in brackets the range over the feasible seeds (the same rule as comparison.png and the report).

goal evolution surrogate-guided best build cantilever, reach past the edge with 8 parts 111.9 mm (95.9 to 135.9), 5/5 feasible 103.9 mm (71.9 to 127.9), 5/5 135.9 mm, 34 % of the clutch bridge over 96 mm carrying 1 N, parts 5 (3 to 5), 5/5 feasible 8 (3 to 8), 3/5 feasible 3 parts, carries 1.46 N tower that survives a 10 mN push, height 118.4 mm (57.6 to 144.0), 5/5 115.2 mm (70.4 to 153.6), 5/5 153.6 mm, 16 parts, 1.64 x the push

Evolution has the better median on all three goals and is the more reliable on the bridge (the surrogate-guided search found no bridge in 2 of 5 seeds), but the margins are smaller than the range over seeds and the surrogate-guided search found the tallest tower, so 5 seeds do not separate the two strategies. For reference, unconnected blocks of the same length reach (L/2) H_8 = 86.7 mm (harmonic stacking), so the stud clutch buys 57 % more reach (135.9 mm), still far below the 255 mm centre-of-mass bound.

Sensitivity. The best cantilever and tower stand over the whole assumed clutch band (0.5x to 1.5x) and with stud shear capped at 0.3 N; the best bridge fails at 0.5x clutch (0.49 N per stud, load factor 0.80) and stands from 0.75x, so its verdict depends on the joint strength.

The three best builds stand in Newton under their goal loads (the bridge with its 1 N dead weight, the tower with the 10 mN push): largest displacement 0.00, 0.00 and 0.03 mm in 0.6 s, no tilt.

Statics against Newton (searched candidates, every joint intact, dt = 0.25 ms): agreement 90 % on cantilevers, 100 % on bridges, 75 % on towers; every disagreement is a statics "mechanism" that Newton keeps standing:

  • cantilever (2 cases): the centre of mass is 0.2 and 0.5 mm past the inset support, inside the 0.5 mm edge inset that the statics assumes and Newton's sharp boxes do not;
  • tower (5 cases): no equilibrium in the statics although the resultant is inside the support; Newton shows a slow drift of 0.1 to 0.8 mm without tilting, which points to sliding at the friction limit. The single-stud torsion assumption explains 2 of 40 tower mechanisms; the rest is not explained.

XPBD friction creeps under a sustained sideways load: the best tower drifts 0.23 mm at dt = 1 ms and 0.03 mm at 0.25 ms in 0.6 s while the statics says friction holds, so the cross-check uses the small step.

Limits. The verdicts rest on the cited 0.98 N clutch, which has no published uncertainty, on rigid parts and the most favourable force distribution (optimistic for brittle clutch), on unbounded stud shear and on an assumed friction coefficient. Nothing here was compared with physical builds.

docs.title: PINNeAPPle from any coding agent: the MCP server
docs.text:
pinneapple-mcp is a Model Context Protocol server (stdio, built on the official MCP Python SDK, 1.x or 2.x). Any MCP client, such as Gemini CLI, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or Antigravity, can then solve, benchmark and validate physics problems with PINNeAPPle, and every result comes back with its physics checks. For agents that read files instead of calling tools, the repository's AGENTS.md covers the same ground as a guide.

pip install "pinneapple[mcp]"
pinneapple-mcp --help            # or: python -m pinneapple_mcp

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
