docs.title: Playground: physics surrogates in the browser
docs.text:
The Playground is a static web page. You draw an airfoil, size a heat sink or drive a lunar-rover wheel, and a PINNeAPPle zoo model answers immediately. Next to each answer the page shows the physics checks and the model's trust verdict. Everything runs in the browser: nothing is installed and nothing is sent to a server. The URL holds the whole state, so a link opens exactly what you were looking at.

Mode Model (zoo) What you change What you get Airfoil airfoil_cst_rans_mlp Drag the CST handles on the airfoil, pick a NACA preset, set the angle of attack Cl, Cd, Cm and L/D with the spread of the 5-member ensemble; the polar sweep, with the OpenFOAM runs the model never saw and an XFOIL polar overlaid for the NACA presets Heat sink heatsink_forced_mlp Fin count, height and thickness, air speed (plus base, material, power) Thermal resistance with its split-conformal 95 % bound, base temperature, pressure drop, and R and ΔP against air speed Rover wheel rover_contact_grc1_viper Slip and sinkage of the VIPER wheel on GRC-1 Drawbar pull, normal load and torque, with held-out points of the analytic Wong–Reece model near the current sinkage Geometry gallery pp.geometries Pick one of the 17 geometries A 3-D view of the light glTF file, its dimensions and sources, and the code that regenerates it

docs.title: The trust verdict
docs.text:
The checks are the library's per-query checks, pp.zoo.query_checks (see the zoo guide). They are evaluated inside the model's ONNX graph on every change. Their rule IDs are the ones pinneapple check uses:

  • PC601, out-of-range query. Is every input inside the model card's validity range? This includes the derived limits: the fin gap and the source fraction of the heat sink. It is the same rule as ZooModel.in_range, tested on thousands of inputs. A query that fails it is labelled an extrapolation, in red.
  • PC403 / PC402, non-finite or unphysical output. For example, a negative drag, or airfoil surfaces that cross.
  • PC602, sparse training region. The ensemble spread is compared with its 99th percentile on the held-out shapes.
  • PC302, model residual. The zoo gate's physics checks, evaluated at the query:
  • the lift slope against thin-airfoil theory, and Cl rising with α;
  • more airflow or a more conductive material lowering the resistance;
  • the Mohr–Coulomb traction limit, My ≥ R·Fx, and the monotonic trends of the wheel.

The Why trust this? panel shows the full model card:

  • the validity range;
  • the held-out metrics against the independent reference, next to the zoo's acceptance limits;
  • the physics checks of the stored trust report;
  • data provenance and known limitations;
  • the SHA-256 and the measured parity of the ONNX file the page runs.

The airfoil design constraints are shown separately: t/c ≥ 11 % and |Cm| ≤ 0.10, the defaults of pinneapple_design.aero.aircraft.Requirements. They say whether a design is acceptable, not whether the model can be trusted.

Note that the NACA 4412 and 4415 presets sit just outside the model's CST box: M1 0.142 > 0.14 and M2 0.123 > 0.12. pp.zoo raises an OutOfRangeWarning for them, and the page marks them red. Their OpenFOAM reference runs, which the model never saw, are overlaid on the polar, so you can judge the extrapolation yourself.

There is no pressure or velocity field yet. The zoo's airfoil model predicts integrated coefficients only, and the field model (MeshGraphNet) is waiting for its training fields to be regenerated and published. The page says so in place of a field view.

docs.title: How it is built: the library does the work, the app draws
docs.text:
The app (apps/playground/site/) is UI code only. Everything it computes comes from library artefacts.

The zoo models. pp.zoo.export_web writes each model as one ONNX graph (pinneapple_hub.zoo.export):

  • input x, for the predictions, and input query, for the query checks;
  • pre- and post-processing included: CST encoding, log features, normalisation, ensemble mean and spread, L/D per member, and the conformal bound;
  • a JSON file next to it with the model card, the check spec (limits, templates, verdict texts) and the reference points to overlay.

The airfoil geometry. pinneapple_design.aero.geometry_onnx exports the CST geometry as two float64 graphs. They reproduce pinneapple_design.aero.geometry to round-off:

  • the outline, thickness and camber, the two validity quantities, and the positions of the drag handles;
  • handle heights back to CST weights, via geometry.shape_from_handles.

The gallery. pp.geometries.export_web writes an index and thumbnails.

The runtime. pinneapple_hub/zoo/web/onnx.js and zoo.js ship with the package. They contain:

  • a ~400-line ONNX interpreter that reads the protobuf directly;
  • loadModel, loadAirfoilGeometry, and evaluate, which turns the check values into statuses and a verdict exactly like pinneapple_hub.zoo.checks.evaluate.

engine=ort in the URL hash runs the same files in onnxruntime-web 1.22.0, loaded from jsDelivr. It is about 10 MB of WebAssembly, so it is opt-in. Pyodide is not used: there is no Python left to run in the browser.

Sizes: the airfoil mode loads 0.67 MB before compression. A 50-point polar with its checks takes 10–60 ms.

What is tested, in CI (.github/workflows/playground.yml):

  • Library, Python (tests/test_zoo_web.py):
  • The ONNX export of each model matches PyTorch to 1e-5 on every held-out and independent-reference input. Measured: 5.1e-7 airfoil, 1.6e-6 heat sink, 5.7e-7 rover.
  • The query checks never change status away from a limit.
  • Range checks fail exactly where ZooModel.in_range is False.
  • Held-out inputs are trusted.
  • The geometry graphs match NumPy to 1e-10.
  • The committed bundle in data/web is current.
  • Library, JavaScript (tests/js/zoo_web.test.mjs): the interpreter, evaluate (statuses and detail texts) and the geometry graphs, compared with Python fixtures.
  • App (tests/test_playground.py and the Playwright test in apps/playground/tests/e2e):
  • Every mode loads.
  • The numbers and verdicts on the page match Python for fixed inputs, in and out of range.
  • Dragging changes the answer and the URL, and a shared link reproduces the state.
  • The trust panel shows the evidence.
  • The page works offline, and the mobile layout has no horizontal scroll.
  • onnxruntime-web gives the same numbers as the built-in interpreter.
  • The app holds no model, geometry or check code.

docs.title: Run it locally
docs.text:
python apps/playground/build.py --serve          # http://localhost:8765/

The build uses only the standard library. It assembles the UI from three sources:

  • the library's runtime and its browser bundles (data/web/zoo, data/web/geometries);
  • three.js, vendored in pinneapple_tools;
  • the light glTF files from data/geometries/.

The output uses relative paths only, so it works under any URL prefix.

When a zoo model or the geometry library changes, regenerate the bundles with the library:

python -m pinneapple_hub.zoo.web data/web/zoo                      # needs torch, onnx, onnxruntime
python -m pinneapple_design.geometry_library.web data/web/geometries
cd apps/playground && npm ci && npm test                           # JS runtime tests + Playwright smoke test

docs.title: Deploying
docs.text:
The page is static, so there are two options, both prepared and neither switched on:

  • Docker + Caddy, next to the other apps. apps/playground/Dockerfile builds the site and serves it with Caddy on port 8095. apps/deploy has the playground service and the PLG_DOMAIN site block.
  • GitHub Pages, under the docs site. Set the repository variable PLAYGROUND_PAGES to true. The docs workflow then publishes the build at https://pinneapple-labs.github.io/PINNeAPPle/playground/.

docs.title: pp.validate: one call, one validation report
docs.text:
Other libraries train a Physics AI model; pp.validate says when to trust it. One call picks the checks that apply to the model and the problem, runs them, and returns a report with per-check evidence, a credibility level per factor and a deploy decision. A check that cannot apply is listed as not applicable with the reason, never skipped silently.

import pinneapple as pp

report = pp.validate(model, "darcy_2d", data={"train": {"a": a_tr, "u": u_tr}, "test": {"a": a_te, "u": u_te}},
                     query=a_new, level="standard")
print(report)                     # verdict, credibility per factor, one line per check
report.to_json("validation.json") # validation-report/v1
report.render("sarif")            # also "junit", "github", "html", "text"
report.to_trust_report()          # the trust card's APPROVED / REVIEW / REJECT

pp.validate(pp.zoo.load("heatsink_forced_mlp"), query=inputs)   # a zoo model: its card is the problem
pp.validate("fno.onnx", "darcy_2d", data=..., query=...)          # an ONNX file, run with onnxruntime

Models: a zoo model or its name, a torch.nn.Module (plain PyTorch, PhysicsNeMo), an .onnx file or any callable. Problems: a zoo model's own card (problem=None), "darcy_2d" (field operators a -> u on the cell-centred grid of operator_benchmarks.darcy_2d, the discretisation of the zoo dataset darcy_2d_li2021), or a small spec {"valid_range": {...}, "outputs": [...], "relations": [...]} for a tabular callable. pp.validate.<name> still gives the names of pinneapple_analysis.validation (pp.validate.PhysicsValidator).

To export an FNO to ONNX: pinneapple_neural.architectures.neural_operators.fno_export.export_onnx(model, example, path) rewrites its spectral convolutions in real arithmetic (the exporters of PyTorch do not handle complex weights), checks onnxruntime against PyTorch and returns the difference (below 1.2e-7 in the tests).

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
Level Adds quick applicability (validity range, training envelope), guaranteed residual bound, flux balance, reference error, the zoo gate, catalog status standard spectral fidelity (#702), metamorphic relations (#698), the data audit (#700), the calibrated error bound (#699) thorough robustness to 1 % input noise against the solver's own sensitivity; fault injection (#697) where it applies

Rollout checks (#701, problem={"rollout": {...}}) run at every level; their long-run statistics from standard on (guide).

docs.title: Credibility
docs.text:
Checks are grouped by factor, modelled on NASA-STD-7009A and ASME V&V 40 (this library's reading of them, not a certification): code verification, solution verification, validation, input pedigree, uncertainty, robustness, applicability. Levels: 0 no evidence, 1 a critical check failed, 2 passes with warnings, 3 passes quantitative checks, 4 passes against an independent reference or a guaranteed bound. The statuses, factors and check IDs are defined once in pinneapple_analysis.validation.schema; a report refuses an ID that is not there.

The decision is fail (REJECT) when a critical check fails, warn (REVIEW) when a non-critical one fails or warns, pass (APPROVED) otherwise; the verdict names the reasons, e.g. fail: out of validity range.

docs.title: What it found
docs.text:
From tests/test_pp_validate.py (Darcy 32², an FNO trained in plain PyTorch on 400 pairs, mean test error 4.2 %):

  • in distribution (thorough): decision warn. Passing: training envelope, guaranteed energy-norm bound (median 0.41, max 0.51: loose, about ten times the actual error), relative L2 4.2 %, reflection and transpose symmetry (worst 5 %), the data audit, the calibrated 90 % bound (mean coverage 90.2 % over 200 splits), 1 % input noise (2 x the solver's sensitivity). Flagged for review: the boundary flux does not balance the source (21 % imbalance), and the high-wavenumber energy is 12 x the reference's (small-scale noise).
  • queries from the contrast shift a in {1, 20}, no ground truth: fail: out of validity range (amplitude 9.5, trained on 4.4-4.5); the residual agrees (guaranteed bound 4.4, flux imbalance 4.9).
  • the same FNO as ONNX gives the same statuses; values agree to 1e-4.
  • heatsink_forced_mlp: pass; the zoo gate's checks (card metrics, acceptance limits, the model's own physics checks), the metamorphic relations and the stored audit card of its dataset all pass, and the decision equals pp.zoo.validate's (APPROVED). An air speed of 20 m/s (range 0.5-6) gives fail: out of validity range.

There is no Darcy model in the zoo, so the zoo case uses the forced-convection heat sink.

docs.title: The report as an artifact
docs.text:
pinneapple_analysis.validation.report_artifact (also pp.validate.diff, pp.validate.badge, ...):

What How Versioned schema REPORT_SCHEMA (validation-report/v1, JSON Schema 2020-12); check_report(report) lists what is wrong, including check IDs outside the vocabulary of schema.CHECKS Provenance provenance.model_hash (SHA-256 of the weights or the ONNX file), data_hash, library_version, physics (problem, tolerances, seed); zoo reports also carry the card's validity range Diff between versions pp.validate.diff(old, new): checks lost (passed before, not now), gained, metrics moved beyond 10 %, validity-envelope changes; .regressed Model card model_card_section(report): verdict, credibility table, checks, model hash Badge badge(report) (SVG, "physics-validated: 16/16 checks"), shields_endpoint(report) (shields.io endpoint JSON) Signature sign_report(report, key) / verify_report(envelope, key) with pinneapple_security.signing (#644)

The zoo stores one report per model (pinneapple_hub/zoo/validation_reports/, scripts/zoo/validation_reports.py build); each Hub card carries its section. The publishing workflow runs scripts/zoo/validation_reports.py check before any upload: a model whose fresh report loses a check its stored report passed is not published. In the tests a heat-sink "v1.1" with a sign error in the resistance loses the zoo gate's checks and is blocked.

Stored reports today: heatsink_forced_mlp, heatsink_natural_mlp, rover_contact_grc1_viper pass; airfoil_cst_rans_mlp is warn because its training split has no recorded Cm (documented missing values).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Built-in physics: Darcy (and steady conduction, the same operator) for fields; tabular models get applicability, reference and metamorphic checks only. Other PDEs: run pp.trust_card on a grid, or add a problem here.
  • The training envelope uses four scalar features of the input field (amplitude, spectral centroid, min, max); a shift that keeps them (a rearrangement of the same values) is not detected by it, only by the residual.
  • Fault injection (#697) and rollout checks (#701) are reported as not applicable until those modules land.

docs.title: Recreate a 3D wear twin (refractory, liner, pipe wall)
docs.text:
This guide shows how to rebuild, with PINNeAPPle, the kind of digital twin that monitors wear of a lining over time: a 3D vessel coloured cell by cell, a remaining-life forecast, and a maintenance schedule that comes out of an executable algorithm. It was written after reverse-engineering five published reference twins (steel ladle, pig-iron ladle, BOF converter, RH degasser and a smelting-reduction reactor); all five are presets.

Everything lives in pinneapple_twin3d.wear; the 3D viewer is the one pinneapple_twin3d already ships.

docs.title: 1. What these twins actually are
docs.text:
Reading the published reference apps (single-file HTML + three.js) showed what is real in them, and it is less and simpler than the visuals suggest:

Piece What it really is Geometry A surface of revolution per zone (wall, cone, floor, snorkel leg), cut into rows x sectors cells. Data Wear depth [mm] per cell and per reading x (heat number). One contract for every vessel. Colour The consumed fraction of the usable thickness, wear / (e0 - emin), mapped to a colour ramp. Forecast Linear least squares of the residual thickness over the last ~30 heats of each cell; remaining life = (residual - emin) / -slope. Nothing more. Process animation Decoration (pours, jets, rotation). Not part of the wear model. Demo data A synthetic generator inside the app (hot spots × growth law). The embedded dataset was empty.

What the originals do not contain: arrival-time (ETA) prediction, geographic maps, an optimizer. The optimizer in this module is new, so it is documented as such (section 5).

So a "wear twin generator" needs only: a spec, a dataset, the forecast, an optimizer, and a viewer.

docs.title: 2. The five steps
docs.text:
from pinneapple_twin3d import serve
from pinneapple_twin3d.wear import (HotSpot, VesselSpec, ZoneSpec, synthetic_campaign,
                                    forecast, optimize, export_wear_twin)

docs.title: Step 1 - Describe the part (VesselSpec)
docs.text:
A zone is a profile polyline (r, y) in metres, revolved around the vertical axis:

wall  = ZoneSpec("wall",  "Wall",  ((1.2, 0.0), (1.2, 2.0)), n_rows=12, n_sectors=24, e0=200, emin=80, group="wall")
floor = ZoneSpec("floor", "Floor", ((0.0, 0.0), (1.2, 0.0)), n_rows=5,  n_sectors=24, e0=250, emin=100, group="floor")
spec  = VesselSpec("tank", "Cylindrical tank", (wall, floor), x_name="batch")
  • wall / cone / neck: points along the hot face from bottom to top (a cone is just two points with different r);
  • floor: (0, y) -> (R, y); rows are rings; a dished floor is a polyline of an ellipse (see the BOF preset);
  • off-axis parts (the RH snorkels): center=(x, z), and theta0 to orient sector 0;
  • e0 is the new thickness and emin the minimum allowed, both in mm. They drive the colour scale and the limit.

Row 0 is the first profile point; sector 0 starts at angle theta0, angles run counter-clockwise seen from above. Use the same convention in your drawings so rows/sectors match the plant's brick numbering.

docs.title: Step 2 - Get a dataset (WearDataset)
docs.text:
• Measured (the real thing): a CSV zona,fiada,setor,valor,corrida (same columns as the reference apps) or the JSON contract. WearDataset.from_csv(spec, text) / from_contract(spec, dict). Missing cells are NaN.
  • Synthetic (before real data exists): synthetic_campaign(spec, hotspots, ...). HotSpot(zone, s, theta, ds, dtheta, amp) places a Gaussian bump of extra wear at position s (0..1 along the profile) and angle theta (None = a band all around). Repairs can be simulated (repairs=, repair_zones=).

Synthetic data is labelled in the dataset (origin="synthetic"), in the viewer title and in the report. Do not remove those labels: a demo that looks like plant data is a liability.

docs.title: Step 3 - Forecast (forecast)
docs.text:
fc = forecast(ds)     # per zone: worst consumed fraction, remaining life (in x), wear rate, critical cell, confidence

Details that matter (all tested, and identical in the JavaScript core of the web suite):

  • the fit window is win_x=30 heats, widened to at least min_pts=8 readings when readings are sparse;
  • a repair (a drop of wear larger than 2 % of the usable thickness between readings) restarts the window, so gunning does not poison the slope;
  • a cell already at the limit has remaining life 0 but its wear rate is still estimated, which the optimizer needs;
  • flat or recovering cells give inf (no trend);
  • confidence ("low/medium/high") grades the fit (points and R²). It is not a probability.
  • remaining_lo / remaining_hi give a 90 % interval from the standard error of the slope (Student-t, needs n >= 3), i.e. the ETA "in ~181 heats (150-230)". It measures the fit; it cannot cover a change of regime. With the 3 readings of the smelting-reduction demo the interval is wide and the confidence "low", which is the honest answer.
  • a >8 % dip between readings is read as a repair; at twice the default instrument noise ~1 % of cells are truncated by that heuristic (measured, see the tests). If your plant logs repairs, prefer passing them explicitly.
  • it is a linear extrapolation: it cannot foresee a change of regime (a new slag, a changed blow practice). backtest(ds) compares past predictions with the heat where the limit was actually reached, when that happened.

docs.title: Step 4 - Optimize maintenance (optimize)
docs.text:
res = optimize(fc, OptimizerConfig(horizon=300, heats_per_day=24))
res.recommended, res.baseline, explain(res)

Three policies are simulated over the horizon on the forecast: run to the limit (reactive), fixed calendar, and predictive grouped stops (stop before the earliest deadline minus a safety margin, serve together the zones whose deadline falls inside a grouping window, search the window). Cost = stops (setup + hours) + zones served + a penalty per heat operated beyond the limit. The recommendation is the cheapest policy with no breach.

docs.title: Calibrating the assumptions
docs.text:
The defaults are relative placeholders. calibrate(stops, ds) replaces what the plant's own records can support and says so for each parameter:

from pinneapple_twin3d.wear import StopRecord, calibrate
cal = calibrate([StopRecord(zones=['fundo', 'cone'], duration_h=11, cost=220), ...], ds)
cal.cfg        # an OptimizerConfig with the calibrated values
cal.report     # per parameter: value, source (calibrated | default | business input), n, standard error, note
Parameter Estimated from Needs setup_hours, hours_per_zone duration = setup + per_zone * n_zones over the stop log >= 3 stops, >= 2 different zone counts cost_per_hour, cost_per_zone cost = c_h * duration + c_z * n_zones >= 4 stops with a cost recovery_frac median wear drop / usable thickness at the repairs detected in the dataset >= 20 repaired cells breach_cost_per_x, safety_margin, horizon, heats_per_day, fixed_interval never inferred: business decisions -

A fit that gives a negative time or cost is rejected and the default kept. The web hub has the same panel (upload a CSV zonas,duracao_h,custo or JSON) and the two implementations are parity-tested.

Be explicit about the three layers when you show it: observed (readings), predicted (forecast), recommended (schedule). The report keeps them in separate sections. Costs are relative and every assumption is an OptimizerConfig field. It is decision support: nothing is sent to equipment.

docs.title: Step 5 - Export and look (export_wear_twin)
docs.text:
export_wear_twin(ds, "out/tank")     # scene.json, geometry.glb, fields.bin, viewer, wear_dataset.json, report.json
serve("out/tank")                    # http://localhost:8765/?field=consumed_fraction&step=last

The viewer's fields: wear_depth, consumed_fraction, residual_thickness, remaining_life. Use the clipping plane to look at the hot face from inside. wear_dataset.json is the same contract the web hub reads, so the twin can also live in the hub next to the others.

docs.title: 3. The four reference use cases
docs.text:
from pinneapple_twin3d.wear import presets
spec, hotspots = presets.get("bof_converter")   # steel_ladle | pig_iron_ladle | bof_converter | rh_degasser
Preset Zones What is special steel_ladle rim, slag line, metal wall, floor conical shell; porous plugs and alloy-jet impact on the floor pig_iron_ladle rim/spout, slag line, metal wall, floor slag-line height derived from the fill level (mass → level); torpedo-jet impact block; KR rotor vortex band bof_converter floor (dished), lower barrel, slag line, upper barrel, cone, mouth arc-length-defined wall (barrel → cone → neck); tap-hole side of the cone rh_degasser lower/upper vessel, floor, up- and down-snorkel off-axis legs; most wear at the immersed tip smelting_reduction_reactor upper/lower shaft, tuyere zone, crucible wall, hearth sector 0 = tap hole; eight tuyere hot spots between tap holes

Geometry comes from the proportions published in the reference twins and is indicative. Replace the numbers with the plant's drawings; nothing else changes. Run all four: python examples/use_cases/refractory_wear_twin/run_use_cases.py.

docs.title: 4. A new part in 25 lines
docs.text: examples/use_cases/refractory_wear_twin/custom_part.py builds a cylindrical tank with a slag band and an impact pad. The recipe for any other part: (1) list the surfaces of the hot face and write each as a profile; (2) choose rows/sectors so a cell matches the unit you measure (a brick course × a sector); (3) set e0/emin per zone from the lining design; (4) pick the real x (heats, days, tonnes); (5) test with synthetic data, then swap in the measurements. Anything that is a surface of revolution fits (vessels, tanks, ladles, snorkels, straight pipe sections). For shapes that are not (a pipe bend, a tundish with flat faces), build the mesh yourself and use Scene.add_trimesh with per-vertex fields, as in pinneapple_twin3d.demo; the forecast and the optimizer only need the dataset contract, not the geometry.

docs.title: 4b. Beyond liners: the gallery
docs.text:
Wear is only one use of the generator. pinneapple_twin3d.primitives (revolve, sweep along a path, loft of airfoil sections, box, cylinder) and pinneapple_twin3d.gallery build complete 3D twins of very different parts, each with time-varying fields and sensors:

from pinneapple_twin3d import gallery
gallery.export_all("out/gallery")      # index.html + one folder per part
Part Built from Illustrative fields runner_channel (blast-furnace trough) sweep of an open U along a curved path wear at the metal/slag lines and under the tap jet, remaining thickness mixing_tank dished revolve, shaft, two pitched-blade impellers, baffles tracer blending, impeller shear (spin-up) oil_pipeline filleted path, circular sweep wall loss at bend extrados and the 6 o'clock line, pressure drop, UT probes airliner revolved fuselage, lofted swept wings, tail, nacelles skin temperature through climb/cruise/descent, wing-root bending rocket ogive + stack, bell nozzle, fins aero heating peaking mid-ascent at the nose, throat heat flux and ablation drone box, arm cylinders, motors, rotor discs motor/arm/battery heating over a flight lunar_rover box chassis, six wheels, mast, dish day/night chassis temperature, wheel wear that grows only when driving wind_turbine tapered tower, three twisted blades leading-edge erosion at the tips, root fatigue satellite bus, two arrays, dish thermal cycling through sunlight and eclipse

(rendered with examples/use_cases/refractory_wear_twin/render_gallery_png.py; the interactive viewer shows the same scenes with the time slider)

All gallery fields are illustrative closed-form patterns that put the physics where an engineer expects it. They are not simulation or measurement results, and every title and source says so. To use real fields, build the same scene and call Scene.add_field(part, name, values) with your (T, V) arrays; the tests check that parts are valid meshes and that the patterns behave (erosion at the bend, heating at the nose, front wheels wearing more, ...).

docs.title: 5. What is real, what is not
docs.text:
• Real and tested: the cell geometry, the dataset contract (validation, CSV, JSON), the forecast (parity-tested against the JavaScript core), the optimizer simulation, the four presets end to end, the exported scene (valid glTF, fields aligned to cells).
  • Synthetic: every wear value produced by synthetic_campaign. It encodes where the process is known to attack the lining, not a physical model. The hot-spot amplitudes are illustrative.
  • New in this module, not in the reference twins: the confidence grade, the ETA interval, the backtest, the optimizer and its calibration. The optimizer's cost structure is an assumption; its numbers must come from calibrate (stop log, history) and from business decisions (cost of a heat beyond the limit).
  • Out of scope: process animation of each vessel, arrival-time prediction, geo maps, plant integration.

docs.title: 6. Checklist before showing a twin to someone
docs.text:
1. The viewer title says SYNTHETIC if the data is synthetic.
  2. Colour scale: consumed_fraction = 1 is the limit; cells above 1 are in breach.
  3. forecast confidence is shown next to every remaining-life number.
  4. The recommended schedule lists its assumptions and says it is decision support.
  5. pytest tests/test_twin3d_wear.py passes.

docs.title: From residual to error bound: how wrong is this prediction, without the true answer?
docs.text:
At query time the physics residual of a surrogate's prediction can be computed without the true answer, but a residual of 0.03 means nothing to an engineer. pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.residual_bound turns it into an error bound in two ways, and reports both.

from pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.residual_bound import (ResidualErrorCalibrator, darcy_problem,
                                                             energy_error_bound)

# 1. theory: guaranteed, no data needed (linear elliptic problems)
P = darcy_problem(a)                                   # -div(a grad u) = 1, the discretisation of darcy_2d
b = energy_error_bound(P, u_pred)                      # ||u_h - u_pred||_A <= b["bound"]; b["relative"] = / ||u||_A

# 2. calibration: tight, guaranteed for queries like the calibration set
res_cal = [energy_error_bound(darcy_problem(a), p)["relative"] for a, p in zip(a_cal, pred_cal)]
cal = ResidualErrorCalibrator(alpha=0.1).calibrate(res_cal, err_cal)          # err_cal: relative L2 errors
bound = cal.bound(res_new)                             # 90 % bound on the relative L2 error of new queries
print(cal.evaluate(res_shifted, err_shifted, "shifted inputs"))   # coverage measured, "BROKEN" if it fails

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
For A u = f with A symmetric positive definite and A >= c L (L a reference SPD operator), ||u_h - u||_A <= ||r||_{L^-1} / sqrt(c) with r = f - A u, because A^-1 <= L^-1 / c. For Darcy and steady heat conduction -div(k grad u) = f in cell-centred finite volumes (darcy_problem, heat_conduction_problem; the matrix is operator_benchmarks.darcy_matrix), L is the same operator with k = 1 and c = min k: every face coefficient is a harmonic mean and never below min k. The residual is evaluated with the reference solver's own discretisation, so the reference solution has a residual of round-off size (a finite-difference residual of the same field is of order one).

The bound is about the discrete solution on the same grid; the discretisation error of that solution is not included. It is loose when the coefficient contrast is large (it scales with 1 / sqrt(min k)).

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: Split conformal prediction (the finite-sample quantile of uncertainty.conformal) on the score error / g(residual), with g the identity (mode="ratio", the default) or a power law fitted on a separate set (mode="power"). The bound of a new query is q * g(residual). Coverage is guaranteed only for queries exchangeable with the calibration set. evaluate measures it and says "BROKEN" when it falls more than two standard deviations (test and calibration sampling) below the target; coverage_study averages it over random calibration / test splits; to_check gives the trust-report check "error bound without ground truth".

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
tests/test_residual_bound.py; Darcy on 32 x 32 cells (Li et al. 2021 coefficients, 400 training pairs, operators trained with pinneapple_neural.train_model), 1000 held-out queries, calibration on 500:

Model Median rel. L2 error 90 % bound: mean coverage over 200 splits Theory violated FNO 4.1 % 90.1 % (std 1.9 %) 0 of 1000 DeepONet 20.9 % 89.9 % (std 2.0 %) 0 of 1000 Heat conduction, FNO (source -> temperature) 1.0 % 90.1 % (std 1.8 %) 0 of 1000

Under the two input shifts of the PhysicsNeMo trust experiment (150 queries each):

Model Shift Median error Coverage of the 90 % bound (ratio map) Theory violated FNO contrast a in 76 % 2.7 % (BROKEN) 0 FNO length scale tau 9 4.8 % 94.0 % 0 DeepONet contrast a in 51 % 100 % 0 DeepONet length scale tau 9 20 % 92.7 % 0

The power-law map breaks under the contrast shift for both models (0 % coverage): it extrapolates the residual-to-error relation outside the calibrated range. These numbers come from one training run each; another seed moves them (the FNO's contrast-shift coverage was 100 % in an earlier run), which is the point: under a shift the calibrated bound must be measured, and only the theoretical bound is guaranteed.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The theoretical bound needs a linear, coercive problem and its discrete operator; for others only the calibrated map applies.
  • The calibrated bound is marginal (90 % of queries), not per query, and assumes exchangeability with the calibration set.
  • Not yet shown in pp.trust_card; pp.validate (#696) reports it as "error bound without ground truth".

docs.title: Rollout validation: when an autoregressive surrogate stops being trustworthy
docs.text:
An autoregressive model (one step at a time, its output fed back as input) can look accurate for a few steps and then lose energy, blur, drift or blow up. A one-step error says nothing about that. pinneapple_analysis.validation.rollout runs the model over a horizon and reports where it stops being trustworthy. Every test is checked against a classical solver.

from pinneapple_analysis.validation.rollout import rollout, validate_rollout

pred = rollout(model_step, u0, 300)                 # (301, n): u0 and 300 model steps
rep = validate_rollout(pred, ndim=1, ref=reference, dt=1.0, conserved=["mass"], chaotic=True,
                       long_ref=long_reference)     # a long run of the solver, from any initial state
rep.evidence["divergence"]["trust_horizon"]         # earliest crossing, in time units
[(c["id"], c["status"]) for c in rep.checks]

import pinneapple as pp                             # the same checks in the validation report
pp.validate(model_step, {"rollout": {"ndim": 1, "dt": 1.0, "conserved": ["mass"], "chaotic": True, "steps": 300}},
            data={"u0": u0, "reference": reference, "long_u0": u1, "long_reference": long_reference})

docs.title: What is measured
docs.text: Function Measures invariant_drift mass, energy (or any callable): drift rate relative to the initial value and, with a reference, the largest relative deviation from the reference's own series (decaying flows lose energy; the model must lose it at the same rate) spectral_drift energy in the top third of the resolved shells, over a trailing window, relative to the reference at the same time (or to a training spectrum) divergence_time first time each of pointwise error (20 %), spectral bias (25 %) and invariant deviation (5 %) crosses its tolerance, each over a trailing window of 10 frames; the trust horizon is the earliest long_run_statistics for chaotic systems: Wasserstein-1 distance between value histograms, decorrelation time, and the time-averaged energy in the low, mid and high thirds of the resolved shells; each also between the two halves of the reference, giving the sampling noise floor

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
ID Fails when rollout.finite a NaN or Inf appears (with the first bad step) rollout.invariant.<name> a declared conserved quantity drifts more than drift (1e-3) relative rollout.horizon never fails: a finite trust horizon is a warn asking for review, with the horizon as its value rollout.spectrum the high-band energy leaves the 25 % band before the pointwise error crosses (with chaotic=True, a crossing after the error crossing is expected and does not fail) rollout.invariants the invariants deviate from the reference's before the pointwise error crosses rollout.statistics any long-run distance is more than 2× its noise floor (with minimum floors of 1e-3 of the field scale, 0.05 in log-band energy and 10 % of the decorrelation time)

pp.validate runs the long-run statistics only above level="quick". Tolerances can be overridden with tolerances={...} (error, spectrum, invariants, drift, floor).

docs.title: Results (from tests/test_rollout_validation.py)
docs.text:
Kuramoto–Sivashinsky (pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.kuramoto_sivashinsky, L = 32π, 128 modes, ETDRK4, the discretisation cross-validated against Exponax), frames one time unit apart:

"Model" error crosses spectrum crosses checks the same solver with dt/2 t = 57 t = 82 all pass; horizon warn at 57 (chaos: the Lyapunov time sets it) solver + 30 % energy removed above mode 20 every step t = 7 t = 1 rollout.spectrum fails; long-run statistics fail (band energy 0.52 vs floor 0.05) FNO trained on one-step pairs finite, < 57 horizon set by the pointwise error

The halved-step solver from a different initial state passes rollout.statistics (0.048 vs floor 0.053). On 2-D decaying turbulence (multiscale.ns2d, 64², ν = 1e-3), the halved-step solver passes everything with no finite horizon over 3 time units.

docs.title: Limits (honest results)
docs.text:
• The pointwise horizon of a chaotic system is set by the Lyapunov time: an exact integrator has one too. Read rollout.horizon against the horizon of a reference integrator, not as a failure.
  • The long-run statistics need a long reference run (here 1500 frames); with short runs the noise floor is large and the check is weak. A per-shell maximum of the spectrum ratio was too noisy to detect 30 % high-band damping; band energies are used instead.
  • Mass conservation is checked as drift of the spatial mean; for a field with zero mean the scale is the mean of |u|, so a drift is relative to that.
  • The invariants are those of a periodic box; with walls or sources supply your own callables.

docs.title: Reduced-order models and meshless methods: measured, not assumed
docs.text: Two studies that answer "which method, at which cost, for which error" on your data, with every number measured on held-out snapshots or against a known solution. They are the library behind the ROM Lab (day 19) and the Meshless Method Lab (day 26).

docs.title: ROM study
docs.text:
from pinneapple_data.snapshots import load_snapshots
from pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom import rom_study, ReducedModel

snaps = load_snapshots([("wake.npz", open("wake.npz", "rb").read())])   # OpenFOAM times, VTU series, npz, CSV
res = rom_study(snaps, ranks=[2, 4, 8, 16], budget_s=5)                # forecast split: the last 20 % of times
print(res.to_dict(tolerance=0.05)["best"])                              # fastest model under 5 % held-out error
m = res.models[("dmd", 16)]
open("wake_dmd.rom.npz", "wb").write(m.to_bytes())                      # arrays + JSON manifest, no pickle
open("wake_dmd.onnx", "wb").write(m.to_onnx())                          # for ModelGateway.publish(kind="onnx")
Method Data What it is pod_rbf both POD + thin-plate RBF regression of the coefficients (in time: interpolation, poor extrapolation) pod_gpr parametric POD + one Gaussian process per coefficient nearest parametric the nearest training snapshot: the baseline every ROM must beat dmd time exact (uncentred) DMD; the mean is one of its modes opinf time quadratic Operator Inference on centred POD coefficients, regularisation chosen inside the training window neural both an MLP trained within budget_s seconds (train_within_budget): parameters to field, or a residual stepper of the POD coefficients

Every row reports the held-out error (time series: relative to the fluctuation about the training mean; several fields: each scaled by its training RMS, with per-field errors), the POD projection error at that rank (the floor), fit time, inference time per snapshot (time_per_query) and the speed-up when the full-order time per snapshot is known (hf_seconds). Time steppers predict from the latest training snapshot at or before the requested time.

docs.title: Meshless study
docs.text:
from pinneapple_simulation.meshless import Problem, domain, meshless_study

res = meshless_study(Problem("poisson", exact="sin(pi*x)*cos(2*y) + x*y"), domain("lshape"), h=[0.1, 0.05, 0.025])
for w in res.wins:
    print(w["criterion"], w["method"], w["value"])

Kansa, RBF-FD, embedded finite differences (Shortley-Weller), P1 finite elements on the Delaunay mesh of the nodes and a PINN on the same nodes, for Poisson, Helmholtz and heat (Crank-Nicolson) with Dirichlet conditions. Measured on the L-shape above (tests/test_meshless.py): RBF-FD (degree 4) converges at order ≈ 4.4, FD and FEM at ≈ 2, Kansa reaches 1e-6 with a condition number of 1e20 (and is unstable when time-stepped), FEM has the best conditioned system. Linear elasticity and Neumann conditions are not implemented yet; R-OAMS is not in the library.

docs.title: The rover that learns the planet
docs.text:
PINNeAPPle Autonomous Physics Lab, demo 4. A mission in plain language drives a full-scale VIPER-class rover across a synthetic site whose true soils are known. The first route is planned on the orbital map, which calls a patch of soft sand "compact regolith"; the rover stalls in it, learns the soil from what its wheels measured, replans with the learned risk and reaches the goal. Every step is checked: the physics of the runs, the agreement between the models, and how close the learned soil is to the truth.

from pinneapple_simulation.rover.autolab import RoverMission, demo_site

m = RoverMission(demo_site(), "Leve o rover até (37, 15) sem atolar, escorregamento máximo de 40%, "
                              "minimizando a energia.")
res = m.run(out_dir="out")               # report.md, trust_report.md, summary.json, figures
[r.meta["ended"] for r in res.runs]      # e.g. ["stalled: mean slip ... > limit 0.4", "goal"]
res.report.decisao                       # APPROVED / REVIEW / REJECT

The full demo, with the renders and the video: python examples/autolab_rover/rover_learns_planet.py (about 10 min for the mission and 15 min for the renders on 4 CPU cores). The numbers of the committed run are in examples/autolab_rover/results/report.md and summary.json next to it; the Flow Studio node is rover.learn_planet.

docs.title: The committed run
docs.text:
Measured in examples/autolab_rover/results/ (2026-10-24 10:02:04 UTC, Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.10GHz, 4 cores, Python 3.13.17, NumPy 2.5.3, Blender 5.1.2); mission 389 s:

Route A (orbital map) Route B (learned soil) outcome stalled: mean slip 0.42 over 2 s > limit 0.4 goal distance driven 12.9 m 28.6 m drive energy 2958 J 2869 J largest 2-s slip 0.42 0.21 largest sinkage, any wheel 319 mm (rear left) 31 mm (rear left) largest sinkage, mean of the front wheels 210 mm 18 mm risk under the learned belief 1.00 0.00

Learned soft sand against the hidden truth: log10 k_phi 4.85 (true 4.78), n0 1.26 (1.20), n1 1.41 (1.40), phi 22.7 deg (24.0); every error within 2.0 posterior standard deviations. Trust decision: REVIEW -- the only failed check is planner_vs_multibody_slip (RMS 0.054 against 0.05): the quasi-static planner is a little off the multibody rover's slip; its energy prediction is within 13 %.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text: Stage Tool What happens mission parse_mission text -> MissionSpec (goal, start, slip limit, risk limit, objective, speed). RuleParser by default; an LLM adapter with the extract(text, schema) interface of CallLLM can be passed, and its values are kept only when their quote is in the text plan agent the fixed tool sequence of RoverMission.plan(); only the tools of TOOLS are called build survey_site soil units of the orbital map -> one Gaussian belief per unit over (log10 k_phi, n0, n1, phi) simulate drive the multibody VIPER (VehicleSimulator, Wong-Reece wheels on several soils, pure-pursuit route following) on the true terrain; a traction monitor stops it when the 2-s mean front-wheel slip exceeds the limit learn estimate_soil the run's log -> noisy measurements -> iterated EKF per unit, then the Birge-ratio check of the residuals; a quarter of each unit's rows is held out learn compare_models analytic Wong-Reece (orbital soil and learned soil) and the zoo surrogate rover_contact_grc1_viper against the measured operating points optimize plan_route risk-aware Dijkstra on the learned belief, from the point the rover backs out to verify verify TrustReport (below)

docs.title: Models and their limits
docs.text:
• Site (site.py): height = tilt + Gaussian mounds (a ridge with a pass); soil units are ellipses. The soft sand is a synthetic truth chosen for the demo (SOFT_SAND_NOTE); compact regolith and firm ground are the library's GRC-1 and JSC-1A with their recorded provenance.
  • Rover dynamics: pinneapple_simulation.vehicle (multibody tree, Wong-Reece wheels with slip-sinkage, multipass and ruts, PI wheel-speed drives, steering, active suspension). VehicleSimulator gained ground of several soils (soil_map), route following and a stop rule for this demo.
  • Planner model (wheel_models.grade_table): quasi-static, equal wheel loads m g cos(a) / n, drawbar pull m g sin(a) / n; no load transfer, no cross-slope. The trust report measures how far it is from the multibody run.
  • Sensors (Sensors): load, slip, sinkage and torque with Gaussian noise; the levels are stated assumptions, not datasheet values. Slip is averaged over a centred 0.3-s window; the slip that sets the sinkage exponent is lagged as the simulator lags it.
  • Estimator (SoilBelief): iterated EKF, observation model = the steady single wheel (sinkage and torque from the measured load and slip), measured-input noise carried through the model, front wheels only (the rear ones run in ruts). Cohesion, K and k_c stay at the orbital soil's values.
  • Risk (RiskPlanner): share of belief samples in which the rover cannot climb a grade at a slip at or below the limit; the soil is checked at both ends, the middle and half a track to either side of every edge.

docs.title: Trust report
docs.text:
Check Meaning goal_reached, slip_within_limit (critical) the final run reached the goal with the monitored slip at or below the limit energy_covers_climb drive energy >= potential energy gained time_step_converged the start of the final route at dt and dt/2 agree within 5 % planner_vs_multibody_energy, _slip quasi-static prediction (learned belief) vs the multibody run of the final route replanned_route_risk, failed_route_risk_learned the final route is within the risk limit and the first one is not, both under the learned belief learned_soil_predictive held-out measurements predicted within 20 % (sinkage) learned_soil_calibrated, learned_soil_closer_to_truth synthetic site only: error within 3 posterior sd, and smaller than the prior's models_used_in_validity the planner uses the analytic law; the zoo surrogate's share of points outside its box is reported

A failed check is reported, not hidden: the decision is REVIEW (or REJECT for a critical one) and the report says which check failed and by how much.

docs.title: Renders
docs.text: render.py (Blender Cycles through pip install bpy): render_overview (terrain coloured by the learned risk, both routes, the rover at the stall and at the goal), render_hero (close-up of the stall on a light studio background with a hard Sun shadow and sand grains instanced on the berms the terrain model computed; the grains are visual only) and render_traverse (chase camera, ruts growing, MP4 and GIF). The rover is the repository's data/geometries/viper_rover/viper_rover.light.glb; VIPER has no blade, so the regolith piles are the berms of the wheel ruts.

docs.title: Running a benchmark
docs.text:
pp.benchmark compares physics-AI methods (PINNs, neural operators, graph networks, MLPs, your own) on physics problems (built-in or your own) under the same compute budget, and tells you whether the comparison can be trusted. One call does everything; each stage can also be run alone.

prepare  ->  validate  ->  run (gates, search, final, equal FLOPs)  ->  report (tables, figures, diagnostics)

docs.title: In one call
docs.text:
import pinneapple as pp

res = pp.benchmark.run(
    problems=["burgers", "darcy", "navier_stokes"],   # built-in ids, or Problem objects (yours)
    methods=["pinn", "fno", "deeponet"],               # built-in ids, or Method objects (yours)
    budget=pp.ComputeBudget(wall_s=300),               # per training run; or flops=..., steps=...
    budget_levels=[1/9, 1/3, 1.0],                     # error-versus-budget curves
    seeds=3, n_trials=4, search_fraction=1/3,          # the same search effort for every method
    equal_flops=True,                                  # an extra arm at equal FLOPs
    n_workers=4, threads_per_run=1,                    # every run gets the same hardware share
    out_dir="results/my_benchmark",                    # re-running resumes from here
)
res.table()            # pandas DataFrame
res.to_markdown()      # the report as Markdown; res.to_csv()
res.report()           # (re)writes table.md, table.csv, summary.json and figures/ in out_dir
res.diagnostics        # the advisor's findings (below)

From the shell, with a YAML file holding the same fields (example):

pinneapple benchmark prepare --config bench.yaml --out results/x     # artifacts + validation only
pinneapple benchmark run     --config bench.yaml --out results/x     # train and report
pinneapple benchmark report  results/x                               # report again from the cache
pinneapple benchmark run --config bench.yaml --out results/x --smoke # tiny sizes: a pipeline check in minutes

Options of run: --force (reuse an out_dir made with another configuration), --skip-checks, --allow-failed-validation, --apply-suggestions (writes config.suggested.yaml with the advisor's edits), --no-prepare (refuse to run when the artifacts are not prepared yet).

docs.title: What ends up in out_dir
docs.text: Path Content config.yaml the resolved configuration; its hash guards the cache (a different configuration is refused unless force) hardware.json CPU, cores, memory, GPU, library versions prepared/<problem>/ solver configuration, data, geometry (for the airfoil: shapes, a complete OpenFOAM case), data-generation cost, manifest.json with the SHA-256 of every file and the validation status validation/ per problem: solver verification, data checks, the validation stack; architecture.json, determinism.json runs/ one JSON per training job (spec, result, hardware, wall time): the cache table.md, table.csv, summary.json the report figures/ summary_table.png (shareable), error_vs_budget.png, pareto_error_vs_inference.png

docs.title: Stage 1: prepare
docs.text: pp.benchmark.prepare(config, out_dir) creates the artifacts before any training and saves them for you to inspect: the solver configuration, the geometry, the generated data, what generating it cost (core-seconds, measured) and the hashes. run consumes only prepared artifacts: it prepares what is missing, and refuses to train when they are stale (a hash no longer matches the configuration or a file changed) or failed validation, unless you pass allow_failed_validation=True, which the table then shows on every page.

docs.title: Stage 2: validation, with PINNeAPPle's own validation stack
docs.text:
Run on the prepared artifacts, stored in out_dir/validation/ and in the report's Validation section:

Check Library entry point Applies to Reference solver against an exact or manufactured solution, observed order the problem's verify_solver (Cole-Hopf, Taylor-Green, a manufactured Darcy solution, NACA 0012 vs the NASA TMR value) built-in problems Grid convergence (GCI, observed order, asymptotic range) pinneapple_design.fitmesh.gci, pinneapple_analysis.verification.richardson_extrapolate problems with grid levels Simulation preflight of the solver case pinneapple_data.preflight OpenFOAM / CalculiX problems Mesh quality pinneapple_data.cae.mesh_report problems with a mesh First-cell y+ verification.mesh_intelligence.estimate_required_first_cell_height wall-bounded flows Physics audit of the solver's assumptions pinneapple_physics.physics_audit (ModelProfile, audit_assumptions) every built-in problem Applicability domain: test inside, OOD outside the training envelope physics_audit.Envelope every problem Data sanity: finite, split sizes, no duplicates or leakage between splits (hashes), OOD really out of distribution, normalisation from the training split FieldOperatorProblem.data_checks every problem (including your arrays) Six-stage trust card pinneapple_lab.curation.trust_stages the report's Trust card section

A failed blocking item stops the run. For a problem you bring (an ArrayProblem or your own Problem), the same checks run against what you provide, and the report says which ones did not apply and why.

docs.title: Stage 3: run, with correctness gates
docs.text:
The gates run by default, are recorded with their measured values, and are never skipped silently:

  • Architecture (before training): forward shapes and dtype, parameter count, FNO modes at most the Nyquist limit and output invariant to the input resolution, DeepONet branch and trunk shapes (and its basis against the POD rank of the outputs), MeshGraphNet permutation equivariance, PINN derivatives against finite differences and the PDE residual of an exact solution through the same compiled residual (a wrong equation or a sign error fails here), and every method overfitting a tiny batch (to 10 % of its initial loss; a model that cannot even halve it is a broken setup, one that learns but more slowly is a warning). A pair that fails an error-level gate is not trained and is INVALID in the table.
  • Training (from every run): loss finite and decreasing, divergence, "did not learn" (judged on the full-budget final runs; the search runs and the short runs of the error-versus-budget curve are expected to learn less), the budget enforced, identical accounting across methods (hardware, threads, timer, FLOP counter), evaluation off the clock, the search touching validation data only, the seed spread (veriphysics tolerance), and a determinism spot-check (same seed, same steps, same loss).

Then the search (n_trials configurations per method, each for search_fraction of the budget, on validation data), the final runs (seeds x budget_levels, test sets) and the equal-FLOPs arm. A row whose error is no better than a trivial prediction is labelled did not converge, not shown as a plain number. skip_checks=True puts a "checks skipped" banner on the table and the summary figure.

docs.title: Stage 4: report, and the advisor
docs.text:
table.md has one section per problem with n in every column header, integral quantities and fields in separate tables (a method that predicts only integrals shows "integrals only" in the field columns), the simulation-data cost, the time per new instance, the break-even number of queries against a per-instance method, a checks badge per row, and, with equal_flops, an Equal FLOPs table (every method trained to the same FLOP count, with the error on the instances all methods share, the FLOPs and wall time used, and what stopped each run).

Diagnostics and suggestions lists what in the setup is likely to hurt the result, each with a severity, the measured evidence, the suggested change and, where possible, the exact configuration edit (res.apply_suggestions() writes them to a new configuration for you to review). It looks for: a budget too small (the error still falling between the last two budget levels), a model that did not learn or converge (with the likely cause for a PINN: loss-term imbalance, nondimensionalisation, collocation density), too few seeds, an OOD set that is not out of distribution or has a single case, leakage, normalisation from all data, FNO modes against the output spectrum, a DeepONet basis smaller than the field's rank, a learning rate that spikes or makes no progress early, and solver or mesh problems (GCI, y+, unconverged runs, CFL).

docs.title: Budget study and setup audit
docs.text:
Two optional parts answer "would this method do better with more compute, or with another setting?":

pp.benchmark.run(...,
    budget_study={"airfoil": {"pinn_rans": [3600, 14400], "pinn": [3600]}},       # wall-clock seconds, seed 0
    ablations={"airfoil": {"pinn": {"lr1e-3": {"lr": 1e-3}, "lbfgs": {"lbfgs": 0.3}}}})   # changes to the best config

budget_study trains the best configuration again at each listed budget (seed 0, on the problem's study instances) and adds those points to the seed-0 runs of budget_levels: a table per instance and figures/budget_study.png. ablations trains the best configuration with each change at the full budget on the problem's audit instance and puts it next to the unchanged run (the Setup audit table). Both only add jobs: adding budgets, problems, methods or variants to them reuses an existing out_dir; changing or removing an entry is refused like any other configuration change (it would reinterpret cached runs).

docs.title: Example: what the gates and the advisor said on PINNeAPPle-Benchmark experiment 09
docs.text:
Experiment 09 is five problems and seven methods through pp.benchmark. From its report:

  • error [airfoil/pinn_rans] Did not converge: the error is no better than a trivial prediction. Evidence: mean velocity rel. L2 on the held-out runs = 0.96 (>= 0.9). Suggestion: check the nondimensionalisation, the loss weights and the collocation density near walls and leading edges; consider more budget or a formulation with fewer stiff terms. With the training gate "no divergence" failing in 2 of its 29 runs, the row is INVALID. The budget study (budget_study: 1 h, 4 h) and the setup audit (ablations: learning rate, Adam -> L-BFGS) show neither more compute nor those settings help: the PINN collapsed to the zero-flow solution of its own equations.
  • warning [airfoil/mgn] Still improving at the full budget: velocity rel. L2 0.368 at 1/3 of the budget, 0.169 at the full one (54 % lower for 3x). Edit: problem_budgets.airfoil.wall_s: 900 -> 2700.
  • warning [darcy] The OOD set is not clearly outside the training data: 9 % of the OOD inputs outside the training distribution (threshold 50 %), 1 of 100 outside the applicability envelope. Suggestion: move the OOD inputs further out. (Its OOD column is read as a second test set.)
  • The setup audit of the potential-flow PINN found that wall and Kutta weights of 1 instead of 10 lower its velocity error from 0.81 to 0.51: a wider search would have helped it.

The gates also caught problems in the benchmark itself before it was published (a preflight that did not know freestreamPressure, a y+ estimate fed the wrong argument, a convergence metric a potential-flow model fails by construction); each was fixed with a test.

docs.title: Your own problem or method
docs.text:
Wrap your arrays (inputs and outputs on a grid) and FNO and DeepONet apply at once; pass pinn_setup to add PINNs:

prob = pp.benchmark.ArrayProblem("my_flow", train=(X_tr, Y_tr), val=(X_va, Y_va), test=(X_te, Y_te),
                                 ood=(X_ood, Y_ood), data_cost_s=3600.0)
pp.benchmark.run(problems=[prob], methods=["fno", "deeponet"], budget=pp.ComputeBudget(wall_s=120), out_dir="r")

Or register new ones (they are then usable by id, in YAML and in parallel workers):

@pp.benchmark.register_method("my_net")
class MyNet(pp.benchmark.Method):
    title = "My net"
    def supports(self, problem): return isinstance(problem, pp.benchmark.FieldOperatorProblem)
    def space(self, problem): return {"lr": [1e-3, 3e-3], "width": [64, 128]}
    def train(self, problem, prepared, cfg, seed, budget, final=True, **job):
        ...  # train under `budget` with pinneapple_analysis.cost.train_within_budget; return a result dict
    def architecture_checks(self, problem, prepared, cfg): ...  # your gates (shapes, overfit, ...)

@pp.benchmark.register_problem("my_problem")
class MyProblem(pp.benchmark.FieldOperatorProblem):
    def generate(self, split, n, n_workers): ...   # (inputs, outputs, solver core-seconds)
    def verify_solver(self): ...                   # checks of your solver against a known answer

The built-in problems: burgers, darcy, navier_stokes (the operator-learning standards), airfoil (the aero app's RANS airfoil; needs OpenFOAM), inverse_heat (h from sensors). Methods: pinn, fno, deeponet, mgn, mlp, mlp_fields, pinn_rans. See Choosing a method for what the published benchmark found.

docs.title: Choose a model by the scale of the question
docs.text: This guide shows how to make an adaptive ensemble respect scales: declare what each model resolves, ask each question at a scale, check closures, and let the ensemble escalate to a finer model when needed. The concepts are in Multiscale ensembles: scales, filters and closures.

docs.title: 1. Declare the scales of every model
docs.text:
from math import pi
from pinneapple_physics.multiscale import Filter, ScaleProfile

L, h = 2 * pi, 2 * pi / 64
profiles = [
    ScaleProfile("fno", Filter("gaussian", 2 * h), h, re_range=(150, 300), fidelity=0),         # surrogate
    ScaleProfile("les", Filter("sharp", pi / 16), L / 48, closure="dynamic Smagorinsky", fidelity=1),
    ScaleProfile("dns", Filter("sharp", 0.0), L / 128, re_range=(0, 6000), fidelity=2),          # resolved
]

Declare the filter the model's output actually carries:

  • a surrogate trained on Gaussian-filtered data carries that Gaussian;
  • a dealiased spectral LES on n points carries a sharp cut-off at k = n/3;
  • a resolved solver carries no filter.

docs.title: 2. Ask each question at a scale
docs.text:
from pinneapple_physics.multiscale import ScaleQuery, ScaleAwareRouter

router = ScaleAwareRouter(profiles, query_fn=lambda case: ScaleQuery(case["filter"], re=case["re"]))
print(router.route(ScaleQuery(Filter("sharp", h), re=3000)))     # only the DNS resolves this
print(router.route(ScaleQuery(Filter("gaussian", 8 * h), re=200)))  # the surrogate is enough

docs.title: 3. Bring every output to the requested filter
docs.text: Use refilter(output, profile.filter, query.filter), not apply_filter(output, query.filter). Filtering an already-filtered output again gives a wider filter than the one asked for. refilter applies only the part of the requested filter that the model's own filter has not applied yet.

docs.title: 4. Check closures without a reference
docs.text:
from pinneapple_physics.multiscale import closure_health, DynamicSmagorinsky, VorticityNS2D

h = closure_health(w_les, w0_les, kc=16, closure=DynamicSmagorinsky(), solver=VorticityNS2D(48, nu))
h.ok, h.reasons      # enstrophy growth, spectral pile-up or collapse, Germano-identity error

docs.title: 5. Put it together
docs.text:
from pinneapple_physics.ensemble import PhysicsEnsemble

ens = PhysicsEnsemble(experts, mode="select", router=router,
                      prediction_checks={"les": lambda pred, case: les_health(case)},
                      error_tolerance=0.25, error_context=lambda case: case["filter"])
out = ens.predict(case)
out["active"], out["failed_checks"], out["escalated_by_checks"]

For every case the ensemble:

  • uses the lowest fidelity rung that resolves the requested scale;
  • skips models whose checks fail;
  • moves up a rung when the models on the current rung last missed the tolerance at this scale.

examples/physics_ensemble/multiscale_turbulence.py runs the whole comparison on 2-D turbulence.

docs.title: Engineering Sensitivity Lab
docs.text:
Which parameters really control the result, and which can you freeze? Day 16 of the apps series: https://sensitivity.pinneapple.org (source: apps/sensitivity_lab).

Give a model (built-in benchmark, pp.zoo model or ONNX graph), runs done in your solver (OpenFOAM, CalculiX: download the Saltelli design, upload the results) or a dataset, the parameters with their ranges or distributions and the responses. The lab returns Sobol first-order, total and second-order indices with bootstrap intervals, Morris screening, main-effect and ICE curves, local derivatives (automatic differentiation for torch models) and the parameters you can freeze, each recommendation checked by re-running the model with them fixed.

On the Ishigami benchmark every estimated index is within 0.003 of the exact value and inside its 95 % interval. On the heat-sink design, fin count controls the thermal resistance (total index 0.54); ambient temperature and power can be frozen (total index < 2e-4) and fixing them changes the output variance by less than 0.1 %. From data alone (3,900 simulations) the app flags that the inputs are correlated (r = 0.66), so the first-order indices add up to more than 1.

Everything shown comes from pp.sensitivity (see Uncertainty and sensitivity studies on any model). Limits, methods and the API are in the app README.

docs.title: Spectral fidelity: what relative L2 does not see
docs.text:
Relative L2 error rewards smooth predictions. A blurred field can have a small L2 error and still miss the small scales that carry heat transfer, mixing or loads, and neural operators are known to under-predict them (spectral bias). pinneapple_analysis.validation.spectral measures what L2 hides. It is NumPy only and works on any field on a regular grid, from any code.

import numpy as np
from pinneapple_analysis.validation.spectral import spectral_fidelity

report = spectral_fidelity(pred, ref, ndim=2)          # arrays (..., ny, nx): leading axes are averaged
print(report.summary())                                # rel. L2, high-band energy ratio and bias, per-band table
print(report.passed)                                   # False when |bias| > tol (default 0.25)

docs.title: What is measured
docs.text: Quantity Function Meaning Energy spectrum E(k) energy_spectrum(u, ndim, periodic=..., window="hann") Shell-summed, integer radial wavenumbers k = rint(|m|), sum E = mean(u^2) for a periodic field. Non-periodic fields are mean-removed and Hann-windowed (unit mean square). Energy ratio per band, high-wavenumber bias spectral_comparison, high_wavenumber_bias E_pred / E_ref - 1 over the top third of the shells where the reference has energy: about -1 for a smoothed prediction, 0 for the reference itself, positive for added noise. Phase error and coherence per band spectral_comparison Energy-weighted mean phase difference [rad]; |sum P R*|^2 / (sum |P|^2 sum |R|^2) (1 = the same modes). Structure functions structure_functions(u, ndim, orders=(2, 3)) S_p(r) = <|u(x + r) - u(x)|^p> per axis, signed S_3, flatness S_4 / S_2^2 (3 for Gaussian increments; larger at small r for intermittent fields). Gradient errors gradient_metrics(pred, ref, ndim, spacing, vector_axis=..., walls=...) Error in grad u and |grad u|; for a velocity field, vorticity and strain-rate magnitude; for a scalar, the mean wall flux -k du/dn on chosen faces. Power-law slope fit_power_law(k, E, kmin, kmax) Least-squares slope in log-log.

docs.title: Where it is reported
docs.text:
• pinneapple check: rule PC704 spectral-bias on every grid result with a grid reference of the same shape (tolerance hf-bias, default 0.25).
  • pp.benchmark: field problems (Burgers, Darcy, Navier-Stokes) add an "HF energy bias" column next to the relative L2 error.
  • pp.validate: part of the validation report (once it lands, #696).

docs.title: How it was checked
docs.text:
tests/test_spectral_fidelity.py:

  • a synthetic field with a prescribed k^-5/3 spectrum: every shell within 1 % (the construction makes it exact to round-off) and the fitted slope within 1 %;
  • a 2-D decaying-turbulence velocity field from the pseudo-spectral solver (pinneapple_physics.multiscale.ns2d, 64², nu = 5e-4, t = 3, spectrum slope about -3.3): the field against itself has zero bias, zero phase error and unit coherence; a copy through a Gaussian filter of half a cell has a relative L2 error of 2.5 % and a high-wavenumber bias of -0.68 (flagged; -0.92 at 0.75 cell, where L2 is 4.9 %); 5 % white noise gives a positive bias above 0.25;
  • closed forms: S_2(r) of a linear field, flatness 3 of Gaussian noise, vorticity and strain of an analytic velocity field, and the wall flux of x^2 + y.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Small added noise is below the default tolerance: 2 % white noise on the turbulence field gives a bias of +0.19 (not flagged at 0.25), 5 % gives +1.09. Lower tol if noise matters for the use.
  • The bias compares energies, not positions: a field shifted by a few cells keeps a zero bias. The phase error and coherence catch that.
  • The band edges are fractions of the resolved range of the reference. A reference with almost no energy at high wavenumbers (smooth solutions) gives a short high band; the check is most informative for multi-scale fields.
  • Non-periodic fields are windowed, which spreads energy across neighbouring shells (leakage). Ratios are robust to it because prediction and reference get the same window; absolute spectra of non-periodic fields are approximate.

docs.title: Surrogates from simulation results: study, regime arena, gateway
docs.text:
Three library pieces turn a table of simulation runs into a model that others can call, and say where it can be trusted:

Piece What it does pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.run_study trains every applicable method on the same splits and budget, measures on unseen data, picks one by validation error, packages it with its limitations and a trust report pinneapple_arena.regimes.run_regime_arena ranks methods per data regime (interpolation, few data, extrapolation, geometry change, steep fronts) over several seeds, with physics violations, solver baselines and a dataset audit pinneapple_registry.ModelGateway publishes versions, runs them behind one predict with the model's OOD policy (warn or refuse), logs every call, aggregates latency / counts / errors, exports TorchScript and ONNX

docs.title: A surrogate study
docs.text:
from pinneapple_analysis import surrogate as S

data = S.examples.airfoil_rans()             # 374 OpenFOAM RANS runs: 6 CST weights + alpha -> Cl, Cd
study = S.run_study(data, budget=3.0, seeds=2)          # 3 s of wall clock per training run
print(study.best, study.ranking("test"), study.ranking("shift"))
print(study.trust["decision"], study.limitations["concentration"])
out = study.model.predict({"T0": 0.15, "T1": 0.12, "T2": 0.13, "M0": 0.02, "M1": 0.05, "M2": 0.04,
                           "alpha_deg": [4.0, 30.0]})
print(out["outputs"]["Cl"], out["ood"][1]["reasons"])      # alpha 30 is flagged: outside the training range
study.model.save("airfoil_model")

Your own data: S.read_table(bytes_or_path, name) reads CSV, Parquet, JSON, HDF5 and NPZ; S.from_table(df, inputs, outputs, group=...) picks the columns. A field output is a set of columns u_0, u_1, ... (with grid_shape= and optionally coords=), or S.from_arrays({"X": ..., "Y": (n, *grid), "coords": ...}).

Which methods apply (S.applicable(kind, n_train, grid_shape, has_pde), each with the reason when not): polynomial ridge and an MLP always; a Gaussian process up to 2000 training samples (on POD coefficients for fields); gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost if installed, else scikit-learn) for scalars; FNO and DeepONet for fields; a PINN only for fields with a declared PDE (pde={"type": "burgers", "coords": {"x": "x", "t": "t"}, "coefficients": {"nu": "nu"}}; types in S.PDE_TYPES).

Equal budget. The iterative methods (MLP, FNO, DeepONet, PINN) train until the same ComputeBudget is spent (pinneapple_analysis.cost.equal_budget.train_within_budget) and keep the best of ten validation checkpoints; the one-shot fits (ridge, GP, trees) are fitted once and report the time they used.

Unseen data. S.make_splits carves out a distribution-shift set first (whole groups, the edge of the input space, or one end of an input) and then a random held-out test set. The model is selected by validation error; the test and shift sets only measure it.

Limitations (study.limitations): training-range validity bounds, the OOD gate (training range plus nearest-neighbour distance, the batched form of physics_audit.Envelope), the error per input quartile and where it concentrates, the worst samples, the extrapolation ratio, and for fields the mean error map and, with a declared PDE, the finite-difference residual of the predictions relative to the reference data.

Trust report (pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport): held-out error against the target (0.10 nRMSE or 0.05 relative L2 by default), R² > 0 on every output (critical), shift error within 3x the held-out error, seed spread, and the PDE residual check for fields. A check that could not run says why.

docs.title: Regime arena
docs.text:
from pinneapple_arena.regimes import run_regime_arena

data = S.examples.burgers_fields()           # exact viscous Burgers fields for 96 viscosities
result = run_regime_arena(data, budget=3.0, seeds=3, baselines={"fdm": S.examples.burgers_fdm_baseline()})
print(result.rankings["extrapolation"], result.overall, result.baselines, result.audit["decision"])

The protocol is in result.protocol: one split for every method and seed (the model seed varies, the data does not), the same budget and stopping rule, default hyper-parameters (no per-method search), the dataset hash, the hardware and date. Physics violations are the share of predictions breaking the dataset's declared constraints (pinneapple_data.audit.constraint_mask, e.g. Cd > 0, the maximum principle abs(u) <= 1.005); the splits are audited by pinneapple_data.audit.audit_dataset (the checks behind pinneapple check PC451-PC453). Regimes the data cannot support (no groups, scalar outputs for steep fronts) are reported as unavailable with the reason; graph networks and R-OAMS are listed in NOT_IN_LIBRARY with why they are not run.

docs.title: Gateway
docs.text:
from pinneapple_registry import ModelGateway

gw = ModelGateway("./models")
v = gw.publish("airfoil-cl-cd", "airfoil_model", ood_policy="refuse")      # or a SurrogateModel
gw.publish("airfoil-zoo", "airfoil_cst_rans_mlp", kind="pinneapple.zoo")    # zoo models too
r = gw.predict("airfoil-cl-cd", [{"T0": 0.15, "T1": 0.12, "T2": 0.13, "M0": 0.02, "M1": 0.05, "M2": 0.04,
                                  "alpha_deg": 4.0}])
print(r["outputs"], r["ood"], r["latency_ms"], gw.metrics()["by_version"])
gw.export("airfoil-cl-cd", None, "onnx", "airfoil.onnx")                    # PyTorch surrogates only

Versions follow ModelStore (vYYYYMMDD_HHMMSS, stages, a REJECT trust report blocks staging and production unless an override reason is recorded). A caller may tighten a model's OOD policy (warn to refuse), never relax it. Surrogates are unpickled only after their sha256 matches their card: publish only directories you produced.

Other servers with the same API (the Surrogate Studio, the Benchmark Arena, any app built on gateway_router) are reachable from Python with pinneapple_registry.gateway_client.GatewayClient(base_url, api_key=...). A gateway can serve them too:

  • gw.publish(name, "https://host/v1/models/<model>", kind="remote") forwards to the remote model;
  • gw.publish_ref(model_ref) publishes from a ModelRef: zoo:<name>, or an http(s) URI whose input ranges become the validity bounds.

The front gateway enforces its own bounds and OOD policy, and logs and meters every call before forwarding.

docs.title: Topology optimisation
docs.text:
pinneapple_design.topology optimises the material layout on a fixed grid of elements (density method, SIMP): each element carries a density rho in [0, 1], a filter and a Heaviside projection turn the design variables into densities, and an optimiser (optimality criteria or MMA) updates them from adjoint sensitivities.

Piece API Density filter (cone weights, any radius), symmetry maps DensityFilter.grid(nelx, nely, r_min), SymmetryMap Heaviside projection with continuation heaviside, heaviside_derivative, DesignChain(n, filter, beta=...) Optimisers oc_update (optimality criteria), MMA (method of moving asymptotes, Svanberg 1987; dual solved with L-BFGS-B) Driver and gradient check optimize(problem, volume_fraction, filter, "oc" / "mma", ...), finite_difference_check Structural compliance on Q4 elements (MBB beam, cantilever) Compliance2D.mbb, Compliance2D.cantilever Thermal compliance ThermalCompliance2D Stokes flow with Brinkman penalisation (Borrvall-Petersson) StokesDissipation2D.double_pipe Rotor iron of an electric machine for torque pinneapple_design.topology.magnetic, on pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics (guide)

docs.title: What is verified
docs.text:
tests/test_topology_optimization.py asserts:

  • sensitivities through filter and projection against finite differences for compliance, thermal compliance and Stokes dissipation;
  • MMA against SciPy's SLSQP on the five-variable cantilever problem of Svanberg (1987): same optimum to 1e-8 relative (1.33995636);
  • OC and MMA reach the same MBB compliance, and the MBB result is a truss attached to the load and supports;
  • the double-pipe problem gives two pipes in a 1 x 1 domain and one merged channel in a 1.5 x 1 domain, the qualitative result of Borrvall & Petersson (2003);
  • the reluctance-rotor optimisation increases torque, and the torque-ripple objective's gradient.

Runs of the examples (2026-10-17, CPU):

Example Result 01_mbb_beam.py (60 x 20, volume 0.5) compliance 233.71 (OC, 146 iterations), 233.49 (MMA, 58 iterations); with projection 190.05, gray fraction 2.3 %; gradient check 1.0e-6 02_heat_and_stokes_flow.py thermal compliance 4.18e8 (uniform) -> 2.49e7; double pipe dissipation 136.4 -> 25.7 (1 x 1) and 179.3 -> 26.8 (1.5 x 1) 03_reluctance_rotor.py 1410 design variables; mean torque 38.10 N m with linear iron, 13.44 N m when the same rotor is re-evaluated with nonlinear iron; Maxwell stress 46.21 vs co-energy 47.07 N m at 5 degrees

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The rotor optimisation uses linear iron; the nonlinear re-evaluation shows that a thin-featured rotor saturates, so the design should be optimised with the nonlinear B-H curve (the adjoint supports it; the example does not).
  • On thin-featured designs Maxwell-stress and co-energy torque differ by about 2 % (46.21 vs 47.07 N m above), more than on smooth geometries; refine the band and air gap before trusting single-angle torques.
  • Grids are structured and 2-D.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• K. Svanberg, The method of moving asymptotes, Int. J. Numer. Meth. Eng. 24 (1987) 359-373.
  • M. P. Bendsoe and O. Sigmund, Topology Optimization: Theory, Methods and Applications, Springer, 2003.
  • T. Borrvall and J. Petersson, Topology optimization of fluids in Stokes flow, Int. J. Numer. Meth. Fluids 41 (2003) 77-107.

docs.title: Physics checks during training (Lightning, PhysicsNeMo, Hugging Face)
docs.text:
Models trained outside PINNeAPPle are usually validated once, at the end, after the whole budget is spent. The callbacks in pinneapple_neural.callbacks run the checks of pp.validate on a fixed validation batch every N steps and log them to the framework's logger. They warn (or stop the run) when a physics metric worsens for K consecutive checks while the training loss improves, and write the validation report and trust card at the end. None of the frameworks is a dependency of PINNeAPPle.

from pinneapple_neural.callbacks import PhysicsMonitor

mon = PhysicsMonitor("darcy_2d", reference=(a_val, u_val), every=50, patience=3, action="warn",
                     report_path="runs/validation.json")        # + runs/validation.trust.json at the end

# PyTorch Lightning: logs to every logger of the Trainer (TensorBoard, W&B, MLflow, CSV)
from pinneapple_neural.callbacks import PhysicsValidationCallback
lightning.Trainer(callbacks=[PhysicsValidationCallback(mon)]).fit(module, loader)

# PhysicsNeMo training loop (PhysicsNeMo has no trainer class): one call per optimiser step
from pinneapple_neural.callbacks import PhysicsNeMoHook
hook = PhysicsNeMoHook(mon)
with LaunchLogger("train", epoch=epoch) as log:                 # physicsnemo.utils.logging
    ...
    if hook(model, step, loss, log=log):                        # True when action="stop" fired
        break
hook.finish(model)

# Hugging Face Trainer: metrics go through trainer.log, i.e. to its report_to integrations
